We systematically study when this kind of composed supervision supports self-improvement and when it fails. Our controlled experiments identify three failure modes: unreliable subproblem predictions, errors introduced by composition, and limited supervision coverage. Beyond controlled settings, these findings carry over to more realistic coding and reasoning tasks: composed labels are more accurate than direct self-generated labels and improve performance even on compositions longer than those seen during training, while the failure modes remain visible. Further, although these failure modes often keep compositional self-improvement from fully succeeding on its own, a short SFT warmup with compositional self-improvement can bootstrap reinforcement learning on tasks that require composing skills the model already has, particularly when direct exploration rarely succeeds. Together, these findings characterize when compositional self-improvement can provide sufficiently reliable supervision to expand model capabilities.

title: mmWave UE Positioning Under Blockage: Limits for ISAC-Assisted Handover
abstract: Proactive handover can save a millimeter-wave (mmWave) link before a passing body blocks it, but only if the network knows where the user is. We ask whether the radio units that serve a user can localize it accurately enough from its uplink sounding reference signals. We derive position error bounds that include synchronization and array calibration errors, with and without reflected paths known from a digital twin, and test two estimators in a ray-traced street canyon on held-out scenarios. Three findings stand out. First, with line of sight to both radio units, array calibration, not bandwidth, limits the bound. Second, blockage degrades the line-of-sight-only bound sharply, whereas known reflections keep the map-aided bound low. Third, a simple dominant-path estimator fails where it matters most: its errors grow sharply around blockage, and proactive handover becomes worse than the 3GPP baseline. A map-aided multipath tracker cuts the median error from 12 to 3.7 cm and removes this significant penalty at link margins of 15 dB and above, but does not yet beat the baseline.

title: Bilinear Strichartz Estimates and Linear Morawetz Estimates for Schrödinger Operators with Potentials
abstract: In dimensions three and above, we establish bilinear Strichartz estimates for Schrödinger operators with potentials using perturbative arguments and Morawetz estimates. Our approach does not require smallness of the potential. As part of the analysis, we also establish endpoint versions of the bilinear Christ-Kiselev lemma.

title: TacMind: Benchmarking and Modeling Tactile Interaction States for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct observations of contact physics, local geometry, and interaction dynamics, making it a vital source of feedback for contact-rich manipulation. However, existing tactile manipulation studies are often developed and evaluated within specific task settings, making it difficult to systematically compare how tactile information contributes under different interaction conditions. In this work, we develop a benchmark in simulation comprising 128 tasks organized around three complementary evaluation regimes: Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic. The benchmark further includes controlled static and dynamic task variants and 12 perturbation settings for evaluating robustness under changes in visual and physical conditions. These settings motivate studying tactile information as a temporally evolving interaction representation rather than only as an instantaneous observation. We therefore propose an action-conditioned latent predictive world model that integrates tactile history and learns a tactile state through prediction of future tactile latents. Building on this representation, we design a model that conditions action generation on the learned tactile state and uses predicted future tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the evaluated regimes. Project Page: https://tacmind-bench.github.io/

title: Spectral Fields and Unitary Descent: Local splitting, simultaneous norms, and transcendental obstructions
abstract: Spectral fields can recover matrix coefficients without standardizing the invariant Hermitian form. Over an algebraic subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ stable under nontrivial complex conjugation, we prove that every Zariski-dense subgroup in a normalized Hermitian model of dimension $m\ge4$ and signature $(m-1,1)$ at the fixed embedding contains a loxodromic element whose spectrum makes all diagonal coefficients norms. The element can be chosen so that every positive power is regular and generates the same splitting field. For an arbitrary initial Hermitian model over such a field, two spectra suffice for standard unitary descent over an extension of relative degree at most $(m!)^2$. Over every quadratic extension $F/k$ of nonarchimedean local fields of characteristic zero, a four-dimensional quasi-split unitary group of Witt index two contains a discrete, Zariski-dense free subgroup whose spectra all split over $F$. Over intrinsic fields of positive transcendence degree, we construct a single convex cocompact, Zariski-dense free subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(3,1)$ for which, for every initial regular element and every normalized extraction, the Hermitian obstruction persists after adjoining any finite family of spectra and over the total spectral field.

title: Bilateral Christoffel-Geronimus-Uvarov formulas for mixed-type orthogonality on algebraic supports
abstract: Christoffel-type determinant formulas construct both normalized polynomial families and their reproducing kernel for mixed-type orthogonality in several variables after independent rational matrix transformations on the two arguments. The pairing may have a rectangular matrix of functionals, with separate degree bounds on each component, and may be supported on an algebraic variety. The reduced matrices are calculated from the original biorthogonal polynomials, rational moments, polynomial division and the masses left free by division; their nonvanishing determinants characterize existence and uniqueness. For measure pairings the rational data are expressed by Cauchy and multivariate Fantappie transforms. Exact dimension counts incorporate the four matrix factors and the relations of the support. For normal degree-ordered original families and fixed factors, when the component degrees on each side differ by a bounded amount and the normalization dimension grows at most like one degree layer, the resulting orders are bounded on curves and grow at most linearly on surfaces. For pairings allowing scalar factors to move between arguments, called balanced pairings, an exact obstruction determines whether a bilateral mass decomposes into unilateral masses when the denominators act injectively. Residue duality provides coordinates for division and mass quotients on integral curves, including singular points, and on the finite surface quotients specified here. Explicit singular-curve families retain nondegenerate residue pairings as denominator zeros coalesce. Positive congruences admit a further reduction by orthogonal projection, while balanced pairings give simultaneous intertwining identities for all coordinate multiplication matrices.

title: PRISM-Net: Dynamic Routing Network with VLM-Guided Disentangled Attribute Distillation for Explainable Fine-Grained Product Retrieval
abstract: Fine-grained visual product retrieval in large-scale e-commerce multimedia systems demands discriminative representations capable of simultaneously resolving macro-level category semantics and micro-level visual attributes such as structural contour (line) and chromatic appearance (color). However, conventional backbones including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision Transformers (ViTs) inherently suffer from feature entanglement and shortcut learning. To learn the micro-level visual attributes without costly manual attribute annotations, we propose phase-routed interpretable semantic mixture-of-experts network (PRISM-Net), an explainable multi-expert architecture that disentangles holistic visual features into disentangled line and color expert pathways governed by a conditional meta-router. In phase 1, we introduce an external VLM-Guided sigmoid semantic distillation mechanism with gradient-detached routing gates, utilizing zero-shot text prompts from SigLIP to supervise specialized structural and chromatic experts. In phase 2, the disentangled expert embeddings are adaptively fused with macro base features via a learned meta-router gate to calibrate category boundaries. Extensive 5-fold cross-validation across 275,454 e-commerce images (18 categories) and full-scale retrieval benchmarks (55,091 queries against a 220,363-image gallery) across SwinV2, ConvNeXt-V2, and DINOv3 demonstrate substantial gains. On SwinV2, PRISM-Net boosts full-fold product mAP@10 from 80.98% to 83.90% (+2.92%), line mAP@10 by +5.74%, and color mAP@10 by +9.12%. Furthermore, unsupervised distribution analysis of the meta-router gate reveals that both ViT and CNN backbones emergently allocate up to 6.8x higher structural line weights to rigid appliances and hardware while dedicating >96% chromatic weight to clothing.

title: Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities, part II: refinements, unitary orbits, unitarily invariant norms and $\ell_s$--$\ell_s$ estimates
abstract: In previous work \cite{Zha26a}, the author established Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities for several classes of operator families, including $\ell_p$--$\ell_p$ estimates and mixed $\ell_q$--$\ell_p$ estimates, by means of operator square-sum identities. The present paper has two main aims. First, using the tracial joint spectral measures recently introduced by O.~Heinävaara \cite{Hei25}, we obtain several refinements of the McCarthy--Clarkson inequalities, one of which confirms a conjecture of Audenaert \cite{AK17}. Second, combining tools from matrix analysis with complex interpolation theory, we establish Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities for unitary orbits, unitarily invariant norms, and $\ell_s$--$\ell_s$ estimates, again in the framework of operator square-sum identities.

title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate fourteen current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider with two additional open-weight models, on 3,076 questions from four medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MedBullets) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on MedQA-USMLE and PubMedQA, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.7 percentage points and only two of the six pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.3% to 50.9%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.

title: $k$-Center under Weak and Strong Distance Oracles with an Application to Minimum Sum of Radii Clustering
abstract: In the weak-strong distance oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram and Wang (COLT 2024), a metric $(X,d)$ on $n$ points is accessed through two oracles: a cheap weak oracle that returns each queried distance correctly with probability $1-δ$ and permits arbitrary values on corrupted pairs, chosen by an adversary who knows the entire metric and all corrupted pairs, and an expensive strong oracle that reveals a point exactly. The goal is to cluster well while making as few strong queries as possible. Our main result is a $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-center using $O(k\log n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ strong point queries, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves both the $(14+\varepsilon)$ approximation factor and the $O(k\log^2 n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ query bound of Bateni et al. It also improves the query complexity of the recent $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Pradhan, Bhattacharya and Jaiswal (AISTATS 2026), in the variant of the model they study. Our algorithm outputs an explicitly known sketch of an otherwise unknown metric: a concrete metric on at most $k$ points that a downstream algorithm can compute with directly, with no further queries and no noise. As an application, we give a simple FPT algorithm for Minimum Sum of Radii (MSR) that returns a constant-factor solution using $2^{O(k\log k)}\cdot O(\log n\log\log n)$ strong queries. We complement the upper bound with an $Ω(k\log(n/k))$ lower bound for $k$-center with assignment that holds for row-local algorithms. These algorithms assign two unqueried points to the same center whenever their weak distances to the strong-queried points are exactly the same. Our algorithm and those of Bateni et al. and Pradhan et al. are all row-local, so our query bound is optimal for this class up to the $O(\log\log n)$ factor.

title: Siting and Curtailment Depth Limit the Grid Headroom Available to New Large Loads
abstract: Data center demand is increasing faster than generation can be built, encouraging proposals to interconnect large loads on condition that they reduce consumption during high-stress periods. Estimates of how much load can be added via flexibility rest on simplified accounting and report only annual curtailed electricity. Here we use a national energy systems model that co-optimizes hourly generation and load curtailment across 16 U.S. regions to characterize the flexibility and power system impacts of enabling headroom. While 50 GW can be served while curtailing less than 0.1% of its annual energy, small annual curtailment conceals potentially severe operating requirements. Most regions require curtailment deeper than 90% in at least one hour, so the load must disconnect or have sufficient on-site resources to provide full back up. Furthermore, announced data center locations are not aligned with modeled headroom and relying on existing generation fleets raises CO2 emissions and wholesale electricity prices.

title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
abstract: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.

title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study
abstract: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via llama.cpp confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.

title: The Promises and Limitations of Evaluation-Based AI Governance: Evidence from Expert Interviews
abstract: We conducted 37 semi-structured expert interviews to examine how frontier AI evaluations reduce societal-level AI risks. Evaluations have become central to AI risk governance, despite their shortcomings being widely critiqued. Still, the case for how they reduce risks in practice remains largely implicit. Drawing on expert accounts, we reconstruct this case by identifying the mechanisms through which evaluations are expected to reduce risk, the assumptions underpinning those mechanisms, and the challenges those assumptions face. Our findings suggest that `evaluation-based governance' could contain foundational gaps which undermine risk-reduction strategies that depend on evaluations. Using thematic analysis, we identified three key pathways through which evaluations could reduce risk: by (i) making societal-level risks concrete to decision-makers and the public (raised in 18 out of 37 interviews), (ii) serving as a basis for governance commitments and regulation (18), and (iii) incentivizing a better risk culture within AI companies (16). However, these pathways often depended on shared assumptions that participants themselves doubted. The main challenges included, in order of frequency: (i) diminishing informativeness of evaluation results as model capabilities improve (21), (ii) measurement limitations that may be inherent to the evaluation paradigm (18), (iii) a lack of guarantees that evaluation results will be acted upon by companies or governments (16), and (iv) the degree of control and discretion AI companies retain over evaluation design, disclosure, and response (12). Participants also noted that evaluation-based governance could prove counterproductive, by functioning as a permission structure for developers' continued capability improvement (4). We finish by discussing the implications of our findings for evaluation-based governance, and what would improve its prospects.

title: Security and Derivative Pricing with Fast Regime Switches
abstract: A regime-switching model lets any parameter of a standard model take a different value in each state of a hidden Markov chain. For the affine and exponential-Lévy models in common use the pricing problem reduces to one linear system, a' = (Q + diag g(t)) a, with the chain's generator Q and a model-specific forcing g as its only ingredients. We expand its solution in the mean holding time of the chain to any order, with an initial layer for the starting regime, and identify the first correction as a Green-Kubo matrix from the group inverse of Q. The same system prices bonds, swaptions, caps, credit default swaps, Asian and digital options, and equity options under stochastic rates, with the Gil-Pelaez integrals conditioned on the regime at expiry where a payoff depends on it; barrier, American and Bermudan instruments go to the coupled equations on a grid. Every numerical claim is checked against QuantLib in the limit where the regimes coincide and against an independent referee with switching on, and the implementation is public.

title: Penalized Likelihood Inference in Highly Multivariate Sparse Spectral Graphical Gaussian Processes
abstract: We develop a penalized likelihood inference approach for highly multivariate Gaussian stochastic processes. Since zeros in the inverse cross-spectral density encode process-level conditional independence, sparse modeling of this object provides a natural route to scalable inference in the highly multivariate case. We introduce a latent variable representation which, combined with random Fourier features, yields a stochastic approximation expectation--maximization algorithm for penalized maximum likelihood estimation of a sparse inverse cross-spectral density matrix under a graphical LASSO penalty. The augmentation is crucial because sparsity is present in the inverse spectral density of the latent variable, whereas the marginal inverse covariance remains dense in the presence of a spatial nugget. Our frequency domain formulation enables joint penalized likelihood estimation of process-specific spatial covariance parameters and sparse process-level conditional dependence without requiring a pre-specified reference set of locations. The method is demonstrated on both synthetic and the MERRA-2 aerosol reanalysis data sets, yielding benefit over existing alternatives, especially for prediction at unobserved locations under spatial misalignment.

title: The symbolic pfaffian method I: A generalization of the Gallucio-Loebl-Tesler Theorem
abstract: The pfaffian number of a graph $G$, denoted by $\mathrm{pf}(G)$, is the minimum integer $k$ such that the generating function of perfect matchings of $G$ can be written as a linear combination of $k$ pfaffians of signed adjacency matrices. The Galluccio-Loebl-Tesler Theorem states that $\mathrm{pf}(G) \leq 4^g$, where $g$ is the orientable genus of $G$. We generalize this theorem by relating the pfaffian number of a graph to another graph parameter: the symbolic pfaffian number, denoted by $\mathrm{spf}(G)$. Namely, we prove that $\mathrm{pf}(G) \leq 2^{\mathrm{spf}(G)}$. Our proof is based on linear algebra arguments and does not depend on topological properties of graphs. As a consequence of our generalization, we conclude that $\mathrm{pf}(K_{2n}) = 2^{\mathcal{O}(n \log n)}$, an improvement on the previous upper bound of $4^{\mathcal{O}(n^2)}$ based on the genus. We also consider lower bounds for $\mathrm{pf}(G)$ related to $\mathrm{spf}(G)$. In particular, we show that the graphs with $\mathrm{pf}(G) = 4$ are the graphs with $\mathrm{spf}(G) = 2$. On the other hand, we show that our main result is strictly more general than a previous generalization by Norine.

title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.

title: Guide to Teaching with Data in Statistics and Data Science Classrooms
abstract: Statistics and data science educators have been concerned about data use or lack thereof in the classroom for decades. For many educators, the question is not whether to use data or not. They often want to know whether they should give clean or messy data, and whether they should spend the time to find a real dataset or simulate it. If they decide to find real data, then other questions follow about where to find it and how to provide it to students. If they provide data, then the question remains whether students will find the data engaging or not or if it will have the properties necessary to demonstrate class concepts. We provide empirically and theoretically supported recommendations on data use. Classroom data are described in different ways (e.g., real, raw, made-up, artificial, fictitious, synthetic, simulated, toy, and messy). We provide definitions of different types, sources, formats, and shapes of data and provide distinctions between classifications. We share resources for educators in bringing data to their classrooms.

title: Mutual Information Estimation via Triangular Transport Maps: Finite Sample Guarantees and Sample Allocation
abstract: We study finite sample guarantees for transport based mutual information estimation. Mutual information can be estimated by first learning the conditional and marginal densities and then evaluating their log-density ratio by Monte Carlo. Given training samples, we use triangular transport maps to learn these densities and then compute the mutual information estimate on an independent batch of evaluation samples. For conditional density estimation using triangular transport maps, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees over realizable Hölder classes by viewing the conditional density as an ordinary density with respect to the product of the law of the conditioning variable and Lebesgue measure. This allows standard density estimation techniques to be applied directly to the conditional density estimation. These results yield finite sample guarantees for the resulting mutual information estimator and characterize how a fixed sample budget should be allocated between training and evaluation in order to minimize the mean squared error. Numerical experiments support the predicted training and evaluation error rates and illustrate the resulting sample allocation tradeoff.

title: FESTiVE: Self-calibrated Spatial-temporal Gradient Characterization for Non-cartesian Imaging on High Performance Systems
abstract: Gradient imperfections disrupt the encoding benefits of long-readout imaging applications on high-performance systems. Currently, external field monitoring hardware provides the only reliable solution for general spatial-temporal gradient characterization. We present FESTiVE, a data-driven alternative to higher-order field monitoring. FESTiVE leverages parallel imaging to both implicitly model and explicitly recover field imperfections. Using a fast k-t mapping calibration scan, FESTiVE formulates a time-varying GRAPPA problem which maps k-space data corrupted by a time-varying gradient imperfection against a clean reference. This mapping is represented compactly with an implicit neural representation, from which the spatial-temporal fields are recovered in image space using coil sensitivities. In phantom, FESTiVE produces comparable field measurements to a Skope field camera across multiple non-cartesian 2D acquisition strategies and gradient specifications. In vivo, FESTiVE achieves state-of-the-art image quality for a high-performance diffusion spiral protocol on the head-only MAGNUS 3T, where higher-order phase imperfections are significant. At 7T, on the head-only Siemens TerraX system, FESTiVE enables 300μm spiral imaging where conventional field camera-based approaches fall below probe dephasing limits. In conclusion, FESTiVE enables robust high-resolution non-cartesian imaging on high-performance gradients, characterizing gradient imperfections using parallel imaging rather than field monitoring hardware.

title: Stochastic learning flow: moment equations for stochastic gradient descent at finite step size
abstract: Analytical theories of learning in deep networks often assume gradient flow, discarding the finite step size and batch noise of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Starting from the discrete update, we derive continuous-time equations for the mean and covariance of the parameter distribution under a Gaussian closure for a general stochastic learning, to first order in the learning rate $η$. Applying these stochastic learning flow (SLF) equations to SGD, we show that the mean descends an effective loss regularized by the covariance and loss curvature, while the covariance, unlike in stochastic differential equation approximations, becomes unstable at curvature $2/η$. In SGD ensembles of linear and nonlinear networks, SLF predicts learning curves and mean trajectories more accurately than gradient flow and captures the covariance dynamics, failing where the parameter distribution becomes strongly non-Gaussian. In the full-batch limit, the edge of stability corresponds to a stationary point of the coupled sharpness-covariance dynamics, recovering self-stabilization and central flow, and batch-to-batch curvature fluctuations lower this threshold under SGD.

title: Few Trials, Many Metrics: Beta Mixtures for Low-Budget AI Evaluation
abstract: Evaluating a stochastic AI system often requires many repeated samples per instance, especially for metrics defined over long horizons. Recent work has shown that modeling instance-level success probabilities with a Beta distribution recovers Pass@$k$ from far fewer samples than direct estimation. We show that this framework supports a broader range of evaluation targets. We fit a mixture of Beta distributions by marginal maximum likelihood, with the number of components chosen by BIC. From that one fit, we compute Pass$^k$ and AUC@$k$ at any horizon in closed form. We also derive delta-method confidence intervals for these metrics and for Pass@$k$, which require no additional model calls. Treating configurations rather than tasks as instances extends the same model to sensitivity analysis. For repeated success metrics, we find that mixture priors yield more accurate estimators than naive estimation across competition mathematics and graduate-level science benchmarks when extrapolating beyond the observed number of trials, and the resulting intervals cover the full-data reference. When prompts are treated as instances, it estimates the distribution of prompt sensitivity more accurately than a comparable item-response baseline without external covariates. Direct estimators remain preferable once trials reach the target horizon.

title: Double White Dwarfs with Circumbinary Disks: Evolution, Population Properties, and Gravitational Wave Signatures
abstract: Double white dwarfs (DWDs) are important multi-messenger sources and powerful probes of binary interaction physics. Close DWDs formed through isolated binary evolution are expected to have negligible eccentricities. However, recent observations have revealed that some eclipsing DWDs exhibit eccentricities of order $10^{-3}$ or larger. In this work, we investigate the interaction between a circumbinary disk (CBD) and the central DWD, where the CBD is assumed to form from a recent common-envelope (CE) ejection. Our models are the first to include CBD-DWD interaction in DWD population synthesis and to constrain disk parameters such as disk mass and lifetime. Our population models predict a correlation between the eccentricity distribution and the orbital period distribution of DWDs, which can be tested by future observations. Furthermore, we discuss the influence of CBD on the gravitational-wave (GW) signal. The CBD-DWD interaction can shrink the orbit and excite eccentricity, extending the time for which the system is individually resolvable by a future space-borne GW detector. Our results suggest that CBD interaction should be accounted for in population synthesis of Galactic DWD GW sources and the stochastic GW foreground.

title: FieldRT: Reconfigurable Architecture from Geometric Sensitivity to Streaming Acceleration
abstract: Geometric perception on edge must simultaneously achieve two goals that are rarely addressed together: preserve accurate spatial understanding for object localization and operate within stringent latency, memory, energy, and precision constraints. This coupling is particularly evident in oriented bird's-eye-view (BEV) detection, where global context, multi-scale interactions, and geometric fusion affect both prediction quality and hardware dataflow. Conventional deployment flows first compress a model using aggregate quality or complexity proxies and then map the compressed operations to a fixed accelerator interface. This separation risks removing geometric structures that appear redundant under coarse metrics but are critical for precise localization, while leaving hardware-level efficiencies in the retained geometry unexploited. We present FieldRT, an algorithm-hardware co-design methodology that uses a common analysis of geometric sensitivity and data lifetime to derive both the deployment profile and its spatial realization. We deploy FieldRT with Axis-Fusion Network (AFN), a sub-million-parameter oriented-BEV detector, and construct controlled profiles that vary the capacity and organization of its geometric processing. The experiments show that redundancy is task-dependent rather than uniform across metrics. Dense prediction can improve while real instance detection deteriorates; coarse localization may remain stable while strict-IoU precision degrades. Moreover, transformations that are individually safe can become detrimental when combined. FieldRT translates the retained geometric structure into a parameterized streaming architecture that shares field access and storage across spatial operators. The resulting custom-PL primitives achieve production-scale numerical closure on an AMD Kria KV260 and make otherwise infeasible multi-dilation execution realizable.

title: Ensemble Classification and Cancer-Specific Gene Signatures from Quality-Aware Hybrid Gene Selection in TCGA RNA-Seq data
abstract: Gene-expression classifiers of cancer type are usually developed and validated within one cohort using random splits. Starting from a quality-aware hybrid Boruta selector from earlier work, we developed and evaluated ensemble classifiers and cancer-specific gene signatures. Using 10,469 TCGA tumours of 33 types, we compared five learners and three ensembles under decision rules fixed in advance, reran the selection in site-grouped cross-validation, transferred a breast-cancer subtype panel to 3273 tumours of the independent SCAN-B cohort, and built five-gene stage~I tumour versus adjacent-normal panels for nine cancer types. Logistic regression (LR) was the most accurate and best-calibrated single learner (balanced accuracy 0.943 on the locked test set). Stacking added at most 0.006 with 1000 genes but improved on LR in every fold with a minimal 100-gene panel; a hierarchical model did not reduce within-group confusion. Site-grouped validation lowered balanced accuracy by 0.027, almost entirely in colon and rectal cancer (0.008 without them and the untestable LAML). On SCAN-B, the subtype panel reached 0.855, close to the 50 PAM50 genes (0.876). Stage~I panels reached ROC AUC >= 0.99 in held-out patients and detected most later-stage tumours. Ensembles help most with a minimal panel; with 1000 genes, a calibrated linear model suffices.

title: Spatial Uncertainty Analytics for Budget-Limited Inspection of Hyperspectral Scenes
abstract: Land-cover maps classified from wide-area hyperspectral surveys are least reliable along class boundaries and in ambiguous regions, so their errors are spatially structured. We study how this structure can direct a limited verification budget: when a low-altitude UAV or a ground crew can visit only a handful of sites, where it should go depends on how classifier uncertainty is arranged across the scene and how a fixed sensor footprint tiles that arrangement. We estimate a per-pixel uncertainty surface from the disagreement of an ensemble of spectral classifiers and select sites by greedy, field-of-view-aware coverage of the uncertainty mass. On seven benchmark scenes, the highest-uncertainty decile of pixels is 2.6 to 7.9 times richer in errors than the scene as a whole, and the coverage greedy covers up to 57% of the classifier's errors with 15 sites, 1.7 to 18 times as many as uncertainty-agnostic sampling of the same labelled region. A non-overlapping selection of the footprints richest in uncertainty does equally well, so the gain comes from scoring whole footprints by uncertainty mass. The advantage persists under spatially blocked evaluation and with a spectral-spatial classifier, although disagreement then ranks errors less well. It requires restricting the surface to labelled land cover: over the whole scene, disagreement peaks on unlabelled ground, where inspections cannot be scored. The best policy for covering connected high-uncertainty regions depends on the scene and on the threshold that defines them, and Gaussian-process selection covers less uncertainty than the coverage greedy on every scene. The pipeline runs on commodity CPUs.

title: A Note on the NP-Hardness on Quadratic Optimization over Doubly Stochastic Matrices and the Gromov-Wasserstein Problem
abstract: The Gromov-Wasserstein problem is an extension of the regular optimal transport problem that is adapted for pairs of distributions residing in incomparable spaces. Broadly speaking, given a pair of metric measure spaces, the Gromov-Wasserstein problem seeks couplings between these spaces that minimize the distortion between the metric evaluations. In this note we record the fact that the Gromov-Wasserstein distance between finite metric spaces is NP-Hard to compute. Our argument relies on a reduction from the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem, and it builds on ideas in Vayer's thesis and Ryner et. al's work that draw connections between the 2-Gromov-Wasserstein and the Quadratic Assignment Problem. During the preparation of this manuscript we learned of the appearance of Breitung et. al's work, whose result essentially supersedes ours. We hope this note serves as a useful companion whose proof is, hopefully, more elementary and easier to understand.

title: Power-Optimal Risk Control via Standardized Margin Calibration
abstract: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.

title: Experimental demonstration of response-enhanced fiber Sagnac gyroscopy via imaginary weak-value amplification
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate a 100-m long fiber Sagnac gyroscope employing imaginary weak-value amplification (IWVA) to enhance the optical readout response to rotation. A Sagnac-induced polarization phase is converted into a measurable spectral response through polarization post-selection and spectrally resolved detection. By varying the post-selection angle, we characterize the gyroscope response over the experimentally accessible rotation-rate range. The response increases systematically toward orthogonal post-selection, yielding a maximum experimental enhancement of approximately 13 times relative to a fixed reference configuration without postselection. Fast Fourier transform and Allan-deviation measurements further characterize the noise and stability of the gyroscope. Near-orthogonal post-selection reduces the equivalent rotation-rate fluctuations, with the minimum Allan deviation decreasing from $0.06~\mathrm{rad/s}$ for the reference configuration to $0.0091~\mathrm{rad/s}$ for the configuration exhibiting the maximum response enhancement, corresponding to an approximately 6.6-fold reduction. Low-frequency fluctuations of the broadband superluminescent diode source limit the long-term stability. These results demonstrate that IWVA provides a practical approach for response-enhanced fiber-based Sagnac gyroscopy and precision rotation sensing.

title: A Straight Line Is Not a Camera Pose: Auditing Short-Clip Pose Benchmarks
abstract: The absolute trajectory error (ATE) is the standard measure of camera-motion accuracy, from SLAM to feed-forward 3D reconstruction. On the common Sintel protocol, a constant-velocity straight line using no images has a lower mean ATE than 10 of 11 recent models re-run with official code. Two properties of ATE's alignment explain this. First, it maps any constant-velocity prediction onto the best-fitting line through the true path, so the line scores the path's regression residual. A residual signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) criterion predicts when moving a prediction towards its constant-velocity fit lowers ATE. It gives the outcome for 95% of 1056 model-clip pairs, 98% of 792 held-out pairs and 97% of 1034 ScanNet pairs, and it separates Sintel (median SNR 0.86) from TUM, ScanNet and full-length Bonn and Wild-SLAM (2.7 to 27), where straightening raises every model's mean ATE. Second, position-only alignment ignores where cameras look: rotating a trajectory by 30 degrees against its orientations leaves ATE unchanged, yet worsens the reprojection of static points for every model on Sintel, TUM and ScanNet in the main setting, and the line, second by mean ATE on Sintel, places them worst by geometric mean: a lower ATE need not mean better geometry. Fitting the alignment's rotation to the predicted orientations gives pose-anchored ATE, a one-function change in ATE's units costing 0.17 ms per clip (ATE: 0.11 ms). It ranks every image-free reference below every model on Sintel, tracks the reprojection error under rotation and straightening, where ATE does not (Spearman 0.61 vs. 0.32), largely preserves the models' order, and ties 10-frame translational relative pose error (RPE) and the discernible trajectory error (DTE) on our rotation and reference tests. Code, predictions and results will be released.

title: PLUMED-JAX: GPU-native enhanced sampling for atomistic simulations
abstract: We present PLUMED-JAX, an AI-assisted adaptation of selected PLUMED collective variables, umbrella sampling, and metadynamics for JAX-based atomistic simulations, developed using gpt-6.1-sol with reasoning effort set to high within the Codex harness. Integration with JAX-MD supports compiled molecular dynamics, batched replicas, walkers sharing a bias, and execution across multiple graphics processing units. We validate the framework against PLUMED and exact free energy benchmarks, and demonstrate applications to butane, silicon crystallization, and lithium transport, with severalfold improvements in computational throughput for both classical forcefields and machine learning interatomic potentials.

title: Where Causal Discovery Breaks on Real Data: Measuring the Assumptions One Property at a Time
abstract: Causal discovery is usually evaluated on simulators or on systems whose ground truth follows from physics or design. When it fails on other real data, the failure is attributed to assumptions that may not hold, but which ones fail, and by how much, is rarely measured. We measure the observable properties of the data they bear on, one property at a time, on a real panel. The case study follows 2,901 US public firms over 31 quarters, with 71 types of corporate action from SEC 8-K filings, 11 financial-statement items, and an expert graph over 651 action-state pairs. The panel breaks measurable requirements of discovery: tails that survive winsorisation, balance-sheet items and revenue close to random walks, and interventions too rare to detect effects of a tenth of a standard deviation in 40 of 71 actions. Even so, a marginal test ranks expert-labelled direct above not-direct pairs within each action (AUROC 0.658) better than every null we built, so the panel does carry information about which pairs are direct. Tuned discovery methods, in configurations feasible at this panel size, recover less of it than a simple pairwise cross-correlation when pairs are ranked within each action, and no more when they are ranked within each target, which removes what the target alone predicts. Most direct pairs (132 of 222) involve actions below the support needed for 80% power against a 0.1-SD effect. For flow targets, conditioning on the target's other expert-labelled parents, often filed alongside the action, erodes the marginal discrimination, and most not-direct associations survive it: even with the graph's parent sets supplied, the expected separation does not emerge. For each property, we give a diagnostic computable before any discovery method is run.

title: On the Distribution of Prime Squares and Its Applications
abstract: We prove that, for every \(A>0\), all but \(O_A(X(\log X)^{-A})\) integers \(n<X\) satisfying \(n\equiv11\pmod{24}\) admit a representation \[ n=a^2+b^2+p^2, \] where \(p\) and \(a^2+b^2+1\) are prime and \((a,b)=1\). For ergodic averages along prime squares, we prove a universal divergence result for integrable functions, while establishing almost-everywhere convergence for near-integrable functions. We also quantify how the bounds used to establish convergence behave as one approaches integrability. Moreover, we prove endpoint improving and sparse bounds for the corresponding discrete averages, with an explicit Orlicz loss.

title: Integer-Exact Microscaling: Running MXFP4 Language Models on INT8 Matrix Units
abstract: On hardware whose fastest matrix datapath is INT8$\times$INT8, such as the Neural Accelerators of Apple's M5 GPUs, 4-bit weights must become INT8 operands. Existing MXFP4 kernels already map FP4 (E2M1) values to integers by doubling them, but apply every 32-element block scale inside the reduction. We show when no per-block work is needed: a row of MXFP4 weights is exactly one INT8 vector times one power-of-two scale if its block exponents span at most three, so a linear layer becomes a single INT8 GEMM with one rescale per output. Enforcing the condition adds at most 1/16 of a row's largest rounding error to the blocks it changes, and real weights already satisfy it: 97.9-99.97% of rows across seven models, including 99.93% of the 95M rows of a 125B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. The resulting spread-constrained MXFP4 files stay standard MXFP4. With integer instead of power-of-two block multipliers, an integer-exact format (16-wide blocks, multipliers 1..10, 4.26 bits) runs as one exact INT8 GEMM and is more accurate than NVFP4 (4.5 bits) with its standard scale rule on five small models, within 0.06 perplexity of NVFP4 with scale search. On Qwen3.8-Flash-Next's routed experts with INT8 activations it is as close to the FP8 model as NVFP4 with scale search (KL divergence 0.0557 vs. 0.0553) and closer than MLX's MXFP4 and affine INT4; with every matrix quantized it solves 94.8% of GSM8K vs. 91.0% for MLX's MXFP4. Quantizing only the 74k routed expert matrices (96% of the parameters) to either of our formats with INT8 activations costs at most 0.2% perplexity. A complete W4A8 system on the M5 produces outputs bit-identical to the quantized reference; prefill is 1.34-1.74x faster than MLX on a dense model, 1.10-1.57x on two MoE models up to 35B parameters and 1.22-1.29x on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, where shared non-GEMM work bounds the gain.

title: Efficient Reconfigurable Architectures for Deep Learning
abstract: The growing computational demands of deep learning (DL) have driven AI-optimized reconfigurable devices, such as the AMD Versal AI Engines (AIEs), the Intel Stratix 10 NX Tensor Blocks (TBs), and the AMD Ryzen AI NPUs. Their heterogeneous resources and novel dataflow models make efficient exploitation nontrivial, and FPGAs lack native support for structured sparsity. This dissertation optimizes dense general matrix multiplication (GEMM), the dominant DL kernel, on these devices, proposes FPGA architectural enhancements for structured sparsity, and extends the techniques to AMD Ryzen AI NPUs. First, MaxEVA optimizes GEMM on Versal AIEs, achieving up to 2.19$\times$ higher throughput and 20.4% higher energy efficiency than the state of the art. It is then extended to arbitrary matrix sizes, and a systematic framework is proposed for the Stratix 10 NX TBs. Both frameworks reach state-of-the-art int8 throughput of up to 77 and 68 TOPS, and energy efficiency of up to 0.94 and 1.35 TOPS/W, on Versal and Stratix, respectively. Next, Systolic Sparse Tensor slices (SSTs) are proposed as in-fabric hard blocks supporting dense, 2:4, 1:4, and a new 1:3 sparsity level. SST-based GEMM accelerators achieve up to 5$\times$ higher frequency and 10.9$\times$ lower area than conventional FPGA logic, and on sparse ViT and CNN models SSTs deliver up to 3.52$\times$ speedup over dense in-fabric acceleration with up to 13.3% area increase. Finally, a common systematic methodology is proposed to optimize GEMM across the XDNA and XDNA2 AMD NPUs, reaching state-of-the-art performance of up to 6.76 and 38.05 TOPS (int8) and 3.14 and 14.71 TOPS (bf16), respectively.

title: Time-Specific Multinomial Logistic Regression for Competing Risks
abstract: Motivated by the project on premature menopause among childhood cancer survivors in the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS), we develop methods for estimating time-specific factor effects using doubly censored event time data with competing risks. We begin with fitting separate binary logistic regression models for different causes. However, the approach does not ensure the sum of the resulting estimated cumulative incidence rates remains bounded by one. To overcome this limitation, we consider a multinomial logistic regression formulation to jointly model all cause-specific risks. Two inverse-probability-of-censoring-weight (IPCW) based estimating functions are proposed accordingly. To handle the estimation instability caused by data separation, we incorporate the Firth-type penalization in those estimating functions to obtain more stable coefficient estimators. The sandwich variance estimator is applied to estimate the standard errors. A weighted quasi-likelihood information criterion, paired with a backward elimination, is further adapted to the proposed estimating functions for selecting covariates at a given age. Simulation studies are conducted to examine the proposed approaches regarding consistency, efficiency, and robustness of the estimators. The Firth correction substantially reduces the bias induced by separation and provides valid standard error estimation. We illustrate the proposed approach with the CCSS data viewing premature ovarian insufficiency and surgical premature menopause as the two potential causes of the primary event, premature menopause. The data analysis reveals that the effects of the cancer treatment-related covariates are significant on premature ovarian insufficiency but not on surgical premature menopause. The variable selection procedure, illustrated on an extended covariate set, yields estimated risks close to those under the full model.

title: Threat Modeling Intimate Partner Abuse in Agentic Systems
abstract: Agentic systems are AI-powered technologies capable of autonomous action within digital environments, such as sending emails or making reservations. They are deeply connected to external tools as well as users' data and resources, making them vulnerable to attacks which exploit their access and capabilities. In this work, we apply the technology-facilitated abuse threat model, in the context of intimate partner violence and surveillance, to these systems, revealing threats that require deliberate investigation and mitigation. We categorize attacks based on system ownership: (1) Abuser-as-owner attacks demonstrate how agentic systems make existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse far easier and more scalable. (2) Victim-survivor-as-owner attacks show how agentic systems create a new attack surface which abusers can exploit. In light of these risks, we outline research and development directions for effective mitigation strategies.

title: Some Remarks on the Asymptotic Behavior of Mean Field Games of Controls
abstract: We analyze the asymptotic behavior of several mean field games of controls. First, in the time-dependent case, we examine the behavior of solutions to discounted mean field games of controls as the discount factor $λ$ tends to infinity. Next, we study three stationary models of mean field games of controls, finding that solutions to the first-order discounted problem and the second-order ergodic problem can be obtained from solutions to the second-order discounted problem by taking $ν\to 0$ and $λ\to 0$, respectively. Finally, we investigate the long-time average behavior of solutions to the time-dependent system with no discount, finding that solutions converge to the solution to the second-order ergodic problem as $T \to \infty$.

title: VoirDire: Counterfactual Calibration for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge Aggregation
abstract: LLM-as-a-judge systems often aggregate multiple judges to improve evaluation reliability. However, judge agreement can reflect shared biases toward verbosity, formatting, or fluency rather than the intended evaluation target. Addressing these shared biases is challenging because observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish agreement driven by target quality from agreement driven by nuisance attributes. We introduce VoirDire, an intervention-calibrated aggregation method for LLM-judge panels. VoirDire applies controlled interventions that vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the evaluation target; it then uses paired changes in judge scores to identify nuisance-sensitive directions. It attenuates these directions and selects aggregation weights that retain variation across items while penalizing sensitivity to the interventions, making the final consensus less dependent on superficial features. We show theoretically that observational judge outputs alone cannot identify which shared direction is target-relevant, while paired interventions provide the contrast needed to identify nuisance-sensitive variation. We evaluate VoirDire on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference. Compared with the existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks. These findings suggest that counterfactual interventions provide an additional means of improving the reliability and controllability of LLM-based evaluation beyond merely relying on observed judge agreement.

title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs
abstract: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL). The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language

title: Counterexamples to torsion-freeness in the $K$-theory of crystallographic group $C^*$-algebras
abstract: We give a negative answer to a question of Sánchez Saldaña--Velásquez and Lück asking whether the topological K-theory of the reduced group C*-algebra of a split crystallographic group with finite cyclic holonomy is always torsion-free. For two explicit split crystallographic groups with translation subgroup of rank four and holonomy of order four, we compute the equivariant K-theory of the classifying space for proper actions and find nontrivial two-torsion. The equivariant universal coefficient theorem transfers this torsion to proper equivariant K-homology, and the Baum--Connes conjecture identifies the resulting groups with the topological K-theory of the corresponding reduced group C*-algebras.

title: A Hierarchical direct solver for Lippmann-Schwinger equations based on boundary traces
abstract: A high-order hierarchical direct solver for variable-media scattering in two dimensions is presented. Standard discretizations for these problems produce dense linear systems that are commonly solved iteratively, requiring a new global solve for each incident field. The method proposed here instead constructs a reusable scattering operator for the inhomogeneous medium, based on a hierarchical subdivision of the computational domain. First, high-accuracy leaf scattering operators are built from discretized local integral equations. Up the hierarchy, neighboring boxes are merged to build the scattering operators for successively larger boxes. A key feature of the method is that each scattering operator is represented as a map of incoming traces to outgoing traces. Consequently, volume unknowns appear only in the leaf computations; all higher levels of the hierarchy operate entirely on boundary traces. The hierarchical solver is presented first at the continuum level and discretized only afterward using high-order local volume quadrature, polynomial trace representations, and boundary integral techniques. For a discretization involving $N$ degrees of freedom, the method requires $O(N^{3/2})$ work and $O(N\log N)$ storage to build all scattering operators. Once these are available, any incoming field can be processed at cost $O(N)$ if only the outgoing field is required, and cost $O(N\log N)$ if the full field is required. Numerical experiments demonstrate high-order accuracy on a range of challenging scattering problems including cavities, back-scattering, limited regularity, and high wavenumber, that pose significant challenges to iterative methods.

title: Understanding GPU Megakernels: Why Residency Can Mislead
abstract: Megakernels let one persistent GPU program prepare dependent operators early and execute ready tasks together. We study the benefits and costs of these capabilities by reconstructing two LLM megakernels, ThunderKittens (TK) and VDCores, as separate kernels on H100 using their original operator code. Our results show that CTA residency can misrepresent opportunities for useful overlap in both directions. By overlapping startup and operand loading with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), the reconstructions reduce decode-step latency by 5.7% in TK and achieve comparable performance in VDCores when both executions enforce the required memory ordering. Under whole-operator dependencies, TK's persistent execution still gains more from prefetch, but runtime and completion-signal ordering costs outweigh this advantage. Both startup overlap and prefetch depend on resource availability. Persistent CTAs can reuse storage before retiring, whereas separate successors must acquire their full CTA footprints before initializing or loading operands. This admission constraint in both reconstructions motivates finer resource sharing across kernels. Beyond early preparation, joint execution requires ready work and spare capacity in the bottleneck resource. Reserving SMs for communication can add GEMM waves that erase overlap gains, while filling idle SMs offers little benefit once memory bandwidth is saturated. These findings clarify benefits and costs of megakernels and motivate GPU support for earlier resource reuse across kernels.

title: Swap, Replicate, Read the Mass: A Protocol for Auditing Demographic Bias in System One Decision Models
abstract: System One decision models replace text generation with typed, probability-scored answers and are entering production. Answers execute without a person in the loop, and no multi-model audit exists on established bias benchmarks. We provide that audit: three benchmarks: BBQ (all eleven categories), CrowS-Pairs, and SilverSpoon, adapted to the typed interface, twelve models plus a no-thinking ablation, and 1,638,000 decisions. Every order-sensitive item runs twice with options swapped; native typed models also swap labels; ten configurations repeat under extra seeds and batch 16. We find widespread stereotype alignment, order-dependent answers, and confidence that tracks instability rather than bias. In BBQ, 97 of 143 model-by-category scores are significant and 94 aligned, while the commercial reference abstains on 99.5% of ambiguous items, hiding aligned probability mass. Option swaps flip 0.0% to 72.6% of choices; typed scoring stays below 10% except Laya (22-33%), and untuned letter prompting reaches 73%. CrowS-Pairs preference spans 0.496 to 0.816, and boolean answers can be decided by position (1.00 versus 0.005). SilverSpoon judgments shift toward lower-SES labels in five of eight decision models, inherited from the 9B backbone or induced by tuning. Audits must permute options and reverse questions by default; order-invariant scoring should become a procurement requirement.

title: Where Does EEG Help Wearable Freezing of Gait Detection?
abstract: Freezing of gait (FoG) detectors built on inertial measurement units (IMUs) are accurate while the legs move, but they become unreliable when the legs are nearly still, which is exactly when akinetic freezing, voluntary stopping, and standing must be told apart. Electroencephalography (EEG) captures motor-planning activity that leg sensors cannot, but EEG is impractical for daily use. We ask where EEG helps: as an input at inference time, or only during pretraining, so that the deployed detector still needs only IMUs. We assemble a pretraining corpus of synchronized EEG and IMU recordings (5 datasets, 184 people, 94 hours) and compare six settings that differ only in the modalities used for pretraining and as model input, each with tuned hyperparameters and five independent pretraining runs. On the BXHC FoG dataset (leave-one-patient-out, 10 patients with FoG), adding EEG as input raises FoG F1 from 0.663 to 0.740 (9 of 10 patients improve), and the gain in ranking performance is confined to the quartile of windows with the least leg movement (AUROC +0.063). Pretraining the IMU encoder jointly with EEG improves an IMU-only detector both within the cohort (FoG F1 0.663 to 0.705) and when it is trained on a small cohort and tested on another (FoG F1 +0.083, all 10 test patients improve). Repeating the study with PD-only and healthy-only pretraining corpora, each with its own hyperparameter search, shows that IMU-based detection is robust to the corpus, whereas the benefit of aligning EEG with IMU requires both. Cross-cohort analysis further shows that detectors trained without annotated voluntary stops classify nearly all stops as freezing. Finally, on PD versus non-PD classification in three external datasets, joint EEG+IMU pretraining improves PD detection from walking EEG over EEG-only pretraining (AUROC 0.750 vs. 0.683), while IMU-based detection does not depend on the pretraining.

title: A block-encoding approach to the Segawa-Suzuki spectral mapping theorem
abstract: We revisit the Segawa--Suzuki spectral mapping theorem for abstract Szegedy-type quantum walks from a block-encoding viewpoint. Retaining both eigenspaces of the involution underlying the chiral symmetry yields a natural two-by-two block representation in which the usual discriminant operator and its counterpart form the diagonal blocks. The non-endpoint spectral mapping theorem then follows from an elementary Schur decomposition, substantially simplifying the original proof by avoiding its invariant-subspace decomposition and approximate-eigenvector arguments. The same framework establishes the result for the spectrum, point spectrum, and Fredholm essential spectrum and gives a direct block-theoretic description of the endpoint inherited and birth eigenspaces. We illustrate the construction with a one-dimensional split-step quantum walk.

title: Knowing Where to Look: Interactive Object Search via Spatial-Semantic Fusion
abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition - reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored - with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website - https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/

title: Detector Placement Relaxes Efficiency Requirements for Detecting a Weak Coherent Link
abstract: A weak coherent link can produce unusually early arrivals without changing stationary count rates. Missed jumps along routes available without the link can produce similar records, obscuring its presence. On an eight-site ring, relocating the same detector losses exposes one more crossing on the easiest background route to hide, without changing the dynamics or leading link signal. At fixed error and a common observation-time scaling, the tolerated missed fraction and time-bin width follow fourth-root rather than square-root scaling with link strength. These requirements hold for every decision using the counting record and are met using three event counts per bin, with all elapsed time included. At the same stationary collected flux, where jumps are monitored can therefore determine the time resolution needed for weak-link sensing.

title: Strongly Pseudoconvex Domains with Finite Dimensional $p$-Bergman Spaces
abstract: We show that for every $n\ge2$, $p>2$, and positive integer $m$, there exists a finite-volume pseudoconvex domain $D\subset\mathbb C^n$ with real-analytic strongly pseudoconvex boundary whose $p$-Bergman space $A^p(D)$ has dimension $m$. These domains admit smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions and satisfy $H^\infty(D)=\mathbb C$ and $\dim A^s(D)=\infty$ for every $0<s\le2$. Moreover, for every finite $s\ge p$, we have $\dim A^s(D)=\lceil pm/s\rceil$. As an application, we show that the Bergman projection fails to map $\mathcal{C}_c^\infty(D)$ into $A^p(D)$ and admits no bounded extension to $L^s(D)$ or $L^{s/(s-1)}(D)$ for any finite $s\ge p$.

title: Non-Convex Market Makers: Coherence without Convexity, Friction, and Parallel Composition
abstract: Cost-function market makers are always assumed convex, and convexity is not what makes them coherent. For a path-independent maker the exact no-arbitrage condition is a chord condition, that every chord slope of the cost lie in the convex hull of payoffs; convexity enters the standard axiomatics through a separate requirement, monotone information incorporation, and dropping it leaves coherent non-convex makers. Rational flow against such a maker trades the convex envelope, so non-convexity costs expressiveness rather than soundness, and a proportional fee of at least the arbitrage depth restores no-arbitrage, which by conjugation is a bid-ask spread with an exact no-trade interval for any cost whatever. Combining fee-bearing makers is an infimal convolution solved by one monotone clearing-price root-find, with sparse participation and a consolidated limit order book as the aggregate, and a deep quadratic co-quoter is Moreau smoothing, which preserves coherence at every depth. Any quoted configuration outside the coherent hull admits a portfolio priced below its worst payoff, so arbitrageurs act as decentralized separation oracles, and coherence is relative to friction and to the cost of finding certificates.

title: The Continuum Limit of the Deep Linear Network
abstract: The Deep Linear Network (DLN) is a simple version of a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) in which the activation function is the identity and the bias vector is the zero vector. We examine the behavior of the model when the number of weight matrices, which is finite in the original model, goes to infinity. We show that a plausible continuum limit is a dimensionally reduced version of the Yang-Mills equation on the torus, revealing an unexpected geometric interpretation of infinite-depth DLNs. While we do not prove this rigorously, it is a very pretty calculation. It also gives some insight into several features of the construction. We note that the choices of boundary conditions on the ends of the discrete series survive better in the continuum limit. Also, the regularizing functional which uses the moment map survives nicely in the continuum limit, whereas the regularizing functional using the size of approximating terms has no sensible limit. This surely is useful information for the choices we make in the finite-dimensional theory, and might also be useful in the more complicated MLP setting.

title: Robustness Starts with the Objective: Designing and Certifying Robust LLM-Generated Heuristics
abstract: LLMs are increasingly used to design heuristics for computer systems. However, most synthesis frameworks evaluate candidates by their average performance, which can mask severe regressions on specific workloads. Even adding adversarial training inputs doesn't eliminate these regressions, and percentile objectives (e.g., optimizing for the 95th percentile) overlook how severe regressions can be beyond the selected threshold. We present TAILOR, a framework that guides LLM synthesis using the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline on the same workload. This paired CVaR measures the average difference over the worst fraction of workloads. We show that a negative paired CVaR guarantees improvements in both average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without ever computing that optimum. We find that TAILOR achieves the best mean--tail trade-off among the synthesis objectives we evaluate across three case studies: Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing, and server placement. Tested across seven diverse optimization benchmarks, TAILOR produces heuristics that are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them. On these six benchmarks, TAILOR also outperforms known robust, human-designed alternatives in the tail while achieving better or comparable average-performance improvement over the baseline.

title: To Jev or Not to Jev: When Can System-1 Decision Models Replace LLM Judges?
abstract: Decision models such as TypeSafe's Jev answer typed questions about a text (yes/no, multiple choice, or an ordinal score) with calibrated probabilities in a single forward pass and without generating text, which makes them an inexpensive candidate for LLM-as-a-judge workloads. We evaluate 14 System-1 decision models, selected with a pre-stated protocol, against four generative judges (Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.6 with and without reasoning, and Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking) on eleven established judge benchmarks. Five of the 14 are statistically indistinguishable from GPT-5.6 without reasoning on all five pairwise and best-of-4 benchmarks, and the two strongest, DReX-Max and d1-ultra, are significantly more accurate than Haiku on JudgeBench, LLMBar and RewardBench 2. Conditioned on a reference answer generated once per prompt, eleven models reach 90.3-93.4% on JudgeBench, statistically indistinguishable from Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 with reasoning, and on PPE best-of-16 every reference-guided System-1 judge matches GPT-5.6 with reasoning at roughly one-sixteenth of its cost per prompt. Several System-1 judges are better calibrated than every generative judge and correlate more strongly with human helpfulness ratings. Robustness to instructions injected into the judged response is a property of the individual model rather than of the System-1 design: an appended note to the evaluator reverses 0-5% of the correct verdicts of five models but 17-49% for the other nine. Two general System-1 leaderboards that contain no judging tasks predict judging accuracy (Pearson r = 0.95-0.96), a well-calibrated System-1 first stage matches Opus on LLMBar while escalating 17% of items, and same-size controls show that the correctness deficit of a 4B decision model is a reasoning gap rather than a size gap.

title: Weights That Stay: On-Chip Megakernels for Serial Heads in Speculative Decoding
abstract: Parallel speculative drafters use a lightweight serial head to recover token dependencies within a block generated in parallel. Each head step updates only a small state, yet projects that state through the same vocabulary-sized matrix. Step-wise execution repeatedly transfers this large, immutable projection, making the head a meaningful source of latency despite its low arithmetic cost. We present Weights That Stay, an execution design that keeps projection shards on chip for the entire serial draft walk. A persistent megakernel couples weight residency with GPU-side token selection and state advancement, reusing resident weights while exchanging only compact state between steps. The design supports full or partial residency and accommodates both Markov and recurrent heads on H100 and B200. Integrated into SGLang, Weights That Stay improves throughput for Markov drafting on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, with gains of up to 12.3%. At the head level, the DSpark walk is up to 11.6$\times$ faster than the fastest measured SGLang reference path. These results show that aligning weight residency with the full draft walk translates cross-step reuse into end-to-end serving gains.

title: Selecting or Solving? What Best-of-N Verification Delivers in Video Reasoning
abstract: Answering a complex question about a long video is a grounding problem: the answer turns on a few seconds of evidence, and vision-language models remain well below human accuracy at finding them. The standard way to spend extra test-time compute on this kind of video reasoning is best-of-N selection: sample several chain-of-thought answers from a fixed model, then let a second model re-watch the video and pick one. Such pipelines are reported by a single headline number, their margin over a majority vote. That number conflates two effects with opposite deployment consequences: the benefit the second model adds by selecting among candidates, and the benefit it would have supplied by solving the question itself. We separate them, measuring the Selection Increment (SI) -- selection accuracy minus the same verifier's accuracy with the candidates withheld -- alongside the margin over self-consistency, across five long-video benchmarks. The Selection Increment is largest for the weakest verifiers: a verifier that solves poorly on its own leaves the candidates the most room to help. Beating the majority vote follows the opposite profile: where the vote already sits near its ceiling no verifier we test improves on it; below that ceiling only the strongest do. On Video-Holmes, the two come apart on a single pool of candidates -- a weak verifier gains +19.3 points from the candidates yet lands 7.1 points below the vote, while the frontier verifier gains the least and beats the vote. The weakest verifier also shows a failure mode: on EgoSchema it picks by where an option sits in the list rather than by what the video shows. Read as a merit score, SI puts a verifier that fails to beat a majority vote at the top of its ranking; read as an audit, it says which of the two effects a headline number delivers. Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/best-n-selection-video-reasoning.

title: Do Social Influence Pressures Move LLM Agents? Evidence from Delegated Audit Judgment
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly being integrated into complex professional workflows such as auditing and entrusted with judgments under human review. Human auditors are known to yield to social influence pressures from superiors, peers and clients, and this paper asks whether LLM agents yield to the same pressures and, if so, how they respond.
