Riemann problems, pressure equilibrium tests and acoustic tests show that in non-stiff regimes the semi-implicit schemes reproduce the results of a fully explicit scheme, while in the stiff regime they allow time steps that are up to 3-4 orders of magnitude larger, avoiding the excessive numerical dissipation of explicit schemes whose numerical viscosity is dictated by liquid sound speed.

title: One Offset, Two Directions: Baseline Adjustment via Subgroup Offsets
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages against the within-prompt mean reward, a baseline shared across the group. In practice, rollouts within a prompt are not always homogeneous, differing in their solution strategies and reasoning trajectories, along which they may group into subgroups. We further find that these heterogeneous subgroups may exhibit distinct reward distributions. The global baseline, however, collapses them onto a single credit axis, where the credit reflects neither a rollout's standing within its subgroup nor the subgroup's standing relative to the rest. We therefore study how to adjust the baseline when the rollouts of a prompt fall into heterogeneous subgroups. We define the \emph{subgroup offset} as the deviation of a subgroup mean from the global mean, and shift the baseline along it by a single signed coefficient $λ$. The sign of $λ$ yields two opposing directions: \emph{Alignment} ($λ{>}0$) adds the offset to the baseline, drawing credit toward a rollout's relative position within its subgroup; \emph{Contrast} ($λ{<}0$) subtracts it, drawing a rollout's credit toward the relative quality of the subgroup it belongs to. The adjustment acts on the baseline alone, leaving the reward signal and the optimization objective unchanged. In this work, we induce subgroups from strategies, grouping rollouts that share a strategy into the same subgroup. We evaluate both directions on Qwen3-8B-Base and Olmo3-7B-Base across four competition-level math benchmarks, against a $λ{=}0$ anchor that shares the same strategy-conditioned sampling and differs only in the baseline. Against this anchor each direction yields modest but consistent gains in multi-sample coverage, with Contrast the stronger of the two.

title: A Tool in the Forward Pass: Frozen Tape Modules as Layers of a Small Language Model
abstract: Calling a tool through generated text adds decoding steps, even when the computation itself is short. We study an alternative: a small neural module that runs inside a language model's forward pass. A learned writer turns hidden states into a symbolic tape, a short sequence of discrete symbols that encodes the computation. The module, trained separately and then frozen, reduces the tape to a result, and a learned reader returns that result to the model. We evaluate arithmetic and object tracking in gemma-3-1b-it. With a writer trained on labelled tapes, the layer answers all 750 items of BIG-Bench Hard's tracking shuffled objects correctly. At seven people it needs about 1/10 of the GPU kernel time of a text-tool baseline that uses the same host model and exact code, with accuracy 1.00 against 0.99. The writer can also be learned from answers alone, guided by a hand-written copying prior, but less reliably: 5 of 6 runs succeed in the 1B host and 2 of 4 in the 4B host. Two independently trained layers keep their task accuracy when attached to one model, and a learned gate keeps them silent on the tested general-text and look-alike prompts. The results support a narrow use case: a bounded computation that returns one symbol can avoid the decoding cost of a textual tool call. Extracting the right input reliably, and deciding when to act, remain the main open problems.

title: ConstraintMatch: Compositional Image-Text Matching through Constrained Regional Evidence Selection
abstract: Local image--text matching can find strong evidence for individual concepts yet favor captions with incorrect attribute--entity bindings. We introduce ConstraintMatch, a training-free inference method that turns entity-level regional consistency into an explicit matching cost. On the same frozen condition--region similarity matrix, it compares independent crop selection for each category and attribute with a shared crop choice within each entity. Their gap quantifies the score advantage obtained by relaxing the shared-region constraint. Spatial references from the same image calibrate this gap by keeping category evidence fixed while jointly shifting an entity's attribute maps. Per-entity clipping prevents cancellation across residuals, and the scaled mean cost is subtracted from global similarity. ConstraintMatch uses pooled embeddings, and spatial calibration requires no additional encoder calls. With parameters fixed per backbone across tasks, ConstraintMatch improves over global matching by 7.70 percentage points on full ARO Attribute and 5.63 points on held-out SugarCrepe++ attribute swaps, averaged across Qwen~2B and CORE~2B. Against SGI adapted to the same 13-crop budget, the respective gains are 4.85 and 3.51 points. Controlled analyses distinguish the effects of shared-region matching and candidate score calibration. The results establish entity-level evidence selection as a practical scoring principle for compositional multimodal retrieval.

title: CheXPoT: Post-Hoc Visual Verification and Correction of VLM-Generated Radiology Reports
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.

title: The Tangled Web They Weave: Exploring Neural Representations with Directed Simplicial Complexes
abstract: Understanding how artificial neural networks (ANNs) represent and combine features internally is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Existing neural circuit-discovery methods represent neuron interactions as pairwise edges in a graph. But distributed neural representations consist of large groups of neurons that are inherently linked by higher-order causal dependencies: suppressing a subgroup of neurons in concert may shift the activation of other neurons in the feature representation. We propose a method to construct filtered directed simplicial complexes (DSCs) that give a topological representation of such dependencies, built from the activation profiles of an ANN on a given set of inputs. Our approach treats ANNs as structural causal models and uses counterfactual ablations to test for causal links between groups of internal neurons within specific input contexts. As a proof of concept, we apply the approach to a pair of small multilayer perceptron (MLP) architectures in a synthetic two-dimensional quadrant classification task. In these examples, DSCs recover the designed feature pathways and coordinated class transitions, and the complexes of trained networks are higher-dimensional than those of their handcrafted references. As validation, we compare our method with graph-based circuit-discovery baselines and find that their 1-skeletons agree within the relations that a weight graph can represent. These results support DSCs as context-dependent descriptions of multi-neuron computation and may thus provide a novel, orthogonal framework to study the phenomenon of distributed feature representations and polysemanticity.

title: Unbiased Low-Rank Approximation for Repeated Matrix-Vector Multiplication: Stability and Optimal Sampling
abstract: Replacing the matrix in an iteration with random low-rank matrices can reduce the cost of matrix-vector multiplication. However, even if the sampled matrices equal the original matrix in expectation, the expected squared norm of the random iterates may grow while the original iteration converges. Under a fixed rank bound, we study how to choose the distribution of these random matrices to minimize this growth when sampling independently at each step. We derive an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic growth factor and use it to determine when the expected squared norm can converge to zero. We then characterize precisely when a fixed sampling distribution achieves this optimal factor and construct finite-support optimal distributions in every attainable case. These results determine the minimum rank required for stability and provide optimal sampling designs under the prescribed rank constraint.

title: Tight Stochastic Sequential Covers for General VC Classes with Unknown i.i.d. Features
abstract: We study hybrid online learning with stochastic features and adversarial labels when the feature distribution is unknown. Prior work gave stochastic sequential covers of log-size $O(d\log^2 T)$ for a general VC class and logarithmic bounds only under stronger star-type structure. We show that finite VC dimension alone is enough: every binary class of VC dimension $d$ admits a distribution-blind exact cover with log-size $O(d\log T+\log(1/δ))$, matching the worst-case $Ω(d\log(T/d))$ dependence on the horizon. The key ingredient is a new local cube weight that counts Boolean subcubes incident to each realizable trace. Unlike the equal splits used in earlier constructions, we split mass unevenly according to these cube weights; a coordinate-deletion inequality shows that VC dimension controls the total cost of these splits. This yields, to our knowledge, the first tight $O((d+1)\log T)$ expected worst-case log-loss regret for general VC partitions with unknown i.i.d. features, and an exact polynomial-time implementation for planar affine halfspaces. We also show that the binary phenomenon does not extend from VC dimension to pseudo-dimension: a fixed pseudo-dimension-one sigmoid class requires $Ω(\log^2 T)$ bits for uniform sequential approximation at accuracy $1/T$.

title: Congruent quotient matrix, nodal domain, and nodal count
abstract: We introduce the congruent quotient matrix along with its inequalities on inertia and demonstrate that these inequalities are the essence of the discrete nodal domain theorem, the bounds on nodal counts, and Fiedler's characterization on tree eigenvectors. Using these techniques, we also extend the existing bounds for the number of nodal domains and nodal counts.

title: Joint Trajectory, Sensing, and Computation Co-Design for UAV-Assisted Federated Edge Vision
abstract: This paper investigates UAV-assisted federated edge vision for training computationally heavy object detection models. Existing studies treat training data as static, ignoring the tight coupling between dynamic visual sensing and massive in place computational burdens. To minimize the expected training time under battery constraints, we propose a four-phase joint trajectory, sensing, and computation co-design. To mitigate data heterogeneity, we use a uniform sensing probability to translate federated convergence requirements into UAV mobility constraints. Furthermore, a two-layer alternating optimization (AO) algorithm is developed to adaptively determine the local data workload, optimally balancing the required training rounds against in-place computation delays. Simulations validate the superiority of our approach in model convergence and accuracy over baselines.

title: PhoneValue-Bench: A Multimodal Benchmark and Datasets for Consumer Smartphone Recommerce Valuation
abstract: As consumer smartphone recommerce scales, buyers must quote binding repurchase prices from seller-uploaded multi-view photos and diagnostic screenshots before devices reach the warehouse. Accurate remote valuation requires fusing noisy cosmetic evidence with identity, battery, lock, and channel risk from screenshots and staff forms, since an error in any modality changes both grade and payout. However, existing multimodal resources mainly target general VLM competence, screen reading, or factory defect detection, and largely overlook staff-aligned trade-in fields, dual appearance/staff ground truth, and executable valuation scorecards. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of large-scale real trade-in data with audited dual annotations and a compact ranking benchmark kept separate from training labels, and (2) the need to jointly reason over unordered multi-view cosmetics and diagnostic screens under operational deduction rules. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-GT evaluation suite with tier-gated scorecards, together with PhoneValue-Corpus, a matched weakly labeled training set of over twenty thousand orders and hundreds of thousands of captioned images. We further present ValueAgent, a staged perception-fusion-valuation reference pipeline aligned with production inspection, plus an executable public scorer and submission schema. Experiments show that ValueAgent reaches a measured 84.1/100 on Bench-Full, with 97.0 appearance fill and 54.1 staff-field fill, establishing a practical dual-GT benchmark for multimodal recommerce valuation.

title: Near-extremal critical dynamics driven by a phantom field in Einstein-Maxwell-scalar theory
abstract: We investigate the fully nonlinear dynamics of Einstein-Maxwell-scalar black holes in the low-mass, near-extremal region of the solution space, which is difficult to access with conventional positive-energy perturbations. An independent phantom field is introduced as a controllable negative-energy channel, and its initial amplitude is varied while the remaining parameters of the initial data are held fixed. The phantom contribution is concentrated during the early-time infall and reduces the quasi-local mass in the black-hole region at fixed electric charge, thereby allowing the evolution to approach near-extremal configurations. Near a critical amplitude $p_\ast$, evolutions on both sides of the threshold enter the same long-lived scalarized intermediate stage before separating toward either a near-extremal Reissner-Nordstrom black hole or a nonextremal hairy black hole. The residence time near this intermediate stage obeys the logarithmic scaling law of Type I critical behavior, and the growth rate extracted from the departure is consistent with the inverse lifetime coefficient. The intermediate stage is characterized by a small horizon surface gravity and finite horizon curvature, with no curvature blow-up resolved at the horizon during the simulated interval. These results demonstrate that phantom-assisted negative-energy transport provides a dynamical route into the near-extremal sector of the EMS solution space and reveals a threshold-mediated transition between bald and hairy black-hole end states.

title: A Second-Order Stochastic Dynamic Mode Decomposition by Richardson Extrapolation
abstract: Stochastic dynamic mode decomposition (SDMD) approximates the Koopman semigroup of an Itô diffusion by a Galerkin generator matrix on a dictionary of observables, computed from samples of the invariant law and evaluations of the generator, and advances observables with a first-order stochastic Taylor step (SDMD-1). The second-order Taylor step (SDMD-2) also needs the matrix of second generator actions, hence a dictionary with four derivatives, evaluations of a fourth-order differential operator at every sample, and a third matrix. We show that the Richardson extrapolation of two SDMD-1 half steps (SDMD-R) is second-order accurate with the data, the matrices, and the regularity of SDMD-1. One error bound covers exact and empirical Galerkin matrices. It consists of the Galerkin error of the dictionary, which is common to all schemes, a time-stepping term, and a data term of order $m^{-1/2}$ in the sample size $m$. The time-stepping term is $O(\dt^2)$ for SDMD-R and $O(Θ_N\dt+\dt^2)$ for SDMD-2, where $Θ_N$ is the norm of the second-order Galerkin residual $\Proj_N\cA(I-\Proj_N)\cA|_{\cV_N}$. The first-order term is attained and, for self-adjoint generators, vanishes only for generator-invariant dictionaries. For reversible periodic diffusions and trigonometric dictionaries with cutoff $K$, the step restriction $\dt\lesssim K^{-2}$ makes all three schemes contractions, and the error against the Koopman semigroup on $H^\ell$ observables is $O(K^{-(\ell-2)}+\dt^p)$ plus a sampling term of order $K^{d+2}m^{-1/2}$ in dimension $d$, with $p=1$ for SDMD-1 and $p=2$ for SDMD-R and SDMD-2. Numerical experiments confirm that SDMD-R matches or improves on the accuracy of SDMD-2 at the cost of SDMD-1.

title: Crop Mapping Evaluation under Sampling Bias
abstract: Government agencies use crop maps to estimate production, monitor food security, and set agricultural policy. These crop maps are usually validated against field labels, but these labels are rarely a random sample of the area the map covers. Field teams tend to label parcels near roads and skip ones that are small or hard to reach, so performance measured on held-out labels mainly describes the places they visited. We call the difference between this reported performance and performance over the whole mapped region the deployment performance gap. To estimate performance over the whole region, we use a weighted form of prediction-powered inference (PPI). The classifier's predictions on unlabeled points across the region give a first estimate, and its errors on the labeled points correct that estimate, with more weight on labels from under-sampled conditions. We test this in five European regions where crop registers label every declared parcel, so the true performance is known. Simulating six documented collection practices there produces gaps of up to 0.20 macro-F1. On the collection rule that creates the largest gap in each region, 5 km block cross-validation still overestimates macro-F1 by as much as 0.18, while PPI with weights estimated from satellite embeddings reduces the largest error across regions to 0.07. Importance-weighted cross-validation with the same weights does almost as well, so most of the improvement comes from the weights themselves. We also apply the method to three Kenyan datasets that have no region-wide reference labels. For a roadside dataset collected with helmet-mounted cameras, the estimated macro-F1 falls from 0.93 under random cross-validation to 0.61, although the correction relies on a small number of heavily weighted labels. Our code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/pappi.

title: BridgeDock: Taming Generative Co-Folding Prior for Molecular Docking with Diffusion Bridge
abstract: Molecular docking aims to predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex; in the conventional structure-based setting, it is conditioned on an input protein structure and ligand, often starting from an apo receptor in flexible docking or a holo receptor in rigid docking. Recent co-folding models exemplified by AlphaFold 3 achieve strong accuracy in protein-ligand complex prediction, but they typically generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and therefore do not directly use apo structures as structural priors in docking, leading to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings. We present BridgeDock, a framework that adapts pretrained co-folding backbones to flexible docking by modeling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, allowing generation from the initial protein-ligand state rather than from Gaussian noise. To make this bridge formulation compatible with pretrained denoisers, we introduce an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model. Experiments on standard flexible docking benchmarks show that BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines. Moreover, BridgeDock is computationally efficient at inference time and remains effective even with very few denoising steps.

title: Steer, Don't Tell: Breaking Reasoning Plateaus with Reachability-Aligned Self-Distillation
abstract: Post training for large reasoning models remains insufficient on challenging problems, whose correct trajectories are hard to sample. Though prior works address this difficulty by integrating supervised fine tuning on expert trajectories with reinforcement learning, such external experts are not always available. Existing self improvement methods instead use reference solutions to create a privileged self-teacher. Yet privileged teacher correctness does not imply student reachability. Solution conditioning shifts the teacher distribution toward actions unlikely under the unprivileged student, producing seemingly "correct" trajectories that are unreachable or even mal-formed learning targets. Accordingly, we identify reachability alignment as the key to self constructed supervision and propose Self-Steered Reasoner (SSR). SSR realizes this principle through student support projection, which transforms the privileged teacher distribution into a directional signal only over reasoning actions locally reachable under the unguided student. Verification then retains correct trajectories sampled from this reachable space. To further boost the sampling efficiency, an iterative refinement framework is adopted, using diagnostic guidance based on current trajectories. On problems with pass@64 = 0 even after extensive RL, SSR recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6% without parameter updates. Fine tuning on these trajectories followed by resumed reinforcement learning improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26. These results show that privileged guidance becomes effective self-improvement data when aligned with the reasoning actions the student can reach.

title: Private Uniform Language Generation
abstract: We study uniform language generation under approximate differential privacy. Given a uniformly bounded number of distinct examples from an unknown target language, a generator must produce infinitely many new examples from that language with probability one while protecting the privacy of its input. We introduce a new combinatorial dimension termed the nested branching dimension and prove that a language class is privately uniformly generatable if and only if both its closure dimension and nested branching dimension are finite. Previous work characterizes non-private uniform generation by the finiteness of the closure dimension alone. Our results therefore identify an additional combinatorial obstruction imposed by privacy.

title: Charge-Order pattern in $κ$-BEDT-TTF salts: A model independent, selection rule approach
abstract: A well known vibrational selection rule is invoked to determine the charge order (CO) pattern displayed by the most interesting members of the widely studied class of $κ$-BEDT-TTF salts and their molecular analogues. The selection rule indicates that an easily identifiable Raman band should be present if intra-dimer charge disproportionation occurs, constituting a sort of model independent ``litmus test''. The absence of such a band in the available Raman spectra of $κ$-BEDT-TTF salts exhibiting static of fluctuating CO, strongly suggests that the CO pattern involves inter-dimer CO, in contrast with the universally accepted intra-dimer disprortionation. This paper therefore poses a challenge for the theoretical modeling of the concerned salts: either the lack of the Raman band sensitive to intra-dimer CO pattern is explained, or the modeling of the multivariate, unique physical properties of these $κ$-phase salts (spin frustration, electronic ferroelectricity etc.) has to start from the perspective of a different ground state.

title: A result of continuous stability for generalized persistence diagrams
abstract: We study persistence modules obtained from the $A$-fundamental groupoids of finite graphs. Moreover, we verify the categorical properties needed to form generalized persistence diagrams, and describe a quotient that identifies equivalent groupoids. A normalized linear presheaf construction places these modules in an essentially small abelian category, where Patel's Continuity Theorem gives a $1$-Lipschitz estimate in erosion distance. Explicit graph filtrations illustrate the groupoid-valued construction, and so we suggest a new approach to interpret persistence diagrams and large data sets in topological data analysis, based on recent works of A-homotopy theory of the last years.

title: A Discrete-Time Variational Objective for Degenerate Diffusion and Equivalence to Flow Matching
abstract: Diffusion models and more recently Flow models have widespread application. In this work we consider degenerate Diffusion models in which the per-step generator is deterministic. We construct a modified variational framework and show a formal equivalence between Flow models and Degenerate Diffusion models. For our discrete-time variational objective we show that the optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of an infinite number of generator steps. Our work therefore provides a unified perspective, showing that discrete-time implementations of flow matching and the discrete-time Degenerate Diffusion model can be considered within the same simple variational framework, removing the need for the continuous-time machinery normally used to justify flow matching models.

title: Joint Transmit Power and Reflection Coefficient Optimization for Underlay Cognitive Radio Ambient Backscatter Communication
abstract: The integration of cognitive radio (CR) technology with backscatter communication offers a promising solution for developing spectrum-efficient and low-power wireless networks. In this paper, we investigate the performance of an underlay cognitive radio ambient backscatter communication (CR-AmBC) system operating under primary network (PN) interference constraints. The objective is to maximize the performance of the CR-AmBC system while protecting the PN from interference. Differing from prior work, our formulation jointly accounts for: (i) interference from the PN on the CR receivers, (ii) interference from the backscatter device (BD) on the PN receiver, and (iii) imperfect successive interference cancellation (i-SIC) at the secondary destination. We propose a joint transmit power and reflection coefficient optimization framework that incorporates the minimum data rate requirements, the PN interference constraint, and i-SIC for decoding the BD signal. The nonconvex problem is decomposed into two subproblems solved via alternating optimization: (a) a closed-form expression for the feasible transmit power given a fixed reflection coefficient, and (b) an efficient one-dimensional search for the reflection coefficient. We prove that the power update is optimal, reducing the joint problem to a one-dimensional search, with monotone convergence and $\mathcal{O}(KN_β)$ complexity for $K$ iterations and $N_β$ search points. We present a comprehensive simulation-based performance evaluation and the results demonstrate that the proposed joint transmission power and reflection coefficient optimization provides an effective strategy to maximize the performance of the CR-AmBC system without violating the PN protection constraints.

title: EduExplain: A Benchmark for Explanation-Set Retrieval and Storyboard Construction in Educational Explanation
abstract: Generating an educational explanation for a learner's query is not a single retrieval step but a pipeline: a system must first retrieve a compact set of complementary resources--passages, figures, examples, activities--that jointly support an explanation, then structure that set into an ordered, timed, role-assigned plan before rendering it as a lesson or video. Existing retrieval benchmarks evaluate neither stage at the level these applications require: they score individual documents rather than explanation sets, and provide no ground truth for how a set should be organised into an explanation. We present EduExplain, a benchmark providing human-validated ground truth for both stages. Built from secondary-level science textbooks, it comprises 6,921 typed, multimodal resources and 2,123 concepts, and pairs each of 321 learner-oriented queries with one or more human-validated explanation sets (retrieval ground truth) and 741 reference storyboards (structuring ground truth). The benchmark exposes characteristics absent from prior datasets: heterogeneous multimodal retrieval units, multiple valid explanation sets per query, and plans whose quality depends on pedagogical role composition, grounding, and timing rather than relevance alone. We describe an LLM-assisted, human-validated construction pipeline, report inter-annotator agreement for both layers, and establish baselines for each stage--lexical, dense, multimodal, and cross-encoder retrieval paired with four selection strategies, and free-form and fixed-template storyboard construction. Our results show that first-stage retrieval quality dominates retrieval-stage performance, that off-the-shelf diversity-based selection underperforms simple top-ranked selection, and that unconstrained and rigidly templated structuring both fall short of the reference plans. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/data-iitd/eduexplain.

title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization
abstract: Topology optimization has become an indispensable design tool in the aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering industries. Yet bringing a new problem from its description to an optimized result remains slow, expert-dependent, and unreliable: the workflow spans many manually connected stages, each new problem requires solver code to be written and debugged manually, and such code often fails or yields incorrect results. We present Agent4FreeFem, a pipeline driven by a large language model that turns a natural-language problem description into a set of verified optimization results without manual solver-code development or debugging. The pipeline keeps the problem definition unmodified, localizes errors using independent sources of evidence, and completes constrained repairs automatically, thereby providing efficient end-to-end automation, autonomous execution, and verifiable results. We evaluated Agent4FreeFem on a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems. Every case passed runtime verification and finished within the repair budget of each stage.

title: Training-free Conditional Object Composition for Multi-object Image Generation with Diffusion Models
abstract: Multi-object image generation in text-to-image diffusion models remains challenging, as existing approaches struggle to reliably generate all objects specified in a prompt. Compositional approaches that generate objects independently often fail to capture the interactions among them, whereas joint generation methods tend to suffer from inter-object interference. In this work, we propose a training-free framework, termed conditional object composition, that relaxes joint generation methods by taking one step back toward compositional approaches. Our framework decomposes the generation of $N$ objects into two stages: it first generates a subset of $N-1$ objects and then composes the remaining object conditioned on the generated content. To enable effective composition, we adopt an inpainting-based formulation with layout guidance to preserve existing regions and encourage spatially coherent placement. To address the challenge of selecting which objects to generate separately, we introduce an attention-based scoring mechanism based on cross-attention maps and further explore the use of off-the-shelf object detectors. We evaluate our method on multi-object image generation using the widely adopted MS COCO dataset. Experimental results show that our approach achieves competitive or improved performance compared to existing methods, particularly as the number of objects increases. Further studies highlight the importance of the proposed design choices. The source code is available at https://github.com/ShampooWang/condComp_imageGen/tree/main

title: Semi-classical analysis of noise squeezing in Kerr microresonators
abstract: Kerr microresonators are integrated nonlinear devices widely used to generate classical optical frequency combs and nonclassical states of light. In particular, they provide a promising platform for squeezed light sources, which are important elements of emerging quantum sensing, communication, and computing technologies. Designing such sources requires numerical tools that efficiently incorporate realistic device physics and noise processes. Here, we show that established semi-classical frameworks based on the Lugiato-Lefever equation and the Ikeda map, instrumental in the development of classical light sources, can also predict the quadrature-noise properties of squeezed light when vacuum fluctuations are properly included. We consider three canonical configurations producing two-mode quadrature squeezing, single-mode quadrature squeezing, and intensity difference squeezing. In each case, the semi-classical simulations produce quadrature variances and noise spectra in close agreement with the quantum theoretical predictions. These frameworks therefore provide practical tools for designing squeezed light sources, with the capability to incorporate additional noise mechanisms, nonlinear effects, and complex resonator arrangements. More fundamentally, our results show that key experimental signatures of squeezing can be modeled as phase-sensitive amplification of properly normalized vacuum fluctuations within stochastic semi-classical field equations. This observation helps distinguish squeezing properties accessible through semi-classical field evolution from those intrinsically requiring a full quantum description.

title: Streaming Virtual Metrology via Lightweight Adaptation under Temporal Distribution Shifts
abstract: Virtual metrology (VM) aims to estimate costly or delayed metrology variables from heterogeneous sensor signals and in-line measurements, and it acts as a critical component of semiconductor manufacturing. While recent data-driven models have improved VM accuracy, most are trained in batch settings and assume stationary data distributions. In practice, however, production environments evolve continuously due to equipment degradation, process adjustments, and maintenance events, making conventional batch-trained VM models difficult to maintain under temporal distribution shifts. In this work, we propose GRAPE (Global Regression with Adaptive Prediction Enhancement), a practical online learning framework for VM in evolving wafer-processing environments. GRAPE integrates a stable global predictor based on interpretable representations with two lightweight streaming adapters that correct feature-level and environment-level shifts through online updates. Experiments on two real-world semiconductor manufacturing datasets, including chronologically held-out blind-test streams, show that GRAPE improves robustness and generalization under real temporal drift compared with both conventional batch-learning methods and existing online learning baselines.

title: AI Data Analysis: A New Approach - Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis
abstract: AI data analysis today is three fragmented worlds: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute; BI aggregates precisely but is stateless; ML processes large-scale data on a stateful kernel but lacks semantics. This paper proposes a combination mechanism, named Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, that fills a still-open gap - the multi-engine joint context: the data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis, where the LLM serves only as the semantic, reasoning, and orchestration layer (not computation) and connects four engines through the 1M context window - Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases, Cypher over graph databases - yielding two multiplications, "semantics and precise computation" and "relational and graph", under enterprise-grade governance. The novelty is a four-dimensional coordinate system: horizontal (engine kinds), vertical (state flow - the watershed), spatial (business generalization), temporal (iterative convergence); a deterministic grounding method (one-shot injection of schema.json + notes.md, M+S) carries the spatial and temporal dimensions. Empirically, all four dimensions are substantiated: horizontally, four engines are quantified - SQL, Cypher (96.5% on CypherBench movie), ML in Python and R (TabReD weather); vertically, state flows across engines and grounding is reused across kernels; spatially, SQL generalizes across three business databases - AdventureWorks 91.3%, financial 95.3%, formula_1 94.6% (average), about 20-23 points above single-shot SOTA 74.45%; temporally, accuracy converges monotonically as notes accumulate. The core invariant - the separation of semantics from computation plus a cross-data-domain persistent context - does not expire as LLMs and agents evolve or engine forms change.

title: Quantum Black Holes in Non-Linear Electrodynamics
abstract: Techniques of AdS/CFT correspondence and braneworld holography have proven to be a useful tool for solving the problem of semi-classical gravity where quantum matter provides the back-reaction to classical spacetime geometry. In this paper, we apply this approach to Einstein gravity coupled to RegMax nonlinear electrodynamics and construct novel type of charged quantum black holes. We then discuss their thermodynamics and horizon structure.

title: Conjectures of Bernstein and Erdős for weighted Lagrange interpolation with Hermite weight
abstract: The classical Bernstein and Erdős Conjectures for algebraic Lagrange interpolation on a finite interval were settled in two consecutive papers by Kilgore and by de Boor and Pinkus in 1978. Extending these results to weighted interpolation on unbounded intervals has proved to be more difficult. In a previous work, we established the Bernstein and Erd\H os Conjectures, together with the ``modified'' de Boor--Pinkus intertwining theorem, for weighted Lagrange interpolation on the half-line with exponential weights. Here we continue this line of research by considering the Hermite weight on the whole real line. Our main result is the Hermite-weighted analogue of the Bernstein and Erdős conjectures together with the appropriate version of the de Boor--Pinkus intertwining theorem. A key ingredient in the classical proofs is the nonsingularity of certain derivative matrices associated with the local maxima of the Lebesgue function. This property already breaks down in the exponentially weighted setting, although the resulting difficulties can still be resolved. In the Hermite-weighted setting, however, the situation becomes more intricate, requiring a substantial refinement of the previous approach.

title: UniCaMo: Unified Camera and Motion Control for Video Diffusion Models
abstract: We present \textbf{UniCaMo}, an unified framework for joint control of camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion models. Given a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory, UniCaMo constructs motion-consistent input noise that directly encodes the desired motion. Our 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a simple and effective motion prior without requiring reconstruction of unseen scene geometry. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications or dedicated control modules and can be adapted using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with low training data volume. Experiments on standard controllable video generation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality with minimal inference overhead.

title: $\ell_{\infty}$ norm SVP in $\widetilde{O}(3^n)$
abstract: We give a classical randomized algorithm for the Shortest Vector Problem in the infinity norm in $\widetilde O(3^n)$ time and space, improving the previous bound of $2^{2.443n+o(n)}$. We adapt Gaussian difference dynamics to the infinity norm by repeatedly taking differences of vectors from two lists, producing lists in successively smaller cubes. The key is to restrict the midpoint of each pair to a fixed inner cube, so that every allowed difference has the same region of possible midpoints. Using random lattice translates, this rule preserves equal expected counts at each point of the smaller cube. We analyze the dependencies created by repeated differencing through the counting moments of Gaussian difference dynamics, together with a weighted packing bound for cubes. Finally, two searches based on coordinate comparisons generate the intermediate lists and recover a shortest lattice vector within the claimed time bound.

title: Biunital Lie Semiheaps and Lie Triple Systems
abstract: We examine the differential geometry of Lie semiheaps that admit biunital elements. Open Ol'shanskii semigroups, which appear widely across causal geometry and harmonic analysis, provide a large class of examples. It is shown that the subset of biunits is a smoothly embedded Lie subheap. Moreover, there is a canonical Lie triple algebroid associated with any proper biunital Lie semiheap. That is, there is a vector bundle over the manifold of biunits that comes equipped with a ternary bracket that satisfies the axioms of a Lie triple system together with a compatible `higher' anchor map. Although every Lie triple algebroid associated with a proper biunital Lie semiheap is trivialisable, it is not canonically so, unlike the case of the tangent bundle of a Lie group. As concrete examples, we examine the Lie semiheap of real $n\times n$ matrices, and the conformal causal Lie semiheap associated with the Lie group $\mathrm{SU}(2,2)$, which is a double cover of the conformal group of Minkowski spacetime, and the future-directed light cone.

title: Stable compatibility for model categories
abstract: By introducing the notion of stable compatibility, we provide a framework in the model category theory which addresses the existence of a stable model structure on the category of modules over a monad. Exact version of such monads have been studied in the setting of triangulated categories, separately as separable monads a la Balmer in tensor triangular geometry and non-separable monads a la Dell'Ambrogio and Sanders in stable homotopy theory. By introducing stable compatibility, we explore their properties together and produce a non-separable monad in Algebraic geometry and more.

title: Polyteam logics for quantum contextuality
abstract: We introduce logics of dependence and independence over polyteams (that is, databases with multiple relation schemes), in a similar way as in arXiv:1704.02158v3 [cs.LO]. On this basis, we develop a logical framework in which we can express (in formulas) relevant properties about the statistics of a repeated quantum experiment. In this framework, we formalize Bell's theorem, and the Kochen-Specker theorem as failure of logical entailments, as it was suggested in arXiv:2107.10817v3 [math.LO]. The key feature of polyteam logics in action here is their power to express both local and global properties, with respect to the set of possible measurements. The point of this is at least twofold. Firstly, as in arXiv:1102.0264v7 [quant-ph], it gives a high-level (information-theoretic) understanding of these physical phenomena, that is not intrinsic to the physical objects involved. Secondly, since logical entailment is often (partially) axiomatizable, this framework incites us to tackle the question of contextuality computationally. We also define semiring-weighted polyteams along with logics on them, and use them to recover the probabilistic versions of the contextuality theorems mentioned above.

title: VCoT-SQL: Enhancing Text-to-SQL Generation through Dual Chain-of-Thought Validation Training
abstract: Open-source LLMs provide a flexible alternative to closed-source models for Text-to-SQL but still struggle with complex queries. Finetuning with chain-of-thought (CoT) data improves reasoning, yet standard datasets lack CoT annotations, requiring synthetic generation. Existing synthesis methods only verify the final answer, allowing flawed reasoning steps to corrupt the training data. We propose VCoT-SQL, a framework that improves Text-to-SQL generation through intermediate-step validated CoT supervision and a dedicated SQL validator, which enables small open-source models to outperform frontier closed-source models. VCoT-SQL trains two complementary models on curated reasoning traces: an SQL generator using clause-level CoT templates where reasoning steps are verified via execution and schema alignment checks, and an SQL validator using diagnostic CoT templates to detect syntactic, semantic, and type level errors. We further design a hierarchical schema filtering pipeline that integrates and refines complementary retrieval strategies to distill relevant database elements. VCoT-SQL achieves 66.82% execution accuracy on challenging dataset BIRD dev and 86.8% on Spider test, improving the base 7B model by 7% on BIRD. Notably, our CoT synthesis relies on 7B models yet outperforms methods that use 72B-scale or even proprietary closed source teachers for data generation, demonstrating that rigorous step-level validation can be more effective than scaling up teacher model size. Our dataset and code are available at https://github.com/INTREBID/VCoT-SQL.

title: SAWs, trails, kites, patterns
abstract: A self-avoiding walk (SAW) on a vertex-transitive graph $G$ is a path that visits no vertex more than once; a trail is a path that traverses no edge more than once. The number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks (respectively, trails) starting at a given vertex has order $μ(G)^n$ (respectively, $μ_{\text{T}}(G)^n$), where $μ(G)$ is called the connective constant and $μ_{\text{T}}(G)$ is the trail constant. It is immediate that $μ=μ_{\text{T}}$ if $G$ either has degree $3$ or less, or is a tree. We prove a necessary and sufficient condition for the strict inequality $μ< μ_{\text{T}}$ if $G$ has degree $4$ or more and is not a tree, and in addition $G$ possesses a so-called height function. This condition is satisfied whenever the height function is transitive. The core of the proof is a pattern theorem for graphs possessing height functions, and this is achieved using an unpublished argument for ${\Bbb Z}^d$ by Hammersley, reported by Janse van Rensburg et al. (J. Stat. Phys. 85, 1996, 103--130). Some ancillary results are included concerning SAWs on the line graph of $G$.

title: Maxima of the Q-index: Forbidden an odd wheel
abstract: In 2013, Freitas, Nikiforov and Patuzzi (EJLA, 2013) proposed the problem of determining the maximum signless Laplacian spectral radius of an $n$-vertex $F$-free graph. Recently, Yuan, Zhai and Zhang (LAA, 2026) determined the maximum signless Laplacian spectral radius of graphs without wheels of sufficiently large order. In this paper, we consider the problem of forbidding a single wheel $W_{2k+1}=K_1\vee C_{2k}$. We show that, for every fixed integer $k\ge 3$ and sufficiently large $n$, the unique extremal graph maximizing the signless Laplacian spectral radius among all $n$-vertex $W_{2k+1}$-free graphs is $K_k\vee(K_2\cup(n-k-2)K_1)$.

title: Well begun is half done: the computation of Eulerian paths
abstract: We characterize the uniform computational strength of finding one-way Eulerian paths in countable graphs. For both directed and undirected graphs, this problem is Weihrauch-equivalent to $\mathsf{lim}\times\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{N}}'$, where $\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{N}}'$ is the jump of closed choice on the natural numbers. This refines the proof-theoretical strength of the existence of an Eulerian path given by the reverse mathematics framework. The $\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{N}}'$ component comes entirely from the difficulty of choosing a starting vertex: with a valid start prescribed, the problem is equivalent to $\mathsf{lim}$. We also study the problem $\mathsf{OrientEP}$ of orienting an undirected graph while preserving the existence of a one-way Eulerian path. We prove $\mathsf{lim}_2<_{\mathrm{W}}\mathsf{OrientEP}<_{\mathrm{W}}\mathsf{C}_{2}'\sqcap\mathsf{Sort}_2$ and $\mathsf{OrientEP}\not\le_{\mathrm{W}}\mathsf{C}_{\mathbb{N}}$.

title: ODC: Orthogonal Drift Correction for Improved Text-to-Image Semantic Alignment at Inference
abstract: Text-to-image models have achieved remarkable success in generating high-quality images from textual descriptions. However, they often struggle with "semantic drift," where the generated output fails to precisely align with complex or nuanced text prompts. While recent approaches have attempted to address semantic errors regarding attribute binding or object presence, there remains a gap for a more holistic method that addresses these issues by directly refining the text embeddings of the initial user prompt. In this work, we introduce Orthogonal Drift Correction (ODC), an inference-time guidance method designed to mitigate semantic drift without requiring model retraining or additional user inputs. ODC guides image generation through a two-stage process. In the first stage, it identifies the semantic drift by evaluating the initially generated image against the user prompt in a shared vision-language embedding space. It then isolates the component of this drift vector that is orthogonal to the prompt's direction and translates it back into text via a vocabulary-based surrogate mechanism. In the second stage, it produces refined text conditioning for a second generation pass by feeding both the initial text embedding and the re-embedded drift representation into an adaptive rank-reduced concept removal module. Our experiments demonstrate that ODC consistently improves prompt-image alignment, increasing CLIP scores by up to 5.4% over the baseline on the COALBench-300 and PartiPrompts benchmarks. Furthermore, on the T2I-CompBench complex subset, ODC improves the average 3-in-1 score by 4.5% over the competing methods. As a plug-and-play module, ODC offers a practical and efficient method for improving the reliability of text-to-image models. Code is available at https://github.com/kasrakamali/ODC.

title: Spectral Theory and Continuum Norm Resolvent Convergence of a One-Sided Discrete Dirac-Type Operator
abstract: We investigate a one-dimensional discrete Dirac-type operator $D_d$ acting on the Hilbert space $\big(\ell^2(\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})\big)^2$, obtained from the classical continuous free Dirac operator by replacing the spatial derivative with the one-sided backward difference operator $I - S_1$, where $S_1$ denotes the right shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})$. We establish the fundamental operator-theoretic and spectral properties of $D_d$: unlike symmetric or supersymmetric lattice discretizations, $D_d$ is bounded and non-normal for every non-zero rest mass $m > 0$, with self-commutator $[D_d, D_d^†] = -2mc^3(-Δ_{\mathrm{disc}})σ_2$, yet it is quadratically normal. We compute the exact operator norm, determine the exact spectral radius in two mass regimes, and show via Fourier--Laurent analysis that the spectrum $σ(D_d)$ is purely continuous and lies on a two-component algebraic curve in the complex plane undergoing a topological transition at $mc^2 = 2c$. Finally, introducing a lattice spacing $h > 0$ and embedding $\big(\ell^2(h\mathbb{Z};\mathbb{C})\big)^2$ isometrically into $\big(L^2(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{C})\big)^2$ via Whittaker--Shannon band-limited interpolation, we prove that the scaled non-normal discrete Dirac-type operator $D_{d,h}$ converges to the continuous self-adjoint Dirac operator $D$ in the norm resolvent sense at the optimal rate $\mathcal{O}(h)$ as $h \to 0^+$, without requiring frequency cutoffs.

title: A semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises theorem at rate $n^{-3/2}$ for frequency estimation
abstract: We consider Bayesian inference for the frequency of a periodic signal of unknown shape, observed in Gaussian white noise on the interval $[0,n]$. The information about the frequency grows like $n^3$, so the frequency can be estimated at rate $n^{-3/2}$, while the shape is an infinite-dimensional nuisance parameter. We endow the frequency and the shape with independent priors, the prior on the shape being a random series in the trigonometric basis. We give conditions on the priors under which the posterior for the signal contracts at a rate that, for suitable choices, is the minimax rate for Sobolev classes of smoothness at least one, up to a logarithmic factor and adaptively to the smoothness of the shape. If, moreover, the prior keeps the shape away from shapes with a shorter period, also the marginal posteriors for the frequency and the shape contract around the truth. Under further conditions, which hold for a Gaussian random series prior conditioned to keep the shape away from shapes with a shorter period, for every true shape with smallest period 1 and Sobolev smoothness larger than $3/2$, the marginal posterior for the frequency satisfies a semi-parametric Bernstein-von Mises theorem at rate $n^{-3/2}$, which we prove by moving the origin of time, a change that leaves the posterior unchanged when the prior on the shape is invariant under time shifts.

title: AdKnob: Ad Intensity Control and Labeling for LLM-Native Advertising
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-native advertising has emerged as a viable monetization channel as LLM service providers seek sustainable revenue streams. However, integrating native ads into LLM responses introduces two largely understudied challenges: (1) controlling ad intensity -- how prominently advertising content appears -- and (2) ad labeling -- identifying which segments of the generated text constitute advertising. We propose AdKnob, a framework jointly addressing both challenges. For ad intensity control, we introduce new ad control tokens without pretrained semantic associations and align the model via direct preference optimization to generate ads at each desired level. For ad labeling, we propose an attention rollout-based attribution mechanism that identifies ad segments by tracing their attribution to input ad-related tokens, requiring no additional inference cost. We further construct MI-KnobSet, the first multi-level ad intensity preference dataset for LLM-native ads. Experiments across six LLMs and human evaluations show that AdKnob achieves uniformly spaced ad intensities where baselines collapse to a narrow range, achieves the highest ad labeling accuracy while being over 500x faster than the strongest baseline, and is preferred over baselines by human evaluators up to 89.6% of the time.

title: Beyond Temporal Overlap: Consumer-Aware Evaluation of Sign-Language Segmentation across Three Corpora
abstract: Sign-language segmentation divides continuous signing into clips. In this study, the downstream consumer is a frozen recognizer that assigns one sign label to each predicted clip. Existing metrics instead compare predicted clips with manually annotated boundaries. They do not directly measure whether a clip preserves the visual evidence needed by the recognizer or whether the segmenter produces too many clips. We therefore ask whether overlap metrics and this consumer prefer the same segmenter. We evaluate 27 outputs from three segmentation architectures, three random seeds, and three corpora. Controlled boundary edits separate the effect of removing sign evidence from that of adding surrounding context. Overlap predicts recognition on average, but it does not always determine model choice. At the same intersection-over-union, different recognizers can prefer the shorter or the longer clip. The real outputs reveal two operating regimes. On DGS, overlap, recognition, and sequence error select the same model. On BSL, recognition-based selection recovers and recognizes more reference signs but increases word error rate (WER). Dicta-Sign shows the reverse trade-off: WER selection reduces in-vocabulary WER by 31.17 points but misses more recognizable signs. Segmenters should therefore be evaluated on four axes: temporal agreement, reference recovery, clip recognition, and sequence error, rather than on overlap alone.

title: Canonic hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium: Reassessing the role of cooperativity
abstract: Hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium is normally studied within the grand canonical ensemble, which assumes that each hemoglobin is immersed in a reservoir of unbound oxygen molecules of the plasma. We show that this assumption is incorrect inside the RBC (red blood cell or erythrocyte), where the hemoglobin concentration is larger than the concentration of unbound oxygen in plasma. We suggest a better model, where a single hemoglobin and a few oxygen molecules around it reach a canonical equilibrium at a fixed volume (determined from the RBC structure) and a fixed temperature. The basic models of hemoglobin-oxygen equilibrium -- Pauling's model and Monod-Wyman-Changeux model -- can be reformulated for this canonical situation. They predict cooperative interaction energies, which are significantly lower than predictions of the same models in the grand canonical ensemble. Larger cooperative energies, in particular those predicted by the grand canonical ensemble, lead to instabilities (cascade processes) in oxygen release within the canonical approach. Oxygen-binding fluctuations within this approach are sizably smaller than those in the grand canonical situation. These results suggest that the hopping diffusion of oxygen from one hemoglobin to another may play a role in oxygen diffusion within the RBC.

title: Identities for generalized Bernoulli numbers from a Lie model of the 2-disk
abstract: We define generalized Bernoulli numbers as appropriate coefficients of the Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff (BCH) product formula, extending the classical sequence of rational numbers to a 2-dimensional setting. We give an identity involving these numbers and the classical Bernoulli numbers which is equivalent to the existence of a particular complete differential graded Lie algebra modelling a cell decomposition of the 2-disk and based on the Lawrence--Sullivan model of the interval. From this identity we derive explicit quadratic relations. The existence of Lie models for the symmetries of the interval and the disk is related to certain properties of the BCH product and to some notable features of the classical Bernoulli numbers: the two choices for $B_1$, the vanishing of $B_n$ for odd $n\geq 3$, and the equality $B_4=B_8$.

title: ROSE: Deep Learning exchange-correlation functional from reduced density-matrix representations
abstract: We introduce ROSE, a deep-learning exchange--correlation energy functional built from the occupied-state density matrix. On GMTKN55 and on additional external benchmarks considered in this work, ROSE improves over modern neural network functionals trained under matched protocols and is on average more accurate than, or on par with, most hybrid and range-separated hybrid functionals considered here. On the experimental benchmarks considered here it has leading accuracy across hybrids, range separated hybrids, and neural functionals. These results motivate nonlocal density-matrix representations as a route to systematic improvement of learned XC functionals with low computational cost.

title: When are dividend barriers optimal? A distributional characterization in renewal risk models
abstract: We study the finite-horizon optimal dividend problem in a renewal risk model with unrestricted dividend payments, examining how claim-size distributions determine barrier optimality. Under general assumptions on a fixed interclaim-time distribution, we prove that exponential claims admit a globally optimal barrier for every positive safety loading, positive discount rate and finite horizon. Conversely, within the class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard, every nonexponential law admits one fixed premium--discount pair for which no barrier is globally optimal at any sufficiently long horizon. These results establish, within this distribution class, an equivalence between exponentially distributed claims and the existence of a globally optimal barrier for every parameter combination in the stated range. Numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims with the same mean and illustrate how the claim-size distribution changes the structure of dividend decisions.

title: Answer Correction with Verifiable Rewards: A Gemma-Family Study of Multi-View Driving QA
abstract: Multi-camera driving question answering provides a discrete test of vision-language models, but post-training gains can reflect changed selected answers or improved answer extraction. We investigate this distinction within the Gemma model family using archived, task-linked WaymoQA evaluations. A zero-shot diagnostic on 5,519 test questions spans effective-small, mixture-of-experts, unified, and dense checkpoints, with serving differences disclosed rather than interpreted as architecture effects. The strongest controlled evidence is a matched-harness Gemma-4-12B base/GRPO pair: accuracy rises from 73.78% to 75.43%, a gain of 1.65 percentage points with a scene-cluster bootstrap interval of [+0.84, +2.41]. There are 215 improvements and 124 regressions; 213 improvements start from an extractable but incorrect base answer, and only two recover previously unextractable responses. Crossing correctness with extraction state shows why correct noncompliant outputs cannot be counted as prediction errors. Category counts reveal a critical safety asymmetry: routine perception gains (+5.93 pp) mask a regression in safety-critical hazard prediction (-1.82 pp), demonstrating that unweighted outcome rewards can trade off rare edge cases for aggregate accuracy. Reward saturation describes sampled training dynamics rather than an architectural ceiling. A separate archived Gemma-31B thinking comparison yields no detected average improvement, with uncertainty that does not establish equivalence. These results support a modest answer-selection gain for the recorded tuning configuration and a reproducible diagnostic accounting, without attributing corrected labels to specific grounding mechanisms or claiming superiority over matched supervised tuning.

title: Dimensional dependence of critical phenomena in black hole interiors
abstract: We numerically investigate the interior dynamics of $D$ dimensional Reissner-Nordström (RN) black holes perturbed by a real scalar field. Strong perturbations destroy the null inner horizon and produce a spacelike singularity, whereas weaker perturbations preserve it with an areal radius that decreases as the perturbation amplitude increases. As the initial scalar field amplitude $A$ approaches its critical value $A^{*}$, the inner horizon radius decreases continuously to zero. Near criticality, this radius obeys the power law $r_{s}\propto|A-A^{*}|^γ$. In four dimensions, different initial scalar field profiles and initial RN black hole charges yield nearly identical critical exponents, $γ\simeq1/2$, supporting the universality of the scaling law. For $4\leq D\leq9$, the numerical results are well described by $γ\simeq1/(D-2)$. The corresponding scaling, $|A-A^{*}|\propto r_{s}^{D-2}$, indicates that the deviation of the initial parameter from its critical value is proportional to the area of the spherical cross section of the inner horizon.

title: On the nonvanishing of Floer lasagna modules
abstract: In this paper, we establish several nonvanishing results for Floer lasagna modules $\mathcal{FL}(W,K)$ for a smooth compact connected oriented $4$-manifold $W$ and a knot $K\subset \partial W$, via the evaluation maps to link Floer homology. We first establish a general criterion: if a certain Heegaard Floer cobordism map associated with a smooth $4$-manifold $W$ is nonzero, then $\mathcal{FL}(W,U)\neq 0$, where $U\subset \partial W$ is a local unknot. Applications include the nonvanishing of Floer lasagna modules for $\#^m\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}$ and for knot traces $X_n(K)$ when $K$ is slice and $n$ is a non-positive integer. In another direction, we show that for every nontrivial knot $K$ and every integer $n$, the Floer lasagna module $\mathcal{FL}(X_n(K),K_n)$ is nonzero, where $K_n\subset S_n^3(K)$ is the dual knot. Moreover, if $K$ is an L-space knot, then $\mathcal{FL}(X_n(K),K_n)$ is infinite-dimensional for all integers $n\ge \max\{2g(K),1\}$.

title: Ultraslow diffusion emerging from local symmetry breaking in quenched disorder
abstract: Many dynamical systems operate in disordered environments. In this Letter, we investigate how quenched randomness modifies particle diffusion. We show that, in finite-strength potential landscapes, low disorder densities can induce logarithmically ultraslow diffusion. The underlying mechanism originates from local symmetry breaking in particular potential configurations: Barrier-well structures form directional channels, causing particles to undergo hierarchical capture, escape, and recapture processes. A coarse-grained channel theory yields an approximate scaling prediction for the mean-square displacement. Counterintuitively, when the disorder density reaches the fully disordered limit, the system returns to normal diffusion, revealing a nontrivial, nonmonotonic relationship between disorder density and transport type. This mechanism is observed in both nonlinear maps and stochastic systems.

title: Coherence controls the visibility of frozen disorder in an open quantum chain
abstract: A Gaussian position distribution need not imply that frozen disorder is irrelevant. We study a resonant quantum chain where neighboring sites couple with opposite signs to auxiliary states that decay with frozen, random return probabilities. Lowering dephasing spreads the effect of each local return bias over more sites. We take dephasing to zero at a fixed, sufficiently weak disorder amplitude. On the scale of a coherent wave packet, the position distribution approaches the same Gaussian for almost every frozen sample. At larger distances and later times, it remains sample dependent and is described by diffusion in a random potential with Brownian spatial statistics. The covariance of bounded, direction-sensitive position readouts from independent trials in the same field distinguishes these regimes. Simulations resolve their separation at finite dephasing. Taking weak disorder before vanishing dephasing also reveals a different packet-scale response from a memoryless random-force model matched in clean diffusion and leading potential strength. The coherent response develops an integrable logarithmic peak near the initial site, where the reference response stays finite. It reflects the correlated duration and displacement of motion between jumps, together with the unfinished packet at measurement.

title: Fewer Tokens, More Answers: Verifiable-Reward Tuning of an Ornith-Style VLM for Multi-View Driving QA
abstract: Reasoning-enabled model derivatives must turn intermediate deliberation into a usable answer within a deployment budget. We study that transition in an Ornith checkpoint adapted to multi-camera driving question answering with verifiable rewards. Paired archived outputs show that, on a selected 400-question development screen with a 256-token cap, GRPO increases answer extraction from 78.25% to 90.25% and accuracy from 55.50% to 63.75%. Of 39 wrong-to-correct transitions, 33 begin with an unextractable base response. The base's 87 unextractable responses all reach the token cap. Checkpoint-verified reconstruction on those same questions gives a much smaller first-pass accuracy gain at 512 tokens: +0.75 percentage points, versus +8.25 at 256. A later answer-cued continuation is analyzed separately; it helps the base more and narrows the adapter difference. On the full 2,511-question development set, this recovery-enabled pipeline reduces mean generated tokens from 108.6 to 47.1, while the paired accuracy interval includes zero gain. We frame these findings as adaptation of answer delivery under finite budgets, with explicit selection and provenance limits. Ornith's self-scaffolding lineage and newer reasoning-enabled derivatives such as Bonsai motivate the problem, but our measured results concern Ornith alone and do not establish a shared architectural mechanism or cross-model transfer.

title: Efficient second-order physics-preserving schemes for incompressible flows with variable density and viscosity
abstract: This paper proposes a novel second-order prediction--filter--projection framework for incompressible flows with variable density and viscosity. In this framework, a constrained $L^2$-projection is enforced to unconditionally preserve the prescribed density bounds and discrete mass conservation, while a generalized-Laplacian reformulation combined with the D-CSAV approach is used to discretize the variable-viscosity momentum equation. In particular, a density-weighted second-order time filter is proposed, which eliminates the additional uniform-in-time bound restriction imposed on the time difference quotient of the discrete density in existing stability analyses. The resulting scheme is shown to satisfy an unconditional modified-energy dissipation law, without the viscosity-related restrictions imposed in earlier work. Then, an additional scalar auxiliary variable and its compatible temporal discretization are introduced to construct a variable-step prediction--filter--projection scheme. This scheme is also bound-preserving and mass-conserving, and satisfies an unconditional modified-energy dissipation law. Moreover, the modified energy is much closer to the ``original'' kinetic energy, differing from it only through the auxiliary-variable corrections. Based on the variable-step scheme, a reliable energy-based adaptive time-stepping strategy is developed. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, physics-preserving properties, and efficiency of the proposed schemes.

title: The Two-Point Inequality for $p>q$
abstract: For $1<q<p<\infty$ we study the $L^p\to L^q$ contractivity of the two-point operator $T_ω(a+bx)=a+ωbx$ with a complex parameter $ω$, extending the Weissler two-point condition, usually discussed in the range $1<p\le q<\infty$, to the reversed order of exponents. For $1<q<p<2$ we prove that the second-order necessary condition $|(p-2)-(q-2)ω^2|\le p-q|ω|^2$, obtained near $(a,b)=(1,0)$, is also sufficient; by duality the same description applies to $2<q<p<\infty$. The proof uses the method of characteristic flows. In addition, for $q\le2\le p$ the contractivity follows directly from $L^2$ contraction.

title: Power Concavity and Log-Concavity for Large-Parameter Robin 2-Hessian Problems
abstract: Let $Ω\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, be a bounded uniformly convex $C^{3,γ}$ domain, where $0<γ<1$. We study the limit as the positive Robin parameter $α\to\infty$. For the $2$-Hessian torsion problem, let $U$ be the admissible Dirichlet solution. For all sufficiently large $α$, we obtain a unique admissible Robin solution $u_α$ and establish the optimal-order estimate \[ \|u_α-U\|_{C^{2,γ}(\overlineΩ)} \le Cα^{-1}. \] Moreover, $-\sqrt{-u_α}$ has a uniform positive lower bound on its Hessian, and hence $\sqrt{-u_α}$ is strictly concave. For the normalized eigenvalue problem, let $(λ_D,φ_D)$ be the normalized negative admissible Dirichlet eigenpair, and assume $φ_D\in C^{2,γ}(\overlineΩ)$. For all sufficiently large $α$, there is a unique normalized negative admissible Robin eigenpair $(λ_α,φ_α)$, which satisfies \[ \|φ_α-φ_D\|_{C^{2,γ}(\overlineΩ)} +|λ_α-λ_D|\le Cα^{-1}. \] The Hessian of $-\log(-φ_α)$ also has a uniform positive lower bound. The main analytic tool is a uniform Hölder estimate for linear Robin problems, with an $α^{-1}$ gain for $C^{2,γ}$ boundary data. A normalized augmented inverse removes the scaling kernel in the eigenvalue problem. A Schur-complement argument combines the $C^2$ convergence with boundary geometry to prove convexity up to the boundary and anisotropic Hessian lower bounds at the scale ${\rm dist}(x,\partialΩ)+α^{-1}$. The convergence rate $O(α^{-1})$ for the Robin solution functions is optimal even in $C^0$, as follows from their boundary conditions.

title: A structure-preserving finite volume scheme for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with nondegenerate state-dependent mobility
abstract: We construct and analyze a fully discrete finite volume scheme for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with nondegenerate state-dependent mobility. The scheme combines a standard two-point flux approximation of diffusion, the L1 approximation of the Caputo derivative on a uniform time grid, and a semiconvex splitting of the potential, and it discretizes the inverse mobility by a secant average multiplying the entire L1 derivative. The key estimate is a lower bound for the accumulated pairing of this weighted L1 derivative with the solution increments in terms of the accumulated L1 quadratic form. Using this lower bound, we derive a discrete energy estimate and the time regularity required for compactness. For twice continuously differentiable semiconvex potentials satisfying sign conditions outside $(-1,1)$ and initial data in $H^1(Ω)$ taking values in $[-1,1]$, we prove existence of at least one fully discrete solution on every admissible finite volume mesh and every uniform time grid. Every such solution satisfies the maximum bound principle and a discrete energy bound relative to the initial energy, without a time-step restriction. In up to three space dimensions, under a mesh regularity condition with a constant independent of the mesh size, we prove that any sequence of fully discrete solutions has a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(Ω\times(0,T))$ to a weak solution of the continuous problem as the mesh size and time step tend to zero. As a consequence, we obtain existence of a weak solution in one and two space dimensions, and in three dimensions whenever such meshes exist.

title: Can Agentic AI Undermine Its Own Assurance Loop? Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance for Cognitive Network Digital Twins
abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Network Digital Twins (NDTs) are increasingly combined to form Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) that translate operational intents into network changes and support closed-loop management. However, a network change may achieve its intended objective while disrupting the monitoring or recovery mechanisms needed for subsequent decisions. For example, a service may be rerouted while its latency-monitoring traffic continues along the original path, producing measurements that no longer reflect the service's performance. We propose Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance (CLDA), an assurance mechanism that augments agentic AI-enabled NDTs with dependency-aware validation. In our framework, an agentic AI planner generates and refines network plans, while the NDT evaluates the projected network outcomes of these plans. CLDA extends this analysis using a Loop Dependency Graph (LDG) that connects service requirements to monitoring mechanisms, forwarding paths, failure domains, and recovery prerequisites. CLDA projects candidate actions onto these dependencies, checks intermediate states of multistep plans, and supports deterministic make-before-break repairs using temporary monitoring mechanisms. Unlike the Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner, CLDA uses explicit, deterministic rules for assurance decisions and repair. We evaluate CLDA through controlled reconfigurations, a 240-trial LLM-based planning campaign, and live network execution. A separate synthetic study examines deterministic assurance scalability across network models representing up to 1,024 routers.

title: Intent-Bound Authorization for Cryptocurrency Withdrawals Under Backend Compromise
abstract: Binance's preliminary account of its October 2026 attack raises a custody question that key protection alone cannot answer: how can a provider prevent unauthorized withdrawals when an attacker controls a service permitted to request signatures? We propose the Intent-Bound Withdrawal Authorization Protocol (IWAP). Before signing, independent enforcement checks customer intent, exact transaction effects, fresh workload evidence, and a committed single-use spending reservation. Administrative actions use a separate authorization path. We specify the protocol's trust assumptions and give conditional arguments for intent preservation, replay resistance, and a fixed-epoch exposure bound. A Python reference monitor authenticates synthetic records with Ed25519 and serializes reservations with SQLite. It rejects 1,200 negative requests, accepts 3,000 valid synthetic requests, and preserves a 100-unit budget under 64 concurrent attempts in each of 20 trials. When the intent authority is deliberately compromised, malicious requests pass, but the independent budget still limits admitted exposure. The study evaluates a normalized policy model, not Binance's infrastructure or a deployed custody platform. Its contribution is an explicit authorization boundary and reproducible tests of that boundary.

title: Three-Dimensional FDTD Simulation of Superconducting Terahertz Emitters Using an Effective Medium Approximation
abstract: Compact and tunable terahertz (THz) sources with controllable polarization are sought for high-speed links, spectroscopy, and imaging. In superconducting THz emitters based on a cuprate Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+δ}$, which have the potential to satisfy such properties, modeling often relies on heavy nonlinear solvers or empirical isotropic dielectrics, obscuring anisotropy, plasma response, and bias dependence.
