We derive an anisotropic, dispersive effective permittivity from the Lawrence-Doniach model for a layered superconductor and implement it as a user-defined material in a commercial Finite-difference Time-domain (FDTD) solver. Simulations of two device geometries reproduce linearly polarized emission from a rectangular mesa and low-axial-ratio (near-circular) emission from a truncated square mesa. This CAD-ready workflow links superconducting theory to device design, enabling rapid searches and parameter optimization for next-generation THz sources.

title: Robust Data-Driven Output Feedback for Systems With Unknown Input Delays
abstract: In a history-feedback realization, an input delay increases memory without increasing the number of unknown physical coefficients. We use this structure to design output-feedback controllers for discrete-time systems with one input, one output, and known undelayed order, using noisy input-output data. For a known delay, we derive a necessary and sufficient linear matrix inequality for common-quadratic stabilization of all models consistent with the data. Optimizing its equation-error bound gives a robustness margin for the measured record. For an unknown constant delay in a known interval, we characterize noiseless delay ambiguity and give a sufficient condition for one controller to stabilize all models for every delay consistent with the error bound. Under stated excitation and nondegeneracy assumptions, this procedure is feasible for all sufficiently small equation errors. Numerical examples compare robustness at equal controller memory and show that certified stabilization can succeed while distinct delay models remain compatible with the same data.

title: Power-optimal allocation in multi-arm cluster randomized trials
abstract: This paper discusses a power-based framework for optimal allocation in multi-arm cluster randomized trials with continuous or binary outcomes, allowing cluster sizes and within-cluster correlations to differ across treatment groups. We consider optimal cluster allocation with prespecified cluster sizes as well as joint optimization of cluster allocations and sizes. Using generalized estimating equations to account for correlated outcomes and a quasi-score test to assess treatment homogeneity, we derive locally optimal designs, which depend on specified parameter values. Since locally optimal designs can be highly sensitive to changes in the parameter values, we also propose maximin designs, which maximize the minimum power over a prescribed parameter space and provide robust allocations under parameter uncertainty. We analytically characterize the maximin designs and the least favorable configurations of treatment means and provide procedures for determining the sample size required to attain a target power. Applications to the WASH Benefits Bangladesh and SCORE trials illustrate gains in calculated power and reductions in the required sample size relative to the original trial designs.

title: Running a 20B Video Diffusion Transformer on Consumer Hardware: A Deployment and Measurement Report for MiniMax H3 on Apple Silicon
abstract: We report the end-to-end deployment and measurement of MiniMax H3, a 20.38-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer (DiT) - the count measured from the safetensors headers of the Q8 checkpoint as deployed locally (Section 3.2) - running entirely on consumer Apple Silicon hardware: an Apple Mac mini with M5 Pro chip and 64 GiB of unified memory. Using the official bf16-to-Q8 (8-bit, group size 64) quantization path executed locally on the machine, we produced a working text-to-video pipeline with no cloud dependency. We document the full deployment procedure, including two non-trivial blockers and their fixes, and report measured figures for build time, peak memory, and per-clip render latency across four resolution tiers (Draft 384x640 through Native 768x1344). A 15.08-second 576x1024 clip rendered in 4838.49 seconds with a measured MLX peak of 27.467 GiB. We further operated the system as an unattended production pipeline, completing 17 clips in 26.49 hours with zero render failures. A blind human review of the 17 production clips (generation prompts withheld) averaged 3.12, 3.18, and 2.94 out of 5 for structural integrity, temporal consistency, and visible artifacts. All figures in this report are our own measurements except where explicitly labeled as third-party data. This is a systems/empirical report; we make no claim of model innovation.

title: Metric Correspondences and Low-Rank Deformations for Conformal and \(m\)-Modified Conformal Vector Fields
abstract: We fix a smooth vector field and a positive parameter $m$, and compare the nondegenerate metrics for which the field is conformal or $m$-modified conformal with the same prescribed smooth factor. Metrics of arbitrary signature are allowed. Passing to inverse metrics gives a linear transport equation and an explicit correspondence on the exact nondegeneracy domains. At a regular point, transverse initial data yield a signature-preserving correspondence of metric germs. For a nowhere-zero field and a Killing background in dimension at least three, every metric satisfying the modified conformal equation and differing from the background by a tensor of rank at most one has factor zero; its inverse-metric difference is $rX\otimes X$ for a unique smooth function $r$. Under a complete flow, such global deformations exist precisely when the field is null for the background and admits a smooth function $τ$ with $Xτ=1$. An auxiliary field satisfying $[X,Z]=X$ gives a second correspondence under orthogonality assumptions. Finally, for a nowhere-zero complete field, a Killing metric and a zero-factor modified conformal metric have inverse-metric difference of rank at least two whenever that rank is constant. In the rank-two case, the pair determines a unique auxiliary field. Examples distinguish the roles of dimension, completeness, constant rank, the zero-factor condition, and orthogonality.

title: Rapid Mobilisation and Organisational Fragmentation: The Telegram Ecosystem during the 2026 Italian Student Protests
abstract: In October 2026, social media pages named \emph{Italia in Piazza} used several platforms to call for demonstrations in Italian cities. The mobilisation brought participants into a rapidly assembled network of Telegram chats, but disagreements over its direction and protest tactics became visible after the first demonstrations. We study how this online environment formed and subsequently fragmented. We first constructed an ecosystem of chats connected to the protests, then compared it with established conspiracy, radical-left and radical-right ecosystems. Few links or observed participants connected the protest ecosystem to these communities. Its messages nevertheless expressed a broader mix of political positions, brought together by a shared focus on the protests. Within this ecosystem, geographically distributed discussions were linked through a small administrative core and connections to TikTok and Instagram. The mobilisation subsequently developed into two distinct spaces: Movimento 17 Ottobre and a re-formed Italia in Piazza chat. The former contained more content classified as promoting violence or hate, while the latter retained part of the original staff and advocated organised, non-violent protest. Their observed populations showed little overlap. After the original chats became inaccessible, discussion was rebuilt on Telegram, while Movimento 17 Ottobre encouraged migration to Signal. The case connects the fragmentation of a shared mobilisation with questions of deplatforming and community governance: the loss of discussion spaces need not end collective activity, while the environments that emerge can develop markedly different norms around protest and violence.

title: Instability of streaky high-supersonic boundary layers over cooled walls
abstract: We investigate the instability of streaks induced by free-stream vortical disturbances in cooled-wall high-supersonic boundary layers. Distinct types of instability modes are identified: modified Mack second modes, a newly discovered varicose secondary-instability mode and sinuous or varicose secondary-instability modes akin to those in incompressible boundary layers. Unique characteristics of the new secondary-instability mode are that its eigenfunctions concentrate in high-speed valley regions near the wall and feature intense temperature fluctuations at the wall. The streaks in high-supersonic boundary layers destabilise the three-dimensional secondary-instability modes, but suppress the growth of the modified Mack second modes, both radiating and non-radiating. The suppression of radiating modes amounts to a reduction of the two-dimensional noise they emit. Numerical results indicate that, unlike streaks in adiabatic-wall boundary layers, whose instability concentrates in low-speed peak regions away from the wall, the secondary instability of streaks in cooled-wall high-supersonic boundary layers occurs both in low-speed peak regions and in high-speed valley regions.

title: Service-Area Robust NOMA for Pinching Antennas Systems
abstract: Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) enable near-field beam focusing using radiating points along a dielectric waveguide, but coherent spherical-wave superposition makes their channels sensitive to small user displacements. This sensitivity is critical for power-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), where successive interference cancellation (SIC) requires the weak-user layer to remain decodable at the strong user. We develop spatially robust PASS-NOMA designs that optimize antenna placement and power splitting over bounded service areas (SAs), with a preset decoding order and explicit SIC-feasibility constraints. We propose a worst-case design for quasi-static users and an ergodic design for codewords spanning representative SA positions, and characterize their achievable rate regions. Numerical results show that, despite SIC requiring weak-user decoding in both SAs, NOMA outperforms orthogonal multiple access (OMA) with a shared placement under both robustness models except when the strong user is served at low rate. In the ergodic regime, this advantage can persist even against OMA with per-user antenna reconfiguration.

title: Toward Counterfactual Learning for Selective Re-Examination in Agentic Visual Search
abstract: Visual search over high-resolution images requires a vision-language model (VLM) not only to determine where to inspect, but also whether another observation is warranted before committing to an answer. Existing prompting, demonstrations, and outcome-based reinforcement learning can encourage re-examination, yet do not directly supervise whether it is beneficial at a particular search state. We introduce ReSee, a benchmark of re-examination decisions comprising 3,227 visual-search trajectories and 8,827 explicit commit-or-re-examine decisions, with counterfactual adjudication that distinguishes states where additional inspection is warranted from those where commitment is preferable. Building on this formulation, we propose CARE (Counterfactual Advantage for Re-Examination), a decision-level reinforcement learning method that compares paired continuations under commit and re-examine verdicts from the same search state. Their cost-aware return difference estimates the counterfactual value of an additional observation and is assigned only to the corresponding verdict tokens, providing localized credit for whether search should continue. Experiments expose limited re-examination selectivity in existing VLMs and show that CARE significantly improves accuracy and decision selectivity over GRPO across two backbones, with higher accuracy and fewer visual requests on six unseen OOD benchmarks.

title: What Is the Dynamic Capacitance of a Memristor?
abstract: Impedance spectroscopy of memristors, nanofluidic channels and halide perovskite devices often shows a low-frequency capacitance that is orders of magnitude larger than any plausible stored charge, or that becomes negative and appears together with an inductive loop. We distinguish two kinds of capacitance that enter the impedance in the same way: a storage capacitance, the derivative of a stored charge, and a dynamic capacitance, produced by the delayed response of a conduction current. Using the conductance-activated quasi-linear memristor (CALM) model, and a general memristor in which an internal state controls the conductance, we show that the dynamic capacitance is the time integral of the transient differential conductance after a small voltage step, measured from its final value. For a single relaxing state it is the product of a relaxing conductance and a relaxation time, with a negative sign. It vanishes at zero bias, and its sign is set by whether the stationary conductance increases or decreases with the magnitude of the voltage. Potentiation gives a negative capacitance and a chemical inductor, and depression gives a positive capacitance that is easily mistaken for stored charge. The analysis gives an explicit formulation of the time-domain criterion for negative capacitance of Jonscher and Ershov. In conical multipore nanofluidic membranes, the dynamic capacitance obtained from impedance and from voltage pulses shows the same sign change at zero bias and reaches values several hundred times larger than the membrane capacitance. The same picture accounts for the capacitive and inductive regimes of halide perovskite memristors.

title: Twisting-free converse theorems for $Γ_0(32)$ and $Γ_0(36)$
abstract: We prove twisting-free converse theorems for $Γ_0(32)$ and $Γ_0(36)$ under the setting of Conrey--Farmer, namely assuming a single functional equation and a suitable Euler product, with particular shapes at ramified primes. The proofs make substantial use of the ramified primes, with methods somewhat different from the existing ones in the literature.

title: Study of pion condensate in nuclear matter based on a Parity Doublet Model
abstract: In this work, we investigate the possibility of pion condensate in isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter within a parity doublet model at zero temperature, treating the baryon and isospin chemical potentials as independent variables. We include the $σ$, $π$, $ω$, and $ρ$ mesons and determine their mean fields from the gap equations. We introduce a novel subtraction scheme to calculate the thermodynamic potential in the no-sea approximation, in which the effective isospin chemical potential is retained in the subtraction term to remove the divergence. We find that the presence of baryons suppresses pion condensate, and that transition to the pion condensation phase is of second order. We further find that the phase boundary depends systematically on the chiral-invariant mass $m_0$: a smaller $m_0$ requires a larger critical isospin chemical potential for pion condensate. The presence of pion condensate also shifts the nuclear Liquid-Gas phase boundary toward larger baryon chemical potentials. Finally we study the existence of pion condensation phase in neutron star matter and find that pion condensate is unlikely to occur.

title: Adaptive-Policy Distillation: Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD), which uses reverse-KL supervision on student rollouts to transfer a context-conditioned model's behavior into student model parameters for closed-book inference, has shown strong results. However, we find that this success does not translate to knowledge injection: across two document-QA benchmarks, OPD injects document knowledge far less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation. We trace this reversal to two failures that are structural, yet sparse across token positions. Reverse KL weights its gradient by the student distribution and therefore barely lifts document-specific tokens the student considers unlikely; after forward KL restores this signal, student rollouts expose later positions on the target trajectory only after generating the preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length. Motivated by the concentration of teacher-student divergence at these hard positions, we propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose per-token gate jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, withdrawing both interventions as the student learns. Without labels or a verifier, APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6%, achieving the best scores of 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 MRR on BioASQ.

title: The structured pseudospectrum of Schwarzschild black hole
abstract: The non-Hermitian nature of black hole quasinormal modes (QNMs) can give rise to remarkable spectrum instability. Such instability is naturally characterized by the pseudospectrum for the operator. However, conventional pseudospectrum analyses permit arbitrary operator perturbations that may not correspond to physically admissible modifications. In this work, we introduce the structured pseudospectrum into black hole perturbation theory. We construct two physically motivated perturbation spaces based on effective field theory and the Rezzolla--Zhidenko parametrization, and get their structured pseudospectra using two distinct norms. Our numerical results show that imposing physical constraints substantially reduces the accessible spectrum instability, especially for higher overtones. More importantly, at sufficiently small perturbation scales $\varepsilon$, the structured pseudospectrum around isolated QNMs exhibits approximately elliptical contours with preferred directions that depend on both the mode and the perturbation space, revealing an anisotropic structure beyond the familiar circular behavior of the conventional pseudospectrum.

title: The Self-repelling Burglar
abstract: In this paper, we study the conditional location of $X_T$ given the local time profile $L_T(\cdot)$ for two non-Markovian self-interacting processes: the polynomially self-repelling motion (PSRM) and the true self-repelling motion (TSRM). For TSRM, our novel approach yields a new proof of Dumaz's clever burglar result [Dumaz 2012].

title: Approximate clearing in financial networks with credit default swaps: hardness thresholds, a box algorithm, barriers, and exact solvency at bounded degree
abstract: We study approximate clearing in financial networks with credit default swaps. For weak notions (W) and (I), we prove PPAD-hardness below a threshold approximately $0.2530$ and give a polynomial-time interval algorithm above a threshold approximately $0.2834$. On networks whose CDS writers are solvent ex ante, the corresponding bounds are $(13-\sqrt{153})/4$ and $3-2\sqrt{2}$, approximately $0.1577$ and $0.1716$. The thresholds are sharp for bounded-radius algorithms: for (I) on writer-solvent networks, and for (I) and (W) in general. On non-degenerate networks, (W) and (I) have identical hardness and tractability threshold endpoints. For exact-solvency notion (D), PPAD-hardness holds at every rational error $\varepsilon<1$ on non-degenerate networks. On a restricted unit-notional class, let $d$ be the maximum number of CDS contracts held by a core bank, counted with multiplicity. For rational $\varepsilon\in[1/2,1)$, writing $ρ=(1+\varepsilon)/(1-\varepsilon)$, the problem is polynomial-time solvable when $d<(\lceilρ\rceil+1)ρ$ and PPAD-complete otherwise. At $\varepsilon=1/3$ the boundary is $d=5$ versus $d=6$; below $\varepsilon=1/9$, degree $2$ is already PPAD-complete, while degree $1$ is exactly solvable. These degree results concern (D) and do not close the (W)/(I) approximation windows. We also establish a barrier to Pure-Circuit reductions certified by interval propagation under stated interface and auxiliary-bank restrictions. A finite-precision interval algorithm reduces writer-solvent (I) to point selection in near-stalled boxes; selection is polynomial-time when the residual matrix is symmetric or monotone on each strongly connected component. The general and writer-solvent approximation windows remain open.

title: Tracking the evolution of sub-Neptunes. I. Gyrochronology of planet hosting stars
abstract: Stellar age is fundamental for reconstructing planetary-system evolution but remains difficult to determine for unevolved main-sequence stars. Stellar rotation provides a sensitive age diagnostic and a temporal framework for investigating the evolution of close-in planets. This is the first paper in a series aimed at tracing the evolution of the sub-Neptune population through homogeneous ages of their host stars. We compiled rotation periods and stellar parameters for 4639 confirmed exoplanet hosts. Gyrochronological ages were inferred using a two-zone rotational evolution model and a Bayesian approach combining rotation periods, dereddened Gaia (BP-RP) colours, and literature stellar masses as Gaussian priors. Rotational tracks were extended to the terminal-age main sequence, beyond the empirical calibration range. We obtain gyrochronological constraints for 2204 host stars. Well-constrained ages have typical formal uncertainties of 10--15%, offering substantially greater precision than is generally achievable through isochrone fitting for unevolved stars. Inferred stellar masses agree with the literature priors, while model effective temperatures are consistent with independent determinations. Ages beyond the open-cluster calibration range remain model-dependent. The resulting homogeneous catalogue provides the age framework for investigating the evolution of sub-Neptune populations and the emergence of the radius valley. Stellar parameters, provenance, and gyrochronological results are publicly available through CDS.

title: Continuous, locally Lipschitz and Lipschitz selections for intuitionistic fuzzy sets, with applications to expert voting
abstract: This paper studies continuous selections in the framework of intuitionistic fuzzy sets. To each intuitionistic fuzzy set $A=(μ,ν)$ on a topological space $X$ we associate the interval-valued map $F_{A}(x)=[μ(x),1-ν(x)]$, whose width is the hesitation degree. Hence, in this setting, a selection of $F_{A}$ is an ordinary fuzzy membership function compatible with the intuitionistic information, and every selection is the membership function of Atanassov's operator $D_{\vartheta}$ for a suitable pointwise parameter $\vartheta$. When $X$ is normal and $μ$, $ν$ are upper semi-continuous, a continuous selection exists by the Katětov--Tong insertion theorem. We show that upper semi-continuity arises naturally in a voting model, in which a panel of experts divides a metric universe into closed regions of acceptance and rejection, and for this model we construct an explicit continuous selection, the consensus selection, illustrated by a non-compact example in the plane. On metric spaces we characterise the intuitionistic fuzzy sets that admit an $L$-Lipschitz selection through a non-local version of the condition $μ+ν\leq 1$, and we give the largest and the smallest such selections in closed form. Finally, we prove that the set of continuous selections depends in a $1$-Lipschitz way on the intuitionistic fuzzy set, with respect to the Hausdorff-type distance of Grzegorzewski. We also characterise the intuitionistic fuzzy sets admitting locally Lipschitz selections.

title: High-order concentric hopfions in a helimagnet
abstract: Magnetic hopfions are three-dimensional topological solitons: ``knots'' in the vector field of magnetization of magnetically ordered materials, which are a key element of the three-dimensional spintronics emerging today. In this work, a simple analytical model for a new type of magnetic hopfions --- ``concentric'' ones --- is constructed and solved. Their size and equilibrium energy are estimated, their stability region on the magnetic phase diagram of a helimagnet is mapped out, and the requirements for materials admitting equilibrium concentric hopfions with high Hopf index on a uniformly magnetized background are determined.

title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
abstract: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

title: Harmonic Quasiconformal Mappings in the BMO-Teichmüller space
abstract: Let $\text{HQS}(\mathbb{R})$ denote the class of increasing homeomorphisms of the real line $\mathbb{R}$ that admit harmonic quasiconformal extensions to the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$. Kalaj and Pavlović proved that a homeomorphism $h$ belongs to $\text{HQS}(\mathbb{R})$ if and only if $h$ is bi-Lipschitz and the Hilbert transform of $h'$ belongs to $L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, and asked whether $\text{HQS}(\mathbb{R})$ is a group under composition. We give a negative answer to this question. Further, we show that the Beltrami coefficients of harmonic quasiconformal mappings of $\mathbb{H}$ can be identified with the open unit ball of $H^\infty(\mathbb{H})$. Finally, we study the topology of $\text{HQS}(\mathbb{R})$ and prove that it is contractible in the topology inherited from the BMO-Teichmüller space.

title: Regions of totally real arrangements of rational curves
abstract: We prove a plane-curve analogue of Zaslavsky's theorem for arrangements of real rational curves for which every complex singularity with more than one local branch is real and all of its branches are real. If at least one component has odd degree, the number of real regions equals the total rational Betti number of the complexified complement. We also give a formula for bounded affine regions which records the number of branches at infinity and the connected components of the real affine curve. Oriented regions generate the middle Borel--Moore homology over $\mathbb{Q}$, and they generate it over $\mathbb{Z}$ when the component degrees are coprime. The relations are described by the circles in the real normalization and, in an affine chart, by winding functions. These results imply equality of combinatorial rank and real combinatorial rank in the framework of Brown--Dupont and Sturmfels--Telen. Examples include singular rational cubics, arrangements of conics, Chebyshev curves, and the plane model of the $27$ lines on a split cubic surface.

title: Low-PAPR Rank-2 DFT-s-OFDM Waveform for 6G Uplink
abstract: Rank-2 discrete Fourier transform-spread orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (DFT-s-OFDM) is attracting renewed interest for 6G uplink, offering not only spatial multiplexing gains but also an additional degree of freedom for peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) reduction. We exploit this freedom by selectively exchanging constellation symbols between the two layers before DFT spreading, preserving the transmitted information while reshaping the resulting waveforms. Building on this idea, we propose Cyclic Layer Assignment with Shared-basis Synthesis (CLASS). CLASS employs carefully designed cyclic assignment patterns to generate diverse waveform candidates, while reusing a small number of waveform components to avoid synthesizing each candidate separately. We further establish the optimality of the cyclic design in maximizing waveform diversity under a minimum-basis constraint when equal group sizes are feasible. With only six inverse DFTs, CLASS explores 16 assignments and reduces the 99th-percentile worst-layer PAPR by 1.41 dB relative to fixed assignment, outperforming representative selected mapping (SLM) and partial transmit sequences (PTS) schemes under the same synthesis budget.

title: Excess inner-horizon entropy and the thermodynamics of Kerr formation
abstract: \noindent We develop a charge-matched thermodynamic framework for the regular rotating black-hole family underlying an exact model of Kerr formation. Since the Kerr endpoint already possesses a Cauchy horizon, hidden entropy is identified with the excess inner-horizon area relative to Kerr at fixed mass $M$ and angular momentum $J=Ma$: $\Sexc=π[h_c^2-(r_-^{\Kerr})^2]$, where $h_c$ is the regular inner-horizon radius and $r_-^{\Kerr}=M-\sqrt{M^2-a^2}$. Under regularity and interior-profile assumptions, we prove $r_-^{\Kerr}<h_c<h$ and establish the sharp bound $0<\Sexc<4πM\sqrt{M^2-a^2}$. The Schwarzschild limit yields $\Sexc=πh_c^2$, while $\Sexc=0$ at the Kerr endpoint. The Kerr reference entropy satisfies $S_+^{\Kerr}+S_-^{\Kerr}=4πM^2$, so rotation redistributes its two-horizon contributions at fixed mass. For the time-dependent model, we derive exact evolution equations for the inner root and $\Sexc$, interpreted as root-bookkeeping identities unless the roots are established as dynamical horizons. In the minimal $N=1$ trajectory, the apparent pole at $n=2$ is removable in the mass profile, giving a logarithmic continuation of the root equation, although the stationary curvature is singular there. The stationary Ricci-scalar density is locally absolutely integrable for $-1<n\leq2$, with the Kerr endpoint $n=-1$ treated separately. Minkowski breaking occurs at $n=0$, independently of inner-horizon disappearance. Quasi-extremal regular configurations approach, but cannot attain, the entropy bound without losing a regular Killing horizon.

title: From MHV Gravity Amplitudes and Hodges map to Pentad Varieties
abstract: We study some geometric aspects behind the Hodges matrix appearing in the context of scattering amplitudes for the $\mathcal N=8$ supergravity. Through a vector bundle construction, we show that the Hodges matrix gives rise to a canonical rational map from the two-step flag variety to symmetric matrices, called the $\textit{Hodges map}$. This construction allows to define the amplitude geometrically: its vanishing locus is a divisor - the $\textit{MHV gravity divisor}$. Inspired by the Hodges map, we introduce the notion of Hadamard ratio of two varieties. In the case relevant to gravity, this is the ratio of two Grassmannians, which we call the $\textit{pentad variety}$, connecting it to the pentad constraint from algebraic statistics. Moreover, we show that the pentad variety is closely related to the combinatorial algebraic geometry of Martin's affine slope variety, and the phirotopes of Below, Krummeck, and Richter-Gebert.

title: Finite-Sample Calibration and Power Benchmarks in Two-Sample Random-Integration Tests
abstract: In high-dimensional two-group studies, a supplied variable set can be used directly or to learn a projection. We study how much attainable power these choices retain at fixed observation and calibration budgets. For complete unbiased random-integration statistics under Gaussian common shape, a fixed-spectrum comparison orders direction-wise power and gives an explicit criterion balancing an oracle advantage against learning loss. Joint regeneration controls level for a specified learner with unknown diagonal shape. A paired construction permits observation reuse and finite-reference calibration of fitted scores and menus. In the paired diagonal experiment, an invariant sparse likelihood-ratio benchmark provides an attainable efficiency target. Finite-amplitude bounds connect a classical bounded quadratic to this target; conditioning on the coordinate maximum yields informative complementary bounds at moderate and strong signals. Both comparisons include finite reference budgets, and null-only simulations certify local comparisons with specified fitted rules. Equal-budget experiments and a leukemia application compare aggregation, projection and fitted quadratic scores. For correlated paired data, classical sign randomization supplies a separate calibration under central symmetry. The efficiency guarantees apply to the stated experiments and signal classes; general small-budget shape efficiency and adaptation to unknown signal allocation remain open.

title: Laplacian Pair State Transfer on Edge Coronas
abstract: Let $G$ be a graph with edge set $E(G) = \{e_1, \ldots, e_m\}$, and let $\mathcal{H} = (H_1, \ldots, H_m)$ be an $m$-tuple of graphs. The edge corona $G\diamond\mathcal{H}$ is obtained from the disjoint union of $G,H_1,\ldots,H_m$ by joining both end vertices of each edge $e_j$ to every vertex of $H_j$ for $1\leq j\leq m$. In this paper, we investigate Laplacian perfect pair state transfer and Laplacian pretty good pair state transfer on edge coronas. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of Laplacian perfect pair state transfer. We also derive sufficient conditions for the non-existence of Laplacian perfect pair state transfer. Further, we identify conditions under which the absence of Laplacian perfect pair state transfer guarantees the existence of Laplacian pretty good pair state transfer. Additionally, we develop constructions based on Cartesian product and tensor product to obtain a few more infinite families of edge coronas admitting Laplacian pretty good pair state transfer. Finally, we investigate the existence of Laplacian pretty good pair state transfer on the edge corona of complete graphs.

title: Harnessing Inter-Waveguide Evanescent Coupling in Pinching-Antenna Systems
abstract: In multi-waveguide pinching-antenna systems (PASS), waveguides are typically modeled as independent signal-transport paths. However, when dielectric waveguides are closely spaced, their evanescent electromagnetic fields overlap, allowing guided signals to exchange energy before radiation. While such inter-waveguide coupling is conventionally regarded as undesirable crosstalk, this paper reveals an opportunity to harness it as an additional analog beamforming resource. The key insight is that coupling, through its interaction with sequential signal extraction by distributed pinching antennas (PAs), can reshape coherent signal combining at the receivers without increasing the available signal power. Consequently, stronger coupling does not necessarily yield better performance; rather, the coupling-induced phase relationships determine whether the radiated signals combine constructively or destructively. To characterize and exploit this mechanism, we establish a physics-based end-to-end channel model, derive coupling-aware waveguide-spacing principles and achievable-rate bounds, and develop joint waveguide deployment, PA placement, and digital precoding algorithms for multi-hotspot communications. Numerical results demonstrate substantial sum-rate improvements over conventional fixed-deployment and optimized minimum-spacing PASS benchmarks. These findings establish inter-waveguide evanescent coupling as a new physical degree of freedom for PASS channel reconfiguration.

title: Noise Stability on the Hypercube: Order $7/8$
abstract: For a balanced Boolean function $f$ on the discrete hypercube, we study the $α$-stability $\mathbb{E}[(T_ρf)^α]$, where $T_ρ$ is the Boolean noise operator and $0<α<1$. Using the asymmetric Hellinger kernel estimates recently established by OpenAI, we prove that dictators minimize the $7/8$-stability in every dimension and at every correlation $0\leρ\le1$. At interior correlations they are the only minimizers. As a consequence, dictators minimize the $α$-stability for every $7/8\leα<1$, maximize the $α$-stability for every $1<α<2$, and maximize the one-sided Shannon entropy stability $\mathbb{E}[T_ρf\log T_ρf]$. This resolves a conjecture of Li and Médard and strengthens the Courtade--Kumar conjecture in the balanced setting.

title: Multi-Antenna Channel Prediction in 5G and Beyond using Data driven approach
abstract: As Wireless Communication evolves towards 5G and beyond, it satisfies Quality of Service (QoS) requirements of users by utilizing beam forming, adaptive transmission and multi antenna communication techniques. It is essential to have accurate channel information at Base station (BS) to provide satisfactory QoS to users. Traditional channel estimation approach involves transmitting pilots from User Equipments (UEs) and estimating the channel at BS, increases computational complexity as it is periodic process. It also increases communication complexity as number of antennas at BS increases which leads to increase in pilots. In this paper, we consider channel vector prediction using Machine learning approach at 7GHz. In this work, we generated data using ray tracing mechanism and used this generated data to train Machine learning models. We Considered XG Boost regression and Multilayer perceptron regression model.

title: A Reproducible Reconstruction and Evaluation Framework for Photorealistic Lunar Analog Scene Reconstruction Toward Digital Twins
abstract: In this paper, we present a reconstruction pipeline that empirically quantifies the photorealistic scene reconstruction accuracy from both human-controlled and rover mast camera monocular feeds against physical ground truth as a function of Lunar traversal effects (e.g., motion blur, haze due to lofted regolith, trajectory bias, and sparse views). First, we benchmark six variants of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) across three Lunar analog scenes on held-out test sets using standard photometric metrics. We then establish how under traversal effects, this test-set-specific Novel View Synthesis (NVS) performance does not proportionally scale to the same photometric metrics in the reconstructed DTs. Our results quantify that splat training metrics alone are insufficient predictors of Cross-Reconstruction Photorealistic NVS Fidelity (CRPNVS), and that factors such as rover trajectory bias and geometric scene coverage play a critical role in determining the photorealistic quality of the reconstructed scenes targeting Lunar analog Digital Twins. Additionally, we pilot study Coverage Score ($S_c$), a geometry-based diagnostic derived from COLMAP poses and point cloud structure that provides a meaningful heuristic about the highest achievable CRPNVS structural fidelity, independently of splat training performance in the absence of a human-controlled reference. These findings establish a standardized, human control-referenced evaluation pipeline for photorealistic scene reconstruction for Lunar-analog Digital Twin development and future planetary exploration. Code and project page: https://rose-lab-admin.github.io/rose-lunar-dt-rec

title: ShiftRAG: Bypassing the Textual Bottleneck via Decoupled Learning and Continuous Soft Tokens
abstract: Despite advances in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), suppressing hallucinations during complex reasoning remains a persistent challenge. We identify that existing RAG pipelines suffer from a textual bottleneck: by passing only raw text to the generator, they discard discriminative signals of the retriever. Furthermore, recent attempts to unify retrieval and generation within a single LLM induce severe objective conflict and exacerbate the rank collapse of decoder-only architectures, degrading performance on both tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce ShiftRAG, a decoupled RAG framework that employs a single LLM backbone but isolates discriminative retrieval learning from autoregressive generation. To bridge these decoupled modes, we project retrieval alignments into continuous soft tokens, establishing a high-bandwidth interface that infuses the generator with retrieval-side signals. Concurrently, our soft orthogonality objective mitigates rank collapse, while layer-wise relevance dynamics preserve the fine-grained latent space required for highly discriminative evidence separation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that ShiftRAG significantly improves retrieval and question answering performance over state-of-the-art baselines. ShiftRAG preserves foundational capabilities of the backbone while maintaining a favorable efficiency-performance trade-off on general text encoding and generative tasks.

title: Entry and position statistics in alternating permutations and Young tableaux
abstract: We study entry and position statistics in alternating permutations and standard Young tableaux using linear extensions and generating functions. For alternating permutations, we give explicit formulas for the mean and variance of the first entry and of the position of any fixed value. For standard Young tableaux, we express the sum of the lower-left entries as the number of tableaux of an associated skew shape. For two-row shapes, we determine the distribution of the entry in each cell of the second row, and for the shape $(n,n)$ we give a closed formula for its sum over all tableaux, which recovers a limit formula of Stanley. Through a bijection of Lewis, the results for the shape $(n,n)$ describe the entries of a random $321$-avoiding down-up permutation of even length.

title: How tightly can PBH abundance information constrain scalar-induced gravitational waves?
abstract: Primordial black hole (PBH) abundances and scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) probe the same primordial fluctuations through different physical weights. We examine the predictive power of precise synthetic information on absolute PBH abundances over a finite stellar-mass interval, together with an exact total abundance and external population bounds. For Gaussian perturbations under a fixed quantum chromodynamics (QCD) formation prescription, two smooth, symmetric lognormal spectra satisfy the same abundance conditions while producing nonproportional leading-order SIGW spectra. The two spectra differ by about 20% when averaged over the lower of two adjacent nanohertz windows but by nearly a factor of 60 in the higher-frequency window, so the difference cannot be represented by a single rescaling of the gravitational-wave background. Peak position and width compensate with amplitude in the abundance calculation, while the higher-frequency window draws almost all its energy from scalar-mode pairs with both wavenumbers above the primordial peak. Under the principal abundance benchmark, local finite-width components yield larger contrasts at a fixed nanohertz frequency through distinct mode couplings under both the QCD and stochastic peak-curvature formation prescriptions. For a separately generated population, extending mass information over most of its abundance restricts the lognormal peak-position and width compensation and reduces the higher-window contrast, while the unequal window responses persist. These results show why joint PBH-SIGW inference must propagate primordial shapes compatible with the PBH abundance information rather than assign one tensor template to a single abundance fit.

title: Multicopy teleportation and quantum program retrieval on superconducting quantum hardware
abstract: Correction-free teleportation protocols offer a probabilistic route around the limits imposed by the quantum no-programming theorem, but have remained largely theoretical. Here, we experimentally implement and benchmark correction-free multicopy teleportation on noisy superconducting quantum hardware. Key to this is an efficient circuit implementation: by suitably decomposing the unitary that maps the multicopy measurement basis onto the computational basis, we substantially reduce circuit depth and gate count. For one- and two-qubit input states, using $k=2$ and $3$ copies, we observe success probabilities substantially exceeding the single-copy bound with fidelities above 0.85. We further explore applications to probabilistic programmable quantum processors, in particular the storage and retrieval of unitary operations encoded in quantum program states. Our results establish the practical feasibility of multicopy teleportation and highlight its potential for near-term quantum processors and distributed quantum computing.

title: HamFormer: A Hamiltonian Flow-based SE(3)-Transformer for Conformation Optimization
abstract: The Transformer architecture plays a central role in modern deep learning, and its SE(3)-equivariant variants have been widely applied to molecular conformation modeling and optimization. Given its importance, many methods attempt to interpret and improve the Transformer through the lens of dynamics. However, they mainly focus on a single attention head rather than the full Transformer architecture and seldom consider SE(3)-equivariance in their proposed models. In this study, we propose an improved SE(3)-Transformer architecture, called HamFormer, which revisits the design of SE(3)-Transformer through the lens of Hamiltonian flow. In particular, we define a parametrized Hamiltonian flow in the phase space of position and velocity, corresponding to optimizing an energy functional that combines an optimal transport-based potential with a damped momentum. The Lie-Trotter splitting framework of the Hamiltonian flow leads to the proposed HamFormer architecture, whose feedforward computation achieves the optimization step of the proposed energy functional. Furthermore, we combine HamFormer with Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN), build a new model for molecular conformation optimization. Extensive experiments on molecular ground-state conformation prediction show that HamFormer provides a strong and physically interpretable surrogate for classic SE(3)-Transformer and generally outperforms state-of-the-art competitors.

title: Radial conditions for global compact finite propagation for divergence-form elliptic operators
abstract: We study global compact finite propagation (GCFP) for the wave equation $u_{tt}=\operatorname{div}(A(x)\nabla u)$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, that is, the property that a disturbance starting in a compact set cannot reach spatial infinity in finite time. For smooth strictly positive matrices $A$ we show that GCFP implies $\int_1^\infty a_*(r)^{-1/2}\,dr=\infty$, where $a_*(r)$ is the minimum over the sphere of radius $r$ of $\langle Aω,ω\rangle$; the proof uses the equivalence of GCFP with completeness of the Riemannian metric $A^{-1}$, of which we prove the necessary direction for the cosine family of the Friedrichs extension. We also prove that the analogous divergence condition with $a^*(r)$, the maximum over the sphere, is sufficient, and that this holds for measurable coefficients $A\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $A\ge I$. Finally, we construct a locally bounded measurable matrix with $a_*=a^*$ for which GCFP holds although the integral converges, so the necessary condition is not stable under the loss of continuity.

title: What Breaks and What Comes Back: Capability Damage and Recovery in Depth-Pruned Small Language Models
abstract: Depth pruning removes whole Transformer blocks to make a language model smaller and faster, but the damage is not spread evenly across what the model can do, and a short fine-tuning run, called healing, decides what comes back. We measure this for small models used as agents. Four instruction-tuned models of 1.2-1.7B parameters (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-2-1B) are pruned and healed, and six capabilities are tracked: structured output, function calling, instruction following, mathematical reasoning, safety refusal and knowledge. Three results hold across the families. First, function calling and math collapse in every model (retention 0.00-0.07 of the unpruned score), and the order in which capabilities break agrees closely across the four (Kendall's W = 0.92; 0.62 after correcting for chance floors). Second, which parameters are trained matters as much as which data: fully tuning the last three blocks instead of adding low-rank adapters to all blocks costs up to 0.18 in capped mean retention on three families, and one 300k-token pilot per scope detects this. Third, we test a planner that allocates a 1M-token healing budget from 21 short pilot heals. At a fixed budget it raises the weakest capability on two families, although only one of these gains survives a test that also resamples training seeds. Once its 3.48M pilot tokens are counted, uniform healing with the same total number of training tokens matches or beats every planned variant on every family and retains math significantly better on three of them in an item-level test (on one when seeds are also resampled). Healing longer is a strong and simple baseline that planned recovery must beat. Code, per-item predictions and every result are public.

title: Experimental Realization of a Nonreciprocal Quantum Battery
abstract: Quantum batteries promise faster and more efficient energy storage and extraction by harnessing quantum mechanics, serving as essential building blocks for future quantum devices. A key practical requirement-unidirectional energy flow during charging-is straightforward in classical batteries via potential difference, yet remains a major challenge in the quantum regime due to the inherent reciprocity of coherent coupling. Here, we realize the first backflow-free, nonreciprocal quantum battery in the few-quantum regime, implemented in a highly controlled trapped-ion system via a qubit-reservoir engineering technique. By subtly tailoring quantum interference between coherent and dissipative couplings of two laser-cooled motional modes, we achieve strictly unidirectional energy flow from the charger to the battery. We observe maximum charging power at an exceptional point and demonstrate a complete charge-discharge cycle with unitary work extraction. This work establishes the foundation for directional energy transfer and storage in micro- and nanoscale quantum devices, with broad implications for nonreciprocal energy harvesting, precision metrology, information processing, and quantum thermodynamics.

title: Flap like a bat: Soft pneumatic wings for biomimetic ornithopters
abstract: This paper describes the development of a bio-inspired ornithopter wing mechanism that uses soft pneumatic actuators, such as PneuNet structures, in place of revolute joints, inspired by the complicated kinematics of bat flight. The proposed design employs pneumatically driven air pockets within a flexible wing skeleton to achieve smooth, lifelike flapping motion. The actuation system is controlled by 3/2-way solenoid valves and an air pump, which manipulate airflow and actuator deformation. We demonstrate, using ANSYS FEA software, the bending behavior of the PneuNet actuators under varying pressures to inform the wing's structural design. The implementation of soft robotics in the flapping-wing system offers potential advantages over traditional mechanisms, such as reduced mechanical complexity, lower acoustic signatures, enhanced adaptability, and wing morphing. This work demonstrates the feasibility of replacing rigid revolute joints with compliant pneumatic actuators, enabling more agile, silent, and biomimetic aerial robots.

title: Structure-Preserving Full Approximation Scheme for Real-Space Hartree-Fock Equations
abstract: We develop a structure-preserving full approximation scheme (FAS) for the real-space restricted Hartree-Fock equations. The method treats the orbital equations, Coulomb and exchange pair potentials, and orthonormality constraints as a coupled nonlinear system on a hierarchy of finite-element spaces. Forced Gram targets, occupied-frame alignment, and auxiliary-variable reconstruction provide constraint compatibility and occupied-rotation equivariance under suitable assumptions. Analysis of the full self-consistent response identifies an elliptic kinetic principal part, motivating the multilevel treatment. The resulting solver, FAS-H, combines FAS cycles with a residual-triggered horizontal Newton correction on the finest grid. Numerical experiments on eight closed-shell systems show convergence in 4-11 cycles across three grid levels. Across 24 system-grid comparisons, FAS-H is 1.60-5.02 times faster than SCF and uses 68-91% less weighted FFT work, while standalone horizontal Newton is faster in some cases.

title: LADS: Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling of Tool Results for Language Model Agents
abstract: Web agents complete multi-step online tasks through repeated browser actions and model calls. Their returned observations lie on the critical path to subsequent decisions. When concurrent browser actions finish in bursts, observations can accumulate on a constrained return path to a shared inference service, while waiting histories compete for reusable cache state. Conventional delivery rules prioritize short transfers or immediate cache reuse but overlook how sending a result earlier can help a request resume sooner and free cache-protection capacity for other waiting requests. We present LADS (Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling), a tool-result scheduler that couples cache-aware delivery with bounded prefix leases. Its key insight is that resumption lets extra protection references retire, making lease quota available to protect another waiting history. LADS prioritizes timely handoffs using current lease ownership and an estimated resumption delay, with bounded departures from Cache-first order. Compared with ReAct using first-in, first-out (FIFO) tool-result delivery, LADS reduces mean complete-workflow latency by 44.6% under bursty tool returns and by 42.4% on Web-derived burst replay.

title: Relative Rouquier linearity and inverse hybrid Kazhdan-Lusztig positivity
abstract: We prove signed positivity for the expansion of a parabolic hybrid basis in the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis of a Hecke algebra. The coefficients have degree bounded by the length of the corresponding minimal coset representative. We deduce this linearity from Elias-Williamson's ordinary Rouquier linearity by a truncation argument. The result does not require the parabolic subgroup to be finite.

title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
abstract: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.

title: When 200 OK Is Not an Answer: Silent Fetch Failures in Agentic Web Content Acquisition
abstract: Web agents and answer engines fetch pages at question time, and liveness checks of cited sources treat an HTTP 200 response as success. We measure how often that assumption fails and what it does to measurements built on fetched pages. We fetched 10,307 URLs in three days with a polite static client and a rendered browser client: pages from 1,507 sites in five strata, random non-existent paths on every site, and the 4,795 URLs cited by expert-verified claims in ExpertQA. We define a taxonomy of what a 200 response contains, label the static 200 responses automatically, and check the labels against 300 items reviewed by an LLM-based assistant; a human check of 60 of them retained every reviewed usability label after discussion. By the automatic labels, 20.9% of the pages that a static client receives with status 200 do not contain the page's main content: app shells, bot challenges, block pages, error and placeholder pages, and partial content. On the held-out test split, the reviewed sample lowers this estimate from 25.5% to 20.0%. 13.1% of the sites whose random-path probe was answered returned 200. The error propagates: for the cited sources, treating 200 as content overstates the share of claim-source pairs that can be checked against live content by 12.2 points and inflates the apparent silent citation-drift rate from 5.8% to 21.9%. Cheap heuristics catch most of it. Text length, probe comparison and redirect-to-root, combined and tuned on held-out sites, recover 86% of unusable reviewed responses at a false-alarm rate near 5%. Content-reading detectors perform comparably: the best, the text classifier, gains five to seven points of recall at more than twice the false-alarm rate. We argue that agents and their evaluations should report fetch outcomes explicitly instead of inferring them from the status line and will release the labelled data and code.

title: Where Does a Variational Quantum Classifier Lose Accuracy? Angle Encoding, Readout and the Fidelity-Kernel Reference in Cyberattack Detection
abstract: When a variational quantum classifier performs poorly at detecting network attacks, it is hard to tell which part is to blame: the encoding, the trained circuit or the readout, which turns measurements into a class. In this work, we build upon a recent amplitude-encoded classifier, and we try to separate their contributions to the NSL-KDD benchmark in noiseless simulation. We compare angle and amplitude encoding, vary one component at a time, and measure each circuit against a classical yardstick: a support-vector machine on the encoded states, whose accuracy estimates what a well-trained circuit can reach. Most of the shortfall lies in the readout. Reading one qubit, or the parity of all qubits, leaves several percentage points unused, while a readout trained together with the circuit recovers most of them from the same measurements. This also explains why some classifiers stop improving as further layers are added. The encodings suit different needs. Angle encoding gives the more accurate detector on traffic like the training data and, from eight features up, shallower circuits; amplitude encoding needs far fewer qubits and catches more attacks of types never seen in training. Finally, we report that classical models, given the same inputs, are about as accurate as the best circuits, thus, registering no quantum advantage.

title: On Ramanujan's cubic continued fraction, II
abstract: We show that all the periodic points with period $n \ge 3$ of the algebraic function defined by the relation $g(x,y) = x^2+2xy^2-y = 0$ are expressible in terms of values of Ramanujan's cubic continued fraction $c(τ)$. It is shown that the values $c(w/2), c(w/6), c(w/6+1/2)$ are periodic points, for specific elements $w$ in the order of discriminant $-d$ in $K = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-d})$, with $-d \equiv 1$ (mod $8$); and all the periodic points are conjugates of these values or specific linear fractional expressions in their conjugates, times cube roots of unity. These periodic points are determined by relating them to the periodic points of the algebraic function defined by $k(x,y)= -xy^2+x^2+y^2+3x = 0$; and these periodic points (for periods $\ge 2$) generate ring class fields over $K$.

title: Multi-quadrotor systems interconnected via structurally unknown forces and moments
abstract: This work addresses the challenge of controlling multi-quadrotor systems subject to tight uncertain couplings. We consider interconnection forces and moments among the quadrotors to be state-dependent functions of the coordination errors, without assuming knowledge of their functional/parametric structures, e.g., no linear-in-parameters assumptions are made. We only rely on general state-dependent quadratic bounds valid for several Euler-Lagrange mechanical systems. We propose a coordination strategy embedding adaptive laws dedicated to compensating for the lack of structural knowledge. Unlike conventional decoupled position-attitude designs, we present a coupled stability analysis accounting for the position-attitude couplings induced by the interconnection forces and moments. The analysis, along with real experiments involving cooperative aerial transportation of rope-interconnected payloads, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed solution in compensating for these complex interconnections. Comparative experiments show that, when a payload drop induces a disturbance propagating through the ropes across the whole formation, the proposed strategy reduces significantly post-disturbance transients.

title: Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality
abstract: The mean log deviation and the Theil index are two widely used measures of income inequality. The organization releasing these measures may be obligated to protect the confidentiality of the individual incomes used in the computations. In particular, the organization may wish to release versions of these measures with formal guarantees of privacy. The organization could do so by satisfying differential privacy; however, typical applications of differentially private algorithms are likely to add so much noise to the measures that they become unusable. We present differentially private algorithms for these indices with reasonable error properties. The algorithms rely on computing or approximating bounds on the smooth sensitivity, that is, the maximum absolute amount the inequality measures change when replacing any subset of the $n$ incomes in the reported data with arbitrarily chosen feasible values. For the mean log deviation, the algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time. For the Theil index, the algorithm runs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We illustrate the performance of each differentially private algorithm using individual-level and household-level income data from the Current Population Survey. We also examine repeated sampling properties of the algorithms using artificially generated data. The empirical results indicate when these differentially private algorithms can be expected to provide accurate estimates and when they are likely to introduce too much noise.

title: Lithography-free, apodized thickness-shear LiNbO3 resonators for piezoelectric DC-DC power conversion
abstract: Piezoelectric resonators have emerged as promising energy-storage elements for compact high-frequency DC-DC power converters. Still, practical implementation requires simultaneously high k_t^2 (electromechanical coupling), Q (high quality factor) and low resistance/impedance fluctuations. Spurious Lamb-wave and lateral modes are particularly problematic because they reduce the usable inductive frequency span and complicate converter operation over variable loads. Here we report a lithography-free, apodized 163° Y-cut lithium niobate thickness-shear resonator with reduced electrically visible spurious responses while preserving the intrinsically large coupling of the thickness-shear mode. Finite-element simulations show that a square plate excites numerous lateral spurious modes near the principal shear resonance. In contrast, a curved asymmetric plate outline redistributes the lateral acoustic boundary conditions and reduces electrically visible spurious responses. Experiments on multiple resonator outlines, interconnection schemes, and device areas are performed to characterize the device responses. The representative 560 mm^2 device exhibits a series resonance near 3.67 MHz, an effective electromechanical coupling coefficient of 53.57%, a series quality factor of 1146, and a series resonance figure of merit of 614. A representative device fitted with a modified Butterworth-van Dyke equivalent circuit model shows excellent agreement between measurement and model, with a maximum Bode quality factor of 2896. These results support lateral-boundary apodization as a practical approach to high-coupling lithium niobate resonators with reduced electrically visible spurious responses for piezoelectric power converters.

title: The covering radius of the first-order Reed-Muller code in nine variables is 242
abstract: We prove that the covering radius of the binary first-order Reed-Muller code RM(1,9) is exactly 242. Equivalently, the maximum nonlinearity of a Boolean function in nine variables is 242. Our proof combines a one-point rigidity theorem with a spectral and computational exclusion of the two larger candidate nonlinearities. We first show that every nine-variable Boolean function of nonlinearity 243 admits a unique one-point modification that raises its nonlinearity to 244: the point to be changed is the vector sum of its support. This part uses exact Walsh-update identities, integer interpolation, rigidity of a quadratic residue, and a sharp Walsh l1 estimate for cubic Boolean functions. To exclude nonlinearity 244, we use Parseval's identity and congruences of integral Walsh coefficients to force an exceptionally restricted spectrum. An associated cubic residue phase must attain the extremal Walsh l1 bound 10240. We eliminate one equality spectrum by hyperplane slicing; the other forces the original Boolean function from the signs of the cubic phase and yields a double-complement-pairing identity for its cubic top part. The classification of alternating trilinear forms over F2, an exact filter of their representatives, and two exhaustive enumerations of 218 quadratic supplements then rule out every remaining candidate. Together with the known construction attaining nonlinearity 242, these arguments establish the asserted covering radius.

title: Beyond Source Compatibility: WebAssembly as a Stable ABI for ARINC 653 Applications
abstract: Thirty years ago, ARINC 653 was introduced to provide a vendor-independent platform for software applications in Integrated Modular Avionics (IMA). A platform is characterized by a well-defined interface abstracting over implementation details; in the case of ARINC 653 this is an Application Programming Interface (API), defined on the source-code level. However, several aspects of this API - such as the memory layout and partially also the integer bit width of data types - remain implementation dependent, so portability across Operating Systems (OSs) requires recompilation, and often also source code adaptation. Our contribution is three-fold; first, we refine the ARINC 653 header file, eliminating remaining ambiguities. Second, building on WebAssembly (Wasm), we define an OS- and processor-architecture-agnostic Application Binary Interface (ABI) at the object-code level, resolving differences in data layout, endianness, and function-pointer representation between host and guest environments. Third, we demonstrate a Wasm-VM-agnostic shim-library that executes ARINC 653 partitions, compiled to Wasm bytecode and following our ABI, on multiple processor architectures using two independent Wasm runtimes.

title: Learning to Group and Order: Cross-Instance Self-Supervised RL for Vision-Centric MLLMs
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become an important paradigm for improving multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially with automatically verifiable rewards. Self-supervised visual pretext tasks provide such rewards without human annotations. However, existing methods mainly exploit within-instance structure, offering limited supervision for cross-instance discrimination and fine-grained comparison. We introduce Group-and-Order Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (GO-SSL), a cross-instance jigsaw framework for vision-centric MLLM post-training. Given two visual instances, GO-SSL mixes their local elements and trains the model to group them by instance of origin while recovering the order within each group, coupling instance-level comparison with spatial, temporal, or geometric structure recovery. This paired formulation turns the same unlabeled data into richer verifiable supervision through diverse pairings, shuffles, and a random-to-hard curriculum. We instantiate GO-SSL mainly on cross-image jigsaw tasks and further extend it to 3D depth and video temporal ordering. Across diverse benchmarks, GO-SSL consistently improves over the base MLLM and prior self-supervised post-training baselines, with clear gains in fine-grained perception and spatial understanding. Further evaluations across model scales and families support its generality. These results suggest that cross-instance comparison provides a useful self-supervised RL signal for improving transferable visual understanding in MLLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SEU-VIPGroup/GO-SSL.

title: On subgroup perfect codes and regular sets in generalized Cayley graphs
abstract: A subset $C$ of the vertex set of a graph $Γ$ is said to be an $(a,b)$-regular set if $C$ induces an $a$-regular subgraph and every vertex outside $C$ is adjacent to exactly $b$ vertices in $C$. A $(0,1)$-regular set is called a perfect code. Let $G$ be a finite group and let $α\in\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ be such that $α^2=\mathrm{id}$. Let $ω_α(G)=\{α(g^{-1})g:g\in G\}$. For a subset $S\subseteq G$ satisfying $α(S)=S^{-1}$ and $S\capω_α(G)=\emptyset$, the generalized Cayley graph of $(G,α)$ with respect to $S$ is the graph with vertex set $G$ in which two distinct elements $g,h\in G$ are adjacent if and only if $α(g^{-1})h\in S$. In this paper, we prove two main results. First, let $H$ be an $α$-invariant subgroup of a finite group $G$, and let $P$ be an $α$-invariant Sylow 2-subgroup of $H$. We show that $H$ is a perfect code of $(G,α)$ if and only if $P[H,α]$ is a perfect code of $(G,α)$, where $[H,α]=\langle h^{-1}α(h):h\in H\rangle$. Second, we consider finite groups $G$ possessing a cyclic subgroup $A$ of index 2 that is invariant under an involutory automorphism $α$. We show that $ω_α(G)$ is a subgroup of $A$. Using this result, we give a complete characterization of all pairs $(a,b)$ for which an $α$-invariant subgroup $H$ of $G$ is an $(a,b)$-regular set of $(G,α)$. In particular, our characterization applies to all finite groups possessing a characteristic cyclic subgroup of index 2, for every involutory automorphism $α$.

title: Microphone Geometry Aware Regional Target Speaker Extraction
abstract: Regional target speaker extraction (RSE) aims to extract speech originating from a specified angular region, relaxing the requirement for precise target speaker location when performing location based speech extraction. However, existing RSE methods typically assume a fixed microphone array configuration and microphone number, limiting their applicability to unseen microphone geometries and varying numbers of microphones. In this work, we propose a geometry-aware RSE framework capable of extract with varying microphone array geometry and microphone numbers. Specifically, we introduce an attention-based multichannel front-end to encode inter-microphone phase information, together with a spatial audio reconstruction-based auxiliary objective to improve the front-end spatial representations quality. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves SI-SDRi by 5.1 dB over geometry-aware baselines across microphone arrays with four-microphones, while maintaining a performance gap of less than 0.6 dB compared with a tetrahedral geometry-specific baseline when evaluated on the tetrahedral microphone array.

title: Radiofrequency plasma spheroidization of lightweight complex concentrated superalloy Al10Nb20Ta15Ti30V5Zr20
abstract: Recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM) have significantly increased the demand for high-quality metal powders with tailored composition. For refractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCA) preparing such powders by conventional metallurgical method remains challenging due to their high melting point and chemical reactivity. In this paper, we present a method to produce spherical RCCA powders (here Al10Nb20Ta15Ti30V5Zr20) via mechanical alloying followed by radio-frequency inductively coupled plasma spheroidization. The resulting powder is suitable for AM processes because of its spherical morphology and a microstructure consisting of major BCC phases with local B2 phase. Complex carbide formation was studied by 3D atom probe tomography.

title: Verifying Test-State Identity in Paired Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Simulation-based VLA evaluation often treats matching task, seed, and episode identifiers as sufficient evidence that two policies faced identical test conditions. Under specific vectorized reset and autoreset conditions, different termination timing can change subsequent initial-state assignment, so the same episode index need not mean the same test state. We present an evaluation-integrity framework for paired comparison - invariants I1-I5, provenance logging, optional scene fingerprints, and an automated checker - and a controlled LeRobot 0.6.1 LIBERO harness study with emulated controllers. Four evidence levels are kept separate: (A) mixed-horizon Sync wave-1 IDs [20, 5, 22, 7] vs [4, 5, 6, 7]; (B) homogeneous separate-job Sync control (16 cells, 0 ID/fingerprint mismatches); (C) Async+Freeze batch-size map differences (12 I3 mismatches; bs=8 incomplete; mechanism unisolated); (D) a synthetic McNemar illustration only. Controllers were emulated and no real-VLA shared-vector experiment was completed. We recommend checking declared/resolved init-state identity and provenance before paired statistics. We do not claim that published VLA leaderboards are generally invalid.

title: A Telescopic Method with Guaranteed B-Stationarity for Partitioned Cardinality and Complementarity Constraints
abstract: We consider the minimization of a smooth function subject to box constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints (PCC): the variables are divided into groups and, within each group, at most a prescribed number of variables may be non-zero. This class contains bound-constrained minimization, cardinality-constrained minimization and bound-constrained mathematical programs with complementarity constraints. We introduce the Telescopic Method, which alternates iterations of a bound-constrained method on the faces of the feasible set with inexpensive one-dimensional "escaping" tests that exchange a variable of the current face by a currently null one within the same group. We prove, without constraint qualifications and without requiring global solutions of subproblems, that every limit point of the generated sequence is B-stationary, i.e., it satisfies the first-order condition defined by the tangent cone of the feasible set. This guarantee is obtained with exchanges of a single variable, whatever the number of non-null entries of the limit point, because B-stationarity for this class of problems decomposes into conditions on single variables. On the 60 bound-constrained mathematical programs with complementarity constraints of the test set of Kirches, Larson, Leyffer and Manns, the method found approximately B-stationary points in all the problems. Applications to separable regression, sparse polynomial approximation and portfolio selection are described and tested numerically.

title: Trading Transparency for Stability: Friction-Cone-Constrained Bilateral Teleoperation for Opening Doors of Unsecured Furniture
abstract: Opening the door of unsecured furniture loads the frictional contacts at its supports; too large a pull slides or tips the object. A friction-cone constraint on the commanded wrench removes this failure mode but costs haptic transparency. We quantify the trade-off: an admissible wrench set built from contact friction cones and support-polygon tipping margins is shrunk for robustness to bounded mass and friction errors, and any command in the shrunken set provably leaves the furniture static (Prop. 1). We call this map the robust friction cone projection (RFCP). RFCP and its haptic guard admit a bounded force transmission error (Prop. 2): transparency degrades only within a band near the constraint boundary, whose width is set by one scalar, the stability factor . A working condition controller handles the door: the operator commands a scalar swing amplitude, the slave orientation follows hinge kinematics, and the grasp wrench is regulated per phase. A pre task certificate decides whether a door can be opened without moving the furniture. Experiments on three cabinets and two supports with five operators (100 trials) measure the stability transparency trade-off and ablate the guard, RFCP and the position baseline. The mechanism is not door-specific: it applies to any body reacted by frictional contacts.

title: FilmTogether: Cinematic Video Generation from Low-Cost Inputs
abstract: The widespread adoption of mobile devices has democratized video recording, but a stark aesthetic divide persists between casual, low-cost captures and high-cost cinematic productions. Bridging this gap requires upgrading heterogeneous production elements, such as lighting, specialized costumes, and materials, without altering the core layout, identity, and temporal motion of the original footage. However, this task is heavily bottlenecked by two important challenges: 1) Lacking a high-quality paired training data specifically designed to handle complex low-to-high appearance shifts. 2) Ignoring the capacity of current video editing models to perceive and enhance the multiple low-cost compositions. To address these issues, we present CineCraft-120K, a large-scale dataset of aligned low- and high-cost video pairs annotated with pair-aware editing prompts. CineCraft-120K features a diverse, high-resolution and high-cost Cinematic Crafting bank spanning decades of media production, meticulously taxonomized into 5 broad domains and 23 fine-grained sub-categories.
