This gives a strict inclusion between the polar of the compact sets of uniqueness and the polar of the union of the classes $H^{(d)}$, answering a question raised in earlier work on these polars. The construction uses random binary increments of size comparable to the reciprocal of a product of square roots. A Gaussian sampling estimate gives a uniform Fourier-tail bound for all pseudomeasures supported by the resulting set, and also bounded atomic approximation and spectral synthesis. A separate energy estimate, stable under deletion of a small number of increments, yields full support for every limiting quasi-independent image of every positive measure absolutely continuous with respect to the constructed measure.

title: Projective relativistic dynamics from a quantum Lorentz algebra: time-dependent deformed Hamiltonians on (anti-)de Sitter spaces
abstract: A (non-standard) quantum deformation of the Lorentz algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)$ is used to construct novel time-dependent Hamiltonian systems on the (anti-)de Sitter spacetimes in $(1+1)$-dimensions. The specific deformation considered here contains, among others, the non-standard quantum deformation of $\mathfrak{sl}(2, \mathbb{R})$ and that of the `book' algebra $\mathfrak{b}_{2}$ as quantum subalgebras. The guiding idea is to apply the theory of Poisson--Hopf deformations of Lie--Hamilton systems to the Lorentz deformation, giving rise to a broad family of time-dependent deformed systems that share the same deformed Poisson--Hopf Lorentz algebra symmetry. In particular, this approach provides Hamiltonian vector fields expressed in terms of certain projective canonical variables, which, in turn, are related to the usual Beltrami variables via a canonical transformation. Under this construction, it is shown that the underlying Lorentizan spaces possess constant curvature $κ$ and the quantum deformation parameter $z$ can be identified with $κ$, such that the cosmological constant is $Λ=-z\equiv -κ$. Therefore, we deal with the anti-de Sitter, de Sitter and Minkowskian spaces for $z>0$, $z<0$ and $z=0$ (the undeformed case), respectively. Finally, as applications, we study time-dependent deformed oscillators on the (anti-)de Sitter spaces in detail, as well as time-dependent deformed Bateman and generalised coupled Caldirola--Kanai Hamiltonians.

title: On the Conditional Consistency of the Bootstrap
abstract: This paper focuses on the conditional consistency of the bootstrap. The target is the conditional law of a statistic given a common shock, and the bootstrap approximates it by the law of a resampled statistic conditional on the shock and the data. We call the bootstrap consistent if these laws are close in the Kolmogorov distance for almost every realization of the shock. The conditioning $σ$-algebras are allowed to be unrelated across sample sizes, and both the comparison law and the dimension of the data may vary with the sample size. We give sufficient conditions for consistency in this sense, show that they yield asymptotically correct conditional coverage for bootstrap quantiles, and provide a finite-sample bound on the coverage error. We also relate the Kolmogorov formulation to the merging of probability measures. The results are specialized to statistics depending smoothly on an estimator or on an estimated nuisance parameter.

title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
abstract: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

title: Modeling Visual Cortex with Layerwise Multiscale Manifold Capacity Maximization
abstract: Task-optimized deep neural networks have risen to prominence as the most predictive phenomenological models of responses in primate visual cortex, but leave much to be desired from the perspective of biological plausibility. One such limitation is the reliance on precise credit assignment through global backpropagation of error signals. Recent work has shown that this weakness can be circumvented by requiring each subsequent stage to solve a distinct and increasingly complex task, allowing for layerwise local learning signals. We propose a novel strategy for crafting such intermediate losses that uses an efficient coding framework formulated in terms of manifold capacity, and which can be computed using a sequence of {canonical cortical computations}. In particular, we leverage the relationship between the multiscale nature of visual signals and the dilation of receptive field sizes in cascaded visual representations to modulate complexity, allowing for the reapplication of these common loss computations at each stage of the hierarchy. We evaluate our approach on its ability to predict neural datasets spanning three areas of the ventral stream hierarchy in macaques, as well as human psychophysical data on an object classification task. We find that our unsupervised layerwise model matches or exceeds the performance of competitive architecture-matched baselines on all evaluations considered.

title: Direct and Indirect Competition in a Two-Prey-One-Predator System : Global Dynamics, Chaos, and the Paine Conjecture
abstract: This paper studies the global dynamics of a three-dimensional Lotka-Volterra system of two prey, with direct competition between them, and one predator. Under a symmetry assumption, the rescaled parameter space is sorted into four generic categories, which yield a complete classification of the global dynamics into 56 meaningful subcases. We determine the existence and stability of the boundary and positive equilibria, including global asymptotic stability and bistability of boundary equilibria, and necessary and sufficient conditions for local asymptotic stability of the positive equilibrium. We identify regimes of periodic solutions and chaos, including a period-doubling route to chaos. We further show that the parameters of Gilpin's chaotic dynamics fall within some cases. Biologically, we introduce the notion of extensive negative competition, which, together with trade-off competition and apparent competition, interprets the interactions among the three species. Our classification shows that the full system largely tracks the dynamics of the prey-only subsystem, and these competition mechanisms explain the differences between them, clarifying how predator-mediated interactions alter competitive outcomes and facilitate prey persistence, thereby providing mathematical support for Paine conjecture.

title: Omitting Types for Infinitary Real-Valued Logic: A Topological Perspective
abstract: For countable vocabularies, we extend the omitting types theorem for countable fragments of infinitary logic to Keisler's general real-valued structures by proving that the space of Henkin types of each such fragment is Čech-complete. The structures interpret function symbols arbitrarily and predicate symbols by bounded real-valued functions, while each formula carries a bound of its own. This extends the setting of Eagle's theorem from metric structures with a prescribed master metric to general structures whose vocabulary prescribes the sorts and bounds of the symbols. Following Keisler and Miller's treatment of logic without equality, we build models from closed terms. Morley's Baire category method then gives every satisfiable theory on a countable fragment a model with countable sorts omitting any countable family of types whose closed-term instances have empty interior in the space of Henkin types satisfying the theory.

title: Metamorphic Testing for Evaluating Robustness of Sentiment Analysis Models
abstract: Machine learning systems are challenging to test using traditional software testing methods because their behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly programmed. This challenge is particularly significant in natural language processing (NLP), where small input variations can lead to unexpected model behavior. Conventional evaluation metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, often fail to capture such inconsistencies. Metamorphic testing addresses this limitation by evaluating expected relationships between original and transformed inputs. With the increasing prevalence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and language-based AI systems, the need for systematic robustness testing has become even more pronounced. Motivated by this growing need, this paper presents a lightweight, batch-based metamorphic testing approach for evaluating the robustness of such systems. In particular, we consider sentiment analysis as a representative NLP task and evaluate a pretrained classifier under four transformations: synonym replacement, typo injection, word-order variation, and negation. Using consistency score, flip accuracy, and confidence change, we identify strengths in handling semantic variations and vulnerabilities to textual noise and logical transformations. These findings highlight the value of metamorphic testing in identifying behavioral inconsistencies beyond conventional performance metrics and demonstrate its potential as a systematic framework for evaluating the robustness of language-based AI systems and guiding performance improvements before deployment.

title: How the eigenvalue region of standardized Laplacians leaves the 2005 polygon
abstract: Let $Λ_n$ be the set of all eigenvalues of $n\times n$ standardized Laplacian matrices, and let $S_n\subseteqΛ_n$ be the polygon introduced in 2005, with upper vertices $λ_0=0,\dots,λ_{n-1}=1$. It is now known that $Λ_n=S_n$, and that $Λ_n$ is convex, if and only if $n\le4$. We study how $Λ_n$ leaves $S_n$ near an edge $[λ_m,λ_{m+1}]$, $2(m+1)<n$. First, we prove a switching law for matrices having a boundary point of $Λ_n$ as a simple eigenvalue: an explicit switching function on the arcs, built from the left and right eigenvectors and the outward normal, forces maximal weight where positive and zero weight where negative; intermediate weights occur only where it vanishes. Second, we perturb the weights of the arcs $k\to k+m+1$ in the circulant digraph (arcs $k\to k+s$, $1\le s\le m$, plus these arcs with weight $τ$) that realizes the point $λ_m+τ(λ_{m+1}-λ_m)$. At second order, the first Fourier harmonic of the perturbation moves the eigenvalue beyond the line of the edge if and only if $τ<τ^*_m=\sin(πm/n)/(2\cos(π/n)\sin(π(m+1)/n))$. For even $n$ and $m$, the point with $τ=τ^*_m$ is the vertex of $S_{n/2}$ lying on this edge, and digraphs with these arcs only at even $k$ give an explicit eigenvalue path that leaves $S_n$ at $λ_m$ and, in all computed cases, ends at this vertex. Third, we give a conjectural, numerically supported picture of $\partialΛ_5$: beyond each edge of $S_5$ not incident to $0$ or $1$, $Λ_5$ forms a cap bounded by four algebraic arcs, which leaves the edge tangentially at its endpoint adjacent to $0$ or $1$ and rejoins it at $τ^*_1=(3-\sqrt5)/2$; the rest of the edge lies on $\partialΛ_5$. In computations for $n\le8$, a cap returns to its edge smoothly at $τ^*_m$, at a corner at $τ^*_m$, or at a corner beyond $τ^*_m$.

title: Q-BWE: Quantum Chaos-Informed Speech Bandwidth Extension
abstract: High-frequency reconstruction in bandwidth extension (BWE) depends on joined interactions among nonlinear spectral, temporal, and perceptual features; assigning a separate discriminator to each such feature may be redundant and may fail to model their joint interactions. We introduce quantum-informed generative model Q-BWE, where we design a five-qubit Quantum Chaos Discriminator (QCD) instead of using separate discriminator for every features, for modeling nonlinear joined-feature interactions efficiently. Our QCD explores a compact five-qubit quantum-inspired inductive bias based on data re-uploading circuit, trainable controlled NOT (CNOT) rotations, quantum entangling gates, and statevector measurement map. Five features for five qubits are selected from a 26-dimensional speech-dynamics bank and are encoded by a two-layer statevector circuit, producing 31 measurements map of local behavior, correlations, mixedness, and Born entropy. QCD guides a Lattice-ConformerNeXt generator with FiLM conditioning and a cosine-masked residual pathway, while delayed-reward Thompson sampling adaptively controls its contribution. The circuit is simulated on classical hardware. Overall, Q-BWE achieves competitive performance on VCTK English, and MLS French datasets in multilingual and multi speaker setups under clean and noisy conditions across a broad set of evaluation metrics with approximately 1.72x fewer parameters (33.5M vs. 19.4M) compared to recent CIS-BWE baseline published in ACL.

title: Retrain, Alert, or Rollback? A Three-Response Decision Framework for Production ML Under Concept Drift
abstract: When a deployed model degrades under concept drift, an operator can retrain it, raise an alert and monitor, or roll back. Yet most drift-adaptation methods consider only retraining. We present RAR (Retrain-Alert-Rollback), a state machine that gives each response an explicit trigger and cost. Retraining is gated on drift detection, label availability, and measured degradation. Every retrained model must pass a two-stage canary before promotion, and corruption-triggered and quality-triggered rollbacks enter different hold states. Under a prospectively specified protocol we compare RAR with six baselines, including a cost-aware retraining policy, on 13 streams: eight real public streams and five semi-synthetic streams derived from them. RAR does not dominate. At low retraining cost, retrain-heavy baselines lead, and no policy's rank differs significantly from RAR's. At higher cost, RAR beats detector-triggered retraining, periodic retraining, and no response simultaneously on four streams, each within a bounded cost window. Its advantage over detector-triggered retraining is consistent with a latency-feasibility condition stated in advance. Against the cost-aware policy, results are heterogeneous. RAR retrains before true drift onsets one eighth to one third as often as detector-triggered retraining, but at lower net utility on most semi-synthetic streams. On H2's designated corruption stream (a registered follow-up), rollbacks fire yet RAR loses to retraining baselines. At $ρ= 1$, removing the canary, and thus rollback, raises utility on 11 of 13 streams. On a post-hoc follow-up stream, cause-specific hold release resumes adaptation where a single cooldown does not. We provide the harness, configurations, and per-cell results for reproduction.

title: $P$-stationary structural equation modeling: Causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations
abstract: Causal modeling of discrete-time processes often involves the assumption that the modeled processes are stationary. A general class of linear causal models for discrete-time stationary processes are structural equation processes (SEP), which generalize the well known structural equation model for i.i.d. observations. In this paper, we extend the SEP model from stationary to $P$-stationary processes, which are non-stationary processes whose $P$-periodically sampled subprocesses are jointly stationary. We will use this model to approach the problem of causal effect identification under temporally incomplete observations from a graphical modeling perspective. To have a notion of generic identifiability, we restrict our analysis to $P$-stationary structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) processes, which are SVAR processes whose underlying coefficients can vary $P$-periodically over time. Our findings allow to detect, in any given temporally incomplete observational setting, if a certain set of instrumental processes qualifies to identify a causal effect between $P$-periodic subprocesses, and if this is the case, that effect admits an explicit expression as a rational function evaluated at the observational spectral density.

title: Calibration-Constrained Diagnostics for Evaluating LLM Self-Evaluation
abstract: We introduce a reusable evaluation artifact for diagnosing whether LLM self-reported confidence can support confidence-gated act-or-defer decisions. The artifact is designed for evaluation rather than safety certification: it provides a black-box protocol, prompts, judge-reference labels, model outputs, reproduction scripts, and calibration-constrained diagnostic metrics for auditing LLM self-evaluation across math, factual, and commonsense reasoning tasks. Our central finding is that aggregate uncertainty summaries can produce deployment-misleading rankings: a model that appears strongest under standard aggregate calibration metrics can fail under category-level calibration constraints, while a model with worse aggregate calibration can exhibit stronger calibration-constrained behavior in the positive-margin region where high self-selection accuracy and tight calibration coexist. To expose this failure mode, we define PVC and C-PVC as category-level diagnostics over an accuracy-by-calibration surface: PVC counts categories whose self-evaluation accuracy exceeds a threshold, while C-PVC additionally requires category-level calibration error below a tolerance. We aggregate these diagnostics using Volume Under Surface (VUS) and a positive-margin restriction; they are VC/fat-shattering motivated but are empirical evaluation proxies, not literal VC-dimension estimates. Across 13 models and four benchmarks, the artifact shows weak confidence-correctness separation, stable diagnostic rankings under alternative categorizations and judge-label perturbations, and persistent positive-margin failures not captured by ECE or Brier score. Confidence-gated self-evaluation therefore requires calibration-constrained, category-level diagnostics, and we provide a reusable artifact for applying them under black-box access.

title: Partial Invariance for Classification under Structural Causal Models
abstract: Making predictions in an unseen environment from data collected across multiple training environments is challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the target-generating mechanism varies across environments. In this work, we introduce environment-label separation, a form of partial environmental invariance that decomposes the target conditional distribution into an environment-invariant component and a label-invariant component. We show that this partial invariance enables estimation of the target conditional distribution in an unseen environment when using labeled training data together with unlabeled test features. Within the structural causal model framework, we provide sufficient conditions for environment-label separation. Building on these conditions, we develop an algorithm, dIMP-Classifier, which jointly minimizes an estimate of the test risk and encourages invariance across environments. We further provide finite-sample guarantees that characterize the test risk in terms of deviations from invariance, estimation error, and sample complexity. Experiments on simulated data and the real-world light tunnel Causal Chamber data demonstrate that the proposed approach can perform under interventions on the target mechanism and consistently outperforms the considered standard and invariance-based baselines.

title: Multiclass Classification with Rare Useful Features: Fundamental Limits and the Optimality of Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding
abstract: We consider classification in high-dimensional feature spaces where only a vanishing fraction of features are useful and the number of classes may be large. While this rare-and-weak useful-feature regime is well understood in the binary setting, its multiclass version raises new questions: a feature can be useful for class discrimination without separating any specific pair of classes. We focus on a rare feature diversity model, in which most features are useless, but a small fraction promote discrimination among classes in a way that can be detected by a per-feature diversity test, such as one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal-Wallis test. For this setting, we propose Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding (DP-HCT), a feature-screening procedure that applies a higher-criticism threshold to the collection of p-values obtained from per-feature diversity tests. We justify DP-HCT under a Gaussian multiclass Rare-and-Weak Useful Feature model with class-mean contrasts of fixed magnitude in random directions, extending the binary model of Donoho and Jin (2008). When the number of classes is fixed, our model recovers the binary phase transition. When the number of classes grows logarithmically with the number of features, however, we derive a new and strictly harder phase transition, driven by the growing degrees of freedom and their effect on the useful-feature tail rate. We show that whenever classification beyond chance is possible, DP-HCT with ANOVA, followed by a simple classifier based on similarity to class means, achieves asymptotically perfect accuracy. Experiments on real multiclass classification benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, and numerical simulations confirm that the derived phase-transition curve accurately predicts the finite-sample behavior of DP-HCT in the growing-class regime.

title: Exact Shortest Paths and Maximum Flow in Planar Networks in the CONGEST Model
abstract: In the CONGEST model, exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) with nonnegative weights and exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks have both been solved in $\tilde O(D^2)$ rounds, where $D$ is the hop diameter, while the lower bound is $Ω(D)$. Given the approximate distance labels of a recent preprint (arXiv:2606.31192), which we use as a black box, we solve exact directed SSSP in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. It rests on a lemma that answers queries from a virtual source with the labels, and on a corrected discretization of the reduction of exact to approximate distances (arXiv:2210.16351). All further bounds of the form $\tilde O(D)$ and $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ use these labels. Through the reduction of arXiv:2303.00811, SSSP with negative weights, or the detection of a negative cycle, takes $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ rounds with high probability. We weight the face-disjoint graph of arXiv:2411.11718 so that its distances are dual distances, which turns distance problems in the dual into problems in a planar network of hop diameter $O(D)$. This gives exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks in $\min\{\tilde O(D^2),D\cdot n^{o(1)}\}$ rounds with high probability, and in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds with $s,t$ on a common face. In undirected planar networks, the value of a minimum $st$-cut and a minimum cut take $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. For this we repair the auxiliary graphs of arXiv:2608.09500 at $s$ and $t$, and we show that its recursion, as we read it, can miss the minimum cut, also with exact shortest paths: on a network with $11$ vertices it reports $37$ for a minimum cut of $15$. Two more shortest-path computations per level make it exact. The virtual-source lemma, the weighting of the face-disjoint graph and the corrected discretization are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib; all other arguments are proved on paper only. Numerical checks are not used in any proof.

title: The 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model for Occupational Safety and Health
abstract: This paper presents the 3-Tier Integrated Technology Risk Model, a progressive framework for Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) management that integrates Job Safety Analysis (JSA), dynamic risk assessment using leading and lagging indicators, and predictive analytics powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). The model provides organizations with a structured pathway to evolve from static, reactive safety practices to a sophisticated, predictive safety paradigm. Each tier builds upon the previous one, creating a comprehensive, data-driven approach that enables just-in-time training and preemptive risk mitigation.

title: Beyond Binary Detection: Type-Aware Hallucination Analysis and Hierarchical Detection in Financial Question Answering
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to answer questions over financial filings, where an unfaithful answer can mislead investment, compliance, or client decisions. Hallucination detectors are a common safeguard, but they are usually evaluated with a single binary score that reveals neither which kinds of errors analysesed nor why. This paper studies hallucination detection on PHANTOM, a long-context benchmark built from SEC filings, at the level of hallucination type. We first analyze 15,443 paired hallucinated and faithful answers without any detector and find that hallucinated answers are more than twice as long as faithful ones, and that lexical grounding separates the two classes only because faithful answers are bimodal. We then generate hallucinations in nine financially motivated categories, confirm each with a separate verification pass, and diagnose an LLM-based detector on 4,086 usable examples. Generation success varies from 66.3% to 100% across categories. The detector reaches 80.2% binary accuracy but only 44.7% subtype accuracy, never assigns two of the nine categories, and misses between 5.3% and 46.8% of hallucinations depending on category; these misses are unrelated to input length but rise with how far an answer departs from the correct one. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose a two-stage hierarchical detector that first decides whether an answer is hallucinated and then assigns a subtype, raising binary accuracy to 95.6% and subtype accuracy to 56.1%. The results show that type-level evaluation exposes detector weaknesses that aggregate metrics conceal.

title: Band Alignment of Grafted versus Directly Bonded Si/Ge Heterostructures
abstract: The electronic properties of semiconductor heterostructures are influenced by the local bonding and electrostatic environment at the heterointerface. Here, we investigate how the interface-formation mechanism modifies the band alignment of Si/Ge heterostructures by directly comparing Al2O3-mediated semiconductor grafting with direct bonding. Interface-sensitive X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy combined with Kraut analysis reveals type-I band alignment for both structures, but with different band offsets: the valence-band offset increases from ~0.08 eV for directly bonded Si/Ge to ~0.21 eV for grafted Si/Al2O3/Ge, accompanied by a corresponding reduction in the conduction-band offset. Raman spectroscopy further distinguishes the two interfacial configurations. The different core-level shifts and band offsets indicate that the electronic structure is sensitive to the interfacial bonding and electrostatic environment introduced by the two integration schemes. These results demonstrate that, even for an identical Si/Ge material pair, the interface-formation pathway provides an additional degree of freedom for controlling heterojunction band alignment, offering a route toward interface-engineered electronic and optoelectronic devices.

title: Towards a Theory for the Design of Rules in Multi-Agent Systems: the case of Homogeneous Fleets
abstract: The regulation of systems composed of many interacting decentralised agents is a long-standing problem. This problem has typically been resolved by the imposition of rules. Rules resolve the limitations of sub-optimal agents whilst simultaneously aligning the behaviour of the agents with the demands of society. Traffic laws, for example, let a driver cross a junction without seeing around the corner, and transport protocols such as TCP let applications share a network without knowing of one another. The problem is more pressing today, as autonomous systems are deployed in society. In this work, we establish the basis of a system-agnostic theory of rule design for multi-agent systems. We first state the rule design problem (RDP) in its generality. It relates a rule to the set of system performances, defined by the regulator, that the agents deployed under it can attain. However, it is not yet possible to solve the RDP in full generality. As such, we introduce the homogeneous rule design problem (HRDP), in which the agents in each environment are identical, and among other interesting properties, show that under worst-case aggregation the two problems have the same solution, bypassing the combinatorial complexity of the RDP. To solve the RDP under worst-case aggregation we propose Rule Branch and Bound (RuleBnB), an anytime branch-and-bound algorithm. Finally, we illustrate the value of solving the RDP on an autonomous driving case study.

title: Normality of closures of conormal bundles to Schubert cells for $\operatorname{GL}_n$
abstract: We prove normality of closures of the conormal bundle to certain Schubert cells in the flag variety for $\operatorname{GL}_n$ coming from Grassmannians. Our argument uses a Zelevinsky-type resolution of singularities, and through a sequence of cohomological computations based on the Borel--Weil--Bott theorem, we reduce normality to a problem about Kronecker coefficients, which we solve by applying results of Knutson and Tao from honeycomb theory.

title: Topological Acoustic Metamaterials with Synthetic Magnetism: Observation of Hofstadter Spectrum and Topological Edge States
abstract: Architected materials are increasingly used to implement topological dynamics, yet realizing the gauge fields and symmetries that protect the topology with purely passive elements remains the central practical challenge. Here we turn a previously proposed theoretical strategy into an integrated platform that accepts a theoretical model as input and returns a passive acoustic metamaterial with identical dynamics. We demonstrate it experimentally on the Hofstadter model at $θ= 2π/3$, fabricating a spin-Chern insulator whose two sectors carry Chern numbers $C_s = \pm 1$, and observe the predicted helical edge states.

title: Lieb-Robinson bounds for Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians via path expansions
abstract: We study the transport properties of Bose-Hubbard-type Hamiltonians. Kuwahara, Vu, and Saito proved sharp bounds on (i) particle transport and (ii) the Lieb-Robinson velocity for initial states with controlled boson density. We provide simpler and shorter proofs for both results using a new set of methods. For (i), boson transport, we use a class of weighted extended particle number operators that directly enables closing the associated differential inequalities. For (ii), the Lieb-Robinson bounds, we develop a bosonic version of the Chen-Lucas path expansion technique and recover the sharp velocity bound $t^{d-1}$ up to logarithmic corrections, where $d$ denotes the lattice dimension. We also extend the transport bounds (i) to long-range hopping with a power-law exponent $α>d$. The range $α\in (d,d+1)$ corresponds to an algebraic light cone for boson transport and has not been previously covered.

title: The Non-Abelian X-Ray Transform on Simple Asymptotically Hyperbolic Surfaces
abstract: We prove a gauge equivalence result for the non-Abelian X-ray transform with connection and Higgs field on simple 2-dimensional asymptotically hyperbolic spaces. Our approach is based on the construction of holomorphic integrating factors. To construct these, we analyze the geodesic X-ray transform on functions on simple asymptotically hyperbolic manifolds of general dimension and prove polyhomogeneous mapping properties and a surjectivity result for the adjoint.

title: The Verification Bottleneck
abstract: This paper studies how generative AI, by lowering the cost of research production, affects scientific verification in a general-equilibrium model of peer review. Privately informed researchers choose observable output, an editor optimally assigns review depth, and reviewers supply time according to its expected scientific contribution. Costly output helps screen research quality, and cheaper production lets weaker researchers imitate stronger ones more readily. Beyond a technological threshold, reviewer capacity and verified knowledge weakly decline even under optimal editorial decisions, and strictly when a screening constraint has positive shadow value. Reviewer withdrawal can amplify the loss. With observable quality, the same progress weakly increases both.

title: Nonpathological submeasures and $F_σ$ ideals
abstract: We study the relationship between nonpathological lower semicontinuous submeasures, $F_σ$ ideals on $ω$, and matrix summability ideals. First, we construct in $\mathsf{ZFC}$ a non-analytic ideal on $ω$ which is representable as an intersection of matrix summability ideals. Then, we show that an $F_σ$ ideal is nonpathological if and only if it can be represented as an intersection of summable ideals if and only if it can be represented as an intersection of matrix summability ideals. We also prove that the random graph ideal is pathological. Finally, we compute the exact degree of pathology of a certain submeasure related to a construction of Topsøe.

title: Overcoming Demand Censoring through Randomization for Risk-Sensitive Newsvendor Learning
abstract: We study online newsvendor learning with bounded demand, censored observations, and convex nonlinear shortage costs. Because stockouts can conceal the shortage magnitudes needed by gradient-based algorithms, we use randomized ordering to construct unbiased subgradient estimates. We characterize admissible randomization distributions within this framework and develop an online inventory policy that combines the resulting subgradient estimates with gradient-based updates. Our regret analysis quantifies the cost of randomization via the estimation variance and an additional loss term. We characterize the randomization distributions that minimize this objective. For piecewise-linear shortage costs, the optimal distribution is computed through a linear-time recursion; for costs with bounded curvature density, it is characterized by a scalar ordinary differential equation. The policy achieves expected regret of $O(T^{2/3})$ against the best fixed order in hindsight over $T$ periods. Under independent demand and suitable curvature of expected losses, the bound improves to $O(\sqrt{T})$. Matching minimax lower bounds establish rate optimality over the corresponding classes with a fixed marginal-cost bound. Both rates extend to nonperishable inventory under uniformly positive conditional expected demand. Numerical experiments on synthetic and retail data show improvements over alternative policies using censored observations.

title: Lattice-Induced Splitting, Connectivity, and Topology of Anyon Bands
abstract: Fractional Chern insulators realize fractional quantum Hall states without external magnetic fields, while their underlying lattice periodicity allows otherwise dispersionless anyons to acquire finite bandwidth. Here we show that flux--lattice commensurability can also give rise to multiple anyon bands with nontrivial topology and symmetry-protected connectivity. In multiband vortexable systems, commensurability between the lattice periodicity and the effective magnetic unit cell of fractionally charged quasiholes leads to the folding of a quasihole Landau level into multiple bands. Interactions lift their degeneracy, producing dispersive bands with Chern numbers distinct from that of the parent quasihole Landau level. We further demonstrate that these Chern numbers can be redistributed through Dirac crossings under continuous deformations that preserve exact electronic flatness, while crystalline symmetries can enforce protected band touchings. Our results establish that fractionalized excitations can exhibit the rich band topology familiar from electronic Bloch bands, opening possibilities for nontrivial anyon dynamics beyond conventional Landau-level physics.

title: Qubrio: High-Performance Quantum Compilation via Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an adaptable alternative to traditional quantum compilation heuristics, which bottleneck progress by demanding costly manual redesigns whenever hardware evolves. However, naive single-pass LLM approaches fail under the unique challenges introduced by quantum compilation. We introduce Qubrio, a practical agentic framework that significantly reduces heuristic redesigns through a three-level decomposition. By (1) partitioning programs into sequential operation stages, (2) deploying specialized agents for placement, routing and optimization, and (3) using disaggregated feedback for precise error correction, our system reliably navigates complex physical constraints. Beyond serving as a direct compiler, our LLM framework also uncovers novel strategies that facilitate convoy-style shuttling, substantially enhancing hardware concurrency without sacrificing fidelity. We further integrate these strategies into the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) compiler, recovering a significant fraction of the LLM's performance advantages. On realistic workloads, our compiler achieves significant improvements in hardware runtime and program fidelity over the SOTA baseline PowerMove, seamlessly adapting to new hardware capabilities. Qubrio features an open user interface for practical use, and its code is publicly available at https://github.com/crosaa/Qubrio.

title: Hinted Scaling Laws
abstract: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most $10^{20}$ FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a $10^{23}$ FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to $10^{22}$ FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

title: Current state of LLMs for Arabic dialectal machine translation
abstract: This work presents an evaluation of large language models (LLMs) for English to dialectal Arabic machine translation on the MADAR dataset. We evaluate both translation directions (English to Arabic and vice-versa) on 16 Arabic dialects. Our experiments cover a diverse set of models, including specialized Arabic models (Jais, Nile), multilingual models (Gemma, Command-R, Mistral, Aya), and commercial APIs (GPT-4.1). We employ multiple evaluation metrics: BLEU, CHRF, COMET (both reference-based and reference-less variants) and GEMBA (LLM-as-a-judge), as well as a small-scale manual evaluation, to assess translation quality. We discuss the challenges of automatic MT evaluation, especially in the context of Arabic dialects. We also evaluate the ability of LLMs to classify the dialect used in a text. The study offers insights into the capabilities and limitations of current LLMs for dialectal Arabic machine translation, particularly highlighting the difficulty of handling dialectal diversity, although the results may be influenced by possible training data contamination, which is always a concern with LLMs.

title: An Amplitudes Approach to Spinning Black Hole Scattering
abstract: The detection of gravitational waves has opened a new era of precision studies of gravity, demanding advances in our understanding of compact binary dynamics. Scattering amplitudes provide a powerful framework for studying these systems using methods from high-energy physics. In this thesis, we study classical black hole scattering, systematically including spin---an important feature of real astrophysical systems---to describe Kerr black hole dynamics. We model Kerr black holes as massive point particles in finite-spin representations and compute their scattering dynamics perturbatively. We resolve an ambiguity mixing classical and quantum contributions using our spin interpolation method, obtaining a classical amplitude for Kerr black hole scattering through quartic order in spin at third post-Minkowskian order. From this amplitude, we extract the gauge-invariant radial action, enabling the computation of classical non-aligned-spin observables---such as the linear and angular impulses---using covariant Dirac brackets. The amplitude exhibits spin-shift symmetry, remaining invariant under a shift of the black hole spin by the momentum transfer. Motivated by this property, we study the conserved quantities governing the scattering process and show that the dynamics of a probe black hole remains integrable at asymptotic infinity through quartic order in probe spin. Finally, we show that the quartic-in-spin radial action for a probe black hole in a Kerr background, at any order in perturbation theory, is completely fixed by the aligned-spin dynamics, provided that it satisfies asymptotic integrability and spin-shift symmetry.

title: When the Text Is Silent: Memory Shortcuts and the Validity of LLM Annotation under Evidence Insufficiency
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate text for social science research, content moderation, and training data. Their broad knowledge of real-world entities raises a concern: when labeling a text, do they rely on its evidence or substitute what they already know? We call this behavior a memory shortcut and examine when it emerges, what amplifies it, and how to mitigate it. Using 995 widely recognized public figures and four matched control names per figure, we construct counterfactual texts that separate textual evidence from prior knowledge, and evaluate three commercial LLMs on 121,594 prompts each across five stages. We find a striking asymmetry. Although all models recognize nearly every figure, none follows memory over the text when the two conflict. Shortcuts instead emerge when evidence is absent: for one model, famous names raise the rate of remembered occupations, ages, and countries by 17.0, 14.9, and 6.8 percentage points relative to synthetic names. These effects occur only for recognized figures, and 98.6% of the resulting labels are factually correct about the namesake while none is supported by the text. Evaluation threats and answer-contingent rewards amplify shortcuts by 8.7 and 12.4 points. Famous names also raise leadership ratings of sparsely documented applicants by 0.22 and 0.28 points in two models. A namesake reminder and name masking each eliminate the shortcuts, with trade-offs in gender annotation. LLM annotations can thus be factually correct yet methodologically invalid. Trustworthy LLM annotation requires audits that test evidence absence, account for incentives in annotation instructions, and evaluate the attribute-specific trade-offs of mitigation.

title: Invertible Graph Aggregation Can Increase ReLU Readout Width
abstract: An invertible graph aggregation preserves the complete feature table, but can increase the size of a classifier that reads one node at a time. For every even $N\ge4$, we construct a labeled tree with $2N$ vertices and maximum degree three. A shared one-hidden-layer rectified linear unit (ReLU) classifier needs one hidden unit on the raw scalar features and exactly $N$ units after one lazy neighborhood mean. All aggregate values are distinct, and the mixing matrix has condition number at most 8. We determine the complete error curve for heads with a free affine term. The width separation persists under scalar perturbations. Under a specified bounded uniform-noise model with one nuisance coordinate, every one-unit aggregate head has expected error at least $1/12$, while a fixed $N$-unit head has zero error. Controlled fits compare trained heads with these explicit feasible scores. On Roman-empire and Tolokers, aggregation improves fitted prediction, and retaining raw features helps at the largest tested parameter budget. Training-only diagnostics include conditional output-layer optimality bounds for eight fixed runs.

title: Data-Scarce, Multi-Granular, Multimodal: Benchmark Design for Biosynthetic Gene Clusters
abstract: Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) are co-located genes that encode the biosynthesis of specialized metabolites, an important source of antibiotics, anticancer agents, immunosuppressants, and agricultural bioactives. Deep learning, particularly self-supervised foundation models, has spurred interest in BGC sequence modeling, but evaluation has lagged behind: existing benchmarks often rely on coarse classification over small curated datasets, providing limited discrimination among models and insight into downstream utility. We propose a benchmark-design framework in which an informative benchmark should be discriminative, separating models with statistical confidence, and applicable, spanning scientifically meaningful tasks under different levels of generalization. We instantiate this framework as BGC-Bench, which derives five tasks from MIBiG, ranging from A-domain substrate prediction to BGC-molecule retrieval, evaluates them under genotype- and phenotype-shift splits, includes an active-learning setting for label-scarce discovery, and is easily extensible to new tasks and encoders. BGCs further provide a shared testbed across granularities and modalities: BGC-Bench compares twelve encoders on nucleotide, amino-acid, or Pfam-domain sequences, including compositional baselines for each input type, and combines BGC and chemical encoders for cross-modal retrieval. No single representation dominates: the best granularity depends on the biological scale of the task, and pretrained encoders do not consistently outperform other representations across tasks and splits. Active-learning experiments show that most tasks remain data-limited, encoder rankings change with labeling budget, and acquisition strategies yield modest gains. These results show that BGC model evaluation requires task-diverse, shift-aware benchmarks, and the framework can be generalized to benchmark design beyond BGCs.

title: Chirality-Induced Angular-Momentum Pumping by Moving Charges
abstract: Chirality-induced spin selectivity is established even in light elements at room temperature; dissipation and electron correlations are implicated, here combined in one mechanism. Injected electron wave packets coherently radiate chiral phonons; electronic absorption competing with phonon decay sets the fraction electrons receive and its temperature dependence. Spin-orbit coupling itself is not renormalized; it becomes effectively large because both the orbital and spin moments it couples are enhanced by Coulomb correlations.

title: Atom-Wise Allocation of Message-Passing Scale for Molecular Property Prediction
abstract: Molecular properties depend on chemical structure at different ranges, from local polar groups governing solvation to extended substructures shaping bioactivity, yet graph neural networks usually fix one propagation scale for every atom. We present PRISM (Per-atom Routing over Intermediate States of Message Passing), in which each atom's encoded features produce a bounded scalar that positions a unimodal distribution over retained message-passing states and matching circular-fingerprint radii. Because one coordinate translates the whole profile, allocated depth responds to the routing scalar in closed form: at fixed temperature it is nondecreasing, its sensitivity scales with the profile variance, and it saturates in the clipped regions. Beyond providing closed-form analyzability, this constrained one-parameter profile matches or significantly outperforms parameter-matched, unconstrained node-wise gates and Jumping Knowledge attention. Under scaffold partitions with equal tuning budgets against eight graph, fingerprint, and geometric baselines, PRISM trained from scratch without three-dimensional coordinates achieves the lowest mean error on aqueous solubility and hydration free energy and strong accuracy on BACE and BBBP. As a general layer-combination rule, PRISM transfers directly to GCN, GIN, and GAT backbones, reducing hydration free energy error by up to 29% relative to last-layer readout. Applied to a pre-trained GIN, it improves on last-layer readout on four of six endpoints and gives the lowest lipophilicity error overall. In trained models, allocated depth differs systematically between atom types in a task-dependent way, and permuting profiles among a molecule's atoms raises prediction error on several endpoints, so the rule acts as a learned counterpart of atom typing.

title: Concise-9B: Removing the Slack from a Reasoning Model's Thinking
abstract: Reasoning models answer better when they think longer, but a thinking trace keeps going well after its answer has formed. We measure this slack in Qwen3.5-9B and remove most of it with concise self-training: two rounds of on-policy rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keep the shortest correct samples, plus a small share of answer-synthesis targets, giving Concise-9B. On 8,983 held-out problems (competition and hard mathematics, SuperGPQA, a five-area confirmation set and MMLU-Pro), Concise-9B generates 0.66x the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B at a 32K thinking budget, with accuracy equivalent within +/-1 point (-0.20 [-0.77, +0.36] points). Forcing each trace on the hard and confirmation sets to answer every 2,048 thinking tokens, we find that 54-64% of Qwen3.5-9B's thinking tokens come after the point from which every forced answer equals the final one (41-48% for Concise-9B). Stopping there would keep every answer at 0.35-0.44x the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight: stopping when three consecutive forced answers agree costs the base model 2.4-9.2 points. Concise self-training removes slack without that cost: 86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed. It has a limit: with traces continued to 80K tokens, Concise-9B solves 25 fewer of 1,276 hard problems (-25 [-49, -1]), mostly in competition mathematics. The measurement also yields a cheap commit signal for adaptive sampling that matched two-sample escalation within +/-1 point at 0.67x its tokens in a pre-registered test. Results on Qwen3.5-4B, on which the recipe was developed, and a replication on Olmo-3-7B-Think suggest that the saving depends on how verbose the base model is.

title: An affine reverse Faber-Krahn inequality via information decay
abstract: We prove that every convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ admits $S\in\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{R})$ such that $λ_1(SK)|K|^{2/n}\le Cn$, where $C$ is universal. For origin-symmetric bodies of volume one, the bound holds in maximal Gaussian measure position. The main step is the spectral estimate \[ λ_1(D)\le C(P)\bigl(n+\sqrt{n I(ν\midγ_n)}\bigr) \] for an even isotropic log-concave probability measure $ν$ supported on a symmetric convex body $D$, with Poincaré constant at most $P$ and finite relative Fisher information. A second-order Stein estimate and an information jump under convolution give entropy decay faster than $m^{-1}$ for normalised sums. Their supports control the Gaussian measure of dilates, and a Brownian bridge expansion gives the spectral estimate. A Gaussian-weighted ground state supplies a measure whose Fisher information is bounded in terms of $λ_1(K)$. The square-root dependence then gives the bound of order $n$.

title: Deterministic Polynomial-Time Primality Testing with a Single Binomial Congruence
abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time primality test whose main verification is the congruence $(1+X)^n=1+X^n$ in $C_n[X]/(X^r-b(Y))$, where $C_n=(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})[Y]/(Φ_r(Y))$. Two identities in the coefficient ring normalize $b$ and ensure compatibility with the main congruence. A finite-field root count and a lattice bound show that an accepted input is a prime power; elementary preprocessing excludes nontrivial perfect powers. We construct $b$ deterministically using Jacobi sums and the uniform Dedekind-zeta zero-free theorem of Cureton and Thorner, which extends OpenAI's Hecke zero-free theorem. The total bit complexity is $L^{32+o(1)}$, where $L=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$, and verification after constructing $b$ costs $L^{6+o(1)}$. More generally, for a fixed real algebraic $1/2\leθ<1$, a common zero-free boundary $\Re s>θ$ for the relevant Dedekind zeta functions gives $L^{\max\{6,(1-θ)^{-1}\}+o(1)}$. This bound reaches $L^{6+o(1)}$ at $θ=5/6$, and hence under GRH. We state a fixed-base modification of Agrawal's conjecture for odd integers passing the base-$2$ Fermat test, using the modulus $X^r-2$ with $r$ the least positive integer not dividing $n(n-1)$.

title: Near-Quadratic Error-Free Graph Matching above Otter's Threshold via Approximate Local Tree Correlation Testing
abstract: This paper presents a near-quadratic-time algorithm that correctly matches almost all nodes of two correlated Erdős-Rényi graphs without any incorrect matches. Each graph has average degree $λ$ and its edges are subsampled from a common parent Erdős-Rényi graph with $n$ nodes, with subsampling probability $s$. The nodes of one graph are then relabeled by an unknown permutation. The algorithm is built on a test for correlated versus independent Galton-Watson trees with approximated likelihood ratios. For every constant $s>\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{Otter}}}$, where $C_{\mathrm{Otter}}\approx0.338$ is Otter's tree-counting constant, and every $λ=ω(1)$ with $λ=(\log n)^{O(1)}$, the algorithm outputs a partial matching of size $n-o(n)$ that contains no incorrect matches with high probability. If, in addition, $λs\ge(1+ε)\log n$ for a constant $ε>0$, a seeded completion step recovers the permutation exactly. In both cases, the time complexity of the algorithm is $n^{2+o(1)}$ with high probability, whereas previous polynomial-time algorithms with the same guarantees either have a time-complexity bound whose exponent goes to $\infty$ as $s$ approaches $\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{Otter}}}$ from above, or apply only when $s$ is close to $1$.

title: Unconditionally $L^2$-stable explicit--implicit--null filtered Runge--Kutta methods for general nonlinear degenerate parabolic equations
abstract: We develop unconditionally $L^2$-stable explicit--implicit--null (EIN) filtered Runge--Kutta (RK) methods for nonlinear degenerate parabolic equations with space-, time-, state-, and gradient-dependent diffusion coefficients. The methods are linearly implicit in the sense that they evaluate nonlinear terms explicitly and require only linear solves. Unlike classical EIN methods that are direct applications of implicit--explicit (IMEX) RKs, our construction is built upon explicit RKs. The key ingredient is two-sided symmetric filtering applied at each RK stage: a high-order filter is applied both before and after evaluating the original nonlinear residual. It leads to a dissipation estimate independent of the time step and retains the underlying RK order formally. Assuming time-dependent splitting operators with stagewise pointwise coefficient bounds, we rigorously prove non-increasing $L^2$ norm for arbitrary time steps. A quadratic matrix criterion covers explicit RK-based methods with positive weights, while strong stability preserving (SSP) compositions yield exact energy identities and weighted dissipation estimates. We present SSP methods through fourth order and a method based on the classical RK4. The framework accommodates spatial discretizations with discrete gradient structures including continuous Galerkin, Bassi--Rebay 1, the method of Brezzi et al., and local discontinuous Galerkin. Compatible summation-by-parts discretizations with simultaneous approximation terms are also covered in their discrete mass norm.

title: The Reference System Loophole
abstract: I argue that the Extended Wigner's Friend theorems have a `loophole' that has previously not been appreciated, coming from the fact that we typically need a reference system to give meaning to a measurement outcome. I show how this loophole can be used in the context of the Local Friendliness theorem to preserve the predictions of quantum mechanics without denying Local Friendliness, and I respond to some objections. I explain how the loophole arises naturally from consideration of relevant symmetry transformations, and then I appeal to the partial/complete observables formalism to argue that the same loophole will work for any type of Wigner's Friend experiment, even if it is performed with a variable that does not obviously look like it requires relativization to a reference system. Finally I compare the loophole to other possible responses to the Local Friendliness theorem, and I show that the same loophole will work for other Extended Wigner's Friend theorems too.

title: SVD-Prune: Spectral Vision Token Pruning under Extreme Compression
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models process hundreds of visual tokens, making visual representations a major computational bottleneck. We argue that visual token pruning should be formulated not as identifying individually important tokens, but as preserving the dominant low-rank spectral structure of the visual representation. Based on this formulation, we introduce SVD-Prune, a training-free framework that leverages Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and statistical leverage scores for globally informed token selection. SVD-Prune is architecture-agnostic and can be applied at different stages of the multimodal pipeline, including encoder-side, decoder-side, and hybrid configurations Extensive experiments across VLM and VLA benchmarks demonstrate strong robustness under extreme compression. SVD-Prune reduces the visual token. SVD-Prune cuts the visual token budget by up to 99.3%, while, at a 16-token budget, encoder-side pruning lowers inference FLOPs by 82.4% and achieves a 4.18x end-to-end speedup, including pruning overhead.

title: Modern Software Engineering with Verification Agents: A Spec-First Architecture for Autonomous Synthesis, Verification IRs, and Organizational Scale
abstract: When autonomous coding agents synthesize implementation code, formal specifications, and mechanical proofs simultaneously, the software engineering hierarchy inverts: the formal specification becomes the primary human-reviewed artifact, while source code and proof scripts become disposable build outputs. This paper presents an end-to-end architecture for agent-authored, formally verified software engineering. First, we establish a logic-agnostic foundation combining a spec-first stack inversion, a zero-code-review workflow gated by automated continuous integration (CI) checks, and a minimal Verification Intermediate Representation (VIR) lowered via a thin, verified translator. Second, we pair an extensional Computational Type Theory (CTT) specification layer with Higher-Order Abstract Syntax (HOAS) and linear resource typing in the VIR--eliminating rewrite friction for synthesis agents while defining an experiment, its protocol frozen before the first reader, to measure whether removing boundary coercions improves human specification readability. Third, we scale collaboration across multi-team organizations using Personal Spec-Copilots and a Shared Synthesis Fleet that detects cross-team Semantic Merge Conflicts and fuses modular contracts into zero-copy binaries. We illustrate this architecture on a zero-copy authenticated message router and distinguish our existing empirical baselines (salt, SaltBench, x86lean, and MetaPRL) from newly proposed components.

title: Toward Agentic AI-Ready Workflows in Built Environment Organizations: Knowledge Structures and Interoperability Challenges
abstract: The rise of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) in the built environment is shifting attention from isolated AI tools toward autonomous systems that reason, plan, and act across project and organizational workflows. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on large language model capabilities, but also on the readiness of heterogeneous data environments across the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. These environments combine structured sources, such as CAD and BIM models, schedules, cost databases, and asset registers, with unstructured ones, including technical reports, design narratives, planning and policy documents, contracts, meeting minutes, and risk registers. This paper reviews how built environment data can be organized to support agentic AI-ready workflows, focusing on knowledge structures, interoperability, and access and integration mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Drawing on existing literature, it examines approaches proposed to organize structured and unstructured data and considers how such data can be contextualized and made accessible to AI agents in a reliable manner. The paper synthesizes current perspectives, highlights challenges around fragmentation and interoperability, and identifies open questions for future research on AI-compatible information management in the built environment.

title: Faster graphic matroid parity: Breaking the $nm$ time complexity barrier
abstract: In the graphic matroid parity problem, we are given an undirected multigraph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices, together with a partition of $E$ into $m$ pairs of distinct edges, and the goal is to find a maximum-cardinality collection of pairs whose union is a forest. This problem generalizes both graph matching and graphic matroid intersection. Graph matching admits the celebrated $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}m)$-time algorithm of Micali--Vazirani~[FOCS'80], and graphic matroid intersection admits $o(nm)$-time algorithms due to Gabow--Stallmann~[ICALP'85] and Gabow--Xu~[FOCS'89]. In contrast, for graphic matroid parity, Gabow--Stallmann~[FOCS'84 \& Combinatorica'86] gave an $O(n^2 m)$-time algorithm, and its $\tilde{O}(nm)$-time implementation by Gabow--Stallmann~[ICALP'85] had long remained the best known bound, except in very dense regimes where $m=ω(n^3)$, in which case the algebraic $\tilde{O}(n^4)$-time algorithm of Cheung--Lau--Leung~[SODA'11 \& TALG'14] is faster. We present a randomized $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2} \sqrt{m} + \sqrt{n} m)$-time algorithm for graphic matroid parity. This is the first algorithm to break the $O(nm)$-time complexity barrier for this problem outside the very dense regime. Moreover, it improves over the previous bounds except in very sparse regimes where $m=\tilde{O}(n)$ and in very dense regimes where $m = \tildeΩ(n^{3.5})$. In particular, when $m=Θ(n^2)$, our algorithm runs in $\tilde{O}(n^{2.5})$ time, which nearly matches the $\tilde{O}(n^{2.5})$-time bounds of Micali--Vazirani for graph matching and of Gabow--Xu for graphic matroid intersection in this regime.

title: Charge-Balanced Control of Linear Systems: Controllability, Stabilizability, and Periodic Regulation
abstract: Electrical neuromodulation is a therapeutic approach that regulates neural activity by delivering electrical currents to brain tissue to treat brain disorders, such as epilepsy and Parkinson's disease. A critical safety requirement is charge balance, which ensures zero net injected charge over each stimulation cycle. Despite its clinical importance, the implications of charge-balanced stimulation for system dynamics and control remain poorly understood. This article investigates the controllability, stabilizability, and regulation of discrete-time linear systems under charge-balanced input constraints, motivated by applications in electrical neuromodulation. We introduce novel notions of charge-balanced controllability and stabilizability and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for both properties. We further demonstrate that nonzero steady states cannot be maintained under charge-balanced inputs, motivating the introduction of charge-balanced periodic orbits as alternative control targets. We characterize the conditions under which convergence to such orbits is achievable and develop optimal feedback controllers to stabilize the origin and track optimal charge-balanced periodic orbits. Finally, we validate the proposed control framework using a Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model, demonstrating successful suppression of tonic spiking and highlighting the potential of our approach for controlling nonlinear dynamical systems.

title: Thirty years of primordial deuterium abundances: A provenance-aware statistical reanalysis
abstract: (ABRIDGED:) Primordial deuterium provides one of the most precise observational tests of Big Bang nucleosynthesis, yet the published literature is built on a comparatively small number of high-redshift absorption systems. We construct a provenance-aware database of 957 published primordial-D/H values from 247 publications spanning 1994--2026 and trace observational entries, wherever possible, to their underlying physical absorbers. Of the 795 observational entries, 80.1 percent represent reused individual or compilation values; only 11.4 percent correspond to new determinations of individual absorption systems. Although 52 distinct absorbers are identified overall, the eight most frequently represented systems account for 62.0 percent of all identifiable absorber mentions. An inverse Herfindahl--Hirschman measure applied to our full database gives an effective representation equivalent to only 16.28 equally represented absorbers, demonstrating that the published literature is strongly concentrated around a much smaller effective subset. Despite this strong internal dependence, the modern consensus value of $10^5({\rm D/H})\simeq2.5$ is robust to alternative absorber-level treatments and survives removal of the eight dominant systems. However, the apparent precision of literature-level compilations is more sensitive to repeated representation than a simple count of published values implies. We also identify a synchronised transition in the compilation literature around 2013--2014, associated with increasingly selective and homogeneous analyses while older individual values continued to circulate. The modern D/H consensus is therefore robust in central value, but the underlying literature is less statistically independent than its publication density suggests. This thus highlights the importance of provenance-aware analysis in precision cosmology.

title: Monotonicity and bounded variation for harmonic mappings with applications to special functions
abstract: We investigate sufficient conditions for the close-to-convexity and univalence of planar harmonic mappings. First, we establish a unified monotonicity criterion for harmonic mappings that incorporates the ordinary and odd harmonic cases. We then develop a criterion based on the total variation of successive coefficient differences. Unlike conventional monotonicity conditions, this approach allows the coefficient sequences to exhibit non-monotone behavior. Several previously established criteria for harmonic close-to-convexity are recovered as particular consequences. Applications are developed for harmonic mappings associated with Gaussian hypergeometric functions and Legendre polynomials, with explicit restrictions on their parameters.

title: Probing non-adiabaticity in a quantum Otto cycle through quantum texture and imaginarity
abstract: Finite-time driving in quantum thermodynamic cycles inevitably generates coherences in the instantaneous energy basis, leading to quantum friction and degrading the operational performance. In this work, we demonstrate that the non-adiabatic inner friction produced during unitary driving of a two-level system can be faithfully quantified by combining two distinct resource-theoretic notions: quantum texture (rugosity) and imaginarity. We show that neither rugosity nor imaginarity alone is sufficient to track the total non-adiabaticity, and we introduce a combined witness, which is strictly non-negative and vanishes if and only if the driving is quasi-static. Applying this framework to a finite-time quantum Otto refrigerator, we establish an exact closed-form relation connecting the coefficient of performance directly to the quantum texture and imaginarity, evaluated at the end of the unitary compression and expansion strokes. Furthermore, we show that local minima of the non-adiabatic witness accurately identify the operating regimes that maximize cooling performance. Our findings provide a geometric and resource-theoretic foundation for inner friction, offering practical diagnostic tools for optimizing finite-time quantum thermal machines.

title: Why Good Experience Can End Joint Activity
abstract: Learning a partner's preferences through joint activity can make both partners worse off than receiving no feedback from the activity. We study a responder who values the partner's payoff but bears a cost when joining is attributed to personal interest. Both partners observe noisy evidence of whether the responder wanted the activity, available only after participation. Evidence of interest raises this cost, discouraging joining on unwanted days; joining only on wanted days would then be too revealing to sustain. With choices based on current payoffs, we derive a condition under which learning can end participation without ever making stopping beneficial to either partner. Feedback accuracy and preference persistence described by couples' diaries satisfy this condition at baseline payoffs. Once activity stops, no further evidence arrives and the belief that the responder generally wants the activity stays fixed, so waiting may never restore it; preference information available without participating can. A separate forward-looking model with highly persistent preferences shows why this remedy can also reduce joint welfare. When participation reveals preferences exactly, a responder may accept at a current loss to establish a lack of interest, making acceptance less revealing and so sustaining participation on wanted days. Free daily revelation outside the activity removes this incentive. At the model's baseline, it lowers the best joint value in monotone Markov equilibria with exact participation feedback, but raises it with feedback as weak as the diary's.

title: Small-time controllability of affine systems and quadratic Lie brackets
abstract: We prove a new sufficient condition for small-time global exact controllability of finite-dimensional control-affine systems. It points out that, under a natural Lie algebra rank condition, quadratic Lie brackets are the only possible obstacles to controllability. This result extends to infinite-dimensional settings such as the global approximate controllability of diffeomorphisms. It also allows us to interpret recent results in PDE control theory.

title: Two teams that cancel: a didactic analysis of a teaching progression for signed numbers from Grade 5 to Grade 7
abstract: Signed numbers make learners revise what addition, subtraction and the minus sign meant for whole numbers. This paper presents the design rationale and a critical analysis of a three-level source progression for signed numbers (Grades 5-7, nominal ages 10-13), from which French-curriculum and International Baccalaureate chapters published at https://commeunjeu.org are assembled. One representation is presented first and taken up throughout: an integer is drawn as a collection of positive and negative units, a positive and a negative unit forming a zero pair that leaves nothing. An integer therefore has many drawings, which makes visible the construction of the integers as classes of pairs of natural numbers. The design hypothesis is that the gesture pupils perform with the units, inserting a zero in the form a + (-a), is shared by the subtraction of a negative number, by the worked examples that accompany the 2026 French programme, and by the derivation of the sign of a product of two negatives through distributivity; the progression does not model that product, it derives it from the zero pair, a derivation that holds only if distributivity is kept. The number line supports position, order and distance; contexts provide applications. The choices are related to the epistemological obstacles described by Glaeser, to studies of counter and number-line models, including a classroom comparison in which a path model gave better results than chips, immediately and five weeks later, and to the French and IB curricula. A block-level audit of the dated source documents found the representation absent from the first level, no exercise asking pupils to draw, and the decisive subtraction never drawn; the revisions made after the audit are recorded. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses for one are stated.

title: On the exponential Diophantine equation $\left(P_{n}^{(k)}\right)^{x}+\left(P_{r}^{(k)}\right)^{x}=P_{m}^{(k)}$
abstract: The Pell numbers satisfy $P_n^2+P_{n+1}^2=P_{2n+1}$, and Bravo, Luca and Pomeo recently found all the cases in which the sum of the $x$-th powers of two consecutive $k$-generalized Pell numbers is again a $k$-generalized Pell number. We ask what happens when the two indices are arbitrary, that is, we solve $\big(P_n^{(k)}\big)^x+\big(P_r^{(k)}\big)^x=P_m^{(k)}$ in positive integers $k\ge2$, $n\ge r$, $m$ and $x$. The answer is that nothing new appears: apart from $1^x+1^x=2$, every solution has consecutive indices. The proof combines linear forms in logarithms with an auxiliary Fibonacci equation which does not depend on $k$, and, for large $k$, with the fact that the dominant root of the sequence is very close to $φ^2$. For the reduction step, the method of Dujella and Pethő fails for large indices and has to be replaced by a criterion of Legendre type.

title: Shallow data-loading circuits for multivariable functions
abstract: We construct shallow QROM, diagonal block-encoding, and quantum state preparation oracles for analytic functions on the $D$-dimensional hypercube $[0, 1]^D$. On $n$ qubits and with $2^{- Ω(n/D)}$ error, these circuits have depths of $O \left( \sqrt{\frac{n \log_2 (n)}{D}} \right)$ in the Clifford + $T$ gate set, albeit using $2^{O(\sqrt{nD \log_2 (n)})}$ ancilla qubits. This is a near-quadratic depth reduction compared to known linear-depth methods.

title: FactorSpec: Serving Exact Relational Constraints as Speculative Drafts
abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM serving by drafting tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, and its gain grows with the drafts the target accepts. Structured outputs should be an ideal case, because much of a record follows from relations among its fields: an itinerary's days follow from its cities' stays and flights. Serving engines, however, draft such text by proposing it from the prompt or a learned head, and their grammar masks enforce only syntax, so the model must satisfy the relations, which it violates: on NATURAL PLAN's trip problems, Qwen3-8B writes a valid itinerary for 10%, and retries that name the violated relation raise this to 14%. We present FactorSpec, which serves exact relational constraints as speculative drafts. FactorSpec compiles a JSON Schema and its relations into a factor graph with an exact feasibility check, drafts every token the constraint determines as certain, verifies each request at a width chosen for it, and computes the masks in worker processes outside the scheduler while the GPU runs. In SGLang, its drafts yield up to 10.5 tokens per verify step, up to 1.9x those of the fastest n-gram drafter, and it decodes up to 1.43x faster than speculators tuned per load, at a grammar mask's cost; it also leads in vLLM. Because every record is also valid, it serves up to 13.9x the valid records per GPU-second of syntax-only baselines.

title: Improved criteria for geometric properties of confluent hypergeometric functions
abstract: In this paper, we establish sufficient conditions for several geometric properties of confluent hypergeometric functions. Using differential subordination techniques, we derive parameter conditions ensuring lower bounds for the real part of the confluent hypergeometric function and sectorial subordination of its derivative. We also obtain criteria for strong convexity and strong starlikeness of prescribed order. In addition, we investigate the close-to-convexity and starlikeness of the confluent hypergeometric functions. Particular cases yield corresponding results for generalized Laguerre polynomials. The obtained criteria are compared with existing sufficient conditions, and their implications for the geometric theory of special functions are discussed.

title: On the exponential Diophantine equation $\left(P_{n+1}^{(k)}\right)^{x}-\left(P_{n-1}^{(k)}\right)^{x}=2P_{m}^{(k)}$
abstract: For the Pell numbers one has $P_{n+1}-P_{n-1}=2P_n$ and $P_{n+1}^2-P_{n-1}^2=2P_{2n}$. We look for all the solutions of $\big(P_{n+1}^{(k)}\big)^x-\big(P_{n-1}^{(k)}\big)^x=2P_m^{(k)}$ in positive integers $k\ge2$, $n$, $m$, $x$, where $P^{(k)}$ is the $k$-generalized Pell sequence. We prove that for $k=2$ the two identities above give all the solutions, and that for $k\ge3$ the only solutions are $(n,m,x)=(1,1,1),(1,2,2),(2,2,1)$. In contrast with the analogous equation for $k$-generalized Fibonacci numbers, there are no parametric families of solutions.
