Part IV separates information attribution, subspace geometry, statistical dependence, and decision-theoretic discrimination for collective systems. Part V evaluates the role and limits of the GSVD across the cognition loop. Part VI covers numerical practice, including a tested reference implementation. Every number printed in this document was verified in double precision. Where a statement is an assumption rather than a theorem, it is labelled as such.

title: Finite Recovery by Extrapolation for the Douglas--Rachford Method on Affine Subspaces
abstract: We completely describe the dynamics of the Douglas--Rachford (DR) method for solving affine subspace feasibility. We characterise the affine hull of the resulting iterates, and we show how the corresponding search space's dimension is an explicit function of the number of distinct nontrivial principal angles. This dimension can be much smaller than the ambient dimension, helping to explain why extrapolation can be so effective. Using this characterisation, we extend the Lyapunov surrogate method (LSM) to higher extrapolation orders and prove that it recovers the DR limit exactly from finitely many iterates. We show that LSM and a least-squares extrapolation (LeSE) share the affine search spaces used by the generalized minimal residual method (GMRES) applied to the DR fixed-point equation (DR-GMRES). The dimension characterisation gives bounds on the number of steps required for exact recovery by all three methods. We develop adaptive implementations that estimate the search-space dimension from differences between successive DR iterates and use this estimate to select the extrapolation order. Numerical experiments show how ill-conditioning affects recovery accuracy, and we identify cases where adaptive extrapolation runs faster than DR-GMRES.

title: 3L-D: A Low-Light Level Dataset from a Sensor-Agnostic, Alignment-Preserving Acquisition Framework
abstract: Supervised low-light image and video enhancement has achieved remarkable progress, yet current models remain fundamentally constrained by the limitations of existing datasets. Prevailing methods typically rely on uncontrolled ambient captures, camera parameter manipulation (e.g., exposure or ISO adjustments), or neutral density filters, failing to replicate authentic night-sky near-infrared spectral content and genuine low-photon noise distributions. Furthermore, capturing dynamic paired sequences without introducing warping artifacts or sensor-specific biases remains an open challenge. In this paper, we introduce 3L-Dataset, a physically calibrated low-light image and video dataset generated using a modular, sensor-agnostic acquisition framework. Our test bench faithfully reproduces the standardized Midavaine night level scale from Level 1 (full moon, approximately 1000 mlx) down to Level 5 (overcast moonless night, approximately 0.1 mlx), spanning the visible to near-infrared spectrum across diverse realistic environments, including countryside, forest, urban, and desert scale models. Using high-precision programmable mechanical actuation, our acquisition framework guarantees sub-pixel spatial alignment across synchronized sextuplets, each composed of one reference image and five corresponding images acquired at the five standardized night levels, without post-processing image warping. We evaluate multiple representative deep learning baselines across varying night levels, revealing critical trade-offs between reconstruction fidelity, perceptual quality, and inference latency under severe photon starvation. The modular acquisition framework can be adapted to different cameras, optical systems, sensor technologies, and resolutions, enabling the dataset to be continuously expanded.

title: Protection challenges and solutions on power systems towards 100% inverter-based resources and energy storage systems
abstract: The decarbonization of the energy sector, driven by the Paris Agreement and the European Green Deal, is increasing the share of renewable energy sources (RES) in power systems. Unlike traditional systems, RES-based systems rely on power electronic converters, which creates unprecedented challenges for reliability and resilience. The future power system is expected to combine a low-level AC layer with an upper-level High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) backbone, which requires new understanding of fault protection, stability, and interaction between AC and DC components, as well as new models and simulation tools. This is especially critical in systems moving towards 100 percent converter-based generation. Protection systems detect, locate, and isolate faults to protect assets while the rest of the system keeps operating. Traditionally, they rely on the large fault currents supplied by synchronous machines. In modern systems, converter controls limit the fault current contribution to about 120 percent of rated current, so relays that distinguish faults from normal overcurrents based on current level may operate incorrectly. In addition, inverter-based resources (IBR) may not inject enough negative and zero sequence current for directional relays to work properly, and converters hold the voltage at a fixed value only within their reach, beyond which it drops quickly. As a result, existing protection schemes may not provide the expected accuracy and reliability. This report reviews the protection challenges identified in recent academic literature for power systems with high shares of converter-based resources. It covers the specific characteristics of RES, the challenges for protection with intelligent electronic devices (IED), the challenges of converter control during faults, and the main solutions proposed in research over the last decade.

title: Two Fast Radio Burst Candidates Detected in the RATAN-600 Blind Survey
abstract: We report the detection of two single dispersed pulses with widths of about 6.7\,ms and 15.6\,ms and flux densities of about 0.8 and 1.7\,Jy. These were found in a blind survey of two circular regions (Dec$\;=+22^{\circ}$ and $+5^{\circ}$,RA: 0--24~h) at high radio frequencies \mbox{(4400--5000\,MHz)} using four 4-channel filter radiometers (central frequencies of 4475, 4625, 4775, and 4925\,MHz) spanning a total frequency bandwidth of 600\,MHz. The survey was carried out with the Western Sector antenna of the RATAN-600 radio telescope, which had an effective area of 1200\,m$^2$ in~2017--2025. The total area of the survey was about 1500~square degrees, and each pointing of the antenna lasted one year. We consider these to be two rare, high-frequency FRB events (MJD~58614.38257 and MJD~58659.62482), detected with estimated dispersion measures of $200\pm20$ and $266\pm10$\,pc\,cm$^{-3}$ at a final signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) level of 8--9 after additional optimal filtration. After subtraction of the estimated dispersions within the Milky Way, we estimated redshifts of approximately 0.09 and 0.13, respectively, using the traditional equation: ${\rm DM}\,[{\rm pc~cm}^{-3}] = 1000\,z$ for the intergalactic medium. The estimated isotropic energies of the FRBs are equal to $10^{40}$\,erg and $2\times 10^{40}$\,erg, respectively. To effectively detect single pulses, we applied machine learning methods using a neural network trained on synthetic FRB pulse profiles.

title: GeoGuesser Bench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Agents on Interactive Geolocation
abstract: Vision-language model (VLM) agents that act in the open world need two abilities: world knowledge to interpret what they see, and exploration to find what they cannot yet see. We study how agents combine the two through interactive visual geolocation. GeoGuesser Bench contains 282 tasks in an offline Street View environment where agents rotate, zoom, and move between real panoramas. Its three task types shift the balance from knowledge to exploration: agents (1) report the coordinates of their starting location, (2) name the enclosing street, city, state, or country, or (3) find, read, and count nearby objects. The coordinate tasks in (1) also include 42 real GeoGuessr World Championship rounds, whose expert guesses provide a human reference. We evaluate 23 VLMs: the best accuracy is 62.5% on place naming and 35.0% on object finding, and the best agent averages 4352.4 GeoGuessr points on the championship rounds, against 4770.3 for the better expert in each round. Beyond these headline numbers, world knowledge and exploration are only weakly correlated across models: agents that localize well do not necessarily explore well. To understand where agents fail, we categorize their errors into vision, navigation, and tool-use failures. Further ablations show that the strongest agents, such as Claude Opus 4.8, still perform well with limited views, while weaker agents degrade; customizing the environment thus adjusts task difficulty. The environment's verifiable rewards and restorable state also support training, and our Planner-Worker-Compressor harness cuts planner tokens by 57-61% by compacting the interaction history. We hope GeoGuesser Bench and its environment serve as a high-quality foundation for simulating real-world exploration at scale.

title: Right Ranking, Wrong Scale: Reproducing the Robotic World Model's Dynamics Model and Testing the Uncertainty of Its Follow-up
abstract: We reimplement the dynamics model of the Robotic World Model (RWM) and test the uncertainty estimate that its follow-up, RWM-U, uses to penalize reward in offline policy optimization. Our implementation matches the released model's gradients. On held-out data, training on the model's own rollouts beats one-step training at the preregistered long horizon for all ten episodes, but loses on short one-step windows. RWM-U's ensemble disagreement ranks rollout errors better than forecast step (Spearman rho = 0.90 at 100 steps), yet its spread substantially understates error: one-sigma coverage on the released checkpoint is 4.6% at 100 steps, versus 68% for a calibrated Gaussian. Rolling ensemble members on their own predictions raises coverage to 33%. The implemented squared-error loss on sampled predictions drives each member's variance toward zero. A horizon-specific rescaling restores one-sigma coverage under leave-one-episode-out evaluation, but not two-sigma coverage. We also identify two defects in the released evaluation pipeline. The study covers one robot, one gait and one dataset; it trains no policy.

title: Keep on growing or change direction? Dependence of clonal plant survival on the probability of side-branching
abstract: In clonal organisms, the genetic individual (genet) may consist of several physiological individuals (ramets). Clonal plants typically grow horizontally by means of stolons or other clonal growth organs. Some species grow linearly for several ramet generations, while others produce side branches frequently. We hypothesize that the probability of side-branching ($b$) affects genet survival ($G$) depending on the ramets' ratio of birth to death rates ($λ$). We used a spatially explicit model of ramet population dynamics to compare three growth strategies. In the neutral case, growing forward and side-branching were equally probable, whereas forward-growing and side-branching plants had lower and higher $b$, respectively. We found that the genet's survival threshold (the critical $λ_c$) strongly depended on the branching probability. The lowest threshold, and hence the broadest range of survival, occurred in moderately forward-growing plants, in which the average length of linear (non-branching) intervals was $1.89$ units. Above the threshold, the $G(b)$ relationship strongly depended on $λ$. Genet survival was promoted by forward growth in sparse ramet populations (low $λ$). However, this advantage gradually disappeared as $λ$ increased, and branching probability became effectively neutral across a broad parameter range encompassing both forward-growing and side-branching plants. This suggests strong selection for low branching intensity in unfavorable habitats, but weak or negligible selection in favorable habitats.

title: Estimates for Ratios of Low-Order Eigenvalues of the Laplacian with Muckenhoupt Weights on Euclidean Domains
abstract: We study low-order eigenvalue ratio estimates for the Laplacian with Muckenhoupt $A_2$ weights. For weights bounded above and below, we prove a universal upper bound for $λ_2/λ_1$ with constant $1 + \frac{4}{n}\,\frac{C}{c}$, linear in the ratio of the weight bounds, and recover the classical Payne-Pólya-Weinberger bound as a special case. For radial decreasing weights, we prove that the ball maximizes $λ_2/λ_1$ among domains of equal volume, assuming that an admissible radial test function exists (Definition 5.8) and that on the ball the second eigenvalue is attained by the $l=1$ mode. The argument adapts the method of Ashbaugh--Benguria to the weighted setting via a weighted Chiti comparison theorem and a monotonicity property of the admissible radial test function (Definition 5.8). Higher-order eigenvalue ratios are estimated in terms of the $(n-1)$-Hausdorff measure of the boundary, under an explicit balance condition on the weight at the covering scale. The generalized Payne-Pólya-Weinberger conjecture for eigenvalue sums remains open in general; conditional results are presented for restricted families of domains.

title: Fine-Grained Complexity Across the Computational Phase Transition
abstract: How does a computational problem transition from easy to hard? In the hard-core model, approximate counting and sampling are polynomial-time tractable up to tree uniqueness, but worst-case intractable at any constant relative distance above it unless $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$. We quantify the transition from polynomial to exponential mixing for classical Glauber dynamics. On $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $d\ge3$, at fugacity $λ=(1+δ)λ_{\mathrm c}(d)$ with sufficiently small $δ\ge0$ that may vanish with $n$, its worst-case mixing time has the form $\exp\{Θ(nδ^2/d)\}n^{1+Θ(1)}$. The upper bound is degree-uniform, and the matching lower bound holds for every fixed $d$. Annealing gives approximate counting with the same running-time upper bound at fixed accuracy. For general sampling and counting algorithms, we establish a robust fine-grained reduction from SAT without assuming a lower bound on SAT's running time. For any fixed $d\ge3$ and $0<γ<1$, a sampling or approximate-counting algorithm running in $\exp\{O((nδ^2/d)^{1-γ})\}\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time along any one suitable inverse-polynomial distance sequence $δ=δ(n)$, yields a randomized SAT algorithm running in $\exp\{\widetilde O(s^{1-γ})\}$ time on inputs of binary length $s$. This power-saving transfer identifies $nδ^2/d$ as the analogue of SAT input length for hard-core sampling and counting at relative distance $δ$ above criticality: beating the Glauber exponent by a fixed power through any sampling or counting method would yield a corresponding power improvement for SAT. At criticality, we establish $O(\sqrt{n/d})$ spectral independence, optimal in $n$ at fixed degree, and degree-uniform Glauber mixing in $\widetilde O(n(n/d)^{1+1/(d-2)})$ time, improving the previous $\widetilde O(n^{4+4/(d-2)})$ bound.

title: Competing interaction driven broad magnetic entropy distribution in triangular net compounds \text{Ba$_3$RE(BO$_3$)$_3$}, RE= Dy and Ho
abstract: Triangular magnetic lattices have attracted significant attention as a model platform for exploring frustrated magnetism and quantum spin liquids, particularly in rare-earth-based systems. These materials also hold considerable promise for cryogenic magnetic refrigeration. In this work, we investigate the magnetic and magnetocaloric properties of the rare-earth (RE) based compounds $\text{Ba}_3\text{RE}(\text{BO}_3)_3$ ($\text{RE} = \text{Dy}$ and $\text{Ho}$). Polycrystalline samples synthesized via a solid-state reaction method crystallize in a hexagonal structure with the space group $P6_3mc$, featuring triangular nets separated by approximately $8.8~\textÅ$ along the $c$-axis. Detailed magnetic investigation reveals a deviation from pure paramagnetic behavior at low temperatures ($T < 20\text{ K}$). This is further corroborated by isothermal magnetization measurements, which exhibit non-overlapping $M$ vs. $H/T$ plots and reduced magnetization moments, suggesting significant crystal electric field (CEF) splitting of localized $f$-states. For an applied magnetic field change of $70\text{ kOe}$, the maximum entropy change (Relative Cooling Power) reaches $4.2\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ ($204\text{ J kg}^{-1}$) and $7.3\text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ ($230\text{ J kg}^{-1}$) for the Dy- and Ho-based compounds, respectively. Overall, the positive slopes of Arrott plots, the universal scaling behaviour of $ΔS_{\text{m}}/ΔS_{\text{m}}^{\text{max}}$ versus reduced temperature ($t$), and the field exponent $c$ of the RCP versus $H$ curves indicate a second-order nature of entropy distribution, making them promising candidates for magnetocalorics in the millikelvin range.

title: Beyond Answers, Traces, and Efficiency: Evidence for Adaptive Reasoning
abstract: Current AI systems are evaluated as reasoners through final-answer accuracy, reasoning traces, process supervision, and computational or human-relative efficiency. Yet these measures do not establish whether reasoning adapts when tasks or evidence change. We distinguish across-task adaptivity, where acquired abstractions transfer or recombine across novel problems, fromwithin-task adaptivity, where hypotheses and actions are revised in response to new observations, feedback, or counterexamples. Using ARC-AGI as a diagnostic case study rather than an alignment benchmark, we examine what existing measures leave unresolved when test-time search, sampling, or adaptation affects performance. We propose intervention-oriented evaluation that tests abstraction transfer and hypothesis revision under controlled changes to tasks and evidence, with explicit reporting of test-time procedures and budgets. This perspective supports evaluating systems for robustness, responsiveness to corrective feedback, and auditability under changing conditions.

title: Rose: Efficient Embodied RL through Graph Optimization and GPU Compute Resource Control
abstract: Embodied reinforcement learning (RL) coordinates policy inference, simulation, and model training with highly heterogeneous resource demands. Although individual components frequently underutilize GPU compute during execution, existing systems only overlap work at coarse component boundaries (e.g., pipelining inference and simulation across simulator groups), leaving substantial low-activity GPU windows within subcomponent phases and nested loops. Exploiting these fine-grained windows manually requires tedious dependency analysis and workload-specific coordination. Furthermore, even when independent work is scheduled concurrently, cross-process GPU time slicing and streaming multiprocessor (SM) contention can negate the benefits of overlap. We present Rose, a runtime-aware system that automates fine-grained overlap and GPU resource management for embodied RL while preserving synchronous training semantics. Through a lightweight programmable interface that exposes execution hierarchy and state accesses, Rose tracks runtime data readiness and GPU activity to perform a two-stage optimization. First, a window-guided graph optimizer identifies low-activity windows and applies graph transformations to overlap complementary work across components and loop levels. Second, leveraging NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) for cross-process GPU concurrency, a slack-aware resource manager tunes process-level SM quotas by exploiting branch synchronization slack to mitigate interference on the critical path. Both stages combine local profiling with end-to-end iteration validation to guarantee throughput gains with minimal tuning overhead. Across diverse policies, simulators, RL algorithms, and GPU platforms, Rose achieves 1.20--1.92$\times$ training throughput improvement and increases average SM activity by 23.8--39.3\% compared with the state-of-the-art systems.

title: Hindsight Credit Assignment over Trees for Agentic RL
abstract: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon LLM agents faces a fundamental dilemma: successful experiences are essential for policy improvement, yet limited policy capabilities make such experiences difficult to discover. Sparse outcome rewards compound this challenge, leaving sampled trajectories with little relative feedback for learning. In this paper, we propose TriGRPO, a tree-based reinforcement learning framework that turns scarce successes into exploration and learning signals through hindsight credit assignment within and across rollout trees. TriGRPO constructs rollout trees through hindsight-guided branching: when an ongoing trajectory reaches a matched decision state, a successful action discovered during rollout initiates a sibling branch that continues autonomously, enabling further exploration and parent-sibling comparisons. Three complementary groups organize policy optimization over these trees: root groups capture within-prompt relative returns, node groups assign credit from parent-sibling outcome differences, and cross groups supplement sparse feedback with historical performance on related tasks. Experimental results demonstrate consistent gains in task performance and rollout efficiency across model scales, highlighting structured hindsight credit assignment as an effective approach to long-horizon agent learning.

title: Weighted Sobolev regularity and failure of profile convergence associated with the scattering operator for the three-dimensional cubic Klein-Gordon equation
abstract: The scattering problem for the three-dimensional nonlinear Klein-Gordon equation \begin{align*} u_{tt}-Δu+u=\pm u^3 \end{align*} is studied. It was shown that the scattering operator $\mathbf{S}$ for the equation is well-defined on a neighborhood of 0 in the Sobolev space $\mathcal{H}^{1/2}:=H^{1/2}(\mathbb{R}^3) \oplus H^{-1/2}(\mathbb{R}^3)$, and that if $Φ_-$ is sufficiently small in $\mathcal{H}^{1/2}$ and belongs to $\mathcal{S} \oplus \mathcal{S}$, then $\mathbf{S}Φ_-$ is also in $\mathcal{S} \oplus \mathcal{S}$, where $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ is the Schwartz space. In the present paper, however, we prove that for any non-zero real-valued $Φ_-\in\mathcal{S}\oplus\mathcal{S}$ whose $\mathcal{H}^{1/2}$-norm is sufficiently small, the corresponding solution $u$ satisfies \[ U(-t) \,{}^t(u(t),\partial_t u(t)) \not\to \mathbf{S}Φ_- \quad(t\to+\infty) \] in the weighted Sobolev space $H^{1,3}(\mathbb{R}^3)\oplus H^{0,3}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ although $U(-t)\,{}^t(u(t),\partial_t u(t))$ converges to $\mathbf{S}Φ_-$ in $H^{1,σ}(\mathbb{R}^3)\oplus H^{0,σ}(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for any $σ<3$. Here, $U(t)$ denotes the free Klein-Gordon evolution group.

title: Mathematical and Numerical Analysis of Tsunami Generation and Propagation: The Initial Tsunami Condition
abstract: This work investigates the appropriate initial condition for tsunami propagation that allows replacing a kinematic system with its corresponding static formulation, where the bottom is fixed at its final earthquake-induced deformation. Using the two-dimensional (2D) nonlinear shallow-water equations (NSW) and a 2D dispersive $abcd$-Boussinesq system, we prove that for the NSW system, the appropriate initial free-surface condition is exactly the final bottom deformation. For the Boussinesq model, this condition is obtained by first applying a \textit{ Boussinesq filtering operator} to the bottom profile. Furthermore, for both models, we establish an error estimate between the kinematic and static solutions that depends linearly on the earthquake rise time. This result provides a rigorous mathematical explanation for the errors observed in previous numerical tsunami simulations. As a direct consequence, the error vanishes as the bottom motion becomes instantaneous. We validate the theoretical results using an Okada solution for the seabed deformation. In particular, both the NSW model and the passive approach, which initializes the free surface with the unfiltered bottom deformation, overestimate the amplitudes of the tsunami waves relative to the linear potential theory for the configurations considered.

title: Sequence-to-Sequence Refinement for EEND-VC Diarization with a Shared Encoder
abstract: End-to-end neural diarization with vector clustering (EEND-VC) separates local segmentation from global speaker assignment, leaving speaker confusion (SC) despite strong segmentation. We propose shared-encoder sequence-to-sequence (S2S) refinement, which reuses DiariZen's self-supervised learning (SSL) representations for speaker-conditioned decoding and prior-constrained assignment. We study frozen-feature refinement with WavLM and structurally pruned w2v-BERT 2.0, and extend the latter to joint training of local segmentation and refinement heads. The heads learn separate layer mixtures while their losses update one acoustic encoder. Across eight domains, frozen-feature refinement reduces macro diarization error rate (DER) from 12.95% to 12.40% with WavLM and from 12.35% to 12.08% with w2v-BERT 2.0, with relative SC reductions of 17.4% and 14.6%. It adds approximately 15% to system real-time factor. The joint system further lowers macro DER to 11.90%, improving seven of eight domains over non-joint refinement. Error decomposition separates SC-driven refinement gains from detection-driven joint-system gains.

title: MicroMouse: Masking Harmful Supervision in Long CoT via Relative Potential
abstract: Even successful long CoTs may contain harmful supervision, motivating the need for methods that can automatically identify and mask such signals during SFT. Inspired by the MicroMouse maze-solving process, we view a long CoT as a search trajectory from the input problem toward the target answer. This perspective motivates maintaining a goal-relative measure, analogous to a MicroMouse's spatial coordinates, to quantify how close the current reasoning state is to the target answer. Building on this perspective, we propose MicroMouse, an automated selective-SFT framework for masking harmful supervision in long CoTs. In MicroMouse we introduce a Relative Potential (REP) to measure how closely each reasoning state supports the gold answer. Unlike the perplexity of the gold answer alone, REP measures relative support by contrasting the gold answer with a matched foil. This contrast cancels likelihood variations shared by the pair, yielding a more stable signal of progress toward the target answer. By tracking the REP trajectory, MicroMouse identifies consecutive potential decreases as erroneous exploration and post-peak reasoning as redundant wandering, and masks these harmful supervision during SFT. Extensive experiments across multiple student model scales and reasoning benchmarks show that MicroMouse consistently outperforms Full-CoT SFT and existing selective-SFT baselines, yielding average relative gains of 5.5% in greedy accuracy and 2.6% in Pass@1 relative to Full-CoT SFT. Meanwhile, MicroMouse improves reasoning efficiency by reducing average output length by 8.8%, while identifying harmful supervision in only 1.7 seconds per long CoT on average.

title: Human-Supervised Artificial Intelligence Researchers in Electric Power Systems: Knowledge, Physics, Simulation, and Governance for Large Language Models
abstract: Conclusions in power-system research require a clear evidential basis. Researchers need to understand the data sources, modelling assumptions, and solution procedures to assess the conditions under which a conclusion holds. Large language models (LLMs) can help researchers extract information from documents and translate research requests into code and tool calls, but their outputs still require physical validation. Focusing on human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) researchers, this review examines power-system LLM applications and related scientific workflows, together with physics-grounded power AI studies, to discuss the conditions for using LLMs in scientific research. In the proposed knowledge-physics-simulation-governance framework, LLMs translate information and coordinate tasks, simulators and validation tools test models, and experts retain authority over critical assumptions, safety boundaries, and final conclusions. Research processes should preserve materials for review so that claims can be traced to their sources, computations can be reproduced, and failed attempts and approvals can be examined. On this basis, a staged development roadmap and requirements for research reporting are proposed. Evaluation should focus on research artifacts and their validation to assess whether LLMs can improve the efficiency of power-system research within clearly defined permissions.

title: Semiprime Rigidity and Growth along Powers in Integer-Sided Cyclic Polygons
abstract: For a positive integer $n$, let $a(n)$ be the largest number of sides of a simple cyclic polygon of circumradius $n$ whose side lengths are positive integers. For primes $p,q$ we show that $a(pq)\in\{6,8,18\}$ and characterize each value by conditions on Gaussian and Eisenstein integers. For every integer $N\ge2$, on the other hand, $a(N^e)\to\infty$ and $\limsup_{e\to\infty}a(N^e)/e\ge2\sqrt2$; a quadratic chord tower combined with Farey neighbors gives explicit polygons, for instance $a(8192)\ge38$. We also show that an odd-sided polygon of radius $n$ exists if and only if $n$ has a prime divisor congruent to $1\pmod4$, and that $a(n)$ is even whenever at most one distinct prime divisor of $n$ is congruent to $1\pmod4$; it is also even when the Gaussian part of $n$ is the product of two distinct primes congruent to $1\pmod4$. Moreover, $a(N^e)=O_N(e^{ω(N)})$ for every fixed $N\ge2$, and $a(q^e)=Θ(e)$ for primes $q\equiv1\pmod4$; exceptional semiprime extremisers have unique side-length multisets. The proofs use a splitting lemma for angle relations by squarefree class, arithmetic in imaginary quadratic fields, bounded zero-sum problems, and a one-dimensional Farey argument. No computer-assisted step is used.

title: A Bayesian quantile mixed model for bounded discrete outcomes
abstract: Quantile regression for longitudinal bounded integer outcomes must accommodate discreteness, finite support, and dependence within participants. We develop a Bayesian quantile mixed model using a discrete Kumaraswamy distribution parameterized through a smooth quantile anchor whose ceiling gives the corresponding integer quantile. Covariates and correlated Gaussian participant effects enter a logit predictor for the scaled anchor, while a separate regression models distributional shape. Posterior computation combines a conjugate Gaussian coefficient update, available for compatible fixed and random effect designs, with slice sampling and covariance interweaving. Simulations showed small biases in regression coefficients and generally near-nominal coverage of 95% credible intervals. An application to repeated cognitive scores illustrates covariate associations across separately fitted quantile levels. Posterior predictive checks captured broad distributional patterns.

title: Triangle Relation Planar Algebras: Cohomology, Classification, and New Families
abstract: We establish a finite system of consistency equations for triangle relation planar algebras. Within the Yang--Baxter relation class, we characterize triangle relations by $H^2(K;\mathbb C)=0$, where $K$ is the fusion complex recording the support of the fusion coefficients. Together with a reconstruction theorem, this gives an algebraic classification procedure. We classify bi-commutative triangle relation planar algebras with $\dim P_{2,\pm}\leq5$. In ranks two, three, and four, the classification yields respectively $2$, $7$, and $19$ realizable fusion-support pair strata, up to relabelling and shading reversal. These results recover the low-rank examples of Bisch, Jones, Liu, and Lu, and extend the rank-four classification beyond exchange relations. In rank five, we obtain two one-parameter families with different duality types whose generic members do not arise from representations of groups or quantum groups.

title: MURFormer: Attention-Based Lightweight Multi-Scale Uncertainty-Guided Refinement Framework for PPG Denoising
abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a widely used physiological signal for its convenience but is highly susceptible to motion artifacts that degrade waveform quality and limit downstream analysis. This paper proposes MURFormer, a lightweight multi-scale uncertainty-guided refinement framework for PPG denoising through noisy-to-clean PPG mapping. MURFormer employs a newly proposed Multi-Scale Attention-Conv Fusion (MACF) block, which is designed to efficiently capture multi-scale temporal dynamics of PPG, as the fundamental building block and performs uncertainty-guided two-pass refinement prioritizing unreliable regions. The method was evaluated on the publicly available CIME dataset and on a Daily Activities dataset collected in this work, comprising paired noisy-clean PPG recordings from 24 subjects. Experimental results show that MURFormer improves both signal quality and physiological fidelity over the raw noisy input, yielding 129\% and 105\% relative signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvements, and 66\% and 81\% relative reductions in heart-rate mean absolute error (MAE), on the Daily Activities and CIME datasets, respectively. MURFormer also outperforms an existing denoising baseline on both datasets with a relatively small parameter count while preserving beat-level timing and waveform morphology. In addition, the model maintains strong denoising performance across varying input window lengths, suggesting that MURFormer is an effective and robust framework for practical PPG denoising. The implementation of MURFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/k-hram/MURFormer.git

title: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk: Semiparametric estimation and inference
abstract: Conditional expectile-based value-at-risk (EVaR) has attracted increasing attention in financial risk management owing to its desirable theoretical properties. However, existing estimation methods for conditional EVaR either rely on potentially misspecified parametric models or suffer from the curse of dimensionality in nonparametric approaches. To this end, we study semiparametric estimation and inference for conditional EVaR in nonlinear time series models with unspecified error distribution. Specifically, we propose a two-step conditional EVaR estimator that achieves the parametric convergence rate. Furthermore, we derive a functional central limit theorem for conditional EVaR process, and then extend to investigate estimating both conditional expectile-based expected shortfall and conditional distribution. A residual bootstrap procedure is proposed for non-expert practitioners to conduct statistical inference. The asymptotic results and their applications are illustrated by numerical studies and an empirical application to S\&P 500 returns.

title: Universal Curve Counting in Calabi-Yau 4-folds
abstract: Recently, Pardon introduced a universal curve counting framework, which allows him to show that curve counting on 3-folds is "generated" by local curves (in a precise sense). We implement this universal curve counting program for Calabi-Yau 4-folds, where a significant technical difficulty comes from the dependence of the virtual dimension on the genus, which leads to more complicated generators than just local curves. Our main techniques are combinations of deformation-theoretic and homotopy-theoretic methods with an adaptation of Pardon's generic transversality results, which allow us to establish a full set of (computable) generators for CY4 curve counting. As a result, we prove (a slight correction of) the Gromov-Witten/Pandharipande-Thomas correspondence with primary descendents for CY4-folds, formulated by Cao, Maulik, and Toda. From this, we additionally obtain integrality of Gopakumar-Vafa style invariants for CY4-folds, as conjectured by Klemm-Pandharipande.

title: A counterexample to Lee's conjecture on pseudo-Einstein structures
abstract: In 1988, J.~M.~Lee conjectured that a compact strictly pseudoconvex CR manifold admits a pseudo-Einstein contact form if and only if the real first Chern class of its holomorphic tangent bundle vanishes. The necessity of this condition was proved by Lee. We show that the condition is not sufficient: in every real dimension $2n+1\ge 5$ there is a compact connected strictly pseudoconvex CR manifold $M$ with $c_1(\Tone)=0$ in $H^2(M;\Z)$ which admits no pseudo-Einstein contact form. The examples are boundaries of small strictly pseudoconvex neighborhoods of a section $D\cong B$ with negative normal bundle in a $\PP^1$-bundle $\PP(E_e)\to B$, where $B=C^n$ is a power of a curve of genus two and $E_e$ is a non-split extension of $\cO_B$ by an ample line bundle $L$ with $K_B\cong L^2$. More generally, if $K_B\cong L^m$, such a boundary admits a pseudo-Einstein contact form if and only if $(m-1)e=0$, where $e\in H^1(B,L)$ is the extension class; the obstruction is detected on the first infinitesimal neighborhood of $D$.

title: A counterexample to a three-step convergence bound for BFGS with exact line search
abstract: We disprove a three-step error estimate for the Broyden--Fletcher--Goldfarb--Shanno {(BFGS)} method with exact line searches. We construct a globally strongly convex function $F\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and a single nonterminating trajectory $x_k\to0$ for which $\limsup_{k\to\infty}\|x_{k+3}\|/(\|x_{k+2}\|\|x_k\|)=+\infty$. The Hessian of $F$ lies between $\tfrac12 I$ and $\tfrac32 I$ everywhere, and $F(x)-\tfrac12\|x\|^2$ is compactly supported with all derivatives vanishing at $0$. The proof first constructs point-gradient pairs satisfying the exact BFGS step identities. A five-step cycle produces a large three-step quotient and restores an invariant plane for the actual updated matrix, allowing the cycle to be repeated with arbitrarily small gradient errors. Disjoint smooth corrections to a quadratic then realize all the pairs by one objective. Strong convexity identifies the prescribed points with the unique exact line-search minimizers. Thus smoothness and strong convexity do not imply the proposed product estimate, even for an objective that agrees with a quadratic to every order at its minimizer.

title: Inverse optimization for divisor methods of apportionment
abstract: The apportionment problem is to allocate a fixed number of seats among regions in proportion to their populations. In this paper, we propose an inverse optimization approach to evaluate how fairly an observed apportionment treats each region. It is well known that every divisor method can be formulated as a separable discrete convex minimization problem. We introduce a weighted divisor method, in which a nonnegative weight is assigned to each region, as the forward problem. Then we formulate an inverse optimization problem that finds the weight vector closest to the all-one vector in the $\ell_1$-norm such that the observed apportionment is optimal for the forward problem. We show that the optimal weight vector is always unique and has a closed-form expression as the median of three values that depend on a single parameter. Based on this result, the inverse optimization problem is reduced to a one-dimensional monotone equation, and it can be solved in $O(n \log n)$ time, where $n$ is the number of regions. We also apply the proposed approach to the apportionment of the single-member districts of the House of Representatives of Japan.

title: IssueLighter: An Issue Type-Aware LLM Agent for Issue Report Validity Assessment
abstract: Invalid issue reports are prevalent in open source software (OSS) projects, imposing substantial burdens on maintainers who already face a high risk of burnout. Prior research has primarily focused on identifying invalid reports for specific issue categories (e.g., bug and wontfix), leaving the broader landscape of OSS issue types largely unexplored and limiting the generalizability of existing approaches. Moreover, existing methods provide little support for explaining or validating their predictions, reducing their practical usefulness for maintainers. With the rise of LLM-based agents, it remains unclear whether a comprehensive understanding of the causes of invalidity across all issue types can improve validity assessment performance while producing well-grounded rationales. To this end, we first manually annotated the validity status of 520 issue reports from three OSS projects, i.e., pandas, scikit-learn, and mypy, resulting in 257 invalid reports and 263 valid ones. Then, we conducted a thematic analysis on these invalid reports and identified 13 causes of invalidity that are closely specific to issue types. Based on these insights, we propose IssueLighter, an agent-based framework with a type-aware validity assessment strategy that dynamically executes commands. Experimental results show that IssueLighter consistently and substantially outperforms all baseline methods, with an average F1 improvement of over 20 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm that both the type-aware strategy and the taxonomy of causes of invalidity contribute to the performance gains. Qualitative analysis further demonstrates that IssueLighter generates rationales grounded in accurately identified causes of invalidity and supported by evidence. Moreover, leveraging these rationales, we challenged maintainers' original decisions in four disputed cases, and all received approval.

title: The Staged Pandora's Box: Reservation Indices for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
abstract: A staged search must decide which candidate to advance next and when to stop. Some observations only inform later decisions; others can be kept as results. We formulate these choices as a staged Pandora's box with a designated set of collectable stages. For independent finite-stage candidates with bounded readings and positive bounded own-history costs, an exact covered-call recursion gives the reservation index, the optimal value and the loss of every advance or stop; advancing an index-maximal candidate while its index exceeds the incumbent is optimal. The representation recovers classical single-stage search, nested inspection and the all-collectable Markov setting, and prices changes in the problem: enlarging the collectable set or lowering costs raises the value by an explicit covered-call overshoot. Resumption can be valuable even when future reward laws do not change, but has no value for deterministic readings. With information sharing across candidates, no rule using only their separate remaining-reading laws is universally optimal, and making an intermediate reading collectable can change which candidate is inspected first. Under a coherent joint path law with own-history costs, an approximate-planning bound controls the recomputed index's regret by changes in untouched candidates' local values; a common-component specialization bounds those changes through predictive total-variation dispersion. Exact finite-law experiments check the representation, the loss accounting and the bounds.

title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VI. Surface diffusion on a nonmetal-terminated surface
abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate surface diffusion of adsorbates on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs (-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb (-1-1-1) surfaces. The mixed coverage consists of Ga adatoms in the first layer with a nonmetal atom attached above them forming a triangular-based pyramid. The pyramidal structures are stable during surface jumps involving rotations around one of the basal Ga adatoms. Thus, the diffusion proceeds via rotation (pivot) of the pair of the other basal Ga adatoms around an immobile Ga adatom moving them into new, originally empty sites. Using an energy-path determination procedure, the diffusion barriers were obtained as the difference between the initial site energy and the activated complex state energy. The detachment energy of the NM adatom was obtained assuming a final state in atomic and molecular form. The energy barrier for detachment to the atomic state is high for all atoms, on the order of 5 eV. For the molecular state these barriers are different: smaller for nitrogen, on the order of 1 eV, which is related to the high dissociation energy of the N2 molecule. For P and As the barrier is above 2 eV. For Sb it was not determined. Accordingly, the surface diffusion length is macroscopically large, indicating that all NM adatoms arrive at the steps.

title: All-Disorder Localization for the One-Dimensional Anderson Model with Power-Law Hopping
abstract: We consider the one-dimensional random operator \[ (H_{λ,ω}u)(n) = \sum_{m\ne n}\frac{u(m)}{|n-m|^r} +λω_nu(n), \] where the random variables $ω_n$ are independent and uniformly distributed on $[-1,1]$ (i.e., \mbox{$ω_n\stackrel{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}[-1,1]$}). For every $λ>0$ and $r>3/2$, we prove that $H_{λ,ω}$ almost surely has pure point spectrum and admits an orthonormal eigenbasis $\{ψ_j\}$ satisfying \[ \sum_{n\in\bbZ}(1+|n|)^{2τ}|ψ_j(n)|^2<\infty \qquad \text{for every }j\text{ and }0\leτ<r-\frac32. \] These conclusions establish spectral localization, thereby rigorously confirming the prediction of earlier analytical and numerical studies in the physics literature, which identified $r=3/2$ as the marginal exponent.

title: AffToM: Benchmarking Recursive Affective Theory of Mind in Dynamic Multi-Party Interactions
abstract: Understanding emotion in realistic social interactions requires more than recognizing facial expressions or assigning affective labels. The same event can elicit different emotions depending on what each participant knows, what they believe others know or feel, and how these nested mental states evolve over time. Existing benchmarks largely study higher-order epistemic Theory of Mind (ToM) and multimodal emotion reasoning in isolation, leaving recursive affective reasoning under asymmetric and dynamically changing information underexplored. Therefore, we introduce AffToM, a benchmark for affective ToM with 1,922 test pairs and 19,759 training pairs. AffToM evaluates Individual Affective Reasoning (IAR), which infers emotions from events and socio-cognitive context, and Multi-party Affective Reasoning (MPAR), which recursively tracks participants' nested beliefs and emotions as new evidence emerges. We develop an event-driven multi-agent generation pipeline grounded in dynamic character interaction graphs that explicitly capture event sequences, interpersonal relations, and mental-state updates. Furthermore, we propose AffToM-R1, a two-stage post-training framework combining supervised fine-tuning with perspective-aware rubric-guided reinforcement learning. Experiments show that MPAR remains challenging, with even the strongest evaluated MLLM achieving less than 60% accuracy, while AffToM-R1 improves MPAR accuracy by 13.38 percentage points over its base model. Our dataset is available at: https://github.com/MindIntLab-HFUT/AffToM.

title: Attention Residual U-Net for Enhanced Cross-Dataset Polyp Localization in Endoscopy
abstract: Precise localization of pathologies in endoscopy is a critical task in medical imaging, with deep learning (DL) frameworks now serving as the primary methodology for automated lesion detection. Today, generic object detection methods, such as YOLO, provide state-of-the-art performance in this context. However, their robustness often decreases under real-world clinical conditions due to variations across endoscopic devices, intestinal content, dataset bias, and the presence of small or low-contrast lesions. Motivated by these challenges, we propose a novel polyp detection framework based on a Attention Residual U-Net offering enhanced polyp localization. Instead of directly regressing bounding boxes from global feature representations, the proposed method learns lesion-focused spatial representations and converts them into bounding-box predictions during inference. Unlike conventional encoder-decoder localization frameworks that directly propagate all encoder activations into the decoding pathway, the proposed method selectively suppresses irrelevant background responses before feature reconstruction. This encourages the network to focus on lesion-relevant spatial evidence under heterogeneous imaging conditions. To achieve this, the framework integrates residual feature propagation, attention-guided encoder filtering, and multi-scale contextual learning. The proposed framework was evaluated on multiple public endoscopic datasets acquired using different devices. The comparative experimental results validate its effectiveness over the relevant state-of-the-art methods, with an improvement up to 22.0% in terms of the area under the receiving operating characteristic (AUC).

title: Charge-Activated Birefringence and Shadow Mimicry around Reissner-Nordström Black Holes
abstract: We discover that electric charge can activates birefringence for a neutral vector field coupled to the Einstein tensor around a Reissner-Nordström black hole. Changing the electric charge of an uncoupled black hole can mimic one parity's shadow radius of a coupled black hole. The coupling makes the two parity looks differently. It separates their shadow edges of two parities and produces a backward-scattered signal with reversed helicity. However changing the charge alone cannot reproduce both effects. They require both nonzero charge and coupling. At weak coupling, the leading correction is the same for both potential. Positive coupling raises the potential, reduces low-frequency absorption and decrease the average shadow radius. Negative coupling reverses these trends. The backward signal is nonzero, this is due to the difference between the complex scattering amplitudes of the two parities. It is entirely helicity reversed. For the uncoupled field, the shadows is the same for both parities and the backward intensity vanishes exactly at every charge. We can use the split edge and backward signal to distinguish the coupling from a change of charge alone. A comparison with observations still requires a mechanism that produces and detects this field.

title: Generalized Wishart processes under nonlinear expectation
abstract: We develop a theory of generalized Wishart processes within the framework of $G$-expectation, with $G$-Dyson Brownian motion and the $G$-Wishart process as two typical examples. In contrast to the classical setting, we show that $G$-Dyson Brownian motion may exhibit collisions and provide a sufficient condition ensuring the non-collision of the eigenvalues of generalized Wishart processes. We then derive the equations governing the high-dimensional limits of the empirical spectral measures under $G$-expectation, leading to the corresponding semicircle law for $G$-Dyson Brownian motion and Marchenko--Pastur law for the $G$-Wishart process.

title: Extension of kappa-additive measures
abstract: We establish an extension theorem for kappa-additive probability measures, where kappa is an arbitrary uncountable cardinal. Starting from a <kappa-algebra, we define an outer measure using coverings of cardinality at most kappa and characterise measurable sets by approximation in outer measure of symmetric differences. We prove that these sets form a kappa-algebra carrying a complete kappa-additive extension of the original measure. The extension is unique on the generated kappa-algebra, and its completion is the minimal domain admitting a complete kappa-additive extension. We also establish attainment of the covering infimum and show why the closure assumption on the initial algebra is essential. Examples include a strict extension of classical Lebesgue measure under the additional hypothesis add N = aleph_1 < cov N.

title: General Form Factors from String Amplitudes
abstract: We extend the string-amplitude construction of single-insertion form factors to multiple operator insertions carrying independent off-shell momenta. By deforming the bulk closed-string punctures onto the open-string boundary, we establish a relation between stringy general form factors and scattering amplitudes. Using this relation, we evaluate the field-theory limit and find that the resulting form factors receive contributions from both separate operator insertions and local contact terms. Furthermore, we uncover several hidden structures of stringy general form factors at finite $α'$: $2$-splits and hidden zeros analogous to those of scattering amplitudes, bulk zeros specific to form factors, and a decoupling split unique to multiple insertions.

title: Maximal correlation and optimal transformations of probability distributions in tensor-train format: a variational algorithm
abstract: The correlation between two subsystems $A$ and $B$ of a many-body system is usually measured through a pair of observables chosen in advance. The Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi maximal correlation removes the choice: it is the largest correlation coefficient between any function of the configuration of $A$ and any function of the configuration of $B$, and the two functions that reach it, the optimal transformations, are the observables that carry the correlation. Both follow from a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the joint distribution normalized by its marginals, a matrix whose dimension is the number of configurations. We show that this SVD can be computed variationally for a classical distribution of discrete variables, such as the Boltzmann distribution of a spin model, given in the tensor-train (matrix-product) format, without ever forming the matrix. The optimal transformations are sought as tensor trains; each step updates a single core in closed form, and the inverse of a small matrix contracted from the distribution and the remaining cores performs the division by the marginals core by core. Every iterate is a feasible pair, so the objective is a lower bound on the maximal correlation that increases monotonically, and the cost grows linearly with the number of variables. The algorithm reproduces the exact SVD on small systems, recovers the known nonlinear optimal transformations of synthetic distributions of up to ten angular variables ($10^{15}$ configurations), and, for the bipartite antiferromagnetic model with $2^{32}$ configurations, returns an optimal transformation that is a function of the group magnetization, linear above the transition and sign-like below it: the staggered order parameter is read off from the distribution instead of being postulated.

title: Capillary $L_p$ dual Minkowski flow
abstract: For $n\geq2$ and $θ\in(0,π/2)$, we study the long-time existence and asymptotic behavior of an even normalized capillary $L_p$ dual Minkowski flow in the Euclidean half-space $\overline{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}_+}$. When $pq\geq0$, the flow exists for all positive time and the evolving hypersurfaces converge smoothly along a sequence of times tending to infinity to a stationary solution of the normalized problem. If $p\neq q$, a dilation of the limit solves the unnormalized problem.

title: Edge spectral invariants and second-order Steklov asymptotics for the regular tetrahedron
abstract: We give a two-term Weyl asymptotic for the Steklov spectrum of a solid regular tetrahedron. Its linear coefficient is the total edge length times an explicit, absolutely convergent dihedral invariant. A trace-class difference of massive Neumann-to-Dirichlet operators computes the full invariant, including the continuous spectrum. The main analytic step is a fixed-time cumulative trace comparison between the compact tetrahedron and its exact half-space or dihedral models. Localized Hilbert-Schmidt defects have vanishing high-energy tails; retaining the time factor in Duhamel's formula makes this sufficient for an $o(L)$ cumulative error. A separate trace-class face comparison fixes the model's infinite exterior primitive and permits one observation time independent of the inner collar width. Compact-band Mourre estimates and a harmonic comparison establish immediate reflection/transmission support for incident face waves. Triangular unfolding gives null periodic and dead-end sets for the maximal branching relation. Actual edge-window bounds, adapted conical annuli and an ordered-limit Fourier-Tauberian argument then prove the sharp remainder. The proof treats guided and continuum channels together in the edge trace and requires neither a guided metric graph nor a lower-departure estimate uniform at zero tangential momentum.

title: Search for dark photon dark matter near $\mathbf{1\,meV}$ using a superconducting mixer
abstract: We demonstrate the use of a superconducting mixer for direct searches for dark photon dark matter (DPDM) in the meV mass range. DPDM couples to the ordinary electromagnetic field through kinetic mixing with a coupling constant $χ$ and can convert into ordinary photons at the surface of a metal plate. For DPDM masses of 1 meV, the conversion photons have frequencies of around 240 GHz. At such frequencies, superconducting mixers enable low-noise spectroscopic measurements. We performed a direct search for DPDM in the mass range 1.0047578-1.0047598 meV, corresponding to the frequency range 242.94935-242.94983 GHz, using approximately one hour of data obtained with a cryogenic millimeter-wave receiver based on a superconducting mixer. No significant excess was found, and we set upper limits of $χ< (1.6\text{-}1.9)\times10^{-9}$ at the 95% confidence level. These limits are comparable to existing constraints from solar dark photons. By applying this method, we plan to extend the search to the wider mass range of 0.7-1.1 meV, corresponding to 170-260 GHz, with improved sensitivity.

title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. VII. Step kinetics
abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate the kinetics of attachment of new segments of the crystalline lattice (pyramids) at steps on the nonmetal-terminated surface of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. These surfaces are wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e. GaN(000-1) surface, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e. GaP(-1-1-1) gallium arsenide, GaAs(-1-1-1) and gallium antimonide GaSb(-1-1-1) surfaces. Diffusion species are gallium adatoms at high coverage or gallium adatoms connected with nonmetal atom creating stable pyramids. These pyramids arrive at the steps, and cannot be attached be directly because the Ga adatom at the pyramid base cannot be attached directly. Therefore they are incorporated into the step by additional nonmetal atoms glue atoms arriving from the vapor or detached from other segments of the surface terraces.

title: Feature extraction for LSTM-based finger-joint angle estimation from sEMG
abstract: Continuous estimation of finger-joint angles from surface electromyography (sEMG) is a promising approach for controlling dexterous myoelectric prostheses. Deep time series models have been applied successfully in this context, typically relying on feature extraction rather than raw signals, given limited subject-specific data. Various time-domain and frequency-domain features can be used, extracted for a given window and step size. This study systematically investigates these three design choices for Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) regression on the Ninapro DB2 dataset. Window sizes from 300 to 1200 ms and step sizes from 10 to 100 ms were evaluated in combination with six time- and frequency-domain features. Models were evaluated using regression performance metrics, inference time, and memory footprint to assess feasibility on embedded microcontroller hardware suitable for a prosthetic device. A 300 ms window with a 100 ms step, paired with either the Mean Absolute Value (MAV) or Root Mean Squared (RMS) feature, yielded the best performance (test PCC of 0.779 +/- 0.080 / 0.779 +/- 0.085). Window size, step size, and feature choice were found to interact non-trivially: jointly tuning them can improve both accuracy and computational feasibility for real-time, embedded myoelectric control.

title: MoviEdit: Long-form Multi-Shot Video Editing Made Easy
abstract: Long-form multi-shot video editing requires an intended edit to remain coherent across abrupt changes in scene, viewpoint, and subject appearance, while processing substantially longer visual context than conventional single-shot editors. We introduce MoviEdit, an end-to-end framework for scalable long-form multi-shot video editing that jointly addresses the challenges of data, modeling, and evaluation. To provide cross-shot supervision data at scale, we develop automatic data-generation pipelines spanning synchronized multi-view footage, real-world multi-shot videos, and generated multi-shot content, yielding 87K paired editing videos without manual annotation. Architecturally, MoviEdit employs a cascaded bidirectional-autoregressive design: a lightweight bidirectional stage first establishes a globally coherent editing draft over a spatiotemporally compressed representation, which is then autoregressively propagated and refined over the full video. We further introduce MoviEdit-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for systematic evaluation of long-form multi-shot video editing. Extensive experiments show that MoviEdit substantially outperforms existing open-source models and performs on par with industry frontier models across text-guided and image-guided editing. Visit our project page for complete results and to access the benchmark: https://multi-shot-edit.github.io/

title: Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System for Bridge Operation and Maintenance based on Large Language Model
abstract: Bridges are critical transportation infrastructure, and reliable operation and maintenance (O&M) is essential for traffic safety and long-term structural performance. However, bridge O&M faces key bottlenecks: no unified architecture coordinates heterogeneous resources; model inferences lack clear links to physical-mechanical laws; and experts' tacit knowledge remains difficult to formalize. This study proposes a knowledge-enhanced autonomy formalization methodology and apply it to construct the Bridge O&M Multi-Modal Multi-Agent System (BOMMA), which integrates heterogeneous diagnostic actions, physics-mechanics-informed representations, long-term memory, and structured experiential knowledge within a coordinated multi-agent workflow, enabling interpretable and traceable scheduling, analysis, and decision-making. On 3,492 multi-source instructions, the proposed method achieves scheduling recalls of 85.37% for simple and 99.40% for composite tasks, with 95.35% BERT F1-score for O&M action reasoning. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the components in the autonomy. This study bridges general LLM reasoning and specialized bridge O&M requirements.

title: Beyond Monotonicity: Stochastic Online Optimization under Semi-Bandit Feedback
abstract: We study stochastic online optimization (SOO) under semi-bandit feedback: in each of $T$ rounds, a policy adaptively observes $n$ independent random variables with unknown distributions, learning only from observed values. First-order stochastic dominance (FSD) monotonicity enables general reductions for learning SOO, but can fail when observations change future feasibility, resource use, or reference points. Our algorithm runs the dynamic program for the optimal policy, replacing each expectation by its most optimistic value over a confidence set of distributions. Its regret depends on the level-set complexity $s_i$ of the computed values as functions of the $i$th variable: the number of intervals needed to describe their superlevel sets. For rewards in $[0,1]$, the regret is $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{ST})$ without this monotonicity, where $S=\sum_{i=1}^n\min\{s_i,k_i\}$ and $k_i$ is the support size of the $i$th distribution, which may be infinite when $s_i$ is finite. For constant level-set complexities, regret is $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nT})$, even for continuous distributions. The algorithm requires no knowledge of $s_i$, $k_i$, or the supports, and it also achieves regret $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nkT})$ for supports of size at most $k$ without any level-set condition, which improves the previous bound $\tilde{O}(n(\sqrt{kT}+k))$ for FSD-monotone problems. We also prove a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{T,\sqrt{ST}\})$ for all positive integers $s_1,\ldots,s_n$ with $k_i=2s_i+1$, which holds even under full feedback and matches the upper bound up to logarithmic factors. We obtain $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nT})$ regret for these problems, all nonmonotone under FSD: stochastic Boolean function evaluation, the full-information secretary problem, optimal stopping with loss aversion, scheduling with deadlines and correlated stochastic knapsack with unimodal rewards, and overbooking with group reservations.

title: Rigidity of shrinking Ricci solitons with low-dimensional focal sets
authors: Matheus Andrade Ribeiro de Moura Horácio
abstract: We prove that, in every dimension, the focal set of the potential function of a complete gradient shrinking Ricci soliton with constant scalar curvature is totally geodesic whenever it has dimension two or three, and that every complete five-dimensional gradient shrinking Ricci soliton with constant scalar curvature is rigid. The first result follows from a Bochner identity for the covariant derivative of the Ricci tensor at the focal set. For the second, when the scalar curvature is twice the soliton constant, we prove that total geodesy implies rigidity through an integral identity on the level hypersurfaces; the case of scalar curvature three times the soliton constant is treated by a separate argument. As further applications, we combine our methods with the rigidity theorem in the recent preprint of Li, Li, Ou, Qu, Wu and Zhou to obtain rigidity in arbitrary dimension when the scalar curvature is twice or three times the soliton constant, and under integral Weyl pinching for four-dimensional focal sets.

title: ATrust: Adaptive Trust Boundary Expansion for Securing LLM Agents
abstract: As large language model (LLM) agents take on more complex tasks with greater autonomy, security has become a major obstacle to their broader deployment. Unlike in attacks that require complex exploitation of operating system vulnerabilities, attackers can easily hijack agents through indirect prompt injection (IPI), leading to privacy leakage, financial loss, and destructive operations. However, existing defenses often make security decisions based on limited static trusted evidence or assess observations in isolation. Such rigid trust assumptions can cause task-essential information to be unnecessarily discarded, resulting in over-defense and degraded agent functionality. To address this problem, we propose ATrust, a defense mechanism that adaptively expands the trust boundary during agent runtime. Starting from the user query as the root trust anchor, ATrust evaluates external observations against the current trust boundary and execution state, progressively admitting task-essential information as new trust anchors. This preserves necessary environmental feedback while excluding irrelevant content, whether benign or malicious, from subsequent decision-making, thereby limiting unnecessary exposure to external environment. We evaluate ATrust on AgentDojo and AgentDyn, where it achieves the strongest overall security--utility trade-off among existing defenses. With GPT-4o as the engine model, ATrust reduces the attack success rate on AgentDyn from 37.80% to 4.37% while enhancing utility by 10.00%, outperforming AuthGraph, the state-of-the-art defense, by 12.33%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and practicality of ATrust.

title: k-uniform l-Eulerian hypergraphs
abstract: We consider $l$-Euler trails and $l$-Euler circuits in finite $k$-uniform directed multihypergraphs, where $k\geq 2$ and $1\leq l<k$. Let $D$ be such a directed multihypergraph. The notions of $l$-connectivity and $l$-balance are defined in terms of the $l$-tails and $l$-heads of its hyperarcs. It is shown that $D$ is $l$-Eulerian if and only if $D$ is $l$-connected and $l$-balanced. Moreover, $D$ is $l$-semi-Eulerian if and only if $D$ is $l$-connected and has exactly two states with unequal $l$-indegrees and $l$-outdegrees, one with $l$-outdegree one greater than its $l$-indegree and the other with $l$-indegree one greater than its $l$-outdegree. The proofs are based on an $l$-transition digraph and the classical Euler theorem for directed multigraphs. The corresponding conditions for $k$-uniform multihypergraphs are also obtained in terms of their orientations. For a given orientation, an expected linear-time algorithm is provided to determine whether an $l$-Euler trail or an $l$-Euler circuit exists and to construct one when it does.

title: Two-point residual step size gradient methods for linear systems
abstract: Kaczmarz-type methods often converge slowly when the coefficient matrix is ill-conditioned. In particular, when the smallest singular value is small, every row of the coefficient matrix is nearly orthogonal to the corresponding right singular direction, so that the iteration stalls along that direction. To break this slow-convergence regime, we borrow the delayed-step-size idea of the Barzilai-Borwein (BB) method and, within the framework of the residual-based surrogate-hyperplane Kaczmarz method, propose two new step sizes for gradient-descent-type methods solving linear systems: a delayed residual step size \(α_k^{\mathrm{DR}}\) and a residual-difference step size \(α_k^{\mathrm{RD}}\), which correspond, respectively, to the BB1 and BB2 step sizes in convex quadratic optimization. We prove that \(α_k^{\mathrm{RD}}\leα_k^{\mathrm{DR}}\), and we analyze the convergence of the resulting method in a canonical model with two singular values: although the step sizes are non-monotone, the residual norm is shown to decrease after finitely many steps. Numerical experiments on some ill-conditioned linear systems illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

title: Subspace Representations for Synthetic-to-Real Transfer in 3-D Surface Inspection
abstract: This paper studies what subspace representations contribute to synthetic-to-real transfer in 3-D surface inspection, where models learn from synthetic defects and the only real data before deployment are scans of good parts. We use three classical constructions as instruments: the nearest-subspace classifier, one-class template subspaces and the generalized difference subspace (GDS). On 1,197 MVTec 3D-AD scans without target annotation we find that every decision rule ranks real defects at a similar window AUC, that image-level detection stays at chance, and that no rule keeps its in-domain threshold. We show that the margin of a nearest-subspace rule moves by at most the part of the feature shift outside its class subspaces, and that this leakage, measured from unlabeled good scans, bounds the displacement observed on unseen scans. On 597 Real3D-AD objects, a one-class subspace of registered templates evaluated at every location on frozen features reaches point AUROC 0.957 on pre-registered scans and a category-mean object AUROC of 78 to 81 with no training on the benchmark. Our results suggest that a subspace helps under shift in proportion to the shift it spans, and that in reference-based inspection the reference and its registration matter more than the subspace.

title: Bilinear maximal functions associated with some degenerate surfaces on the Heisenberg group
abstract: Motivated by the works of Lee--Shuin and Borges--Foster on the Euclidean space, in this article we consider bilinear averages on the Heisenberg group $\mathbb{H}^n$ corresponding to some degenerate surfaces associated with the Korányi norm as well as Nevo--Thangavelu type averaging structures, and study the boundedness of the their full and lacunary maximal functions on various $L^{p}(\mathbb{H}^n) \times L^{q}(\mathbb{H}^n)$ spaces, for $n \geq 2$. For the full maximal functions, we obtain optimal range except possibly at the end points.

title: Replay for LLM Continual Learning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) distills several domain experts into one student and is used in the post-training of recent large language models. It trains on all domains at once, so every expert must be available at the same time. In practice, capabilities often arrive one after another, and the experts of earlier domains may be gone when a new domain is learned. Distilling the experts in sequence then suffers from catastrophic forgetting of the earlier domains. Some recent pipelines store a snapshot after every stage and end with a multi-teacher recovery stage taught by all snapshots. The number of stored models then grows with the number of stages. Different from these pipelines, this paper formulates continual MOPD by what is kept from earlier stages and studies replay toward the previous student. Inside every stage, prompts of earlier domains are replayed with the student of the previous stage as their teacher, so neither earlier experts nor stage snapshots are kept. Two design choices of replay are explored. The replay budget of a stage is either shared among the earlier domains or fixed per earlier domain. Replay steps either distill the token distribution alone or add alignment of hidden states, region-pooled self-attention scores and value relations. A five-domain benchmark of logic, math, code, safety and instruction following is built from public experts of one 1.5B student. Experiments on its 14 benchmarks show that, without storing any snapshot, replay toward the previous student closes most of the gap between sequential distillation and joint MOPD. With a fixed replay share per earlier domain, it performs on par with recovery from all stored snapshots.

title: What Drives the Zero-to-One Jump? Diagnosing and Steering Hard-Prompt Learning in RLVR
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved mathematical reasoning, yet progress on hard prompts often stalls: a prompt can remain unsolved for many training steps before abruptly transitioning to solved--a discrete "zero-to-one" jump whose underlying dynamics and steerability remain poorly understood. We investigate two questions: what drives this transition, and can it be steered? Through event-based analysis measuring the time-to-first-positive (TTFP), we find that negative rollouts preceding successful transitions consistently retain higher early-stage generation entropy, distinguishing near-solvable failures from dead ends. This signal motivates NAPO (Negative-Augmented Policy Optimization), a method integrated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that ranks negatives in unsolved groups via an early-branching driver and assigns graded advantages, injecting informative gradients precisely where standard group-relative updates vanish. Under fixed rollout budgets, NAPO accelerates early solution discovery and improves Pass@256 by 10.0 points on AIME24 and 6.6 points on AIME2025, demonstrating that zero-to-one transitions are diagnosable and steerable through driver-guided negative learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/jameszhu-pixel-time/Z2O.

title: When GL(2) cusp forms meet CM points in GSp(4)
abstract: Duke's equidistribution theorem shows that the nonconstant contribution of the $\mathrm{GL}(2)$ automorphic spectrum to CM packets becomes asymptotically negligible. CM packets on the Levi base index the fibers of Bessel quotients in $\mathrm{GSp}(4)$, and the symmetric cube correspondence carries $\mathrm{GL}(2)$ cusp forms to $\mathrm{GL}(4)$. In the holomorphic setting considered here, these two constructions meet inside $\mathrm{GSp}(4)$. We prove averaged decay for the resulting class group periods over imaginary quadratic fields, expressed as averages of conditional fiber integrals. More precisely, let $f$ be a non-CM holomorphic Hecke newform with trivial central character. The mean absolute value of the associated class-group averages tends to zero along the transverse unipotent direction.

title: Generalized parabolic Demazure modules and the N!/2-conjecture for two-row diagrams
abstract: We study a family of generalized parabolic Demazure modules, i.e. of gl[x]-submodules of tensor products of integrable representations of the affine Lie algebra generated by tensor products of extremal vectors, and describe these modules by generators and relations. Realizing the Garsia--Haiman modules of two-row diagrams as fusion products of two local Weyl modules, we show that their y-graded components admit filtrations whose associated graded modules are isomorphic to tensor products of these generalized parabolic Demazure modules with the cohomology rings of Grassmannians. As a consequence, the Garsia-Haiman modules of two-row diagrams of a fixed size generate a distributive lattice, and the N!/2-conjecture holds for two-row diagrams.

title: Investigating the effects of the patch size in Time Series Foundation Models
abstract: Patch size is a central design choice in patch-based time-series foundation models, controlling temporal resolution, sequence length, and computational cost. We study how this choice interacts with transformer architecture through a controlled comparison of encoder-only and decoder-only forecasting models trained with the same data mixture and optimization budget. Across 97 GIFT-Eval tasks, encoder-only models consistently benefit from smaller patches, whereas decoder-only performance follows a U-shaped trend, with an intermediate patch size performing best in aggregate. Dataset-level results further show that the preferred decoder patch size increases with the forecasting horizon. For encoder-only models, increasing context length improves performance across patch sizes, although the gains diminish beyond a context length of 2048. Finally, training-compute and CPU-latency Pareto analyses reveal complementary regimes: decoder-only models provide efficient low-cost alternatives, while encoder-only models attain the highest overall accuracy. These results show that the choice of patch size and architecture should be made depending on the forecasting horizon and deployment constraints.

title: Pair-Relative Partial Equivariance for Rotation-Robust Keypoint Descriptor Matching
abstract: Learned keypoint descriptors trained on upright imagery often fail under large in-plane rotation. Steerers address this by applying a single exact SO(2) representation to the descriptor space, but this global group constraint can be too rigid for keypoint descriptors, whose angular responses need not follow a single group representation.
