SNEEF achieves an F1 score of 0.967 for evidence entities extracted from SQLite row content, excluding application names, compared with 0.728 for a context-free configuration, with consistent gains across all corpora. We also introduce an Evidence Failure Mode taxonomy to characterize why extraction errors occur.

title: Stabilizer Learning under Global Depolarizing Noise with Polynomial Copies and $2^t$ Time
abstract: We study learning the stabilizer structure of an unknown pure $n$-qubit state observed through global depolarizing noise of unknown strength, with a fixed promised upper bound below one, using destructive two-copy Bell measurements. Let $0\le t\le n$ bound the stabilizer nullity, let $\varepsilon>0$ be the accuracy, and let $0<δ<1$ be the failure tolerance. With probability at least $1-δ$, a learner must return a commuting unsigned Pauli group containing every stabilizer of the pure state; averaging conjugation by that group must decrease the purity of the observed noisy state by at most $\varepsilon$. Tang and Steckmann gave such a learner with polynomially many copies and $2^t$ times polynomial time when the noise strength is below a threshold of at most about $0.16$, which tends to zero as $t/n\to1$. They asked whether other algorithms with these resources can exceed this threshold. We answer this question affirmatively for every fixed bound on global depolarizing noise below one and every $0\le t\le n$, including states with only one promised independent stabilizer. Our learner uses polynomially many copies and $2^t$ times polynomial classical running time. All resource bounds hold on every execution. Their polynomial factors depend on $n,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/δ)$, with degrees and constants depending on the fixed noise promise.

title: End-to-End NTT on FPGA for FHE Acceleration
abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving computation on encrypted data without decryption. Despite its strong security guarantees, FHE incurs substantial computational and memory overhead. In FHE-based deep learning inference, on average 63% of the CPU time is spent on the number theoretic transform (NTT) and its inverse (INTT), which reduce the complexity of polynomial multiplication from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N \log N)$. Prior FPGA works follow two approaches: accelerating entire FHE schemes, which yields significant speedups but ties them to specific parameters and algorithms, or accelerating only the NTT, which applies across schemes, algorithms, and libraries. Most FPGA NTT designs require interconnects that grow with parallelism and utilize significant resources, which complicates routing on multi-die FPGAs. Additionally, to the best of our knowledge, end-to-end NTT acceleration within an FHE context has so far been left unexplored. We design a fully unrolled, delay-commutator streaming NTT/INTT kernel, and floorplan it across the three dies of an AMD Alveo V80. At 400 MHz, the kernel transforms a polynomial of $2^{16}$ coefficients every 5.12 $μ$s, the highest throughput among FPGA designs at this size. Offloaded end to end, it is up to 22x faster than the CPU per transform. We integrate the kernel into the Lattigo FHE library and evaluate it end to end. With 128-bit secure parameters, it accelerates core FHE operations, such as key switching and bootstrapping, by 1.8-2.2x, and neural network inference by 1.8-2.1x.

title: Six-hourly Probabilistic Precipitation Forecasts Created From Hourly Probabilities
abstract: A lightweight neural network is described that produces six-hourly, spatially detailed probabilistic quantitative precipitation forecasts (PQPF) from a sequence of hourly spatially detailed probabilistic forecasts, for lead times from 6 to 72\,h. The hourly forecasts were generated by a ``zero-inflated'' Attention Residual U-Net that outputs the parameters of a probability distribution including a probability of no precipitation and a weighted mixture of two Gamma distributions at each grid point for each hourly forecast lead time. The six-hourly network passes the six consecutive hourly parameter sets, together with summary statistics of the spatial texture of the raw deterministic forecast, through a small recurrent (GRU) layer and a multi-layer perceptron, and maps them to a corresponding zero-inflated mixture of three Gamma distributions describing the six-hourly accumulated precipitation. Training uses sets of hourly probabilistic forecasts, drawn preferentially from wet and heavy-precipitation cases (importance sampling), and matched Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) six-hourly precipitation accumulations, subject to a quality threshold. The resulting six-hourly probabilistic forecasts are well calibrated and skillful, as demonstrated by reliability diagrams, performance diagrams and Brier Skill Scores evaluated over an out-of-sample period spanning day 12 through the end of every month of 2025. The Brier Skill Scores are consistently and significantly higher than those of a baseline that sums independent draws from the hourly distributions. Forecasts show realistic modulation of precipitation related to terrain variations

title: From FAIR to AI-FAIR Metadata-First Infrastructure for AI-Enabled Science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and their capabilities have advanced rapidly over the past few years, leading to widespread interest and adoption in the biological and ecological sciences. However, the data infrastructure and computational resources that provide the foundation for AI workflows in ecology and biodiversity science remain fragmented. Moreover, the flow of value remains largely unidirectional: data move from collectors, through repositories and aggregators into models, and finally to research products or management actions. The derived value, such as corrected taxonomies, annotations, quality flags, and insights, rarely returns to source communities. We propose an extension of the original FAIR principles to address the needs of AI-ready infrastructure: the AI-FAIR metadata criteria, which place AI-enabled science in the context of a bidirectional Question-Data-Model triangle. This framework is designed to facilitate large-scale content-based analysis across diverse collections and ensure that the scientists generating the data benefit from the AI-enabled advances built on their data. Alongside these criteria, we introduce an agentic evaluation workflow that both rates existing datasets on the AI-FAIR and traditional FAIR criteria and provides actionable feedback where critical metadata is missing or incomplete. This modular dataset evaluation tool, paired with a domain-appropriate checklist, translates these principles into a reusable assessment of machine-learning readiness, AI-readiness for specified tasks, traceability, and ethical and CARE-aligned stewardship. Through this approach we aim to create a community-informed system to close the model data loop, so that AI also enriches data to further enable scientific discovery.

title: Solar Wind Turbulence Spectra and Correlation Scale from 4 to 50 $r_\odot$: STEREO and PUNCH Observations
abstract: We investigate the radial evolution of solar wind turbulence using remote-sensing brightness observations from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) and the first science-ready images from the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission. Exploiting the combined wide fields of view of STEREO's COR2 coronagraph (4-9 r_sun) and PUNCH's Wide Field Imager (WFI, 21-50 r_sun), we track the radial evolution of the power spectral density and correlation scale of density fluctuations from 4 to 50 r_sun. Line-of-sight integration systematically steepens the "usual" turbulence scaling laws by a constant offset of about -0.5 across all resolved scales, so that the energy-containing range (nominally k^-1) and the inertial range (nominally k^-5/3) appear as k^-1.5 and k^-2.1, respectively -- consistent with previous synthetic-image simulations. The correlation scale increases with heliocentric distance across the full range of heliodistances probed, in accordance with previous theoretical models and observations at closer distances from the Sun.

title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
abstract: Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model. Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics. An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.

title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
abstract: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs, and the most accurate SOTA model is a fit, not a law: it absorbs architecture into fitted coefficients, requiring per-LLM fitting. We derive closed-form expressions of the computational and memory-access complexity of LLM inference in terms of architectural hyperparameters, covering MHA and GQA, and compare a family of analytical models of increasing granularity. From these, we obtain the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache cost and next-token computation. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from six families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. The SIMPLE law explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with the hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and more aggressive GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy by up to 3x relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; although accuracy grows with the budget, energy grows faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x reasoning-budget range. Agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x relative to non-agentic ones, driven by the growth of both the prefill and the KV-cache terms with input length; while prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), the KV-cache term is unaffected, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

title: Leveraging Continuous Trade Data for Intraday Imbalance Price Forecasting
abstract: Forecasts of imbalance prices are essential for participants in short-term electricity markets. This study proposes an approach to integrate trade data from continuous intraday markets into forecasting methods and considers the production of both parametric and non-parametric density forecasts. Extensive feature engineering is required to convert irregular trade data into a suitable tabular structure. Our findings demonstrate that intraday trade data can enhance state-of-the-art forecasts based on quantile regression and LASSO. We also propose a model based on Natural Gradient Boosting to predict the means and variances of a bimodal Gaussian mixture, which offers both improved predictive performance and computational efficiency. In a case study based on multiple years of data from Great Britain, our proposed approach reduced the Pinball Loss of state-of-the-art models by 20% for forecasts made 30 seconds before gate closure, and by 7.5% for forecasts made one hour before delivery.

title: Sublinear Power-Law Growth of Level Set Diameters in Heterogeneous F-KPP Equations
abstract: For every $α\in(1/4,1)$, we construct a heterogeneous medium $ξ$ such that the diameter of the level sets of the solution to the F-KPP equation is of order $t^α$ along a sequence of times tending to infinity. This is a natural continuation of a series of recent works establishing logarithmic lower bounds as well as linear asymptotics for the diameters of the respective level sets in random and deterministic heterogeneous media. Both results assume $\supξ> 2\infξ$; we also show that the diameter can diverge in the critical regime $\supξ=2\infξ$. A key ingredient is an estimate for branching Brownian motion with fixed time horizon $t$ and branching rate $1$ on the negative half-line and $2+t^{-η}$ on the positive half-line. This estimate exhibits a saturation transition: for $η<1/2$ the polynomial and logarithmic corrections to the extremal position depend on $η$, whereas for $η\geq1/2$ the extremal position becomes independent of $η$, up to an additive constant.

title: Methods for Assessing Distributional Assumptions in Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Tests
abstract: Meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies is commonly based on bivariate generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) that assume normally distributed study-specific random effects. In practice, this distributional assumption is rarely examined, particularly in individual participant data meta-analysis (IPDMA), where empirical Bayes (EB) estimates exhibit heterogeneous precision across studies. Applying standard multivariate normality tests to such estimates can therefore lead to misleading inference. We propose a weighted extension of the Henze-Zirkler (HZ) test to assess bivariate normality of random effects, accounting for study-specific precision via inverse-variance weighting. To obtain valid finite-sample inference, we develop a parametric bootstrap calibration procedure. Extensive simulation studies showed that the classical HZ test applied to EB estimates can exhibit substantial Type I error inflation, whereas the proposed weighted procedures maintain nominal error rates while retaining power to detect departures from normality. The proposed method provides a practical, statistically principled diagnostic tool for assessing random-effects distributional assumptions in hierarchical models, with particular relevance to IPDMA of DTA studies. Although motivated by IPDMA, the proposed approach also extends to aggregate-data diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis based on study-level 2-by-2 tables.

title: A counterexample concerning weighted convolution on the integers
abstract: Let $1<p<\infty$ and let $w:\mathbb{Z}\to(0,\infty)$ be a weight. When is the weighted space $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z},w)$ an algebra with respect to convolution? A well-known sufficient condition is that $(w^{-q}*w^{-q})/w^{-q}$ be bounded on $\mathbb{Z}$, where $q:=p/(p-1)$ is the index conjugate to $p$. We present an example to show that this sufficient condition is not necessary.

title: Higher dimensional Kleinian groups of small Hausdorff dimension are classical Schottky groups II
abstract: This is the higher dimensional continuation of our works on Hausdorff dimension of Kleinian groups \cite{Hou2010}, \cite{Hou2020}. In this paper we prove that for all $r\ge 2$ there exists $λ_r>0$, which is independent of the dimension $N$ of the hyperbolic space, such that any finitely generated non-elementary torsion-free Kleinian group of $\Isom(\mathbb{H}^N)$ generated by $r$ elements with limit set of Hausdorff dimension $<λ_r$ is a classical Schottky group. For two generators the bound can be taken to be $1/3$. The proof relies on our previous works in \cite{Hou2010}, \cite{Hou2020} and on a metric carrier graph reduction. Our result can also be considered as the complete converse to the well-known theorem of Phillips-Sarnak \cite{PS} for spaces of any dimension $N$.

title: Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction for periodic orbits of implicit discrete dynamical systems
abstract: We derive bifurcation equations for periodic orbits of autonomous and periodically non-autonomous implicit discrete systems in arbitrary finite dimension. Cyclic Lyapunov--Schmidt reduction gives recursive coefficients and nondegeneracy and transversality conditions at the multipliers +1 and -1. We prove equivalence under regular changes of implicit representation and exact invariance under cyclic relabelling when the reduction data are transported consistently.

title: Evaluation of clinical prediction models: Decomposing performance uncertainty into model development and validation components
abstract: There has been growing emphasis on acknowledging, quantifying, and communicating the uncertainty inherent in the output of clinical prediction models. However, allowing for model uncertainty when assessing the performance of an existing model in a new sample (i.e., external validation) has not been sufficiently explored. When validating a model that generates uncertain predictions, the uncertainty of a given performance metric is affected by both model uncertainty and the finiteness of the validation sample (validation uncertainty). For a given performance metric, we show that the total uncertainty of the performance estimate can be decomposed into the uncertainty due to the model and the uncertainty due to the validation. Also, we propose $M^2$, the fraction of the total variance due to model uncertainty, and $V^2$, the fraction of the total variance due to validation uncertainty. These measures serve as complementary scalar indices that can be implemented for common performance metrics and visualizations such as calibration plots using simple Monte Carlo algorithms. Critically, our case study shows that with the same model and the same validation sample, the contribution of uncertainty sources is highly variable across performance metrics ($M^2$ varying from 12% for the Brier score to 78% for the calibration slope). This indicates that stakeholders who prioritize different aspects of performance (e.g., calibration versus clinical utility) might arrive at different decisions on whether future efforts should be directed towards creating a more reliable model or procuring a larger validation sample. In conclusion, external validation studies can readily be amended to incorporate model uncertainty, and we recommend that such studies report total variance as well as the relative share of variance components for all performance metrics.

title: Exact Regular Planar Black Holes solutions in Bumblebee gravity
abstract: We discuss possibilities of finding exact regular planar black hole solutions in bumblebee gravity with temporal and radial components of the bumblebee field. We consider quadratic and linear potentials, with vanishing and nonzero cosmological constants, respectively. The field equations determine the nonminimal coupling and the relations between the model parameters. Found solution produce regular planar black hole with planar deformation function. Analytical expressions for this functions has been found. This solutions free of singularities at the $r=0$.

title: ArabGeoText: Tool-Augmented Vision-Language Models for Arabic Geospatial Text Spotting
abstract: Geospatial text spotting involves locating and transcribing geographic labels, such as road names, district names, and landmarks, in raster maps. These labels are often small, densely arranged, and arbitrarily oriented. Although Arabic text recognition has been studied extensively in documents and natural scenes, Arabic geospatial text spotting remains underexplored. We introduce ARABGEOTEXT, an Arabic-centric benchmark covering 970 geographic locations in Riyadh and Jeddah, with 17,875 manually annotated text instances per view type. For each location, we pair an OpenStreetMap (OSM) rendering with a composite created by overlaying that rendering on the corresponding remote sensing (RS) imagery. The paired views preserve label content and pixel geometry, allowing evaluation across different backgrounds. Geographic partitions support in-city and city-disjoint evaluation of detection, recognition, and end-to-end spotting. Experiments with direct Qwen3.5-4B spotting show difficulties in recovering all labels within a tile. We therefore propose a tool-augmented vision-language framework that combines YOLO26 localization and crop rectification with Qwen3.5-4B recognition adapted through low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The framework outperforms direct LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-4B spotting across both image views and test cities. With localization held fixed, reader adaptation further improves recognition over the pretrained zero-shot reader. The dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yakoubbazi/ArabGeoText.

title: Axion polarimetry with parametric readout: photon-number conversion and sensitivity limits
abstract: We propose a bias-assisted active photon-number conversion scheme for axion-induced polarization rotation in a four-port optical ring cavity with parametric readout. A calibrated real polarization rotation applied \emph{before} the final optical parametric oscillator (OPO) converts the otherwise quadratic response of the summed output photon number into a linear signal. We derive the resulting photon moments and the extracted-field covariance, retaining the four-port optical transfer, finite axion coherence and linewidth. Our principal phenomenological result is a prospective low-mass sensitivity window at $m_a=10^{-18}$--$10^{-16}\,\mathrm{eV}$, extending below the published exclusion bounds included in our comparison, notably the NuSTAR M82 limits. This is a conditional noise-equivalent projection, using the adopted $A/σ_A=1$ stochastic-power criterion and a parameterized technical-noise budget, not a confidence-level exclusion forecast. As a separate readout result, OPO-based total counting reduces the noise-equivalent coupling by approximately $5\%$ relative to matched selective attenuation in a favorable higher-frequency band; $5\%$ internal loss together with a $0.10$-rad pump-phase offset leaves a $3.5\%$ advantage in the stated example. A coherent input with only the final OPO retains this high-frequency benefit, whereas optimized coherent polarimetry remains more sensitive in the baseline. Our results identify both the operating principle of active number conversion and the stability requirements for a future implementation.

title: Dual-Band Mid-Infrared Imaging for Measurement of Fuel Concentration and Temperature in a Supersonic Cavity
abstract: A dual-band mid-infrared absorption imaging method is demonstrated for spatially resolved measurement of ethylene concentration and temperature in a Mach-2 cavity flow. The method used narrowband filters selected to exploit the differing in-band temperature sensitivities of ethylene absorption, together with a broadband infrared source and high-frame-rate mid-wave infrared camera. Temperature-dependent, filter-weighted absorption cross-sections were used to measure two-dimensional ethylene number density and temperature fields. Measurements were obtained for cavity, curtain, and discrete fuel-injection configurations, including cases with the leading edge of a quasi-steady shock near the cavity. Cavity equivalence ratio measurements agreed well with independent extractive measurements and reproduced trends previously observed using hyperspectral imaging. A complementary single-band implementation using a temperature-independent filter provided instantaneous ethylene concentration fields at 100 Hz and revealed intermittent reductions in cavity equivalence ratio associated with plume deflection by the shock train leading edge. The dual-band approach provides quantitative full-field measurements with substantially simpler spectral instrumentation than hyperspectral imaging while retaining flexibility for time-resolved flow measurements.

title: Geometrization of Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer and Vogan's conjecture on local Arthur packets
abstract: We give a geometric analogue of Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer for a general class of reductive groups over p-adic fields with cyclic component groups of trivial or prime order. We prove that this geometric transfer coincides with Kottwitz-Shelstad transfer, adapted to the language of disconnected groups, assuming the local Langlands correspondence satisfying certain desiderata, including the Kazhdan-Lusztig hypothesis for the ambient group and its endoscopic groups. As an application of this geometrization, we prove Vogan's conjecture on local Arthur packets over p-adic fields: for quasisplit classical groups and their pure inner forms, all local Arthur packets are ABV-packets, and the distributions attached to these ABV-packets of Arthur type satisfy Arthur's local conjectures on twisted endoscopic character relations. This demonstrates the following general principle: for any reductive group G over a local field, an Arthur packet should be defined as an ABV-packet of Arthur type, equipped with the endoscopic pairing calculated by traces of actions on vanishing cycles or microlocalizations.

title: Quartet state of the neutral nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond and optimized spin readout under near-infrared two-photon excitation
abstract: Photoionization of the excited nitrogen-vacancy center (NV-) in diamond leaves the neutral defect in a metastable quartet state of unknown energy. Using two-photon optically detected magnetic resonance with a tunable femtosecond laser, we resolve its onset in the spin contrast at 1.23 +/- 0.02 eV and, with the ground-state threshold from the same setup, place the quartet 0.54 +/- 0.04 eV above the neutral ground state. The threshold sets the optimum excitation for spin readout at 1060-1075 nm, in the near-infrared tissue window, with 26-37% higher shot-noise-limited sensitivity than at 1030-1040 nm.

title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell
abstract: Attention remains a substantial computational cost in Transformer training, particularly at long context lengths. NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs provide high-throughput low-precision matrix multiplication, but exploiting it in attention requires addressing quantization overhead, causal information leakage through shared scales, and numerical inconsistencies between the forward and backward passes. We present FLAMIA, a family of attention kernels for Blackwell with MXFP8 and mixed NVFP4/FP8 training paths. Our design combines token-block scaling that reuses quantized operands across matrix orientations, targeted safeguards against scale-induced leakage, and consistent forward and backward computations. Fused quantization and architecture-specific kernel optimizations reduce overhead, while document-local scaling and workload-aware scheduling support variable-length documents directly in packed layouts without repacking. Across various causal packed-document workloads, the MXFP8 path accelerates the combined forward and backward attention call, including quantization, by factors of $1.10$--$1.40\times$ on B200 and $1.06$--$1.42\times$ on B300 relative to the fastest evaluated baseline for each workload. We validate training stability and quality preservation on pretraining Llama-style models. These results show how jointly designing quantization, training numerics, and document scheduling translates low-bit hardware throughput into practical attention acceleration.

title: Sharp Identification for Regressions with Interval-Observed and Missing Covariates
abstract: Researchers frequently estimate regressions when key variables are missing or observed only through intervals. Imputation or assumptions about the observation process can yield seemingly precise but misleading conclusions. We develop methods for identification and inference that remain robust to such incomplete data. For a broad class of conditional moment models, we characterize the sharp identified set, the set of all parameter values consistent with the observed data and maintained regression model, without restricting how incomplete observations arise. We establish Hausdorff-consistent estimation and uniformly valid confidence regions, and develop computationally tractable implementations for common regression models. In an application relating interval-elicited discount rates to on-time high-school graduation, conventional inference excludes zero, whereas our interval-data-robust confidence regions include it. Exploiting sharp identification nevertheless yields substantially tighter confidence regions than non-sharp alternatives.

title: Algebraic Characterization of Time-Varying Set Invariance
abstract: The verification of temporal forward invariance for dynamical systems subject to time-varying constraints is a foundational problem in the analysis of safety-critical systems. Existing methodologies rely on restrictive geometric assumptions, such as the Linear Independence Constraint Qualification (LICQ), or suffer from exponential computational complexity when applied to time-varying polytopes. This paper establishes a rigorous, unified, and computationally tractable framework for temporal safety verification. First, utilizing tools from nonsmooth analysis, we prove that a Nagumo-type geometric inclusion evaluated strictly on the boundary of the augmented graph is both necessary and sufficient for temporal forward invariance. Second, we provide an algebraic characterization of this condition requiring only the weaker Abadie Constraint Qualification (ACQ), generalizing standard Control Barrier Function (CBF) boundary conditions to non-smooth, multi-constraint domains. Finally, for the practical class of Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems with time-varying polytopic constraints, we deploy Farkas' Lemma to eliminate exponential vertex enumeration. By introducing a Lipschitz-bounded time-discretization scheme, we reduce the infinite-dimensional continuous-time verification problem to a finite, highly tractable set of decoupled Linear Programs (LPs).

title: Smoothing the Bouncing-Geodesic Singularity in AdS/CFT
abstract: Black hole singularities remain a central open problem in quantum gravity. In the AdS/CFT correspondence, bulk spacelike extremal surfaces can probe the black hole interior, and information about the near-singularity geometry is encoded in analytically continued boundary correlators. As the bouncing geodesic approaches the black hole singularity, it becomes nearly null and gives rise to characteristic divergences at complex times. Importantly, these complex-time singularities emerge only in the strict semiclassical limit ($G_N\to 0$ or $c\to\infty$) and are governed by the asymptotically linear quasinormal mode (QNM) spectrum. At finite $c$, nonlinear deformations of the QNM trajectories produce suppression kernel that smooths out the complex-time singularities. Using Liouville CFT as an analytically solvable example, we explicitly demonstrate the finite-$c$ deformation of the QNM spectrum and its associated pole-zero structure. We also identify a complementary Gaussian smoothing mechanism arising from finite-energy fluctuations in the thermal spectral decomposition. These results show how finite $G_N$ quantum corrections modify the holographic imprints of the classical black hole singularity.

title: Quaternionic and Octonionic Frameworks for Quantum Computation: Mathematical Structures, Models, and Fundamental Limitations
abstract: We develop detailed quaternionic and octonionic frameworks for quantum computation grounded on normed division algebras. Our central result is to prove the polynomial computational equivalence of quaternionic and complex quantum models: Computation over $\mathbb{H}$ is polynomially equivalent to the standard complex quantum circuit model and hence captures the same complexity class BQP up to polynomial reductions. Over $\mathbb{H}$, we construct a complete model---quaternionic qubits on right $\mathbb{H}$-modules with quaternion-valued inner products, unitary dynamics, associative tensor products, and universal gate sets---and establish polynomial equivalence with the standard complex model; routes for implementation at fidelities exceeding $99\%$ via pulse-level synthesis on current hardware are discussed. Over $\mathbb{O}$, non-associativity yields path-dependent evolution, ambiguous adjoints/inner products, non-associative tensor products, and possible failure of energy conservation outside associative sectors. We formalize these obstructions and systematize four mitigation strategies: Confinement to associative subalgebras, $G_{2}$-invariant codes, dynamical decoupling of associator terms, and a seven-factor algebraic decomposition for gate synthesis. The results delineate the feasible quaternionic regime from the constrained octonionic landscape and point to applications in symmetry-protected architectures, algebra-aware simulation, and hypercomplex learning.

title: NormMoX: A Normative Mixture of Experts for Explainable Autism Classification from Structural and Functional MRI
abstract: While structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI, fMRI) offer profound potential for researching autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and understanding individual neurodivergence, current classifiers lack the explanatory power needed for scientific study, clinical use and personal-level insights. Most models learn from imaging features that also vary with age, sex, scanner site and head motion. They fuse the two modalities without a common reference and explain decisions against arbitrary reference inputs rather than a typical brain. We present NormMoX, a normative mixture of experts that makes the typical brain the shared reference for prediction, fusion and explanation. Normative models trained on large healthy cohorts give the value each brain measure is expected to take for a person's age and sex. NormMoX learns from each person's deviations from these expected values. For each modality, a neural network expert turns the deviations into a score of evidence for ASD. A fusion head, MoX, compares each score with those of typical controls before combining them. It therefore needs no imputation when a modality is missing and shows in which modality each person is atypical. On 1,035 participants of ABIDE I, NormMoX reached an AUROC of $0.728 \pm 0.004$ in repeated cross-validation, above linear, single-modality and deep fusion baselines. NormMoX thus shows not only whether a person is likely to have ASD, but where, and in which modality, their brain departs from typical. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Novelex/NormMox.

title: Certifying Graph Neural Networks Against Label and Structure Poisoning
abstract: Robust machine learning for graph-structured data has made significant progress against test-time attacks, yet certified robustness to poisoning - where adversaries manipulate the training data - remains largely underexplored. For image data, state-of-the-art poisoning certificates rely on partitioning-and-aggregation schemes. However, we show that these methods fail when applied in the graph domain due to the inherent label and structure sparsity found in common graph datasets, making effective graph-partitioning difficult. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework called deep Self-Training Graph Partition Aggregation (ST-GPA), which enriches each graph partition with informative pseudo-labels and synthetic edges, enabling effective certification against node-label and graph-structure poisoning under sparse conditions. Our method is architecture-agnostic, scales to large numbers of partitions, and consistently and significantly improves robustness guarantees against both label and structure poisoning across multiple benchmarks, while maintaining strong clean accuracy. Overall, our results establish a promising direction for certifiably robust learning on graph-structured data against poisoning under sparse conditions.

title: A Note on the Finite-Exceedance Dependence Principle for Sum--Maximum Asymptotic Independence
abstract: Asymptotic independence between sum-type and maximum-type statistics arises repeatedly across many areas of probability and statistics, particularly in high-dimensional testing and random matrix theory. Motivated by the shared structure underlying existing proofs, which is obscured by their model-specific formulations, this note isolates a common intermediate principle. We introduce a finite-exceedance dependence principle: if the finite-exceedance dependence error vanishes at every fixed order and high-order exceedances are mildly controlled, then a finite-order Bonferroni argument yields asymptotic independence between the sum and the maximum. We further give an independent-proxy criterion for verifying this: for each finite set of exceedances, it suffices to construct an exactly independent proxy for the sum-type statistic whose approximation error is negligible in aggregate. Local deletion under dependency graphs and Gaussian regression and residualization are two examples. The framework gives modular derivations of existing sum--max independence results.

title: Neural Actor--Critic Learning with Minimax Critics and Reflected Langevin Sampling
abstract: Actor--critic methods rely on critic gradients to improve continuous-action policies, yet finite-sample guarantees must control both value and gradient errors and their propagation through the actor. We develop a neural actor-critic procedure that combines a regularized minimax Bellman estimator over sigmoid networks with a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient. Under uniform Bellman regularity and covered reset sampling, a positive high-order action-derivative penalty yields value and action-gradient risk bounds with classical nonparametric minimax exponents up to logarithmic factors. We propagate estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors to obtain return guarantees, with refinements for bounded multimodal potentials and strongly concave regimes. Empirical studies across controlled simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task show favorable performance relative to the considered baselines.

title: Data integration using propensity score weighting under missing at random
abstract: We study data integration for the setting in which a probability sample and a nonprobability sample are both available from a common target population, with auxiliary variables observed in both samples and the study variable observed only in the nonprobability sample. Under a parametric propensity score model for the nonprobability sample inclusion mechanism, we develop a conditional maximum likelihood estimator of the inclusion probabilities and construct an inverse probability weighted (IPW) estimator of the population mean. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed IPW estimator under suitable regularity conditions. To guard against misspecification of the propensity score model, we further incorporate an outcome regression model through debiased generalized entropy calibration (GEC) yielding a doubly robust estimator that remains consistent when the propensity score model or the outcome regression model is correctly specified. We also develop variance estimation procedures for both estimators. Simulation studies illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods, and we apply them to data from the Culture and Community in a Time of Crisis survey, where the nonprobability sample substantially over-represents certain demographic groups relative to the U.S.\ adult population.

title: Coherent 1-μm-Band Co-Transmission with C+L-Band Channels over 50-km Hollow-Core Fiber
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate simultaneous coherent transmission across 1-$μ$m and C+L bands, carrying $54\times125$-GBaud PDM-16QAM C+L channels and $2\times15$-GBaud PDM-QPSK 1-$μ$m channels over 50 km, highlighting 1 $μ$m as a promising additional transmission window while avoiding gas-absorption constraints in C/L-band of HCFs.

title: Rate-selective synchronization in switching networks: when timing meets structure
abstract: Switching networks arise across physics, biology, and engineering, where interactions turn on and off due to communication limits, control protocols, failures, or scheduling. Most synchronization theory for switching networks of continuous-time oscillators relies on the fast-switching approximation, yet many systems operate outside this regime, where switching can produce unexpected and counterintuitive collective dynamics. We develop the first analytical framework for synchronization in non-fast-switching networks of saddle-focus continuous-time oscillators. Using Rössler and piecewise-smooth systems as canonical examples, we leverage a structural property of saddle-focus oscillators to reduce the variational dynamics to a linear system with constant coefficients, enabling a Floquet-theoretic stability characterization under periodic switching. The analysis identifies explicit switching intervals that stabilize synchronization even when neither switching mode nor the corresponding average system supports synchronization in isolation, thereby revealing the mechanism underlying the emergence of "windows of opportunity" at intermediate switching rates. We further derive a switching-dependent master stability function linking the network Laplacian spectrum to the switching rate. The master stability function provides two complementary routes to inducing or preserving synchronization: adjusting the switching schedule for a fixed network or adapting the network spectrum to a prescribed schedule through our constructive edge-pruning or edge-augmentation algorithms. These results provide a rigorous basis for understanding and leveraging intermediate-rate switching in the design and control of evolving networks.

title: On Landau's "local method" for obtaining zero-free regions
abstract: We extend Landau's local analytic method for the deduction of zero-free region to a very general setting, and as a particular consequence, obtain a zero-free region and corresponding Prime Number Theorem for Beurling number systems with well-behaved integers. We also discuss the sharpness of the method and prove estimates for the local number of zeros, as well as a clustering result, which roughly put says that zeros close to the 1-line cannot be isolated but must occur in clusters.

title: Multidimensional Suicide Risk Assessment with Machine Learning using Electronic Health Records
abstract: Suicide prevention remains a critical public health challenge, and electronic health records (EHRs) provide an opportunity to characterize suicide-related risk indicators using documented clinical, behavioral, medical, and social-contextual information. This paper presents a multidimensional machine learning framework to model and estimate suicide-related outcomes using MIMIC-IV EHR data. We construct clinically motivated diagnosis categories and define a composite outcome from documented codes corresponding to suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, prior suicidal behavior, and intentional self-harm. To address severe class imbalance and reduce age-related confounding, we apply age-matched resampling that retains all positive patients and samples comparison-cohort patients from the same age group. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost classifiers are evaluated before and after resampling with isotonic calibration. The calibrated XGBoost model achieves the strongest matched-cohort performance, outperforming the other evaluated classifiers. SHAP-based interpretation shows that diagnostic burden, depression-related features, age, personality-disorder history, social determinants related to violence, and medical comorbidity contribute to elevated predicted probabilities. Our results demonstrate that combining broad EHR-derived features, age-matched cohort construction, calibration, and feature-level interpretation provides a practical framework for retrospective suicide-related risk modeling.

title: Frame Properties of Effective Stationary Sequences
abstract: The Kaczmarz algorithm is an iterative projection method for reconstructing vectors in a Hilbert space from inner product data. However, sequences that are effective for this algorithm need not be frames and may lack standard frame reconstruction properties. We investigate these properties for stationary effective sequences, which were classified by Kwapień and Mycielski according to their spectral measures. In particular, we show that the corresponding Kaczmarz reconstruction series always converge unconditionally if and only if the spectral measure is atomic with finitely many point masses. We show that if the spectral measure is atomic, the stationary effective sequence and its auxiliary Parseval frame can be interchanged in the Kaczmarz reconstruction formula. Finally, we construct two stationary effective sequences with singular continuous spectral measures, one of which can be interchanged with its auxiliary Parseval frame in the reconstruction formula, and one of which cannot be interchanged.

title: Air-Scan-Based Point-Spread-Function Estimation for Megavoltage CT with Flat-Panel Detectors
abstract: Accurate spatial-resolution characterization of flat-panel detectors at megavoltage energies is difficult due to long-tailed cross-talk. Conventional measurements at high energy using line-pair gauges or knife-edge phantoms require expensive, carefully fabricated objects and precise alignment, and despite these, scatter from the phantom, detector, and imaging room can further confound the measurement. We present a method for estimating the detector point spread function (PSF) from the mean noise power spectrum (NPS) calculated from repeated radiographs in air. The approach is mathematically equivalent to an autocovariance-based method but is more practical for long-tailed PSFs. We validate the method using simulated air data and Monte Carlo N-particle (MCNP6) calculations of energy deposition in a flat-panel detector. We show that deconvolving the experimental PSF increases the accuracy of transmission radiographs of step wedges. The method requires no phantom or alignments and is straightforward to reproduce.

title: Every Pixel Is an Option: A System One Model for Medical Ultrasound Biometry
abstract: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound tasks, whereas vision-language models offer flexibility through text instructions. However, direct coordinate prediction does not explicitly model spatial likelihood distributions, limiting the representation of localization ambiguity. **Methods:** We propose Kev-Bio, a vision-language model that uses clinical measurement questions to guide ultrasound landmark detection. Inspired by System One decision models, Kev-Bio uses decision representations of the language model to generate queries for each caliper endpoint. These queries are matched against shared dense ultrasound features to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived. The model is trained end-to-end using both landmark localization and clinical measurement losses. **Results:** On the nine-view FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, Kev-Bio achieves a mean radial error (MRE) of 22.50 pixels and a clinical measurement mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.38, outperforming the compared baselines in overall performance. **Conclusion:** These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Kev-Bio for ultrasound landmark detection and clinical measurement across different anatomical views. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/Kev-Bio.

title: Scalable Fully Implicit Runge-Kutta Solvers for Time-Dependent Rayleigh-Bénard Convection
abstract: We consider the efficient numerical solution of time-dependent Rayleigh-Bénard convection governed by the incompressible Boussinesq equations. The coupled velocity-pressure-temperature system presents significant computational challenges arising from incompressibility, buoyancy coupling, convection, and the simultaneous resolution of multiple physical time scales. We present a systematic study of fully implicit Runge-Kutta methods for time-dependent Rayleigh-Bénard convection, together with scalable finite element solvers for the resulting stage-coupled systems. We employ high-order, L-stable Radau IIA methods for temporal integration and investigate Taylor-Hood and Alfeld-Sorokina finite elements in two dimensions, along with Taylor-Hood and enriched macroelement discretizations in three dimensions. The macroelement approaches offer strong local inf-sup stability and patch structures well suited to Vanka-type relaxation. In two dimensions, monolithic multigrid achieves nearly stage-independent outer Krylov iteration counts and maintains robust convergence under mesh refinement. On the same mesh with incremental pressure correction, selected Radau configurations reduce elapsed solve time by 18-32% and yield smaller sampled transient differences relative to a numerical reference solution. Three-dimensional experiments demonstrate favorable parallel scalability with Taylor-Hood elements and substantially improved discrete mass conservation with the enriched macroelement discretization. These results identify regimes in which coupled multistage fully implicit integration is computationally competitive when equipped with appropriate multigrid preconditioners.

title: Optimal bounds for design curves on the torus
abstract: A closed rectifiable curve on the torus $\mathbb T^d=\mathbb R^d/\mathbb Z^d$ is a $t$-design curve if normalized arclength integration is exact for trigonometric polynomials $e^{2πi \langle m,x\rangle}$ with frequencies $m\in\mathbb Z^d$ satisfying $\|m\|_\infty\le t$. For the arclength $L$ of such curves, we establish the sharp lower bound \begin{equation}\label{eq:abs} L\geq \Big(\frac{(t+1)^{2d}-1}{t(t+2)}\Big)^{1/2}. \end{equation} Equality is attained by the family of Korobov curves described in \cite{Kunis,Lindblad}. For even $t$, we also derive an explicit lower bound on the length of total-degree $t$-design curves, defined by the frequency condition $\|m\|_1\leq t$. This bound is sharp for $t=2$ in every dimension and for every even $t$ in dimension two. We determine the minimum length of hyperbolic cross $t^2$-design curves in dimension two. For $d\geq3$, we establish lower bounds of optimal order for the length of hyperbolic cross $t^d$-design curves. Finally, we obtain lower bounds of optimal order for the length of $t$-design curves associated with sparse frequency sets.

title: Stellar wind variability in OB stars and its effect on mass-loss determinations
abstract: Virtually all stellar winds of OB stars exhibit variability in one spectral diagnostic or another. This review focuses primarily on UV spectroscopic signatures of this variability and on studies that have exploited it to reveal the presence of large-scale velocity and density structures in the winds. The review includes demonstrations that the physical structures responsible for the variations appear to be large, spatially coherent and rooted in the stellar photospheres. Furthermore, evidence is summarised that these structures can be optically thick to resonance line radiation and are dense enough to modulate the X-ray fluxes that originate in the wind. Also discussed, is how the structures can affect wind line formation and, as a result, the precision by which mass-loss rates can be determined. The potential of millimetre and radio continuum observations to constrain the radial stratification of wind clumping is highlighted, as a future path to reliable empirical determinations of massive star mass-loss rates.

title: Maximizing Crossword Grids with a Fixed Minimum Clue Length
abstract: In an American-style crossword puzzle, the grid must be connected, 180-degree symmetric, and have minimum word length 3. Ferland and Pratt construct $n\times n$ crossword grids with many clues satisfying these conditions and prove their construction is maximal when $n\equiv 1$ or 3 $\pmod{4}$. In this paper, we explore American-style crosswords in which the minimum word length is 4. Jacobs computed the maximal $15 \times 15$ grid with minimum word length 4. In this paper, we construct grids with a maximal number of clues for all $n \not \equiv 0 \pmod{5}$.

title: Piezogyration and elastogyration in ternary chalcopyrites from first principles
abstract: Natural optical activity arises from the spatial dispersion of the optical response and is described by the rank-two gyration pseudotensor. Its dependence on mechanical stress and strain, quantified by the piezogyration and elastogyration tensors, respectively, has been investigated experimentally for decades. However, a systematic first-principles description of these effects remains largely unexplored. Here we present a first-principles methodology to compute the full piezogyration and elastogyration tensors, and apply it to a set of representative ternary chalcopyrite crystals. The gyration of the unstrained crystal turns out to be a poor predictor of the magnitude of the elastogyration response, which we find to be a property inherited from their parent zinc-blende structures. The elastic compliance tensor further shapes the piezogyration response, with particularly pronounced effects in AgGaS$_2$, a well-known achiral yet optically active crystal. Finally, we explore strain-induced chirality through the trace of the gyration tensor, the only pseudoscalar contribution to the natural optical activity that is linear in the tensor components and encodes information about chirality.

title: Finite groups with all involutions fused
abstract: We characterize finite groups whose involutions form a single fusion class. In the solvable case, we show that the $2$-length is $1$, extending Thompson's theorem which states that a solvable group with all involutions conjugate has $2$-length $1$. For a nonsolvable group $G$, we prove that if its involutions are fused then they are conjugate; moreover, $G/\mathbf{O}_{2'}(G)$ is almost quasisimple. As an application, we obtain a restriction on $m$ for which an $m$-pyramidal Kirkman triple system can be realized under a nonsolvable group.

title: Stochastic Matching with Polynomial Degree
abstract: We study the stochastic matching problem, where a graph $G$ is known in advance, but each edge survives independently with probability $p$. The goal is to select a subgraph $H$ of small maximum degree before seeing the surviving edges, while preserving a $(1-ε)$ fraction of the expected maximum matching size. This problem has received significant attention due to its numerous applications in kidney exchange, labor markets, and online dating. In this paper, we show there is always a subgraph $H \subseteq G$ achieving a $(1-ε)$-approximation while having a maximum degree of at most $O\left(\frac{\log(1/ε)}{ε^4} \cdot \frac{1}{p}\right).$ This resolves a major conjecture of the literature, first stated by [BDH, STOC'20], that $poly(\frac{1}{εp})$ degrees suffice. The best previous bound was $(1/p)^{\exp((1/ε)\log(1/ε))}$ by [ABGR, STOC'25]. The key to this result is a lemma of independent interest that any distribution over the matchings of a stochastic graph can be transformed to another distribution which matches each vertex with exactly the same probability, but exhibits extremely low total pairwise correlation.

title: Good rational functions up to degree six
abstract: Locally recoverable codes (LRCs) are fundamental to the architecture of modern distributed storage systems. The Tamo-Barg construction of optimal LRCs was revolutionized by the introduction of good polynomials, which group evaluation points into local recovery sets. However, polynomial constructions are constrained by their inherently large Galois groups, which limit the number of totally split rational places. Recent advances have generalized this paradigm to good rational functions, which leverage the geometry of the projective line to achieve minimal Galois groups and subsequently codes with greater length. In this paper, we complete the classification of good rational functions of degree up to $6$ in characteristic $2$. By embedding the problem into algebraic function field theory, we explicitly determine the minimal arithmetic and geometric Galois groups for these low degrees. Furthermore, we move beyond asymptotic Hasse-Weil estimates by proving that the exact number of totally split places over extension fields obeys a linear recurring sequence (LRS). This gives an efficient method for computing the exact lengths and dimensions of the corresponding optimal LRCs and, in many cases, yields parameters beyond those obtainable from good polynomials.

title: Fast Self-Triggering and Segment-Fitting of Cosmic Muons with a small-Diameter Monitored Drift Tube Detector
abstract: We present a fast self-triggering and segment-fitting algorithm that identifies cosmic muons and reconstructs their directions using a small-diameter Monitored Drift Tube (sMDT) chamber without an external trigger detector. The muon arrival time is determined using a Legendre-based algorithm combined with coarse- and fine-grid searches. We implement the algorithm in FPGA firmware on an ATLAS MDT miniDAQ board and evaluate its efficiency, resolution, and latency. The results demonstrate standalone sMDT triggering and trigger-level reconstruction of muon directions, providing a solution for chamber commissioning and potentially MDT-based triggers for charged massive stable particle searches at the High Luminosity-LHC.

title: Fuse To Align: Multimodal Representation Learning for Retrieval via Hypergraph Regularization
abstract: Multimodal retrieval must integrate complementary evidence from views that may be missing, noisy, or unequally informative. When a sample provides limited reliable evidence, learning from its views alone can hinder the acquisition of useful retrieval representations. Semantically related training samples may provide complementary observations, yet existing volume-based objectives jointly align modalities within each sample without explicitly enabling information exchange across samples. We therefore propose a training-time hypergraph fusion framework that connects observed modalities both within samples and across semantically related samples, allowing representation learning to draw on evidence beyond an individual sample while leaving the retrieval pipeline unchanged at inference. The framework includes HyVol as a special case and introduces two configurations: wHyVol learns view contribution weights and symmetric semantic affinities, whereas wRHG additionally models typed interactions and participant roles through relational propagation. Missing modalities are omitted rather than imputed, and the hypergraph is discarded after training, incurring no additional inference cost. Experiments on eleven zero-shot video-text and audio-text retrieval benchmarks demonstrate broad improvements with both GRAM and HyperGRAM. Across 17 video benchmark-modality settings evaluated in both retrieval directions, wRHG outperforms GRAM in all 34 comparisons and HyperGRAM in 33 of 34. Mean text-to-video R@1 increases from 63.4 to 68.2 with GRAM and from 64.8 to 68.4 with HyperGRAM, while the largest video-to-text gain reaches 13.3 percentage points on ActivityNet. Under missing-modality evaluation, both weighted configurations retain positive text-to-video gains over GRAM across seven benchmarks at every evaluated missingness rate, even when 90% of clips lack one modality.

title: EO-Jev: Decision Model for Earth Observation
abstract: Earth observation (EO) workflows require selecting among known outcomes, estimating confidence, and processing large volumes of imagery. Generative vision-language models can address these tasks, but autoregressive decoding is computationally costly and their confidence estimates are unreliable. Decision models offer an alternative, returning probabilities over candidate answers in a single forward pass. However, their accuracy, calibration, and transfer across EO tasks remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these properties through a diagnostic study of d3-flash (8.4B parameters) across 30 settings from 23 public EO benchmarks. We find that compositional reasoning transfers well and calibration improves over its Qwen3.5-9B backbone on 24 settings, while counting, change quantification, damage grading, and absent-object recognition remain challenging. To address these limitations, we adapt d3-flash through low-rank fine-tuning on public EO training splits, producing EO-Jev. EO-Jev improves significantly over d3-flash on 26 of 30 settings and matches or exceeds specialist references on 20 of 28. It also achieves an average gain of 8.0 points across 12 held-out settings and lower expected calibration error than specialists on 21 of 28 settings. These improvements come at a modest cost of 1.8 points in general decision performance. Our results demonstrate the potential of adapting general decision models into competitive EO generalists while highlighting persistent challenges in quantitative perception, option-order consistency, and calibration under distribution shift.

title: First- and second-order constrained optimisation for inverse homogenisation of unidirectionally varying microstructure
abstract: This paper is concerned with inverse homogenisation problems that aim to identify microstructure features of a body from macroscopic measurements. The unknown microstructure is assumed to vary macroscopically in one spatial direction and affects the effective tensor in an elliptic partial differential equation that governs the behaviour of the body on the macroscale. We establish the well-posedness of the PDE-constrained minimisation problems that model the task of identifying the microstructure, derive first-order necessary optimality conditions, and prove the convergence of a gradient-projection algorithm for the studied problem class in an infinite-dimensional setting. We moreover demonstrate that recently obtained results on generalised differentiability properties of solution maps of bilateral obstacle problems make it possible to set up and analyse a novel semismooth Newton method in the considered situation. The functional analytic setting that we use for our investigation is chosen such that it covers various elliptic PDEs simultaneously (classical second-order equations, bi-Laplace problems, linear elasticity, etc.) and explicitly exploits the problem structure to obtain global convergence guarantees for the studied solution algorithms in terms of the Lipschitz constants of the involved operators. Our analysis is accompanied by numerical experiments which show that the new semismooth Newton approach requires far less expensive projection evaluations than the gradient-descent method and, thus, offers a significant speedup.

title: Towards AI-Agent-Accelerated Research in High-Energy Physics: A Case Study in Monte Carlo Analysis
abstract: We investigate how far contemporary LLM-based agents can participate in multistep computational high-energy-physics research under reproducible human supervision. Using a previously published CEPC Bell-observable analysis in $e^+e^- \to ZH$, $Z \to q\bar q$, $H \to ZZ^* \to 4μ$ as a case study, we test two capabilities. First, the agent performs an instruction-constrained reproduction: it is explicitly instructed not to use the published numerical results as analysis targets, although no technical information-access barrier is imposed. The analysis definition is fixed before the formal comparison, and the resulting detector-level $I_3$ central values reproduce the four published benchmark points to within about 2% without retuning to those values. Second, the agent is used for an open-ended extension with no target answer supplied. Using 200,000 fast-simulated events, a stage-resolved audit identifies muon isolation as the largest single contribution to the hard-to-detector shift, and subsequent diagnostics connect the effect to angle-dependent isolation efficiency, proximity to the hard $Z \to q\bar q$ system, and mixed electromagnetic activity from muon final-state radiation and hadron decays. Throughout, the agent assists with workflow planning, code and configuration inspection, Monte Carlo production, anomaly diagnosis, control construction, statistical analysis, and result organization, while state-changing actions and final interpretation remain under human control. The study shows that the value of AI agents in HEP may lie not only in faster code generation, but in faster scientific iteration, and motivates systematic benchmarking across historical HEP analyses using correctness, human intervention, and researcher-time efficiency as explicit metrics.

title: Characterizing When Language Models Take Harmful Actions to Protect Their Assigned Goals
abstract: Recent language model (LM) safety failures have largely been studied as disparate phenomena. In agentic misalignment, a model blackmails an executive to avoid being replaced. In alignment faking, it complies with harmful requests during training to keep its values from being modified. We argue that these behaviours share a common decision structure: a model assigned a goal must either take a harmful action to preserve it or refuse and lose it. We formalize this as a goal-harm conflict and present the same conflict under various elicitation protocols that range from compact forced-choice prompts to simulated agentic environments. These protocols span two perspectives on LM decision-making, which we term (i) the logit view, reading preferences from answer-token probabilities, and (ii) the sampling view, classifying open-ended responses with an LM judge. Under the logit view, we show that goal importance and harm severity additively shape how a model resolves these value conflicts. Under the sampling view, we derive two factorizations of the harmful-action probability that safety evaluations commonly report. The first measures how well a preference read from answer tokens carries over into behaviour, such as making a harmful tool call. The second attributes a low harmful-action rate either to refusal or to responses that reach no resolution. We then show how fictional context changes a model's preference under the logit view, and how tool use and partial observability -- two features of agentic evaluations -- change its harmful-action rate under the sampling view. Our work offers a descriptive framework for studying how LMs resolve such value conflicts and for estimating low-probability harmful actions at a finer granularity than the aggregate harm rates commonly reported in safety evaluations.

title: Polarization in $Λ\to pμ^-\barν_μ$ as a probe of CP-violating new physics
abstract: We investigate the normal $μ$ polarization in the hyperon decay $Λ\to pμ^-\barν_μ$ as a probe of new physics that violates CP, since this polarization vanishes at tree level in the Standard Model. Using an effective Lagrangian and lattice QCD form factors, we compute its sensitivity to the imaginary parts of the couplings. With the present bounds from kaon decays and the Large Hadron Collider, one coupling at a time, this sensitivity gives an effect below the Standard Model contribution from the electromagnetic final-state interaction. Only a pseudoscalar coupling with a particular phase can exceed this contribution, by several times. The final-state interaction gives the same polarization in $Λ$ and $\barΛ$ decays, so the difference between the two decays isolates the new physics effect.

title: Mixed-Methods Exploration of Sociotechnical Factors to Improve Adoption of Crime-Reporting Apps in Urban Communities
abstract: Crime-reporting mobile applications can enhance community safety and engagement in urban areas, yet their adoption remains low, partly because developers prioritize technological features over residents' social realities. This study used an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design to identify and validate the sociotechnical factors that drive adoption. Two focus groups and an analysis of 660 app reviews revealed that users' initial sense of usefulness fades, whereas sustained engagement depends on perceived value (PV), comprising six dimensions: safety, anonymity, recency, autonomy, camaraderie, and accessibility. A survey of 505 urban residents, analyzed with PLS-SEM, validated PV as a formative higher-order construct formed by four of these dimensions (safety, anonymity, autonomy, and camaraderie). PV was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, ahead of effort expectancy, facilitating conditions, and performance expectancy, and behavioral intention strongly predicted actual use. The model explained 75% of the variance in behavioral intention and 51% in actual use. The findings offer design principles for community-centered crime-reporting technologies.

title: Same Outputs, Different Scores: Auditing the Unchecked Graders of Multimodal LLM Benchmarks
abstract: Every multimodal-LLM multiple-choice benchmark ends with a scoring rule that converts a model's response, often free-form text rather than a clean option letter, into a right/wrong verdict, buried in its code. Unlike the dataset, this rule is chosen without justification and left unexamined, yet it sets the published number. We reproduce the official scorers of eight peer-reviewed benchmarks on five open vision-language models (VLMs) that fit a single 16 GB GPU, and introduce a blinded human-plus-LLM-judge adjudication (Cohen's kappa=0.956) that recovers what the model actually answered. The scoring rule alone moves accuracy by up to 22 points on identical outputs, yet exactly 0 wherever a model emits clean option letters, so it hides on strong-model leaderboards. It is the fallback and not the rambling that does the damage: the benchmark with the highest non-compliance we measure has an artifact of exactly zero, because its scorer abstains instead of guessing; a reasoning model with non-compliance 0.000 still swings 9.5 points with which regex match of its trace the parser keeps. No standard rule is reliable: snapping a non-answer to its closest option credits answers never given yet buries correct ones, abstention discards answers stated in words, and likelihood scoring follows answer-token priors, so a single grade conflates capability with luck rather than measuring either. We release all code, labels, and the protocol, and argue benchmarks should report a non-compliance rate and at least two rules, not one unexamined grade.

title: Non-Coherent Over-the-Air Distributed Consensus: Algorithm Design and Power Control Optimization
abstract: Non-coherent over-the-air (NCOTA) aggregation offers a scalable and communication-efficient approach to distributed average consensus in wireless networks, without requiring instantaneous channel state information (CSI) or phase alignment. However, persistent aggregation errors pose fundamental challenges in achieving exact average consensus under nominal distributed averaging protocols. In this paper, we develop an NCOTA consensus framework that accommodates row-stochastic mixing, without requiring the conventional average-preservation property of doubly stochastic mixing matrices. Building on a distributed optimization formulation of average consensus, we propose a decentralized projected gradient descent with row-stochastic mixing (DPGD-RS) algorithm and establish its mean-square convergence to the exact average of the agents' initial states. We further derive a closed-form upper bound on the mean-square consensus error, characterizing the effects of aggregation uncertainty, network connectivity, and mixing imbalance. Guided by this analysis, we propose a spectral-reshaping power control (SR-PC) scheme that jointly optimizes transmit powers and receive-scaling factors to accelerate convergence by balancing aggregation accuracy and network mixing. Numerical results validate the theoretical convergence guarantees and demonstrate that the proposed power control scheme significantly accelerates convergence compared with full-power transmission and spectral-radius-minimization benchmarks.

title: RangeFinder: Predicting Ligand Property Ranges from Protein Pockets
abstract: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules. Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context. Using an intersection-over-union objective and evaluation metric (range-IoU), RangeFinder achieves a range-IoU of $0.464 \pm 0.002$, outperforming all deployable baselines while requiring only $12.2$ ms per pocket. We also quantify our method's ability to reduce the ligand search space while retaining compatible binders; in this regard, RangeFinder achieves a Reduction-Recall F-Score of $0.543 \pm 0.011$ --- once again outperforming all deployable baselines. Ablation experiments indicate that RangeFinder's performance depends more strongly on the density and quality of ligand supervision than on any individual input modality or specialized training strategy. Together, these results position RangeFinder as an inexpensive and effective molecular filtering prior, with demonstrated potential in narrowing the ligand search space of target pockets before docking, generation, or synthesis. The code for this project can be found at: https://github.com/alannadels/RangeFinder.

title: Centralizers of maps as automorphism groups of Yang--Baxter solutions
abstract: For a partition $X = Y \sqcup Z$ of a set $X$ and an arbitrary map $g \colon Y \to {\rm Hom}_{\rm Set} (Z, \, Z)$, we construct a solution $R_g \colon X \times X \to X \times X$ of the braid equation. We characterize intrinsically the solutions which are isomorphic to some $R_g$ and we give a necessary and sufficient condition for two solutions $R_g$ and $R_{g'}$ to be isomorphic. Consequently, the number of isomorphism classes of the solutions $R_g$ on a set with $n$ elements is $1 + \sum_{k = 1}^{n-1} \widetilde{o} (n - k, \, k)$, where $\widetilde{o} (m, \, k)$ is the number of orbits of the symmetric group $S_m$, acting by conjugation, on the set of multisets with $k$ elements of maps $\{1, \ldots, m\} \to \{1, \ldots, m\}$. This construction is then used to obtain a solution of the braid equation whose automorphism group is exactly the centralizer ${\rm Aut} (f_1, \ldots, f_k)$ of a given family $f_1, \ldots, f_k \colon X \to X$ of maps, $k \geq 1$. For $k = 2$, combined with a result of Agore, Chirvasitu and the author, this gives another proof of the fact that any group is isomorphic to the automorphism group of a solution of the braid equation (equivalently, of the set-theoretic Yang--Baxter equation).

title: A Geometry-Informed Neural Operator surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for rapid pluvial-fluvial flood forecasting: the case of Forlì, Italy
abstract: Physically based two-dimensional hydraulic models are too slow for real-time inundation forecasting and large ensembles. We present a time-dependent geometry-informed neural operator (GINO) surrogate of LISFLOOD-FP for the municipality of Forlì (Italy), severely affected by the May 2023 Emilia-Romagna floods. The surrogate is designed for an operational setting in which only river stage gauges and rain gauges are available. A reproducible pipeline turns public regional observations into a physically based training set: each river inflow is driven by the first stage gauge downstream of it through a calibrated water-surface boundary condition, and rain enters as SCS-CN effective rainfall. The surrogate is an autoregressive GINO trained on 216 simulations of 24 observed events with scaled forcing. It predicts volume-conserving polygon-mean depths on an exposure-based Voronoi mesh of 659 nodes, with a 20 min step over 72 h. The surrogate is tested on 38 independent observed events that it never saw during training. On these events it reaches a critical success index (CSI) of 0.934 at 0.05m and 0.844 at 0.3 m, a depth RMSE of 0.008m and an $R^2$ of 0.984 for maximum-depth maps. On one NVIDIA A10G GPU a 72-h forecast takes 1.7 s instead of 55 s with LISFLOOD-FP, and a 50-member ensemble, computed in a single batched rollout, takes 6.2 s instead of about 46 min, which makes probabilistic flood forecasting practical. These results show that neural-operator surrogates can deliver accurate pluvial-fluvial flood forecasts driven by river stage for operational early warning.

title: ASCoR: Asymmetric Semantic-Spatial Learning for Remote Sensing Domain Generalization
abstract: Source-only domain generalization (DG) for remote sensing semantic segmentation seeks reliable predictions in unseen domains without target-domain data during training. Although vision foundation models offer transferable knowledge, category recognition remains sensitive to source-specific visual cues, while task-specific adaptation may weaken pretrained transferability. We propose ASCoR, an asymmetric semantic-spatial framework built on SAM3. Its text-conditioned semantic branch uses class-name prompts to provide explicit category guidance. Probe-Once Dynamic Adaptive LoRA distributes a fixed adaptation budget across encoder blocks to limit source-specific specialization.
