The hypothetical stirrers are always larger in size than the planetesimals, but they do not necessarily contain most of the disc mass. In agreement with previous work, the observed dust masses can be explained by steady-state collisional models with reasonable disc masses. The measured vertical scale-heights can be explained by gravitational stirring from embedded large bodies of reasonable properties. However, more advanced models are needed to address the observed non-Gaussian vertical profiles, along with the dependence of disc scale-height on particle size and stellocentric distance.

title: GeoFaham: Domain-Specialized Multi-Agent Geospatial Analytics for Disaster Response
abstract: Real-world geospatial decision support requires more than single-step retrieval or code generation. Disaster-response questions often involve multi-source workflows that combine spatial databases, map-derived features, satellite imagery, raster products, and reusable geospatial artifacts, where correctness depends on preserving spatial scope, temporal context, and intermediate execution state. While large language models and coding agents offer a promising interface for such workflows, they struggle with geospatial-specific failure modes, including handling large artifacts, selecting the wrong evidence source, losing spatial or temporal metadata, and applying invalid geometric operations. We introduce GeoFaham, a domain-specialized multi-agent system for geospatial disaster analytics. GeoFaham decomposes workflows into specialist agents for vector operations, map feature retrieval, imagery discovery, and raster analysis, coordinated by an Orchestrator with a dual-ledger control loop for dependency-aware planning, progress tracking, validation, and replanning. To support artifact-centric collaboration, GeoFaham uses a Response Store that persists full geospatial outputs and typed metadata outside the LLM context window while agents exchange compact identifiers and summaries. We also introduce GeoFaham-Bench, a 40-task benchmark grounded in 17 real-world disaster records, designed to evaluate multi-step geospatial reasoning, cross-source integration, raster-vector computation, artifact generation, and recovery under non-rigid ground truth. We evaluate GeoFaham on GeoFaham-Bench against strong general-purpose coding-agent baselines, including Codex, Claude Code, and OpenCode. GeoFaham achieves the best overall performance, scoring 0.940 versus the next-best 0.879, while using 7.5 times fewer tokens. Our code and benchmark are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/GeoFaham.

title: Weyl Rescalings: A First Order Approach
abstract: Weyl transformations, --local rescalings in which the metric transforms as $g_{μν}(x)\longrightarrow Ω^2(x)\, g_{μν}(x)$--, are expected to be a symmetry of nature at extremely high energy, that should be (spontaneously) broken at low energy. In Cartan's first order formulation of gravity this translates into the condition that the local frames (vielbein) scale as $e^a(x) \longrightarrow Ω(x) e^a(x)$. In this construction, the Lorentz connection one-form fields $ω^a{}_b$ are independent from $e^a$, and since Lorentz transformations and dilatations commute, $ω$ and $R(ω)$ must be Weyl invariant, while in the second order metric formalism the Ricci tensor undergoes a non-homogeneous transformation. This generates a tension between the two formulations, which should be equivalent in the vanishing torsion limit. Here we show how the puzzle can be resolved taking into account the role of torsion. This also sheds some light on the conformal coupling of matter fields to gravity.

title: Scaling Laws For Data-Constrained Dense Retrieval
abstract: Dense retrieval models are typically obtained by fine-tuning pretrained language models on supervised retrieval data, where high-quality annotations or interaction logs are often limited and reused across many epochs. This data-constrained regime differs from the abundant-data setting assumed by standard scaling laws, making it unclear how the best attainable retrieval performance changes with model size and unique fine-tuning data. We study this question through the minimum achievable evaluation loss (MAEL), defined as the lowest evaluation loss reached during training under fixed model-size and data-budget constraints. We first show that learning-rate choices strongly affect optimization trajectories but have little effect on the final attainable MAEL: after rescaling the optimization-step axis, learning curves collapse across learning rates, and CKA analysis shows that checkpoints reaching MAEL learn highly similar representations. We then fine-tune 35 BERT-family dense retrievers on MS MARCO subsets and find that MAEL is accurately described by a simple multiplicative power law over non-embedding parameters and unique samples, outperforming commonly used additive scaling formulations. We further derive a scaling law for the training step at which MAEL is reached and show that optimal weight decay follows an approximately invariant EMA timescale, yielding lower MAEL and stronger retrieval performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Finally, combining loss and step scaling suggests that, in our observed regime, increasing pretrained model size is approximately 1.46 times as fine-tuning-compute-efficient as increasing unique in-domain data for reducing MAEL.

title: ProAlign: Progressive Positional and Prototype-Guided Alignment for Aerial-Ground Person Re-Identification
abstract: Aerial-Ground Person Re-Identification (AG-ReID) aims to match pedestrian images captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground-based surveillance cameras. The task remains highly challenging due to severe viewpoint discrepancies, frequent occlusions, and substantial domain gaps between aerial and ground imagery. Beyond these observable factors, existing methods often overlook two fundamental structural issues: cumulative positional drift during hierarchical feature extraction and semantic inconsistency across cross-view feature distributions. To address these challenges, we propose ProAlign, a Progressive Positional and Prototype-Guided Alignment Network for AG-ReID. ProAlign comprises two key components: a Layer-wise Progressive Positional Embedding (LPPE) module and a View-Aware Prototype Contrastive Learning (PCL) module. LPPE performs adaptive positional calibration throughout transformer layers by employing conditional positional encoding in shallow layers to mitigate local spatial distortions, while introducing learnable static positional embeddings in deeper layers to reinforce global semantic priors. Meanwhile, PCL maintains view-specific aerial and ground prototypes for each identity and enforces cross-view semantic consistency via a dual-prototype contrastive objective. Extensive experiments on CARGO and two real-world AG-ReID benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of ProAlign, achieving state-of-the-art overall retrieval performance on CARGO with improvements of 1.60% in Rank-1 accuracy and 5.01% in mAP over the strongest competing methods.

title: Renormalization and Factorization Scale-Invariant Predictions for the $e^+e^-\to J/ψ+η_c$ process at $B$ factories
abstract: We perform a NNLO perturbative QCD analysis for exclusive double charmonium production $e^+e^-\to J/ψ+η_c$ within the NRQCD factorization formalism using the Principle of Maximum Conformality (PMC). It is well known that this charmonium process suffers poor pQCD convergence, as well as large renormalization scale uncertainty. The PMC is used to remove conventional renormalization scale uncertainty. Based on two fundamental physical processes of charmonium, $J/ψ\rightarrow e^+e^-$ and $η_c\rightarrowγγ$, and using the NNLO perturbative results together with experimental measurements, we extract the factorization-scale-dependent long-distance matrix elements for $J/ψ$ and $η_c$. Combining these two matrix elements with the factorization-scale-dependent short-distance coefficient, we obtain predictions that are independent of the factorization scale for the $e^+e^-\to J/ψ+η_c$ process. Our predictions agree with the measurement from the BaBar collaborations within errors. Remarkably, we provide a new way to eliminate conventional renormalization and factorization scale ambiguities for the $e^+e^-\to J/ψ+η_c$ process. We further demonstrate that the slow convergence of the pQCD series is an intrinsic property of this double-charmonium process.

title: Ta-based S-I-S junctions for integrated superconducting Electronics
abstract: In this work, we have presented S-I-S Josephson junctions with $\rmα$-Ta electrodes and a ${\rm TaO}_x$ barrier. We grew base and top $α$-Ta electrodes using seed layer engineering, showing both Nb and ${\rm TaN}_x$ are viable seed layer choices, and particularly emphasize that at room temperature a re-seed layer is required to nucleate $\rmα$-Ta for the top electrode. However, we note that the choice of seed layer can have subtle implications on the electrical tunneling behavior of the junctions. We used room-temperature probing of variable junction areas, combined with Ambegaokar-Baratoff physics, to characterize the wafer scale critical current densities. For 0.4 $μ$m$^2$ junctions, we found junction spreads as low as 2.0% across the 20 x 20 mm chip relevant for device performance. The entire process was carried out using standard industry foundry processing using 150 mm wafer tooling, which is an important step towards proving that Ta-based junctions can be implemented at scale. We have successfully fabricated and tested junctions with $\rmα$-Ta electrodes and a ${\rm TaO}_x$ insulating tunnel barrier, demonstrating that this is a material platform which merits further investigation and studies for potential application in classical and quantum superconducting technologies.

title: Algebraic ellipticity of double covers of $(\mathbf P^1)^3$
abstract: We show that every smooth complex double cover of $(\mathbf P^1)^3$ branched along a smooth divisor of tridegree $(2,2,2)$ is algebraically Gromov elliptic. These irrational Fano threefolds form Mori--Mukai family 3-1 and have anticanonical genus seven and Picard rank three. Their three coordinate projections define degree-four del Pezzo fibrations. Each threefold also admits a dominant rational map of degree two from $\mathbf P^3$.

title: SrMn$_2$Ge$_2$: A metallic system with anomalous magnetotransport properties
abstract: The structural, electronic, and physical properties of previously unexplored layered tetragonal compound SrMn$_2$Ge$_2$ are reported. The compound crystallizes in the ThCr$_2$Si$_2$-type structure with a crystallographic parameters $c/a$ ratio of $2.535(3)$, significantly smaller than those of the related BaMn$_2$$Pn_2$ compounds ($Pn =$ P, As, Sb, Bi), indicating enhanced interlayer interaction between the moment-bearing Mn-ions. Magnetic susceptibility measurements suggest an antiferromagnetic ground state with a high Neél temperature $T_{\rm N} > 350$~K\@. A large and positive magnetoresistance (MR) of approximately $50\%$ is observed at low temperatures, which follows a power-law field dependence with exponent $n = 1.50(8)$. Low-temperature electrical resistivity data reveal Kondo-like features. Heat capacity measurements show no signs of a phase transition below 300~K and further confirm a metallic ground state. Electronic structure calculations reveal a three-dimensional Fermi surface and suggest the presence of substantial electronic correlation effects.

title: Deep Learning for Longitudinal Asymmetry in Heavy-Ion Collisions at RHIC Energies
abstract: We developed a deep neural network framework to predict the longitudinal asymmetry and the corresponding rapidity shift in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. The model was trained using sufficiently large datasets for Au+Au and Cu+Cu collision systems at center-of-mass energies of 62.4 and 200 AGeV at RHIC. It successfully learns the underlying relationships between the input parameters and reconstructs the corresponding target quantities with good precision. Its predictions agree well with theoretical simulations across both trained and untrained centrality intervals. The influence of longitudinal asymmetry on final-state flow observables has also been studied, and the model results are in reasonable agreement with the simulation. A SHAP-based correlation analysis further supports the physical consistency of the learned feature dependencies and suggests that the observed correlations are not primarily driven by feature redundancy. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient approach to estimating event-by-event results, potentially reducing the computational cost of large-scale theoretical model simulations. This work presents an initial study exploring the use of deep neural networks to investigate longitudinal asymmetry and rapidity shifts in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

title: Optical Ceiling on Polaron Mobility in Disordered Molecular Semiconductors: Lessons from Eumelanin
abstract: Polaron hopping in disordered molecular semiconductors such as eumelanin is set by energetic disorder $σ$ and reorganization energy $λ$. We show that the reduced polaron absorption band encodes this transport problem. Its value at zero energy fixes the mean hop rate, which bounds the mobility in any dimension. For Gaussian disorder and classical vibrations its centroid is $E_\mathrm{op}=λ+(1-c)σ^2/k_BT$, its variance obeys the Hush relation, and the bound is the Marcus rate at $λ\to E_\mathrm{op}$; a 1D lower bound vanishes at $k_BT^*=(1-c)σ^2/λ$, read from optics.

title: ZEMA: confidence-calibrated signed descent with only one state
abstract: Recent work characterizes the Adam optimizer as sign descent modulated by gradient uncertainty: the update is the sign of the batch gradient, scaled by how strongly the batch supports that sign. We apply this view directly and introduce ZEMA (Z-score Evidence Momentum Adaptation), which measures that support with a per-coordinate $z$-score computed from the per-example gradients in the current batch, converts it into a sign probability, and smooths the resulting update with a single exponential moving average. Because the probability is formed before smoothing rather than after, ZEMA keeps one state per parameter instead of Adam's two, at a $4.6$ increase in per-step time; the per-example variance it requires can also be estimated from a small fraction of the batch. In fine-tuning and pretraining experiments, ZEMA is competitive with Adam, reduces the variability of the validation loss, and in some settings recovers the sign of the full-dataset gradient more consistently. We close with two directions this opens: extending confidence adaptation beyond the sign geometry, to methods such as Muon, and to differentially private training.

title: From Roadside Sensing to Risk-Informed Safety Control: Surrogate Safety Measures as a Cyber-Physical Interface
abstract: Proactive intersection safety analysis depends on trajectory data whose reliability varies by sensing modality, yet infrastructure-perception and surrogate safety measure (SSM) research have only recently begun to converge. This paper synthesizes both literatures alongside control theory to clarify how sensing choices, safety metrics, and predictive control connect end-to-end, and where infrastructure-derived risk signals could inform autonomous vehicle decision-making. Searches covered light detection and ranging (LiDAR), cooperative perception, time-to-collision (TTC), post-encroachment time (PET), extreme value theory, model predictive control (MPC), and signal control. Screening considered trajectory-based safety and control relevance, excluding detection benchmarks without safety linkage. This structured narrative synthesis retained 56 sources. No single SSM is universally valid: one-dimensional TTC and modified TTC suit longitudinal conflicts, two-dimensional TTC extends time-based measurement to crossing geometries, and observed PET captures crossing and vulnerable road user (VRU) conflicts but only after the event. LiDAR consistently outperforms camera-only sensing for continuous three-dimensional trajectory extraction, illumination robustness, and privacy, though its range degrades in heavy rain, fog, and snow. Its output becomes control-ready only when paired with filtering--Kalman, Savitzky-Golay--that stabilizes noisy detections. This review complements it from the infrastructure side: it examines how roadside sensing affects that chain's reliability, classifies SSMs by conflict geometry and temporal availability, and maps risk components onto control objectives and constraints for infrastructure and connected and automated vehicle (CAV) applications.

title: Synchronization in one-dimensional arrays of photon condensates
abstract: We investigate the synchronization of coupled photonic Bose-Einstein condensates in dye-filled microcavity arrays, subject to a potential gradient. We show that in the absence of noise the desynchronisation threshold is the result of a dynamical instability. For a two-site system, we analytically derive the maximal potential difference that allows for a synchronized solution as a function of the system parameters and find that it crucially depends on the thermalization rate. For systems with $N$ sites, we find a $N^{-3}$ power law scaling for the critical potential difference. When quantum fluctuations are included, stochastic phase slips broaden the sharp transitions, yet the phase velocity and first order spatial coherence still reliably identify the instability threshold.

title: Basic Reproductive Numbers in Host-Parasite Systems with Demographic Bistability
abstract: The basic reproductive number, $\mathcal{R}_0$, is widely used to determine whether an infectious disease can persist in a population. However, its interpretation may become unclear when the underlying disease-free demographic dynamics exhibit multiple types of stable attractors. In this study, we investigate how demographic bistability between fixed points and periodic cycles affects the calculation and interpretation of $\mathcal{R}_0$. We consider two discrete-time host-parasite models with infection: a tick-host model motivated by Borrelia burgdorferi transmission and a Nicholson-Bailey host-parasitoid model with intraspecific competition and infection. For each model, we calculate reproductive numbers associated with different disease-free attractors using the next-generation operator method and compare their invasion thresholds. In the tick-host model, the reproduction number calculated on the stable demographic cycle differs from that calculated at the positive coexistence fixed point, resulting in parameter regions where infection can invade at one demographic attractor but not the other. In contrast, in the host-parasitoid model, the host-driven invasion threshold is necessarily the same at the positive coexistence fixed point and on the host-only periodic cycles. These contrasting results demonstrate that demographic bistability alone does not necessarily produce attractor-dependent invasion thresholds. Rather, the effect of demographic dynamics on invasion depends on the structure of pathogen transmission. In particular, a complete host--vector--host transmission pathway can allow differences between demographic attractors to alter the invasion threshold. Our results emphasize the importance of considering both demographic dynamics and transmission structure when interpreting $\mathcal{R}_0$ in populations with multiple stable disease-free states.

title: Pionization experiments in light nuclei
abstract: The zero-energy antiproton absorption in light nuclei is considered. The ratios $R_{n/p}$ of antiproton-neutron versus antiproton-proton capture rates in the lightest nuclei $^2$H, $^3$He and $^4$He are analyzed, both from the experimental results and from some selected theoretical models. These models are used as key input in determining the level shifts and widths of the lowest states. We establish the capture orbit in $^3$He to be states of angular momentum $L=2$. Several N-N optical potentials are used to compute the $R_{n/p}$ values for several heavy nuclei and the results are found to be consistent with the data. However, the old chamber experiments studying pionization in Helium, are not consistent with models. Only the Paris potential is likely to succeed provided baryonia states predicted by this model are better understood.

title: BaCon: Band-Concentrated Exponential Random Graph Models
abstract: Exponential-family random graph models ERGMs provide a parametric interpretable framework for modeling real graphs including the Web and social networks Fitted ERGMs may suffer from degeneracy matching observed graph statistics in expectation does not guarantee that the observed graph and similar ones are highly probable under the fitted distribution We introduce Band-Concentrated ERGMs BaCon a framework that avoids degeneracy by imposing a probabilistic constraint requiring at least $1-δ$ of the distribution probability mass to lie on the set of graphs with statistics within an $\varepsilon$-tolerance band around the observed statistics BaCons maximumentropy distribution still belongs to the exponential family while including a factor checking for inclusion in the tolerance band We derive the exact Metropolis-Hastings acceptance rule for this target and use a practical stochastic approximation procedure with a smoothed band membership during fitting Experiments on social networks across increasingly challenging model specifications show that BaCon substantially increases the probability mass assigned to graphs whose statistics are close to the observed ones while remaining estimable for specifications where standard ERGM estimation fails These results demonstrate that probability mass constraints are a principled way to mitigate degeneracy while retaining the benefits of exponential-family graph models

title: Linking as Evaluation: Correct Separate Compilation via First-Class Environments
abstract: Separate compilation is central to modular software: components are compiled independently and linked into an executable. Separate compilation is correct when a linked program behaves like the program formed by merging its sources. This property is less routine to prove than type soundness because it requires a formal account of linking. We present $λ_{\mathsf{SCE}}$, a simply typed calculus in which linking, modules, and environments are all first-class. Programmers control module linking through a link operator, which a type-directed elaboration translates into ordinary terms of a core calculus of first-class environments. The core calculus's existing evaluation rules then perform the linking: linking as evaluation. Linking independently compiled modules yields the same core term as elaborating their source link. Therefore, compilation and linking commute by construction. As a result, separate compilation correctness follows directly from the semantics preservation for both static and dynamic linking. All meta-theory is mechanized in Lean 4, and we implement a compiler to WebAssembly in OCaml.

title: Synchronization Mpemba Effect
abstract: We introduce the synchronization Mpemba effect, in which a less synchronized initial state overtakes a more synchronized one, and demonstrate it in dissipatively coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators. Within a graph-Laplacian framework, we show that for two oscillators, the mechanism is a competition between a slowly decaying collective background and a fast transverse transient, equivalently an exchange between relative-mode displacement and phase-fluctuation errors. The same decomposition extends to networks: the synchronization error splits into transverse Laplacian modes, yielding closed-form crossing times from eigenvalue separations and initial mode weights, and a sufficient screening criterion. With only these eigenvalues entering, the rule is topology independent: crossing times of different networks collapse onto a single spectral-gap line. Thus, quantum many-body dynamics can be designed and controlled at low dimension without constructing the exponentially large Liouvillian, opening a route to quantum synchronization as a resource.

title: Exact Selective Inference for Spectral Clustering via Piecewise-Constant Graph Perturbation
abstract: Cluster labels are often used twice: first to discover groups, and then to test whether the discovered groups differ. This double use of the data makes ordinary two-sample $p$-values anti-conservative. Selective inference fixes this by conditioning on the clustering event, but for spectral clustering the event appears difficult because the algorithm combines an affinity map, an eigendecomposition, and a rounding step. We show that, for spectral clustering based on unweighted $\varepsilon$- or $k$-nearest-neighbor graphs, the obstruction is the affinity construction rather than the eigendecomposition. Along the one-dimensional perturbation used by the truncated-$χ$ selective test, graph changes occur only at finitely many real roots of data-dependent quadratic distance comparisons. Between these breakpoints, the graph, Laplacian spectrum, embedding, rounding, and reported cluster pair are deterministic functions of a finite graph state. Consequently, in real arithmetic and under a known-scale spherical Gaussian model, the selection set is an exact finite union of intervals, yielding finite-sample selective $p$-values for selected spectral-cluster pairs. The same argument gives feature-wise truncated-normal tests. We also record direct extensions to known feature covariance, eigengap-selected $K$, and auxiliary-coordinate graphs. We validate null and partial-null calibration, operational power, numerical sensitivity, and model-scope diagnostics, and give a working-model PBMC algorithmic illustration. Smooth kernels such as RBF affinities fall outside the finite-state guarantee.

title: Symmetry-protected isolation of the quantum metric in chiral type-II semi-Dirac semimetals
abstract: Quantum geometry, comprising the Berry curvature (BC) and the quantum metric (QM), underpins a wide array of topological and transport phenomena. However, in most solid-state platforms, BC and QM signals are inherently entangled, making their experimental separation highly challenging. Here, we demonstrate that the chiral limit of type-II semi-Dirac semimetals provides a symmetry-protected mechanism to cleanly isolate the QM. At the chiral limit where the spin-orbit gap $m_z=0$, chiral and $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetries strictly suppress the BC, its dipole (BCD), and the shift current, leaving the QM and its dipole (QMD) as the sole sources of the optical and nonlinear Hall responses. This pure-QM regime exhibits distinct experimental fingerprints, including a divergent longitudinal optical conductivity and a QMD-induced nonlinear Hall conductivity that exhibits a pronounced singularity as the chemical potential approaches the nodal point. Turning on a finite $m_z$ reactivates the BC channels, transitioning the system from a pure-QM phase into a mixed geometric phase. By deriving a scaling law for the nonlinear Hall conductivity, we establish a direct experimental strategy to separate the mixed Drude, BCD, and QMD contributions based on their distinct relaxation-time dependencies. Our findings identify chiral type-II semi-Dirac semimetals as highly tunable platforms for isolating and probing intrinsic quantum geometric effects.

title: Auditing Multi-Proxy Explanations of Web User Preferences: Identification Boundaries and Abstention
abstract: Web systems infer user preferences from behavior, ratings, text, and LLM-generated profiles, yet explaining a proxy may reveal its measurement process rather than the preference of interest. We develop an audit framework distinguishing point identification, partial identification, and abstention relative to an explicit reference distribution. Under feature-dependent, arbitrarily signed proxy bias, a strict majority of uncontaminated proxy attributions lets the coordinatewise median recover latent-attribution support and direction and, with externally justified positive scales, magnitude. We prove this threshold sharp using response-valid indistinguishable worlds, characterize sharp minimax error and exact compatible-target sets under approximate cleanliness and scale uncertainty, and propagate clean-proxy attribution error. A frozen known-truth benchmark spans two response families, four proxy counts, all contamination counts, three bias strengths, and eleven methods, with a focal comparison confirmed on twenty unseen seeds. Under correct budgets, a direct attribution-tensor audit achieved 100% coverage, 95.40%-97.05% active-driver sign decisions, and no false signs. In a temporally separated Amazon study, median aggregation reduced comparator-relative conditional sign error for all four targets; six of eight prespecified target-metric contrasts had Bonferroni intervals excluding zero. A controlled real-covariate perturbation favored the median on the prespecified focal metric for all four targets. Compatible sets showed that the current proxy configuration rarely licensed strict-sign conclusions. Weak comparator calibration limits the Amazon evidence to fitted-surface alignment rather than latent-preference recovery.

title: ForgeKernel: Self-Evolving Kernels Catching and Surpassing Experts and Agents
abstract: Purpose-built kernel agents can write high-performance GPU kernels, but existing systems generally lack cross-run knowledge accumulation and architectural evolution. Each run starts from the same initial knowledge, and later iterations largely optimize within an architecture fixed early in the search. We present ForgeKernel, a kernel-generation system that accumulates and reuses knowledge across runs while enabling continued evolution of kernel architectures. It analyzes the hardware behavior of a high-performance reference and distills validated architectural decisions into reusable knowledge of hardware mechanisms rather than imitating source code. It then seals a kernel that passes correctness and performance validation and uses it as the reference for the next optimization run, enabling architectural decisions to be revisited. Across 27 operators and 29 input configurations on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, ForgeKernel matches or beats its expert reference on 25 configurations, with a geometric-mean performance gain of 10%. On Ascend 910C, it outperforms the per-operator public best on the public case set of all 8 level-4 operators in the CANN-Bench Season 1 final leaderboard, with a geometric-mean gain of 25.1%, while its full-suite submission ranks first on the A3 leaderboard. As of 2026-10-30, public submissions generated by ForgeKernel rank first on all three CANN-Bench 2.0 solution leaderboards (Ascend 910C, 950DT, and 950PR) and on the SOL-ExecBench FlashInfer-Bench track.

title: Two-Player Zero-Sum Hybrid Games with Set-Valued Dynamics
abstract: In this paper, we formulate a two-player zero-sum game under dynamic constraints defined in terms of a hybrid inclusion. The game consists of a min-max problem involving a cost functional that depends on the actions and corresponding (potentially non-unique) solutions, defined as functions of hybrid time and, hence, can flow or jump. We present sufficient conditions given in terms of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs-like equations to establish a bound and to exactly evaluate the worst-case cost under the optimal strategy. Under additional conditions, we show that the proposed optimal state-feedback laws render a set of interest pre-asymptotically stable for the resulting hybrid closed-loop system. The results are illustrated in an application with sporadic jumps and linear quadratic hybrid dynamics.

title: Almost primes in short intervals and averages of long Dirichlet polynomial approximations to $(ζ'/ζ)^{k}$
abstract: We study the asymptotic behaviour of the mean square of long truncations of the Dirichlet series for $\bigl(ζ'/ζ\bigr)^{k}$ on the critical line; we establish the connection between this problem and the short-interval variance of the convoluted von Mangoldt function $Λ^{*k}$ in short intervals and in arithmetic progressions. Under a shifted moments conjecture and the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we prove that the short-interval variance leading coefficient is the derivative of the mean-square leading coefficient. A unitary trace-sum average governs the variance of sums of $Λ^{*k}$ over monic polynomials in $\mathbb F_q[T]$; we denote its leading coefficient by $δ_k(c)$, where the total trace degree and matrix size grow with a fixed ratio $c$. Under a weaker shifted moments conjecture and RH, we recover this $δ_k(c)$ as the leading coefficient of the variance of short-interval sums of $Λ^{*k}$ over the integers. It is the counterpart of $γ_k(c)$, the piecewise polynomial from the variance of divisor sums, with the Dirichlet coefficients of $ζ(s)^k$ replaced by those of $\bigl(-ζ'/ζ\bigr)^k$.

title: For You, Not for Everyone: Bystander-Aware Delivery of Critical Feedback in Robot Tutoring
abstract: Robots in shared settings may expose information intended for an individual user to nearby bystanders. Robot tutoring makes this concern particularly salient: critical feedback is directed at an individual learner, yet bystanders may overhear or see it. To address this, we compared context-invariant and context-adaptive robot behaviors in a between-subjects study with 40 participants. Following an initial phase without a bystander, a bystander entered the setting. Participants then received two scripted critical feedback messages concerning their pronunciation and handwriting, independent of their actual performance. With the context-invariant behavior, the robot tutor delivered both messages aloud. With the context-adaptive behavior, the robot tutor scanned for the bystander, turned its body and display away after detecting them, gave a spoken attention cue, and presented the same feedback messages silently on its display. Participants rated the robot tutor higher in perceived privacy awareness and perceived social competence in the context-adaptive condition than in the context-invariant condition, while evidence for reduced experienced embarrassment was inconclusive. These findings inform the design and evaluation of robots that respond to bystander presence by adapting how they communicate potentially sensitive information.

title: Hecke Relations from Self-Duality
abstract: Hecke operators can be used to relate characters of rational conformal field theories with different central charges, but it has remained a mystery how to interpret these relations physically. We offer a simple explanation in terms of self-duality under asymmetric orbifolds. Self-dual orbifolds also give more general identities beyond the familiar Harvey-Wu construction, which we illustrate through examples.

title: Unifying and Beyond the Theory of Pervasive Capability Degradation in LLM Post-training SFT from Feature Interference
abstract: Pervasive Capability Degradation (PCD) refers to the phenomenon in which supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while adapting a large language model (LLM) to a target task, often erodes the general capabilities acquired during pre-training. Prevailing explanations attribute PCD to macroscopic distribution shift and therefore lack microscopic manipulability, leaving existing mitigation methods without a complete theoretical foundation. In this paper, we first develop a bottom-up geometric theory of PCD grounded in feature interference under superposition: narrow-domain SFT data disrupt the almost-orthogonal feature structure formed during pre-training, and the resulting interference drives activations across decision hyperplanes in the output Laguerre-Voronoi geometry, flipping predictions on general tasks. This theory unifies existing methods into six paradigms and reveals both the source of their efficacy and their theoretical limits. We then prove that cross-entropy under one-hot supervision cannot resolve PCD on its own, and accordingly propose the AEGIS loss, which directly constrains the drift of activation margins along all competing token directions, thereby decoupling interference suppression from task adaptation. Across 3 model families and 14 SFT tasks, AEGIS outperforms representative methods of every paradigm on target tasks and pervasive capabilities simultaneously, at only about 1.3 times the computational cost of standard SFT. Its generality, scalability, and mechanistic interpretability offer a new perspective on fully resolving PCD.

title: ScoreDial: Precise Control of Visual Attributes in Image Generation via Regressor Guidance from Limited Human Ratings
abstract: Requested-value control is stricter than continuous steering: given $c$ on a human-rating scale, the generated image should attain that value from only limited ratings. We present ScoreDial, which fits a differentiable regressor $R$ to 100-479 human-rated images; once $R$ is fixed, a requested value $c$ is defined on its output scale, and learned target conditioning is paired with error-adaptive guidance that repeatedly reduces $|R(\mathbf{x})-c|$ during sampling. Across tire slip resistance, interior visual complexity, food desire-to-eat, and soap translucency, using one set of sampler settings shared across all four, ScoreDial reaches requested values and achieves, on all four attributes, $R$-MAE at most 0.013 over a range of width 0.8 and Spearman $ρ=0.980$, the maximum attainable under our evaluation protocol. Because $R$ also drives sampling, we evaluate agreement with $R$ separately from matched sweeps, an independent auditor fitted to the same ratings on a backbone none of the deployed regressors uses, and blinded human judgments. MPGD-flow also reaches the requested values under $R$, but ScoreDial has larger auditor displacement on every attribute, the largest among all compared methods, and a stronger MPGD-flow setting gives up target agreement without closing this gap. On every attribute, removing target conditioning leaves low $R$-MAE but more than halves auditor displacement, separating precise score correction from attribute movement. Blinded rating studies with 15 raters per attribute show that mean human ratings track $c$ on tire and soap, with linear $R^2=0.665$ and $R^2=0.786$, and in forced-choice comparisons of matched sweeps, raters chose ScoreDial's as the clearer progression in at least 84% of judgments against every baseline.

title: Rate-dependent gradient flows of integral currents via varicurrents
abstract: Motivated by the analysis of recent models of dislocation motion in crystalline materials, this work introduces space-time varicurrents, a form of Young measures over integral currents, to describe their evolutions with rate-dependent dissipation potentials. This addresses the problem that rate-dependent versions of the (rate-independent) space-time variation suffer from a lack of lower semicontinuity with respect to the natural weak topology. This causes a dynamical relaxation to occur by means of infinitely fine oscillations. Varicurrents retain a description of this ``microstructure'' (in space-time) and, based on this theory, we are able to establish the existence of solutions to a rate-dependent gradient flow. This is in contrast to the classical formulation using integral currents, which does not have a solution in general.

title: When Category Means Move: A Paired-Support Audit of Recommendation Logs with Random Insertions
abstract: Content-category dashboards summarize production recommendation logs, although the serving policy selects the users, items, and contexts behind each mean. Using KuaiRand random-insertion impressions, we audit these summaries on the same 12,472 users and 5,486 videos in both logs. Standard means have absolute/centered mean absolute error (MAE) 0.1935/0.0491 and rank correlation 0.7833. User demeaning plus a random grand-mean anchor reduces absolute MAE by 80.0%, but centered MAE by only 21.0%, without reliably improving rank. A complete-support ledger allocates weighted squared error mainly to within-video residual (72.41%) and video mix (23.90%), with 3.65% from random support. In a frozen later test, early category calibration reaches MAE 0.0251 versus 0.0531 for scalar calibration; their direct difference is -0.0280 [-0.0296, -0.0172]. Decision evidence is cutoff-specific: the nominal top-10 regret change for row-weighted demeaning versus naive is -0.0062 [-0.0084, -0.0003], while top-5 and top-20 intervals include zero. The six-contrast family-wise top-10 interval [-0.0136, 0.0013] includes zero. An outcome-free disjoint randomized-reference split also leaves all six nominal contrasts covering zero. A known-truth stress test shows incomplete improvement under a mean-additive positive control and failure under item mix and weak overlap. All decompositions are descriptive and each result is conditional on its overlap cohort. KuaiRand intervals quantify user-cluster variation conditional on the realized catalog and calendar; we claim neither intrinsic category effects nor a universally valid correction.

title: Throughput-Optimal Control of Distributed Computing Networks for Service DAGs
abstract: Executing service workflows with directed acyclic graph (DAG) dependencies over wireless distributed computing networks requires joint control of function placement, routing, and scheduling, together with synchronization of inputs from the same request at merge points. We study throughput-optimal control of these networks under stochastic request arrivals, time-varying wireless links, and interference constraints. We use a valid mapping abstraction that assigns each service function to a computation node and each DAG dependency to a routing path. Using this abstraction, we characterize the network capacity region to support service DAGs, and prove that synchronizing the packets of a request at merge points does not shrink the region. We develop Dynamic Computing Network Control for service DAGs (DCNC-DAG), a dynamic control policy that selects queue-aware valid mappings and schedules service DAG execution by nearest-to-origin (NTO) while enforcing input synchronization at merge points. With exact minimum-cost valid mappings, DCNC-DAG is throughput-optimal and ensures rate stability of the physical queues under bounded arrivals. These guarantees hold for any fixed finite interval between mapping updates, even when mapping decisions rely on boundedly stale queue length information. For larger service DAGs, we develop DCNC-DAG-H, which replaces exact mapping optimization with a queue-aware heuristic. Simulations show that DCNC-DAG supports $2.7\times$-$5.5\times$ the throughput of queue-blind baselines, while DCNC-DAG-H achieves up to $2.68\times$ those of the corresponding baselines on larger workflow and AI service DAGs.

title: Learned Smartphone ISP on Mobile GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
abstract: With the increasing importance of mobile camera quality in modern smartphones, growing attention has been directed toward computational photography and advanced image signal processing (ISP) algorithms aimed at enhancing various perceptual attributes of captured images. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose the participants to design fast solutions that can reconstruct RGB photos from RAW Bayer camera data while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale Fujifilm UltraISP dataset consisting of RAW-RGB image pairs captured with the Sony IMX586 Quad Bayer mobile sensor and a professional 102MP medium format FujiFilm GFX100 camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to reconstruct high-quality 5MP RGB image from raw data on both platforms under 100 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

title: Periodically poled lithium niobate with submicrometer periodicity using electric-field poling technique
abstract: A series of monocrystalline lithium niobate (LN) thin films on low-resistivity silicon (LNOS) substrates, with thicknesses ranging from micrometers down to tens of nanometers, were prepared through chemical-mechanical polishing of pristine crystal films. By employing the electric-field poling technique, high-quality periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) structures with submicrometer periodicity were fabricated in these LNOSs, and full-thickness polarization reversal beneath the poling electrodes with a well-defined depth profile was achieved. The coercive field was found to follow the Kay-Dunn scaling law, while the lateral domain broadening generally increased with increasing film thickness, and it remained approximately constant across different electrode linewidths at a given film thickness. PPLN structures with periods ranging from 6 $μ$m down to 200 nm were demonstrated. These findings provide guidance for poling electrode design and lateral domain broadening pre-compensation, offering a practical route toward scalable domain engineering in LN thin films with promising potential for compact and highly integrated nonlinear photonic devices.

title: Ergotropy Activation and Coherence in Dissipatively Charged Quantum Batteries
abstract: Quantum batteries can exploit quantum resources to enhance energy storage and work extraction, and recent experimental progress has brought their implementation closer to reality. In realistic settings, however, environmental dissipation is unavoidable, making dissipative charging a physically relevant operating regime. Here we investigate ergotropy in dissipatively charged quantum batteries, focusing on interaction-induced work extraction. For two coupled two-level systems (TLSs), we derive exact analytical expressions for the total, coherent, and incoherent ergotropy in both resonant and detuned configurations. We show that, in the resonant case, ergotropy is activated only above a critical coupling associated with an interaction-induced energy-level crossing, whereas detuning enables ergotropy already in the weak-coupling regime. Moreover, quantum coherence, although necessary for coherent work extraction, is not by itself sufficient to guarantee nonzero coherent ergotropy. In the strong-coupling regime, the resonant setup reaches the maximum ergotropy at a finite coupling strength, whereas the detuned setup approaches the same limit only asymptotically. Extending the analysis to a periodic XX spin chain of $N$ TLSs, we analytically derive the finite-temperature coupling threshold for ergotropy activation and show that it scales as $1/N$ in the large-$N$ limit. These results identify frequency detuning, interaction strength, and system size as key control parameters for ergotropy generation in open quantum batteries.

title: Can saliency maps flag chest radiograph classifier errors at a new hospital? An external validation study
abstract: Saliency maps are offered as a safeguard for medical image classifiers, but whether they reveal individual errors at a new hospital remains largely untested. We trained a convolutional network and a vision transformer on NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated 303,768 decisions per model at the training hospital and at two external sites, in the USA and Vietnam, with radiologist-consensus labels. We scored each explanation by its anatomical enrichment, the area-normalized concentration of attribution in a segmented thoracic region, and tested whether it detects errors beyond the model's confidence. Grad-CAM localized findings less often than radiologists (hit rate at most 0.575 versus 0.888). Adding enrichment to a confidence-based error detector calibrated at the training hospital never raised its area under the curve by more than 0.011, and for the convolutional network the relation between enrichment and correctness reversed between hospitals, degrading the transferred detector. Model confidence, not saliency, should anchor deployment monitoring.

title: Rethinking GA2Ms: performance and out-of-distribution generalisation
abstract: Generalised Additive Models (GAMs) are a cornerstone of interpretable machine learning, offering transparent predictions through structured additive decompositions. Despite advances from classical GAMs to modern neural and spline-based variants, two notable gaps remain. First, comprehensive benchmarking of spline-based GAMs on large-scale tabular learning tasks, the dominant modality in applied settings, is lacking. Second, their robustness under distribution shift, a setting where structured inductive biases should confer advantages, remains unexplored. We propose a multi-resolution, higher-order Composite Generalised Additive Model (CoGA2M) and evaluate it on the TALENT benchmark suite. CoGA2M ranks in the top third across all baselines (29 for regression, 32 for classification), establishing competitive performance with state-of-the-art tabular methods. We further extend TALENT with out-of-distribution (OOD) splits exhibiting train-test distributional shift and benchmark CoGA2M against LightGBM, a consistently top-performing model on TALENT. Under distribution shift, CoGA2M outperforms LightGBM, demonstrating a clear structural advantage. Our results position spline-based GAMs as strong contenders for tabular prediction and reveal a previously unrecognised benefit of additive structure in the OOD regime.

title: One Strategy Does Not Fit All: Rethinking Data Labeling for Just-in-Time Vulnerability Prediction
abstract: Just-In-Time Vulnerability Prediction (JIT-VP) identifies security risks in code changes at commit time, enabling early feedback before vulnerabilities enter software systems. However, its practical reliability is challenged by the difficulty of constructing accurate labels. Multiple strategies with different trade-offs have been proposed to identify vulnerability-fixing commits (VFCs) and vulnerability-introducing commits (VICs) for dataset construction, leading to substantially different datasets. This makes it difficult to separate model performance from dataset construction. Moreover, real-world quality assurance requires not only classification but also prioritizing high-risk commits and localizing vulnerable causes. This paper presents an extensive empirical study of how labeling strategies affect these downstream tasks. We constructed 28 datasets using four VFC and four VIC labeling strategies across OpenSSL and Linux kernel, then evaluated six representative JIT-VP models for classification, prioritization, and localization. Our results show that labeling effectiveness is strongly task-dependent. Manual VFC labeling combined with vulnerability-specific VIC labeling provides the most reliable performance for classification and prioritization, significantly outperforming 11 of 15 alternatives. Meanwhile, precision-first VFC labeling combined with LLM-assisted VIC labeling performs best for localization, significantly outperforming 7 of 15 alternatives. These findings demonstrate that no single labeling strategy is universally optimal and highlight the importance of task-oriented dataset construction.

title: The APN Property of Two Families of functions over $\F_{2^{n}}$ from the Switching Construction
abstract: Let $m\geq5$ be odd with $3\nmid m$. Helleseth, Ichanska, and Kaleyski \cite{HIK} conjectured that two norm-perturbed Budaghyan--Helleseth--Kaleyski functions $F_2,F_3$ over $\F_{2^{2m}}$ are APN. In this paper, we prove this conjecture. First, by using the basis $(1,β)$ of $\F_{2^{2m}}$ over $\F_{2^m}$, we show that $F_2$ and $F_3$ are EA-equivalent to two functions $\mathcal G_1$ and $\mathcal G_0$, respectively. Their derivatives can be written as two trace equations for a matrix $P\in\mathrm{GL}(2,\F_{2^m})$. We then prove that these two equations have no solution. The proof uses only identities over finite fields, the characteristic polynomial of a $2\times2$ matrix, and elementary properties of Frobenius automorphisms. The repeated-root case and all parity cases are considered separately. It follows that the derivative of each function has kernel of size two in every nonzero direction, and hence both $F_2$ and $F_3$ are APN for every admissible $m$.

title: The integer spectrum of a superintegrable quantum field theory
abstract: In our previous article CMP 407 (2026) 131, we explored the rich algebraic structures arising from a specific quantum many-body Hamiltonian quartic in the bosonic creation-annihilation operators. This Hamiltonian originated from the works of Gérard and Grellier on classical turbulent energy transfer in a Lax-integrable setting, and its quantum version respects hierarchies of polynomial conservation laws all of which possess purely integer spectra, as does the Hamiltonian itself. The latter feature, known from numerical studies, has previously remained unproved. Here, we present an elementary solution of the quantum Gérard-Grellier Hamiltonian. The eigenstates are labelled by partitions and the corresponding eigenvalues admit simple explicit expressions in terms of the principal hook lengths. The key ingredient in this construction is a specific basis we introduce, inspired by the classical multisoliton coherent states, in which the Hamiltonian is upper-triangular. The expressions for the eigenvalues then immediately follow, while the full eigenbasis can be recovered via a Gram-Schmidt procedure.

title: Estimating Treatment Effects with a Single Arm Clinical Trial and Data Summaries from an External Control Group: is it Possible?
abstract: Randomized controlled trials are crucial for assessing new treatments, but they are often infeasible due to ethical or practical constraints. In these cases, single-arm trials combined with external control data constitute an alternative approach for estimating treatment effects. However, individual patient-level data on external controls are frequently inaccessible due to privacy and economic concerns. Therefore, investigators rely on data summaries published by previous studies of the control therapy. We propose a method for inference on the treatment effect of an experimental therapy using patient-level data from a single-arm trial and a few published data summaries from an external control group. We introduce and study the Interval of Potential Effects (IPE), described as the range of plausible levels of the treatment effect that are compatible with the patient-level data from the experimental treatment and the available summaries on the control group. The width of the IPE quantifies the uncertainty on the treatment effect attributable to the lack of individual patient data from the control group. We demonstrate, through simulations and a case study, how the IPE indicates whether the available summaries are sufficient for accurate estimation of the treatment effect. We also illustrate that IPEs can support decision-making in the early phases of development of new treatments.

title: Vortices in a two-dimensional fermionic superfluid
abstract: Quantized vortices are a hallmark of superfluidity. They have proven to be an indispensable probe for systems ranging from superfluid helium to type-II superconductors. In ultracold two-dimensional (2D) Fermi gases, where phase fluctuations are enhanced and the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) mechanism governs the superfluid transition, their observation has remained elusive. Here, we report on the controlled creation of quantized vortices in a homogeneous 2D gas in the BEC--BCS crossover. By continuously tuning the velocity of two moving obstacles, we observe quantized steps in the absolute vortex charge. Matter-wave interferometry reveals the characteristic phase winding, quantized in units of $2π$. Measurements on 2D and 3D gases show a striking difference: only in 2D does the vortex number grow with temperature, reflecting thermal activation of BKT vortex pairs. Our approach provides evidence of fermionic superfluidity in 2D and offers a means to study BKT physics, vortex-controlled transport and resistance, as well as to detect unconventional superfluidity in spin-imbalanced 2D gases.

title: Long-time Brownian dynamics of hard and sticky colloids by geometric projection
abstract: Particle-resolved colloid simulations are often limited by the fastest microscopic time scale retained in the model, which can be many orders of magnitude shorter than the collective process of interest. This is especially restrictive for aggregating colloids, where explicit near-contact potentials force the time integration to resolve the rapid positional relaxation of bonded pairs within narrow attractive wells. Here we introduce an overdamped constraint-based Brownian dynamics method that replaces the time-resolved integration of stiff near-contact forces by a geometric projection step. After each free Brownian update, hard-sphere exclusion, sticky bonds, and hard-wall interactions are enforced by projecting the particle positions onto the constrained configuration set. The method preserves hard-sphere structure and diffusion, recovers the aggregation kinetics of sticky hard spheres, and extends the physical time reached at fixed computational cost by one to two orders of magnitude relative to the explicit-potential simulations tested here. This acceleration makes Brownian-dominated, low-Péclet electrophoretic deposition accessible to particle-scale simulations, revealing a pathway in which the suspension first densifies and only subsequently develops a bonded network. Implemented as a LAMMPS fix, the framework provides a modular route to long-time Brownian simulations of dense constrained colloidal systems.

title: Faster Planar Diameter using Pseudoline Envelopes
abstract: We give an improved algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter that runs in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ time. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ time algorithm for weighted directed planar diameter of Gawrychowski, Kaplan, Mozes, Sharir, and Weimann [SIAM J. Comput. 2021] and the recent $\widetilde{O}(n^{8/5})$ time algorithm for unweighted undirected planar diameter of Fredslund-Hansen, Mozes, and Weimann [SOSA 2027]. The main new result is an improved data structure for computing the farthest vertex when given feasible planar distances to the vertices on the outer face. The critical insight is the fact that normalized distances to the vertices of a face behave like pseudolines, for which we can leverage range searching and upper envelope data structures. Using the farthest vertex data structure, we are able to compute all vertex eccentricities and diameter in $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$.

title: ConvexAD: differentiable phase retrieval with geometric regularization for high-strain, low-signal Bragg coherent diffraction imaging
abstract: Bragg Coherent Diffraction Imaging (BCDI) relies on phase retrieval (PR), a non-convex, ill-posed inverse problem whose conditioning is degraded by factors like noise, partial coherence, and strain or crystallographic defects in the imaged nanocrystal. Conventional approaches, including alternating projections and deep learning methods, represent the object on a dense voxel grid, which is prone to amplitude-phase mixing and becomes increasingly ill-posed under these factors, often preventing reliable three-dimensional mapping of the particle's shape and strain. Here we present ConvexAD, a gradient descent PR model that parametrizes the object shape as a convex polyhedron, built by the intersection of half-spaces and enforces flat amplitude within it by construction. This geometric regularization eliminates amplitude-phase mixing and reduces the number of trainable parameters, hence facilitating the convergence of the PR. Implemented in JAX for native GPU acceleration and forward-model flexibility, ConvexAD is validated on simulated and experimental BCDI data, where it outperforms conventional and deep learning assisted PR at high strain, low signal, and reduced coherence, extending the conditions under which quantitative BCDI reconstruction is achievable.

title: Nearly-Linear Query Algorithm for Submodular Maximization subject to a Matroid Constraint
abstract: We consider monotone submodular maximization subject to a matroid constraint. The seminal continuous greedy algorithm of Calinescu, Chekuri, Pál, and Vondrák~[SICOMP'11] achieves the tight approximation of $(1-1/e)$. Since then, a line of works by Badanidiyuru and Vondrák~[SODA'14], Buchbinder, Feldman, and Schwartz~[SODA'15 \& MOR'17], Kobayashi and Terao~[ICALP'24], Buchbinder and Feldman~[FOCS'24 \& SICOMP'25], and Buchbinder and Feldman~[STOC'25] has developed efficient $(1-1/e-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for this problem. We present a combinatorial randomized $(1-1/e-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm that requires $\tilde{O}_{\varepsilon}(n)$ independence-oracle and value-oracle queries, where $n$ is the number of elements in the matroid. This is the first $(1-1/e-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm with both independence-oracle and value-oracle query complexities nearly-linear in $n$ and polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$. To achieve this, we develop a new local search algorithm, which we call \emph{protected local search}, based on the potential function of Buchbinder and Feldman~[FOCS'24 \& SICOMP'25].

title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
abstract: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.

title: HiLo-WAM: Decoupling Long-Horizon Task Evolution and Local Dynamics in World Action Models
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.

title: RGB Photo Enhancement with Deep Learning on Smartphone GPUs: Mobile AI 2026 Challenge Report
abstract: On-device RGB photo enhancement is a popular task that is needed for quality improvement of photos captured with mobile devices as well as for retouching of images acquired through other sources. This creates a need for efficient deep learning models for this problem that are not only performant but can also be deployed on constrained mobile hardware. In this Mobile AI challenge, we address this problem and propose participants to design fast solutions that can perform comprehensive enhancement of RGB photos while running on popular smartphone GPUs from Qualcomm and Arm. For this, the participants were provided with a large-scale DPED dataset consisting of RGB image pairs captured with an old iPhone 3GS smartphone and a professional Canon 70D DSLR camera. The runtime of all models was evaluated on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and Dimensity 9500 chipsets with the Adreno and Mali GPUs, respectively. Top solutions proposed in this challenge are able to enhance Full HD resolution RGB images on both platforms under 300 milliseconds. A comprehensive description of the models developed in the challenge is provided in this paper.

title: Ferron polariton Hall effect: Deflecting optically rectified polarization with magnetic fields
abstract: Ferrons are elementary excitations of ferroelectric order that can propagate and transport polarization when excited with light. Here, we show theoretically that ferron polaritons exhibit a Hall effect: an applied magnetic field generates polarization transport perpendicular to the propagation direction of a ferron polariton excited by an incident terahertz pulse. We demonstrate this effect for the example of ferroelectric SnTe using first-principles calculations and a microscopic theory of the phonon-polariton current. The direction and magnitude of the transverse polarization transport can be controlled by the polarization of the terahertz pulse and the applied magnetic field. Our results establish a route toward light-controlled directional transport of electric polarization in ferroelectrics.

title: A Unified Isoparametric Moving Mesh PDE Method for P1 and Q1 Elements with Certified Local Nonsingularity
abstract: We develop a unified isoparametric moving mesh partial differential equation (MMPDE) method for $P_1$ simplicial and $Q_1$ tensor-product elements, including elements on embedded surfaces. Mesh movement follows a prescribed symmetric positive-definite metric through equidistribution and alignment. For $Q_1$ elements, we prove that bounded, exactly integrated adaptation energy prevents local Jacobian rank loss on a fixed finite mesh at sharp critical exponents. The result also gives local full-rank preservation for embedded bilinear surface elements. A complete physical-coordinate gradient accounts for metric variation at moving quadrature points. For the discrete MMPDE, we use whole-element validity tests and develop sufficient Bernstein certificates for trilinear hexahedra. An explicit positive-margin bound on each fixed stage is provided by an optional certificate barrier. Numerical examples illustrate metric-driven movement on one-dimensional, planar, volume, and graph-surface meshes. Limitations of pointwise hexahedral Jacobian sampling are also presented.

title: Haptic Shared Control for Multi-Robot Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems offer significant advantages in terms of flexibility and redundancy, enabling the efficient distribution of complex tasks among multiple robots. However, their deployment requires advanced control strategies to ensure optimal cooperation between autonomous agents and human operators. We propose a modification of the global connectivity maintenance algorithm to incorporate measurements taken in agent's local frame, using sensors with limited fields of view. This algorithm, responsible for the autonomous behavior of the multi-robot system, is combined with different adaptive supervision strategies, allowing the user to exert control at varying scales over the entire group. (i) Single Agent Control (S): The operator directly controls a single robot, (ii) Pinning Control (P): The operator imposes constraints on multiple robots to influence the group, (iii) Centroid Control (C): The operator acts on the system's center of mass to steer the entire fleet. In conjunction with the connectivity maintenance algorithm, these methods ensure compliance with inter-agent constraints while providing haptic feedback to the user regarding the system's connectivity state. The effectiveness of these approaches was evaluated through a user study, comparing performance with and without haptic feedback across multiple scenarios tailored to the different control modes.

title: Observation of Scaling of Higher-Order Flow in a Unitary Fermi Gas
abstract: Collective flow emerging from spatially anisotropic many-body systems is a fundamental manifestation of strongly interacting quantum matter, from ultracold quantum gases to the quark-gluon plasma created in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Yet how collective flow emerges across different spatial harmonics and how dissipation modifies its evolution remain largely unexplored. Here we investigate the nonequilibrium expansion of a unitary Fermi gas initially confined in nearly homogeneous potentials with engineered angular deformations. By suddenly releasing the confinement, we resolve anisotropic flow harmonics up to the seventh order. Remarkably, after normalization and rescaling by the characteristic expansion timescale, the different harmonics and system sizes exhibit a universal early-time evolution. At longer times, this universality breaks down and we observe an approximately quadratic dependence of the harmonic attenuation on harmonic order, consistent with viscous acoustic scaling. Furthermore, temperature-dependent measurements reveal the role of shear viscosity in the dissipative evolution of higher-order flow. Our results open a new route to exploring the interplay between universal hydrodynamic expansion and dissipative transport, connecting collective dynamics in ultracold quantum gases with anisotropic flow in strongly interacting nuclear matter.

title: DRAP: Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity for Continual Learning in Physical AI
abstract: Continual learning in physical AI differs from conventional continual learning because small per-step policy errors can accumulate over a trajectory. Each deviation may move the agent outside the training distribution, increase subsequent prediction errors, and ultimately cause closed-loop task failure. This work introduces Dynamics-Risk Adaptive Plasticity (DRAP), a replay-free method that estimates the historical importance of adaptable model tensors from sample-level action gradients weighted by local trajectory-amplification risk. A ridge-regularized local linear model is fitted to expert state-action transitions, and the largest singular value of its state-transition matrix provides a policy-independent, Lyapunov-inspired estimate of one-step perturbation amplification. After each task, risk-weighted squared gradients are accumulated in a tensor-level importance memory. During subsequent tasks, DRAP uses normalized cumulative importance to scale the effective AdamW learning rate of each tensor, immediately reducing the plasticity of components that supported previous behavior at dynamically sensitive trajectory points. We instantiate DRAP on a fixed KappaTune-selected subnetwork of OpenVLA and evaluate replay-free sequential adaptation across the LIBERO Spatial, Object, and Goal suites. Compared with standard AdamW fine-tuning and EWC, the results show substantially improved retention of previously learned behaviors while preserving strong new-suite acquisition.

title: On Revolutionizing Power Systems: Suitability of Quantum Computing-Ready Pipelines for Stochastic Unit Commitment Optimization
abstract: Modern unit commitment (UC) scenarios, particularly those involving uncertainties from demand fluctuations and renewable energy sources, pose significant challenges to traditional optimization methods due to the large search spaces they encompass. This paper proposes a quantum computing-ready optimization pipeline for deterministic and stochastic UC, integrating classical, quantum-inspired, quantum annealing, and hybrid quantum-classical solvers across test systems, including the IEEE 118-bus system. A novel Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) reformulation accommodates generator scaling and 24-hour scheduling horizons with compact Boolean logic penalties for startup, cooldown, and spinning reserve constraints. A divide-and-conquer strategy and Quantum Computing Monte Carlo (QCMC) simulation address scalability across 27,730 uncertainty scenarios, reducing compilation time by up to two orders of magnitude. Experimental results demonstrate the pipeline's ability to achieve efficient, scalable, and accurate UC optimization under uncertainty: the hybrid quantum method approach matches the classical baseline, reduces stochastic UC runtime from 40.76 to 14.79 hours, and characterizes pure quantum annealing as limited to small systems with 0.22% to 2.18% encoding errors and constraint violations. These results provide an analysis of the scalability and computational practicality of hybrid quantum optimization for generator scheduling in UC.

title: Comparing model representations and fitting methods for port-Hamiltonian system identification
abstract: Port-Hamiltonian models describe physical systems by separating stored energy, dissipation and external inputs. Learning such models from data requires a choice of representation and fitting method. We compare using neural networks, analytic expressions and combinations of the two for representing the different components of the port-Hamiltonian system, and compare fitting the models with gradient-based optimisation or sparse regression. Testing on simulations of mechanical and electrical systems, with and without added noise, we present prediction accuracy and computational cost of the different approaches.

title: Curvature Estimates and Prescribed Curvature Problems for Sum Hessian Equations on Star-Shaped Hypersurfaces
abstract: Let $M$ be a closed star-shaped hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ and let $η=Hg-h$ be the first Newton transformation of its second fundamental form. For a fixed constant $α>0$ and $2\le k\le n-1$, we study the prescribed sum Hessian curvature equation \[ σ_k(λ(η))+ασ_{k-1}(λ(η))=f(X,ν). \] Under the natural admissibility condition \[ λ(η)\inΓ_{k-1}\cap \{λ:σ_k(λ)+ασ_{k-1}(λ)>0\}, \] we establish a global curvature estimate for closed star-shaped solutions with a general positive right-hand side depending on the position vector and the unit normal. A key point is that the sum Hessian operator is nonhomogeneous; the resulting lower-order term in the maximum-principle calculation is controlled by a partial curvature estimate. We also use the augmented-variable identity \[ σ_k(λ)+ασ_{k-1}(λ) =σ_k(λ_1,\ldots,λ_n,α) \] to recover the relevant ellipticity and concavity properties. As an application of the a priori estimates, we prove existence and uniqueness for the corresponding prescribed curvature problem under suitable spherical barrier and radial monotonicity assumptions.

title: Whose Effect Is It? How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions
abstract: Interpretability often locates concepts by copying part of a language model's state from one input into another (activation patching). A larger output change counts as stronger evidence that this part carries the concept. Methods that learn which part to copy often change the output more than the whole state does. By that reading, learned parts isolate the concept more cleanly. Yet the whole contains the part. So whose effect is this excess, the network's or the method's? Copying the whole state learns nothing, so it shows what the network produces. We prove that, to first order, the effects of orthogonal parts add up to that of the whole. A part therefore exceeds the whole exactly when the rest moves the output back, which does not require isolating the concept more cleanly. Objectives that reward a larger effect select such parts. Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy, for example, exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks, and inside the network at most sites. In both, changing only its objective to target what the network produces removes most of the excess. It therefore comes largely from the objective, so a larger learned effect alone is not stronger evidence.

title: A Short Proof and Generalization of the Rainbow Cycle Theorem and Improved Bounds for Binary Even-Query LCCs
abstract: A \emph{rainbow cycle} in a list-edge-colored graph is a cycle where no color appears more than once. We give a short and simple proof of a result of [ABSZZ] showing that a properly edge-colored $n$-vertex graph with average degree $Ω(\log n\log\log n)$ always contains a rainbow cycle, and generalize it to weighted graphs with edges list colored with list size at most $\ell$ and where the total weight of all edges containing a given color $i$ incident to a vertex is at most $Δ$, showing that $Ω_\ell(Δ\log n\log\log n)$ average degree guarantees a rainbow cycle. Using the reduction of [AG26] and the new generalized rainbow cycle theorem, we prove that for $r\geq 3$, every binary linear $r$-query locally correctable code $E:\mathbb{F}_2^k\rightarrow \mathbb{F}_2^n$ satisfies $k\leq \tilde{O}(n^{1-2/(r-1)})$ by showing a rainbow analogue of the odd $r$-LDC lower bounds of [BHKL25,JM25], closing the gap between the best known lower bounds for odd- and even-query binary linear $r$-LCCs.

title: Federated Transfer Learning for Medical Image Classification under Mixed Skew
abstract: Deep learning in medical imaging is constrained by data scarcity and by privacy regulations that make centralizing patient data across institutions impractical. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these constraints by keeping data local, but its distributed nature exposes training to strong statistical heterogeneity. Multicentric medical data is particularly affected, exhibiting a mixed skew that combines feature, label, concept, and quantity shifts across centers. Personalized FL mitigates heterogeneity by tailoring a model to each client, yet most methods assume training from scratch, which is unrealistic given the high dimensionality of medical features relative to the limited data available. We propose the Personalized Aligner Federated Pretrained (PAFP) framework, a personalized FL approach built on a pre-trained backbone. PAFP inserts client-specific Feature Alignment modules before the fine-tuned blocks to realign hidden feature distributions toward a server-aggregated target.
