abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) can have wavelengths comparable to the Schwarzschild radius of their lenses, and detectors record their phase, so lensing requires wave optics. Its standard tool, the diffraction integral, follows from the particle path integral of a scalar wave on a static weak field, under the eikonal (one-way) and paraxial approximations, plus the thin-lens limit. We give a self-contained account of how the proper-time (worldline) representation overcomes these steps. An auxiliary proper time makes the wave equation exactly first order, with frequency as $1/\hbar$, so geometric optics and, for paraxial thin-lens paths, the diffraction integral follow from stationarity of an exact integral. For a point mass, the Duru-Kleinert (DK) gauge and Kustaanheimo-Stiefel map give the exact propagator; for a distant observer the DK time and fibre angle become the radius and azimuth of a lens plane, the result is the point-lens amplification factor with the offset set by the excess path, and geometric optics requires $w\gg1$ and $wy\gg1$. This agreement reflects the Coulomb potential, not the approximations: the exact eikonal condition, $\varepsilon_E\simeq\barλ/d+GM/c^2d+\mathcal O(\sin^2θ/2)$, fails near the lens and at large angles, and the one-way step is a non-relativistic limit. We then treat the bound lens, a GW source orbiting its lens, which emits a backscattered echo and moves during the lensing delays. Its exact time-domain signal gives each worldline its own retarded time and Doppler factor, so no single amplification factor describes it. In the diffraction regime the Shapiro phase alone misses all lensing beyond it, geometric optics misses 46-100% of it near conjunction at $w=0.3$, the paraxial geometry fails on the far side, and the static amplification factor along the orbit errs by $\approx(1-2)\,wM/R$ near conjunction and by the echo amplitude elsewhere.

title: Information content of the Gamow Teller Resonance: Bayesian inference with self-consistent Skyrme models
abstract: Many important charge-exchange weak processes, such as beta decays, double beta decays, and neutrino-nucleus and neutrino-nucleon reactions, are closely related to the spin- and isospin-dependent nuclear force, yet few of them can be precisely measured, or even observed, in terrestrial experiments. The Gamow-Teller resonance (GTR) in finite nuclei is one of the few experimental probes of this spin-isospin force. In a companion letter, we obtained the probability distribution of the Landau-Migdal parameter $G'_0$, which characterizes the main part of the spin-isospin force, from GTR measurements using Bayesian inference. In this follow-up work, we quantitatively study the correlations emerging from this Bayesian analysis. From the posterior, we identify two standard Skyrme parameterizations (nuSky*) that reproduce, in a unified manner, ground-state observables of finite nuclei, the salient features of the GTR, and the bulk properties of neutron-star matter. Since collective excitations in finite nuclei and in neutron-star matter are related, we use the Skyrme interactions sampled from the posterior to constrain the axial-current, charged-current neutrino-nucleon reaction rates in hot and dense compact-star matter, as the first astrophysical application of this study. The GTR-informed calculations substantially reduce the spread of the neutrino opacity; nevertheless, significant uncertainties remain due to the poorly constrained symmetry energy at sub-saturation densities. Constraining this quantity on top of a well-constrained spin-isospin interaction would pave the way towards a systematic determination of neutrino interactions in dense matter.

title: Stein's generalized spherical maximal operator
abstract: This survey concerns Stein's analytic family of generalized spherical means and the associated maximal operator. We review Stein's original theorem, the sharp necessary conditions for boundedness, and the complete theory for radial functions. We then explain the connection between positive results and local smoothing estimates for the half-wave propagator and, more generally, for Fourier integral operators. This point of view yields the sharp two-dimensional result through the work of Guth, H. Wang, and R. Zhang and, when combined with the recent local smoothing theorems, an improved higher-dimensional range. As a byproduct, the maximal operator associated with the first radial derivative of spherical means is bounded on $L^p(\R^4)$ for $2<p<3$, a case left open in recent work of Kwaśnicki. We keep track of the relation between the local smoothing exponents and the resulting maximal estimates, and identify the region that remains open.

title: Asynchronous Robot Policies
abstract: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

title: Decompositions of homomorphisms of abelian $p$-groups with $p^2$-bounded target
abstract: Let $p$ be a prime. We classify homomorphisms $H:V_1\to V_2$ between abelian $p$-groups that are direct sums of cyclic groups, under the assumption $p^2V_2=0$. We prove that every such homomorphism is isomorphic to a direct sum of finite indecomposable representations and that this decomposition is unique up to isomorphism and reordering of the summands.

title: Macrocanonical Generator Networks: Data-Efficient Neural Surrogates for Amortized Physics Simulation
abstract: Many scientific simulations are computationally expensive, limiting their use in simulation-based inference, uncertainty quantification, and decision making. We introduce macrocanonical generator networks, a framework for learning fast, data-efficient neural surrogates for amortized simulation of stationary physical processes by matching multiscale statistics of a target process. Inspired by microcanonical maximum-entropy synthesis, which matches feature statistics per sample by inner-loop optimization, our approach instead trains a neural generator to satisfy the same constraints in expectation, preserving physically realistic sample-to-sample fluctuations. We prove that gradient-descent training induces preconditioned gradient-descent dynamics in sample space that inherit the symmetry-preservation properties of the microcanonical gradient descent of Bruna and Mallat, amortizing its per-sample inner-loop optimization into a single training run after which every sample is generated in one forward pass. We further show that residual generator parameterizations initialized near the identity, trained with a small learning rate, preserve entropy locally during early optimization and mitigate mode collapse. Experiments on cosmology and fluid simulations show that macrocanonical generators recover realistic samples from extremely small training sets, in some cases a single training example, while generating new realizations more than $10^6$ times faster per sample than the reference simulator and more than $10^3$ times faster than microcanonical gradient descent. The trained generators can be reused for downstream pretraining, including simulation-based inference, providing a data-efficient route to multi-fidelity scientific machine learning workflows.

title: Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding
abstract: Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on static supervision from stronger external judges or curated hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers through a closed perturb-verify-repair-verify loop. Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.

title: In-situ azimuthal sample rotation within a horizontal-field cryomagnet for small-angle neutron scattering
abstract: We present an in-situ azimuthal rotation stage for small-angle neutron scattering measurements. The stage provides an azimuthal rotation range of $315^\circ$ about the stage normal. At the reference sample-stick orientation, the stage normal is parallel to the incident neutron beam, so that the sample rotates in the plane perpendicular to the beam. Combined with a sample stick rotation about a second, orthogonal axis, the stage provides control of the magnetic-field direction relative to the crystal axes, while the field remains fixed in the laboratory frame. For a 5 mm diameter incident beam, sample-stick rotations of approximately $\pm315^\circ$ are accessible with negligible additional attenuation from the holder. The commercial rotator is specified for operation between 1 and 373 K and in magnetic fields up to 35 T, making the stage nominally compatible with the full temperature (1.8 to 320 K) and field (0 to 6.8 T) ranges of the used cryomagnet. As a working example, we characterize its performance on a spherical single crystal of MnSi between 20 and 35 K and in fields up to 183 mT, observing local sample heating during operation of $\sim$20 mK per $5^\circ$ step. We illustrate the design considerations behind the holder construction, with specific notes for mounting spherical samples, and discuss the resulting performance and limitations.

title: On partitions with bounded multiplicity restrictions on even parts and with the largest part being odd
abstract: Andrews and El Bachraoui (\textit{RACSAM} \textbf{119}, \textit{Article Number 4 (2025)}) established identities relating $4$-regular partitions to partitions with distinct even parts whose largest part is odd. As an extension to their work, in this paper we define partitions of a positive integer $n$ with bounded multiplicity restriction on even parts and whose largest part is odd. We prove some identities relating our partition functions and $2r$-regular partition function, and show that identities due to Andrews and El Bachraoui follow as particular cases.

title: An elementary proof of a tangent-cone identity for rank-one planar Lipschitz maps
abstract: We give an elementary proof of a tangent-cone identity which might be known to specialists in geometric measure theory. It concerns Lipschitz mappings $g$ from the closed unit ball $B\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$. Let $x$ be an interior point of differentiability of $g$ at which $Dg(x)$ has rank one. If the upper one-dimensional Hausdorff density of $g(B)$ at $g(x)$ is at most one, then the tangent cone to $g(B)$ at $g(x)$ coincides with the image of $Dg(x)$. This property is used in the proof of rigidity for the four-gradient problem. We provide a detailed, self-contained proof based on differentiability, connectedness and elementary estimates for one-dimensional Hausdorff measure, without using advanced methods from geometric measure theory.

title: Uniform asymptotics for the Kleitman-West problem
abstract: Two distinct $r$-element sets are adjacent if their intersection has size $r-1$. The Kleitman-West problem, equivalently formulated as the edge-isoperimetric problem on the Johnson graph $J(n,r)$, asks for the maximum number $M_r(n,m)$ of unordered adjacent pairs in a family of $m$ $r$-element subsets of an $n$-element set, and for the families attaining this maximum. For every fixed integer $r\ge2$, we determine this maximum asymptotically as $n\to\infty$, uniformly over the entire range of family sizes. Specifically, for each integer $1\le j\le r$, define $F_j(p)=\max\{p^{1+1/j},\,2p-1+(1-p)^{1+1/j}\}$ for $0\le p\le1$, and $G_j(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor+F_j(x-\lfloor x\rfloor)$ for $x\ge0$. With \[ P_r(n,m)=\sum_{j=1}^r\frac{n^{j+1}}{2(j-1)!}G_j\!\left(\frac{j!m}{n^j}\right)-\frac{r(r-1)}4mn-\frac m2, \] we prove that \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\max_{2\le m\le\binom nr}\left|\frac{M_r(n,m)}{P_r(n,m)}-1\right|=0. \] The remaining cases satisfy $M_r(n,0)=M_r(n,1)=0$. The proof first establishes the asymptotic formula for dense families using a sharp inequality for bounded random variables, with equality attained by a random variable taking at most two values. To extend the result uniformly to all family sizes, we extract groups of sets sharing a fixed subset, apply the dense estimates after deleting that subset, and control the adjacent pairs not contained in any one group.

title: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.

title: Basin2Vec: Learning Basin-Centric Embeddings for Scalable Hydrological Modeling
abstract: Reliable streamflow prediction across time and in ungauged basins requires representations that capture hydrologically relevant basin characteristics. Existing methods rely on either fixed handcrafted attributes or general-purpose Earth observation embeddings not tailored to basin structure. We introduce \textbf{Basin2Vec}, a self-supervised framework that learns compact basin representations from hydroclimatic and physiographic data without observed streamflow. Basin2Vec organizes representation learning around basin scale and relationships across space and time. Across multiple forecasting architectures, it consistently outperforms predefined attributes and general-purpose geospatial embeddings in temporal generalization and zero-shot spatial transfer. Basin2Vec provides average relative gains of up to 8.3% temporally and achieves 3.5x the median predictive performance of the strongest baselines on unseen basins. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of basin-centric pretraining for transferable hydrologic prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/Muhammad-Talha-MT/basin2vec

title: QPP-Aware MCX over Tactical Edge 3D Networks in Public-Safety Communications
abstract: During disasters, public mobile networks may become unavailable, congested, or degraded, requiring deployable communication systems to support emergency operations. This article proposes a mission-critical communications system supporing Mission Critical Push-to-Talk (MCPTT), Mission Critical Video (MCVideo), and Mission Critical Data (MCData) over a private 5G standalone network with Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) connectivity. A context-aware Quality, Priority, and Pre-emption (QPP) mechanism is proposed to dynamically adapt network resource allocation according to the operational state of Mission Critical Services (MCX). Extensions to the Open5GS Policy Control Function (PCF) and Session Management Function (SMF) enable priority and pre-emption updates for existing flows without session re-establishment. The architecture supports tactical edge deployment of service and media functions while retaining centralized service control. Experimental evaluation considers three configurations: terrestrial backhaul with centralized media processing, satellite backhaul with centralized media processing, and satellite backhaul with edge media processing. Results show that tactical edge processing reduces communication delay and packet loss. Under satellite backhaul, edge processing reduced the 95th-percentile MCPTT audio transport delay by 60.03 ms and packet loss by 9.42 percentage points, while achieving a 95th-percentile MCPTT access time of 184.52 ms. These findings demonstrate the benefits of tactical edge media processing and provide an experimental foundation for context-aware priority mechanisms in public-safety networks integrating terrestrial and non-terrestrial components.

title: When Self-Verification Hurts: Calibrated Answer Repair for Financial Question Answering
abstract: Financial question answering can fail even when a model extracts a plausible number from the supplied evidence: the answer may attach it to the wrong entity, period, unit, or accounting concept. Asking the model to verify and revise its draft can help, but open-ended revision may alter content that was already correct or inspect the wrong relation and reinforce the original error. We formulate repair as a decision that balances the information it may recover against the correct content it may damage. Based on this trade-off, we introduce Calibrated Answer Repair (CAR), which first estimates whether a draft is likely to benefit from repair, then selects a targeted check, localizes the relevant evidence or draft span, and limits the permitted edit. Across FinRank, Fin-RATE, and FinQA with three open-weight models, CAR outperforms generic verification in all dataset-model settings. At the system level, it recovers 14.6% of initially missed answer requirements while damaging 2.1% of initially correct ones. Its post-draft token cost is over 30 percent lower than the iterative revision alternatives. Ablations on two dataset-model settings show that evidence localization and bounded editing are the main contributors to CAR's gains.

title: Learning Behaviorally Relevant Dynamics in Multimodal Neural Recordings
abstract: Multimodal neural data can enable a more complete understanding of brain dynamics underlying behavior. Modalities such as spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), and behavior capture diverse spatiotemporal aspects of brain processes, yet prior neural-behavioral models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality. By leveraging these complementary strengths, multimodal neural fusion can provide a unified, rich representation of brain-behavior processes and address the limitations of single-modality analyses. Here we develop BREM-NET, a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that integrates behavior with multiple neural modalities having distinct statistical characteristics and temporal resolutions. BREM-NET performs multimodal neural fusion during inference while separating behaviorally relevant and residual neural dynamics via a structured learning framework. In a public multimodal non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and local field potential recordings during a 2D reaching task, BREM-NET separates these two types of dynamics and learns them more accurately, as reflected in better behavior decoding, better neural prediction, and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and it retains these capabilities when neural modalities are asynchronous or suffer dropouts, which are major challenges in real-world recordings. This framework provides a new tool for studying behaviorally relevant neural computations across spatiotemporal scales of brain activity.

title: DSL-Bench: Evaluating and Explaining LLM Code Generation Across Domain-Specific Languages
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software-engineering workflows, but code-generation benchmarks largely focus on general-purpose languages. Domain-specific languages (DSLs) have distinct syntax, semantics, and validation requirements, making results from individual DSL benchmarks difficult to compare. We present DSL-Bench, an executable benchmark and analysis framework for cross-DSL code generation. Starting from 13,045 DSL-related papers, LLM-assisted open card sorting identifies 18 representative application domains. For each domain, we select an evaluable DSL and provide a syntax checker and task-level semantic oracle. Evaluating 7 LLMs on 18 DSLs, we observe mean syntax and semantic pass rates of 31.37% and 11.64%, respectively, revealing a substantial gap between syntax acceptance and semantic correctness. A variance decomposition attributes 76.99% of semantic pass-rate variation to differences among DSLs and 7.86% to differences among models. Among four DSL-level factors, Knowledge Demand has the strongest negative association with semantic correctness (r = -0.508). We evaluate prompt engineering across all 18 DSLs and study five improvement methods on five targeted DSLs. Prompt engineering yields uneven gains; RAG-Refinement, the strongest targeted method, improves semantic correctness by 16.29 percentage points on average over matched baselines. We further derive capability profiles and DSL-Profiler summaries for interpreting data-scarce DSLs. These results highlight toolchain-specific semantic bottlenecks and the need to evaluate DSL code generation beyond syntax acceptance.

title: Unified Motion Correction and Reconstruction for Accelerated Zero Echo Time MRI
abstract: Zero echo time (ZTE) MRI is near-silent, but dead time gaps, head motion, and undersampling jointly degrade reconstruction. To develop an accelerated ZTE MRI reconstruction framework that jointly estimates the 3D image and rigid-motion parameters, this work introduces Energy-based Motion Correction (EnMoCo), a regularized maximum a posteriori (MAP) formulation that also compensates for missing k-space center data and angular undersampling artifacts. Solved by alternating between k-space rigid-motion updates and conjugate-gradient data-consistency updates, the framework incorporates regularization via a pre-trained Multi-Scale Energy-based model (MuSE) implemented in a data-efficient 2.5D form. Evaluations on simulated and in vivo 3D ZTE data, spanning dead time gaps of 1.5 to 5 samples, rotations up to 17 degrees and translations up to 10 mm, demonstrate that EnMoCo significantly improves PSNR and SSIM relative to CG-SENSE and Autofocusing baselines (achieving roughly 10 to 15 dB higher PSNR for gaps >= 3.5) while reducing motion blur and tissue contrast inconsistencies.

title: Constraining tau-sterile neutrino mixing with high-energy astrophysical neutrinos
abstract: Whether a sterile neutrino mixes with the three active ones remains an open question. Its mixing with the tau neutrino, $|U_{τ4}|^2$, is the least constrained, since terrestrial experiments probe it only indirectly and over limited ranges of sterile-neutrino mass. We show that TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrinos probe it differently. Their sources make almost no $ν_τ$, but oscillations over cosmological distances turn about one third of them into $ν_τ$ before they reach Earth. Mixing with a sterile neutrino would make these $ν_τ$ scarcer, lowering the $ν_τ$ fraction that neutrino telescopes measure, whatever the sterile-neutrino mass. In contrast, sterile mixing with $ν_e$ or $ν_μ$ is nearly undetectable. Fitting the flavor composition measured by IceCube, with the composition at the sources left free, we find $|U_{τ4}|^2 < 0.88$ at 90% C.L. Combining IceCube with present and planned neutrino telescopes, including IceCube-Gen2 and HUNT, could lower this limit to 0.24-0.29 by 2040 and to 0.12-0.14 by 2050. By 2050, these limits would match some present terrestrial limits, though not the strongest.

title: AgentAM: An AI Agent for Spatter- and Defect-Aware Process Optimization in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
abstract: Predictive models for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) are rarely used on the shop floor because querying them requires programming and model-specific knowledge. We present AgentAM, a large language model (LLM) agent that gives process engineers natural-language access to CFD-trained surrogates of spatter and melt pool geometry for SS316L through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Polynomial surrogates trained on 279 single-track simulations predict melt pool dimensions ($R^2 \geq 0.95$) and spatter volume ($R^2 = 0.83$ on test data) at any power-velocity point in the trained range, and geometric criteria assign each point a geometry-derived defect regime (keyhole, lack of fusion, balling or stable) that matches the regime obtained from the simulated geometry in 93.4% of tracks under cross-validation. The agent selects and parameterizes tools for prediction, process-window scans and constrained optimization. Minimum-spatter optima often sat within 10 $μ$m of the lack-of-fusion boundary; a margin-aware optimizer moved them away from all thresholds and raised the estimated probability of remaining classified Good from 0.94 to 1.00 under an assumed 2% process drift, and from 0.72 to 0.91 when jointly sampled cross-validated geometry residuals were added. About 40-50 well-spread simulations sufficed to reproduce the defect map. To evaluate the agent layer, we introduce a 145-prompt benchmark scored against direct tool calls, plus eight prompts (40 runs) on margin-aware requests. Over the 725 runs of the main benchmark the agent passed the intended inputs in 98.5% of parsing prompts, reported the scored spatter values and defect classes faithfully and met every stated constraint in the 65 feasible optimization runs, within a median 1.0% of the brute-force optimum.

title: PadLoc: Training-Free Floor-Plan Localization by Sparse Geometric Matching
abstract: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,θ)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc's offline refinement from $T=35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc's published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23-32 pp under wheel odometry and 35-43 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches 100% SR@1m at 9-10 cm median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at 0.90-0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.67-0.92 with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.

title: Correctness Firewalls for Synthesized Database Components
abstract: For the first time in history, high-performance code is cheap. Today's coding agents can generate bespoke, instance-optimized data systems with excellent performance, and such agents will continue to improve as LLMs advance. But a purely agentic approach, even when validated with strong testing techniques, does not automatically inherit the correctness guarantees our community has spent decades building. We propose a middle ground between hand-crafted and agent-crafted systems: correctness firewalls, lightweight design patterns under which a synthesized component can affect a system's performance but never its results. Behind a correctness firewall, agents are free to synthesize fast components while the overall system remains correct. We present three case studies, each demonstrating a different type of firewall: cardinality estimation (advisory), searching sorted data (guarded), and data compression (certified). In early experiments, synthesized components search sorted data up to 3x faster than human-designed learned indexes and can compress text 1.5x smaller than Zstd. Drawing on these case studies, we outline a research agenda for how data management systems can exploit coding agents without giving up their hard-won correctness guarantees, from protecting synthesized code to measuring the cost of correctness.

title: Evidence for a Dirac Spin Liquid in the Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet from High-Precision Neural-Network Quantum States
abstract: The spin-1/2 kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet is a central model in the study of quantum spin liquids, yet its ground-state properties remain unresolved. We perform large-scale variational Monte-Carlo calculations using neural-network quantum states (NQSs) with kagome-geometry-aware message-passing convolution on two-dimensional tori containing up to 300 spins, and achieve exceptionally low variational energies for the kagome model. The spin and dimer structure factors show no evidence of magnetic or valence-bond long-range order. Moreover, the dominant symmetry-resolved spin and dimer correlations exhibit a common scaling behavior consistent with the emergent $SO(6)$ monopole multiplet of the Dirac spin liquid. Finally, the fidelity of the optimized NQSs with Gutzwiller-projected mean-field states increasingly favors the Dirac state over the competing $Z_{2}$ candidates as the system size grows. Together, these complementary results provide evidence for a $U(1)$ Dirac spin-liquid ground state in the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet.

title: The Novelty Horizon H_N: Why Large Language Models Fail to Generate Scientific Data beyond Their Training Distribution
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) lack physical grounding and extrapolation. This paper formalises the Novelty Horizon as tasks needing extrapolation beyond training support, causal reasoning absent from learned correlations, or post-frontier information. A forensic analysis tests LLMs on unguided, guided, and ground-truth data from an underrepresented diode-clamped short-circuit experiment using temporal, spectral, and statistical validation against a first-principles Modified Ohm's Law. Both script-based approaches fail catastrophically with physical and spectral inconsistencies, extreme statistical pathologies, zero Generative Fidelity Score, and linear-regime outputs. Direct prompting corroborates distinct failure modes. This paper introduces the Past Information Boundary and physics-based authentication. LLM data generation cannot extrapolate past the Novelty Horizon essential for novel discovery. Hybrid neuro-symbolic systems must preserve human causal reasoning and experimental design.

title: Extending the MM-AR Metamodeling Platform with Process Mining Capabilities
abstract: Process mining derives process models from event data recorded by information systems, but its results are usually presented as two-dimensional visualizations that are separate from the environments in which enterprise models are created and maintained. Metamodeling platforms for extended reality (XR), such as MM-AR, allow users to define modeling languages and to display models in 2D and 3D, but they do not provide access to event data or mining algorithms so far. In this paper we therefore present a first proof-of-concept for showing how an XR-based metamodeling platform can be extended with process discovery capabilities without changes to the platform core through a separate Python service based on the open source PM4Py process mining library. We demonstrate the approach using three common discovery algorithms for obtaining Petri nets and BPMN models based on CSV or XES event logs. A technical evaluation using four public event logs shows that the element counts of the created model instances match those of the PM4Py models in all 16 configurations. The integration adds between about 8 and 53 seconds per run, and this overhead grows with the size of the discovered model rather than the size of the event log. Although the prototype does not yet use the third dimension to encode process information, it established the foundations for studying such approaches.

title: A Smooth Shioda-Tate Isomorphism for Elliptically Fibered 4-Manifolds
abstract: This paper studies a subgroup of the mapping class group of an elliptically fibered $4$-manifold $π: M\to B$, inspired by number theory. The smooth Mordell-Weil group $\mathrm{MW}(π)$ is the group of isotopy classes of smooth sections of $π$. We construct a smooth analog of the Shioda-Tate isomorphism, identifying $\mathrm{MW(π)}$ with the quotient of $H^2(M;\mathbb{Z})$ by the trivial lattice of $π$. This shows that $\mathrm{MW}(π)$ can be computed explicitly from $H^2(M;\mathbb{Z})$. As an application, we show that the natural inclusion of the holomorphic Mordell-Weil group into the smooth one is an isomorphism if and only if $M$ is a rational elliptic surface. As another application, we show that $\mathrm{MW}(π)$ satisfies a strong version of Nielsen realization: any torsion element of $\mathrm{MW}(π)$ is represented by a holomorphic translation of $M$ of the same order.

title: Weighted Max Cut in Subcubic Graphs
abstract: For a graph $G$ with nonnegative edge weights, let $\operatorname{mc}(G,w)$ denote the maximum total weight of a cut and let $w(G)$ denote the total edge weight. We prove that every edge-weighted triangle-free subcubic graph satisfies $\operatorname{mc}(G,w)\geq \frac{15}{19}w(G)$, improving the bound of $\frac{8}{11}$ due to Gutin and Yeo. For subcubic graphs of odd girth at least seven and nine, we strengthen this bound to $\frac{47}{59}w(G)$ and $\frac45w(G)$, respectively, establishing the conjecture of Gutin and Yeo for graphs of odd girth at least nine. Our proofs combine structural properties of vertex partitions with randomized cut constructions and convex combinations of the resulting bounds.

title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
abstract: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of $399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover $265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.

title: Analog signal processing, storage, and demultiplexing via in-materia wave-based computing
abstract: The ability of mechanical systems to perform basic computations has gained traction in recent years, providing a robust supplement to digital computing in off-grid, low-power, and extreme environments where electronics are inaccessible or risk failure. However, prior work has focused on Boolean logic applied via bistable structures, snap-through mechanisms, or origami lattices. Digital signal processing (DSP) underpins a wide range of computational tasks, providing the foundation for information encoding, manipulation, and analysis. In contrast to conventional DSP approaches, we present a new paradigm for analog information processing, where an elastic substrate houses a spatial wave-based platform for mechanical signal manipulation in the temporal domain. The proposed metasurface-based system exploits temperature-dependent phase transitions of shape memory alloys (SMAs) to realize key signal-processing functionalities, including gating, retention, and programmable delay of impinging mechanical loads. In doing so, we address a new set of challenges by manipulating transient mechanical waves through dispersive and lossy media. Building on this capability, we introduce the concept of mechanical wave-based memory, in which a locally resonant metamaterial's dispersion characteristics are actively reconfigured to achieve programmable delays while preserving spatial waveform integrity, and demonstrate its utility in the context of input shaping and frequency demultiplexing of superimposed waves. More broadly, the modular and scalable nature of the demonstrated framework paves the way for advanced mechanical computing architectures, enabling higher-order operations such as signal classification, parallel processing, and reservoir computing through the controlled sequencing and temporal alignment of mechanical signals.

title: What Does the Model See? Representation Validity in Multimodal LLM-Based Video Analysis
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) allow social scientists to analyze video at scale, but researchers must decide which parts of a video to provide as input. We use the term representation validity to examine how text, audio, video, and combined inputs affect measurement and subsequent analysis. We compare input representations across six open-weight MLLMs and three human-annotated video datasets. No representation consistently performs best. On seven news-related constructs, native-video performance varies little across models (macro-F1 = .70-.77), while extracted-text performance ranges from .52 to .80. Three models perform better with text and three with video. Combining inputs rarely improves performance. Higher classification accuracy also does not reliably produce estimates closer to those based on human codes. The highest-F1 representation best reproduces human-coded regression coefficients in 17 of 42 comparisons. Even when each model uses its highest-F1 deployable representation, 45% of sample-prevalence estimates differ from the human-coded benchmark by more than ten percentage points. Input representation therefore requires validation for both the construct being measured and the quantity estimated from the resulting labels.

title: A Holographic Weyl Semimetal in an Effective Gauss--Bonnet Geometry
abstract: We study how an effective Gauss--Bonnet deformation of the thermal geometry changes the competition between the conducting Weyl-semimetal and insulating flavour phases of the probe D3/D7 model. The phases are represented by horizon-reaching and smoothly capped D7 embeddings, respectively, whose free energies exhibit a first-order transition. At the temperatures examined, positive Gauss--Bonnet coupling shifts coexistence toward larger flavour mass and expands the thermodynamically preferred Weyl-semimetal region, while negative coupling shifts the boundary in the opposite direction. The normalized zero-temperature transition remains unchanged. An on-shell analysis shows that the leading finite-temperature shift is largely explained by an effective rescaling of the thermal scale, opposed by an intrinsic fixed-horizon geometric contribution. The enlargement of the conducting phase does not imply stronger electrical response: the longitudinal and anomalous Hall conductivity jumps at coexistence can decrease, and the coupling response of the longitudinal jump reverses with temperature. The mass-dependent maximum of the longitudinal DC conductivity can also cease to occur on the thermodynamically preferred branch. Thus the geometric deformation changes both which phase is favored and how the Weyl-semimetal phase conducts.

title: Base change between canonical basis and path basis
abstract: Almost 30 years ago Littelmann conjectured that there is a unitriangular base change between the dual canonical basis and the path vector basis for all symmetrizable Kac-Moody Lie algebras. In this paper we give a positive answer to the conjecture for the case of classical Lie algebras and type $G_2$, when the path model is given by standard Young tableaux.

title: Provably Learning Mixtures of Linear Experts
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely deployed in modern machine learning. However, few convergence guarantees exist for gradient-based training of MoEs: the objective is nonconvex, and even simple mixtures trap first-order methods in spurious local optima. We analyze a canonical gated mixture featuring linear experts and a gate induced by Gaussian clusters in the input space, and give, to our knowledge, the first global convergence guarantee for jointly training the gate and the experts of such a model by gradient EM on its likelihood. Given a logarithmic overparameterization relative to the true number of experts $m$, gradient EM converges from randomly initialized gates and least-squares-initialized experts to any prescribed accuracy in polynomially many iterations, under a separation condition on the gate centers. Our analysis establishes a gradient-dominance inequality for the coupled dynamics by decoupling the loss into per-cluster subproblems. Empirical results validate the predicted $m\log m$ phase transition and suggest that the least-squares warm start required by our analysis is not needed in practice: randomly initialized experts perform nearly as well. We also find that leaving the mixing weights unconstrained concentrates routing onto the true number of experts, whereas load-balancing penalties spread it, so that the fitted model can be pruned to a fraction of its width without loss of accuracy.

title: Efficient simulations of spectra and transport for multiorbital quantum impurities
abstract: Quantum impurity calculations become challenging when multiple correlated orbitals are treated explicitly, particularly in nonequilibrium steady states. We introduce Coupled-Cluster Coupled Lindblad (C$^3$L), a deterministic approach that combines the recently developed coupled-Lindblad compact bath representation with coupled-cluster theory to compute steady states and Green's functions directly in imaginary and real frequency. C$^3$L has favorable polynomial computational complexity and avoids the sign problem of quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). In a real-time multiorbital benchmark, it agrees closely with state-of-the-art QMC while reducing computational cost by four to five orders of magnitude, with a further 10--100-fold speedup on a GPU. Beyond the practical reach of established real-time QMC solvers, four-orbital nonequilibrium impurities with general interactions and biased reservoirs become accessible with C$^3$L. We obtain resonance-resolved transport signatures relevant to scanning tunneling microscopy experiments on molecular junctions.

title: Rasterization-based discontinuous integration on the GPU
abstract: In this paper, we propose a method based on rasterization in computer graphics for the integration of discontinuous functions accurately and efficiently on the GPU. The proposed method takes advantage of the massively parallel architecture of GPUs via a modified graphics pipeline, where discontinuities are encoded through geometric primitives and processed in the rasterization stage, and multisample anti-aliasing (MSAA) is used to improve integration accuracy across subdomain interfaces. We present both hardware- and software-based pipelines and compare their performance in terms of accuracy as well as computational effort on modern GPU hardware with adaptive quadrature on the CPU. For the tested hardware, at approximately comparable median relative error, the hardware pipeline is up to around $100\text{x}$ faster than adaptive quadrature, while the single- and double-precision software pipelines achieve up to $840\text{x}$ and $1200\text{x}$ speedups compared to their adaptive quadrature counterparts. We use the finite cell method as model problem, where cutcells represent discontinuous integrands at the interface of the physical and fictitious domains and demonstrate the performance of the proposed method using numerical benchmarks. The end-to-end finite cell solution runtime is reduced by a factor of $8.3$ to $9.5$ in the single-precision pipeline and by a factor of $62$ to $72$ in the double-precision pipeline at the prescribed integration settings. Therefore, results indicate that the rasterization-based integration method is a promising alternative for the accurate and efficient integration of discontinuous functions in demanding applications on the GPU.

title: Hopf algebra polynomial identities in the Sweedler algebra
abstract: Using Mac Lane's PROPs, one can introduce multilinear polynomial identities that involve all the operations of a Hopf algebra: the (co)multiplication, the (co)unit and the antipode. We find bases for polynomial identities and calculate their codimensions for the Sweedler algebra, treating it first as an ordinary associative algebra over a field and second as a Hopf algebra.

title: Bang-Bang Correlation Sensitivity: A Local-to-Global Dichotomy for Correlation Preference
abstract: Binary choice under risk can depend on how the alternative outcomes are jointly distributed. We show that in a finite outcome space, continuity, completeness, and betweenness impose a local-to-global restriction on this dependence: indifference between two alternatives with one common marginal distribution, however their outcomes are jointly distributed, implies correlation insensitivity for all lotteries supported on the same outcomes. In the correlation-sensitive case, these three axioms alone characterize correlation weighted utility, which combines statewise comparisons with a bilinear function of the marginal lotteries. In the correlation-insensitive case, an additional projective independence axiom yields Fishburn's (1982) skew-symmetric bilinear representation. Strong independence reduces correlation weighted utility to Lanzani's (2022) correlation expected utility representation. We extend the correlation-sensitive characterization to finitely supported lotteries on general metrizable outcome spaces. The resulting framework distinguishes correlation effects from departures from classical independence, and yields testable restrictions linking choices between identically distributed lotteries to correlated Allais behavior.

title: Logarithmic Embeddings into Probabilistic Spanning Trees for Distances and Capacities
abstract: We prove that every connected $n$-vertex graph admits a probabilistic embedding into its spanning trees with expected distance stretch $O(\log n)$. This settles the logarithmic stretch conjecture of Alon, Karp, Peleg, and West, whose spanning-tree game appeared at the 1991 DIMACS Workshop on On-Line Algorithms and in SIAM Journal on Computing in 1995. A weighted form of the theorem also yields a distribution over spanning trees with capacities exactly equal to their fundamental graph cuts. Every tree dominates every graph cut, every cut is approximated within $O(\log n)$ in expectation, and the same capacity distribution defines an $O(\log n)$-competitive fractional oblivious routing. The distance and capacity distributions may differ. Diamond graphs give matching logarithmic lower bounds for stretch, congestion, and cut distortion. For rational input, both distributions are constructed deterministically in polynomial time and use at most $m$ trees, where $m$ is the number of graph edges. We prove an $Ω(m/ρ)$ support lower bound for congestion $ρ$; in particular, $(1-o(1))m$ trees can be necessary for near-unit congestion, even when the optimum tends to one. Thus linear dependence on $m$ is unavoidable in this regime. The weighted theorem combines a protected-geodesic petal decomposition with a pathwise entropy bound for locally selected centers. A local averaging inequality derandomizes the radii, and an adaptive rational packing procedure constructs the distributions.

title: Cosmological evolution and late-time attractors in axion-monopole interacting dark energy
abstract: We investigate the cosmological dynamics of axion-monopole interacting dark energy, examining whether a microscopically motivated dark-sector interaction can sustain stable late-time acceleration. In particular, magnetic monopoles constitute dark matter and an ultralight axion contributes to dark energy, with their interaction arising from the Witten effect through field-dependent dyon masses. We formulate the autonomous system, classify its critical points and stability, and investigate the evolution analytically and numerically. We find that stable de Sitter attractors at finite positive Hubble parameter require a positive cosmological constant and correspond to axion-potential minima, whereas those at maxima are unstable. Nevertheless, transient axion-driven acceleration remains possible without an explicit cosmological constant. Furthermore, the interaction induces matter-era tracking, namely an attracting slow-drift regime rather than an exact critical point. The interaction-effective dark-energy equation of state can cross the phantom divide, although the physical equation of state remains non-phantom. Extending the analysis to the full Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield dyon mass, we find that the main dynamical features persist, while the field evolution and interaction strength depend on the microscopic dyon properties. Our results demonstrate how a microscopically motivated dark-sector interaction can give rise to distinctive cosmological evolution and effective dark-energy behavior.

title: Stepsize modulation for cross entropy from local quadratic optimization
abstract: Two methods are presented that perturb a given learning rate schedule in stochastic gradient descent with cross entropy loss. Both methods use an extra forward pass to estimate various derivatives of the minibatch loss. The first method selects a value $η$ by linearising the softmax values and minimizing the squared error $\tfrac 1 2 ||y - q - ηq'||_F^2$, where $q$ is the matrix representing the softmax values of the minibatch and $y$ is the matrix with one-hot encodings of the labels. The second method considers a quadratic Taylor approximation of the minibatch loss under the outer approximation of the Hessian. Thus, it minimizes $L(0) + ηL'(0) + \tfrac 1 2 η^2 L''(0)$. Here, the derivatives $L'$ and $L''$ are computed from the derivatives of the logits (using the outer approximation of the Hessian of the loss). We observe that both methods give very similar values of $η$. Finally, these estimated $η$ are used to slightly increase or decrease the learning rate of an existing schedule. The method is evaluated on Cifar10 and Cifar100 datasets for training Resnets, where they decrease the loss faster than the schedule that is perturbed and increase monotonicity. For Cifar10 it also leads to a small improvement of test accuracy, but in Cifar100 test accuracy remains the same.

title: From Natural Images to Medical Scans: Transferability of Diffusion Models for Medical Image Generation
abstract: Transfer learning from natural images is standard in supervised and increasingly adopted in self-supervised medical image analysis, but its role in generative modelling, and in particular diffusion denoisers, remains underexplored. Medical diffusion models typically train the denoiser from scratch, with no systematic evaluation of natural-image transfer. We analyse this across latent and pixel paradigms, model sizes (131M-952M) and two radiology datasets (RadImageNet, BraTS), and ask which aspects of transfer support generation. We find that: i) Natural-image initialisation consistently improves generation, by 21-34% relative gFID in pixel space against 14% in latent space, where the tokeniser supplies much of the prior. gFID gains mirror downstream pathology classification and radiomic-feature FD, both proxies for clinical fidelity. ii) Benefits reflect spatial structure, not semantics: semantic probing does not predict generation quality, whereas a spatial-structure metric adapted to internal denoiser representations tracks gFID at $|r|=0.85$, positioning spatial organisation as a channel through which pretraining manifests. iii) Mixed-domain denoiser training shows that natural and medical images share similar layer-wise representations up to the late blocks, and mixing natural images into medical training improves fidelity. iv) Transfer benefit is tied to natural image initialisation, outperforming in-domain medical pretraining and several reinitialisation schemes. Overall, natural image denoisers transfer positively to medical ones in our setup. Code is available at https://github.com/CAIROLab-Bern/rad-dit

title: Factorized MLLM Embeddings for Composed Image Retrieval
abstract: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.

title: A Resonant-Tunneling Quantum-Dot Demultiplexer for Scalable Cryogenic Single-Electron Routing
abstract: Scaling quantum electronic systems such as quantum-dot spin qubits and single-electron devices is increasingly limited by the wiring overhead between cryogenic devices and room-temperature control electronics. Multi-channel quantum-dot architectures that selectively route electrons using a few shared control lines, analogous to demultiplexers in classical networks, offer a promising solution. Here, we propose and theoretically investigate a gate-defined architecture of three parallel quantum dots sharing a common source reservoir and coupled to independent drain channels. Using an analytical electrostatic model and tight-binding quantum transport simulations, we show that the device can act as an on-chip single-electron demultiplexer based on resonant tunneling in the cryogenic regime. Closed-system eigenstate analysis reveals localized orbital states in each dot, and open-system transport calculations show resonant conductance peaks when these levels align with the incident electron energy, consistent with the closed-system eigenenergy evolution. By engineering the barrier-gate spacing and the relative plunger-gate dimensions, we obtain well-separated resonances with minimal overlap between channels. Bond-current density calculations show that transport is confined to the resonant channel with negligible leakage into neighboring outputs, yielding channel selectivity approaching unity for all resonant modes. The architecture is compatible with Si/SiGe and GaAs/AlGaAs platforms and can be extended to more channels, offering a route toward programmable quantum routing and resonant-tunneling-based quantum circuitry.

title: Ensembles of Random Partition-Based Models under Covariate Shift
abstract: Distribution shifts, including covariate shifts, are ubiquitous in real-world applications of machine learning. Empirical evidence suggests that, across a variety of models with and without downstream adaptation, ensembles tend to be more robust to covariate shift than single models. We extend the theory of covariate shift severity from single models to ensembles, providing theoretical justification for the empirical trends. We introduce new discrepancy measures of covariate shift severity to control the risk of partition-based kernel estimators. We then show that with sufficient ensemble size, these models can achieve minimax-optimal risk convergence rates under covariate shift. Our results suggest that modelers can expect to need larger ensemble sizes for more severe covariate shifts.

title: Divisibility Properties of Odd Part and Even Part Sums in Cubic Partitions
abstract: A cubic partition of a positive integer $n$ is a partition of $n$ in which even parts may appear in two distinct colors. The purpose of this paper is to study the arithmetic functions $COS(n)$ and $CES(n)$, which denote the sums of all odd and even parts, respectively, in all cubic partitions of $n$. We obtain their generating functions and divisor-sum formulas, and establish Ramanujan-type congruences modulo $3$, $4$, $5$, and $7$. To prove these congruences, we use Lambert series, classical theta-function identities, dissections, coefficient extraction, and weighted Euler identities.

title: Robust Reconstruction of Power Lines from Incomplete Mobile and Aerial LiDAR Data
abstract: Accurate vegetation-encroachment assessment and risk mitigation require electric utilities to accurately locate and characterize distribution-network assets, including poles and power lines, and distinguish among medium-voltage, low-voltage, neutral, and telecommunication lines. Mobile and aerial Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds provide detailed 3D representations of these assets and their surroundings. However, power-line detection and reconstruction remain challenging because conductor returns are often sparse, incomplete, noisy, or occluded by vegetation. These challenges are especially significant in distribution networks, where lower pole heights and complex line configurations place conductors close to trees. In addition, mobile and aerial LiDAR datasets differ substantially in point density, viewing geometry, spatial coverage, and occlusion patterns. We propose a robust and automated reconstruction method combining scaled density-based clustering, robust polynomial fitting, and iterative fragment merging to recover individual conductors under severe data incompleteness and occlusion. Following semantic classification, the same reconstruction pipeline processes both mobile and aerial LiDAR data without modality-specific code or parameter tuning. The method is evaluated through degradation experiments, benchmarking, parameter sensitivity analysis, and large-scale validation. On the aerial dataset, it achieves 96.87% precision, 96.66% recall, a 96.76% F$_1$-score, and a geometric RMSE of 0.127 m. On the mobile dataset, where conductor-level reference annotations were unavailable, it achieves a point-to-model RMSE of 0.045 m and a reconstruction coverage of 95.27%. Source code, documentation, and evaluation data are publicly available at https://github.com/varen-project.

title: The P-Ideal Dichotomy and the Failure of Two-Cardinal Square Principles
abstract: We prove that the $\mathrm{P}$-ideal dichotomy implies the negation of the square principle $\square(λ, ω)$ for every regular cardinal $λ\geqω_2$.

title: Response to "Late Time Dynamical Dark Energy and the CMB-Distance Ladder Tension"
abstract: We respond to the recent paper by Efstathiou (arXiv:2607.29562) who makes several statements that appear to be in conflict with our recent paper (Turner & Huterer, arXiv:2606.05358). We stand by our primary result that direct determinations of $H_0$ can be sensitive to the late-time expansion history. We also point out where there is significant agreement between his work and ours.

title: The Galah survey and symbiotic stars. II. Discovery, validation, and intensive follow-up of 44 new systems accreting at the lowest detectable levels
abstract: We report the discovery, validation, and characterization of 44 new symbiotic stars (SySts) accreting at the lowest detectable levels (Lacc =< 3 Lsun). Candidates were initially selected from the Galah survey among non-pulsating M-type red giants exhibiting Halpha excess. Between 2021 and 2025, these targets were subjected to intensive multi-wavelength campaigns, including ground-based, high-resolution Echelle spectroscopy over 544 nights, multi-epoch flickering searches down to 1 mmag, and UV/X-ray observations with the Swift satellite. Our high-resolution spectra allowed for a detailed investigation of Halpha flux and line-profile variability. Crucially, the radial velocities measured for the M-giant components yielded reliable spectroscopic orbits for 22 objects and preliminary orbits for an additional eight, corroborated by binary-induced modulations in ASAS-SN photometry. Measured accretion levels vary by factors of up to 20X, emphasizing the need for high-sensitivity, long-term monitoring. Swift X-ray data exclude neutron star companions in all targets, consistent with predominance of white-dwarf degenerates in known SySts. Combined with the 33 objects from Paper I, this sample of 77 new SySts significantly exceeds the number of previously known, accreting-only Galactic symbiotic stars, constituting the bulk of the low-accretion (LowAcc) variety discovered to date and representing >10 percent of all known SySts in the Galaxy. As SySts likely spend most of their lifetimes in LowAcc faint states, characterizing this population is essential for estimating the total Galactic SySt population and evaluating the role of SySts as Type Ia supernova progenitors or sources of UV excess in elliptical galaxies.

title: Excitation factors and exceptional points of Kerr--Newman quasinormal modes
abstract: We study excitation factors and investigate exceptional points (EPs) of Kerr--Newman quasinormal modes using the exact separated gravitoelectromagnetic equations. At fixed charge, the magnitudes of the excitation factors for the gravitational-led modes studied here decrease with increasing spin, whereas those for electromagnetic-led modes exhibit both monotonic and nonmonotonic behavior. The magnitude of the excitation factor for the first overtone can be comparable to or larger than that for the fundamental mode. We identify 42 EPs at which pairs of modes coalesce in the gravitational-led and electromagnetic-led sectors. Some EPs form sequences involving successive overtone pairs, with higher-overtone pairs coalescing progressively closer to the extremal limit. The additional EPs identified outside these sequences all share the same mode-pair labels as sequence members, but occur at different values of the black hole spin and charge. These findings clarify how rotation and charge shape the relative excitation strengths of different modes and the pattern of mode coalescence in the non-Hermitian spectrum of Kerr--Newman black holes.

title: Empirical Bayes Flow Matching for Continuous Cryo-EM Heterogeneity
abstract: We address the problem of learning generative priors over high-dimensional latent variables from indirect, noisy observations, with a focus on continuous heterogeneity in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). In this setting, 3D atomic structures $x \in \mathbb{R}^{3N_a}$ are never directly observed and must be inferred from 2D projection images $y$ generated by a complex, non-linear forward operator. We propose Empirical Bayes Flow Matching (EB-FM), a method that learns a flow matching prior $p_θ(x)$ directly from observations using a Monte Carlo stochastic approximation Expectation-Maximization framework. EB-FM alternates between an E-step that performs approximate posterior sampling from $p_θ(x \mid y)$ via guided flow-based generation while maintaining persistent latent estimates through stochastic approximation, and an M-step that updates the flow model using these stabilized latent variables as training targets. This approach eliminates the need for pretraining on clean data and naturally accommodates non-linear forward models. We validate our method on controlled inverse problems using two-moons and MNIST data, and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated cryo-EM data with known poses, showing that EB-FM can recover continuous distributions of protein conformations directly in atomic-coordinate space.

title: Exact association-test distributions for prior-informed stepwise SNP prioritization
abstract: Prioritizing causal variants in Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) is challenging due to linkage disequilibrium and high dimensionality. We propose an iterative algorithm for the selection of genetic variables that allows the integration of biological priors. The proposed algorithm requires the specification of the power function of a test statistic and incorporates a priori information on each SNP. We derive the approximate and exact distributions of several commonly used test statistics. At each step of the proposed algorithm, we select the SNP with the largest a posteriori probability of being causal. We consider several stopping criteria for the algorithm. We conduct comprehensive simulation studies to assess the performance of several versions of the proposed algorithm and to make a comparison to some existing competitors. The use of the proposed prioritization algorithm is illustrated with a cis-eQTL application to a human gene-expression data, using European discovery and Yoruba cross-population replication.

title: Signature of exocomet transits observed with Ariel
abstract: We investigate the potential of the Ariel space telescope to detect and characterise exocomet transits through their wavelength-dependent photometric signatures. Building on a radiative-transfer framework, we model exocomet transits for three representative dust morphologies, three grain-size distributions, and four homogeneous dust compositions using synthetic photometric bands covering the Ariel wavelength range. The modelled events typically last 1-2 days and produce photometric variations of a few millimagnitudes. We find that the wavelength dependence of the transit signal provides stronger diagnostics of the dust properties than transit morphology alone. In particular, colour variations relative to the VISPhot band and their wavelength-dependent slopes separate the considered compositions into two broad groups: carbonaceous dust and graphite, and olivine and pyroxene. While the compositions within each group show similar behaviour, the two groups remain distinguishable across the dust morphologies and grain sizes considered. We further assess the detectability of these signals using the $β$~Pictoris spectral energy distribution and ArielRad simulations. Integrating over broad synthetic photometric bands substantially improves the signal-to-noise ratio, allowing millimagnitude-level signals to be detected with short integration times for sufficiently bright targets. Ariel's simultaneous optical-to-infrared coverage therefore offers the possibility not only of detecting exocomet transits, but also of characterising their chromatic signatures and constraining broad classes of dust properties. We also discuss the limitations of the modelling assumptions and the potential of coordinated observations with long-baseline photometric missions.

title: TAQ-MOTR: Tracking-Aware Detection Query Formation for End-to-End Multiple Object Tracking
abstract: Tracking-by-propagation (TBP) methods perform end-to-end multi-object tracking by propagating track queries across frames, jointly handling detection and identity association without heuristic post-processing while naturally modeling temporal information. However, as detection and association are tightly coupled, detection queries in TBP are expected to discover currently untracked objects and provide complementary current-frame evidence for challenging tracks whose queries and identities are retained. Existing methods largely inherit detection-query formation from single-frame detection and construct such queries before the decoder with little awareness of trajectory states. Consequently, currently untracked objects may be missed, while challenging tracked objects with reduced visibility under occlusion may lack complementary evidence, causing association failures or duplicate responses. To address these issues, we propose TAQ-MOTR, a tracking-aware detection query formation framework that employs a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator (HQG) to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory. By conditioning detection queries on trajectory states, TAQ-MOTR adapts them to \rev{the discovery of currently untracked objects and tracked-object complementation We further introduce a training-only auxiliary detection branch whose one-to-one label assignment is decoupled from that of the main tracking branch, providing additional detection supervision to strengthen the shared HQG and decoder for the discovery of currently untracked objects. TAQ-MOTR improves performance on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and BFT, achieving 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set. Code is available at https://github.com/Magicmiya/TAQ-MOTR

title: Diffusion Plug-in Priors for Self-Supervised Ultrasound Video Restoration
abstract: \textit{Objective:} Ultrasound videos are limited by hardware-constrained spatial resolution and signal-dependent speckle, while paired low- and high-resolution acquisitions for supervised restoration are rarely available. We aim to jointly super-resolve and despeckle ultrasound videos without paired training data or network retraining. \textit{Methods:} We propose UltraDiff, which uses a frozen pre-trained diffusion model (DM) as a plug-in prior and restores each frame by optimizing the latent seed of the DM sampler under a range-constrained maximum a posteriori formulation. We derive a speckle-aware data-fidelity term from a Rayleigh scale-family model and characterize its relative-residual and variance-adaptive weighting properties. We further introduce a stabilized fidelity that is bounded below and strictly convex in log intensity for positive observations in its unclamped form. A total-variation regularizer complements the DM prior, and a temporal seed update warm-starts each frame from the optimized seed of its predecessor. \textit{Results:} On EchoNet-LVH videos with simulated speckle and additive noise, UltraDiff with a natural-image prior improves PSNR by 1.24\,dB over the strongest baseline, and ultrasound-related priors improve it further. On real clinical echocardiography videos, UltraDiff reduces the mean absolute error of zero-shot ejection fraction (EF) prediction from 7.31 to 6.37 EF points relative to DUP, the strongest baseline. \textit{Conclusion:} Combining a speckle-aware fidelity with frozen diffusion priors enables ground-truth-free ultrasound video restoration that benefits downstream measurement. \textit{Significance:} UltraDiff needs neither paired data nor retraining and is not tied to a specific diffusion checkpoint. Code associated with this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
abstract: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.

title: Privacy for Free in Efficient Agnostic Halfspace Learning
abstract: We provide the first computationally efficient, differentially private algorithms for agnostically learning halfspaces. In particular, we study three different settings of agnostic learning: improper learning under Gaussian and log-concave marginals; proper learning under Gaussian marginals; and semi-agnostic learning under Gaussian marginals. In all three aforementioned settings, the added cost in the sample complexity due to privacy matches the respective non-private sample complexity, implying that we get privacy for free.

title: Relative cohomology and base-change
abstract: In this note we prove a simple generalization of cohomology and base-change which seems to be missing from standard sources. We illustrate its usefulness by providing an alternative proof of a result of Ishimura on descent of vector bundles along blowups at a smooth center.

title: Non-local approximations for the Schrödinger operator with a general point interaction via the non-relativistic limit
abstract: We consider the one-dimensional Dirac operator $D_{A,c}$ with a general, not necessarily self-adjoint, point interaction at the origin, whose strength is described by an arbitrary complex $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ and suitably rescaled by the speed of light $c$, together with its non-local approximations $D_{A,c}^ε$ obtained by replacing the Dirac distribution by a rank-one projection onto a scaled function $v_ε$. It is known that $D_{A,c}^ε\to D_{A,c}$ as $ε\to 0+$ and that $D_{A,c}-c^2/2$ converges, as $c\to+\infty$, to the Schrödinger operator $H_A$ with the general point interaction, both in the norm resolvent sense. We prove that the first convergence is uniform with respect to $c$ in a neighbourhood of $+\infty$, and we provide explicit rates of convergence. Combining this with an explicit computation of the non-relativistic limit of $D_{A,c}^ε$ for fixed $ε$, we show that the two limits can be interchanged and that the corresponding double limit exists. As a by-product we obtain a family of non-local, rank-two approximations $H_A^ε$ of $H_A$ that converge to $H_A$ in the norm resolvent sense.
